He relieves his servant of a personal injury by telling him the injury is his own, and greater — and then files the request alongside four centuries of idolatry. And says yes. Three times in this chapter God says obey their voice.

The warning is built on one verb, used six times in seven verses: he will take — sons, daughters, the best fields, a tenth of the grain, the servants and the livestock, and a tenth of the flocks — and you shall be his slaves, which is the word for what they were in Egypt. They hear all of it and say no, but there shall be a king over us... that our king may go out before us and fight our battles — which God had done with thunder, in the open, within their own adult memory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Your Sons Do Not Walk in Your Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel grows old and makes his sons judges over Israel, posting them to Beersheba in the far south (vv. 1-2). And they are corrupt: they did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice (v. 3). So the elders come to him at Ramah with a request built on two facts and a comparison: you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who carried God's message against Eli for failing to restrain his sons (3:13) has appointed his own to office and sent them where he cannot see them. The narrator does not say a word about it. He does not need to.
verseByVerse.examples: The elders' two reasons are true and both of them are Samuel's doing. It is the third clause that is the problem, and they will say it again more plainly in v. 20: like all the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second, Abijah; they were judges in Beersheba. Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second, Abijah; they were judges in Beersheba.'

Read that verse slowly, because of who is doing it.

This is the boy who was woken three times in the dark and given his first message from God, and the message was that Eli's house would be destroyed for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them (3:13). He carried it to the old man himself in the morning. He was afraid to say it and he said it all.

He is now old, and he has made his own sons judges over Israel.

Note where he posted them. Beersheba is the southernmost town in the country — the far end of the phrase from Dan to Beersheba — and Samuel lives at Ramah in the hill country, on his annual circuit of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah (7:16-17). His sons are as far from his sight as it is possible to put them and remain in Israel.

Note also that the office was never hereditary. Not one judge in the previous book passed the work to a son, and when Israel offered Gideon a dynasty he refused it in the plainest terms — I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you (Judg. 8:23). Samuel installs one without being asked.

'Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice.'

They are exactly what Eli's sons were.

The charge is specific and it is judicial. They turned aside after gain — the word is unjust profit, money got by bending something. They took bribes. And they perverted justice, which for a judge is not a sin alongside the job; it is the destruction of the job itself.

Put the two households side by side, because the writer has built forty years of narrative so that we would. Eli's sons stole the offerings and God said his father honoured them above him. Samuel's sons sold verdicts, and Samuel appointed them.

The narrator says nothing. There is no oracle here, no man of God, no sentence on the house of Samuel; the writer states the facts in three verses and moves on to the elders.

That silence is more damning than a comment would be, and it is honest about something most histories will not admit. The best man in Israel, whose words never fell to the ground, who broke a famine of the word and judged the nation faithfully all his life, made precisely the mistake he had been sent as a child to condemn.

Be careful how that is applied. The failure is real and the book records it, and it is not the reason Israel asks for a king — verse 20 gives that reason and it is something else. But it is the occasion, and the elders will use it, and they will be right about the facts.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him, "Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him, "Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations."'

They come to his house, and they open with two statements that are simply true.

You are old. He is. Your sons do not walk in your ways. They do not, and the previous verse has just said so in the narrator's own voice. The elders are not slandering anybody and Samuel cannot contradict a word of it.

Both facts are also his responsibility. He got old, which is nobody's fault, and he appointed the sons, which is entirely his.

Then the request, and it has three parts. Appoint for us a king — the institution. To judge us — the function, and a fair one, since the judging is precisely what has broken down at Beersheba. And then: like all the nations.

Everything turns on the third clause, and it needs saying clearly that the first two are not the problem.

God had legislated for a king. Deuteronomy anticipated this request, in these words, generations before it was made: when you come to the land... and then say, I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me, you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose (Deut. 17:14-15). There follows a job description — he must not multiply horses or wives or silver, and he must write out a copy of the law and read it every day of his life.

So a monarchy was never forbidden. Israel's ultimate hope is a king; Hannah sang about one in chapter 2 before anybody had thought of asking, and Jacob had promised the sceptre to Judah before that. The problem is not the office.

The problem is the phrase like all the nations, and what it means will come out plainly in verse 20 when they say it a second time and add what they want him for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The request displeases Samuel, and he prays (v. 6). God's answer is the hinge of the whole monarchy: obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (v. 7). And he classes the request with everything since the exodus — forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you (v. 8). Then: obey their voice, only warn them solemnly and show them the ways of the king who will reign over them (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel heard the request as a rejection of himself, which is what any of us would hear. God corrects him, and the correction is not comfort — it is worse than he thought. The sting is taken out of the personal insult by enlarging the offence.
verseByVerse.examples: Obey their voice is said three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 9, 22). God grants a request he has just filed alongside idolatry. Being given exactly what you asked for can be the judgment: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15).

verseByVerse.quote: But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, "Give us a king to judge us." And Samuel prayed to the LORD. And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them. According to all the deeds that they have done, from the day I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you. Now then, obey their voice; only you shall solemnly warn them and show them the ways of the king who shall reign over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, "Give us a king to judge us." And Samuel prayed to the LORD.'

He is stung, and the narrator tells us exactly which words stung him.

It was not like all the nations that displeased Samuel. It was give us a king to judge us — because judging Israel is what he has done every year of his adult life, on a circuit, at Bethel and Gilgal and Mizpah and at home in Ramah. They are asking for a replacement, to his face, in his own house, while he is still doing the work.

What he does with the sting is the best thing about him. He prays.

He does not argue with the delegation, or defend his record, or point out that he has never taken a bribe in his life — all of which he will say later, in chapter 12, and all of which would be true. He takes it to God first.

'And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them."'

God's answer is one of the most remarkable pastoral sentences in Scripture, and it is not comfort.

They have not rejected you. That is the consolation, and it is real: the old man is being told that this is not about him, that forty years of faithful work have not been repudiated, that he has not failed in the way he fears.

Then the second half enlarges the wound rather than closing it. They have rejected me from being king over them.

God relieves his servant of a personal injury by telling him the injury is his own, and greater. Samuel goes from thinking he has been sacked to understanding that he has been standing next to something much worse than his own dismissal.

A lesson sits in that for anybody in Christian work who has been passed over, replaced, criticised or quietly moved aside. The first instinct is always that it is about you. Very often it is not, and the discovery is less flattering than it sounds, because what it usually means is that somebody is refusing God and you were merely in the way.

'"According to all the deeds that they have done, from the day I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you."'

Now God files the request, and the folder he puts it in is idolatry.

Read the comparison exactly. Everything they have done since the exodus — every Baal, every Asherah pole, every high place, the golden calf, the whole four-hundred-year record of forsaking me and serving other gods — and so they are also doing to you.

The request for a king is not a constitutional preference that God happens to dislike. It belongs on the same list as the calf at Sinai.

Pause on that, because on the surface the two things look nothing alike. Nobody in this chapter is bowing to an image. They are asking for a perfectly ordinary form of government, one that God himself had made provision for. And God says it is the same act.

What makes it the same is not the object but the transfer. An idol is anything you put in the place where God was, to do the job God was doing. These men want somebody to go out before them and fight their battles, and God had been doing that, personally, with thunder, within living memory.

'"Now then, obey their voice; only you shall solemnly warn them and show them the ways of the king who shall reign over them."'

God says yes.

That is the hard thing in this chapter, and the whole book turns on it. He has just called the request a rejection of himself and classed it with four centuries of idolatry, and his instruction is obey their voice. He will say it again in verse 22. He says it three times in this chapter.

No blow falls, no refusal, no plague. He gives them precisely what they asked for, having told them in advance and in detail what it will cost.

The psalm that looks back on Israel's wilderness years puts this in one line, and it is one of the most frightening sentences in the Bible: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15). Paul says the same thing three times in a single paragraph about a world that exchanged the truth for a lie: God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28).

There is a judgment that consists in being told no. And there is a heavier one that consists in being handed the thing, with a receipt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel tells them the ways of the king, and the speech is built on one verb. He will take your sons for his chariots and his armies and his fields (vv. 11-12); take your daughters as perfumers and cooks and bakers (v. 13); take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards for his servants (v. 14); take a tenth of your grain and wine (v. 15); take your servants and your best young men and your donkeys (v. 16); take a tenth of your flocks (v. 17). And the last clause is the destination: and you shall be his slaves. Then the warning: you will cry out because of the king you chose, but the LORD will not answer you in that day (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Six times, in seven verses, the same verb. The grammar of the king Israel is asking for is extraction, and every category of what they own is named in turn — children, land, produce, labour, livestock.
verseByVerse.examples: The word in v. 17 is 'abadim, the word for what they were in Egypt. God brought them out of slavery and they are asking, in writing, to go back into it under new management. And v. 18 reverses the engine of the entire book of Judges, where the cry was always heard (Judg. 2:18).

verseByVerse.quote: So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking for a king from him. He said, "These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and to run before his chariots. And he will appoint for himself commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and some to plow his ground and to reap his harvest, and to make his implements of war and the equipment of his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking for a king from him. He said, "These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and to run before his chariots."'

Samuel does exactly what he was told: he warns them solemnly, and shows them the ways of the king.

The whole speech is built on one verb. Watch for it, because it is going to appear six times in seven verses: he will take.

The first thing taken is the sons. Not for the harvest and not for the family — for the chariots, as horsemen, and as men who run before his chariots, which is the most expendable job in an ancient army: outriders who go ahead of the king's vehicle on foot.

Note the chariots in particular. Israel does not have chariots. Chariots are what the Canaanites had at the Kishon and what Judah gave up the plain for in the first chapter of Judges. Asking for a king like the nations means asking for the nations' military, and the nations' military has to be paid for out of somebody's children.

'"And he will appoint for himself commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and some to plow his ground and to reap his harvest, and to make his implements of war and the equipment of his chariots."'

An officer class, and then a labour force, and the pronouns tell the story: his ground, his harvest, his war, his chariots.

Their sons will farm land that is no longer theirs and make weapons they will not own.

'"He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers."'

Take two, and this time the daughters.

The roles named are domestic and they are palace roles — a court needs perfume and bread and cooking on a scale a village does not. The girls go into service, and the phrasing repays hearing plainly: he will take. Nobody is applying for a position.

'"He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants."'

Take three, and now the land.

Not any fields — the best. And what happens to them is the thing that makes a court: they are given to his servants. A class of men who did not clear that ground or plant those vines will be granted them for loyalty, and the families who did will watch.

Vineyards and olive orchards are the detail that hurts, because neither is a one-year crop. An olive tree takes a decade to bear and a lifetime to mature; a vineyard is planted by a man for his grandchildren. Confiscating them takes three generations of somebody's work in an afternoon.

Ahab will do this to Naboth, and the story will be remembered for three thousand years as the definition of a king who takes (1 Kings 21).

verseByVerse.quote: He will take the tenth of your grain and of your vineyards and give it to his officers and to his servants. He will take your male servants and female servants and the best of your young men and your donkeys, and put them to his work. He will take the tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his slaves. And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"He will take the tenth of your grain and of your vineyards and give it to his officers and to his servants."'

Take four, and the number is the sting.

A tenth is the tithe. It is God's portion — the fraction Israel had been giving to the LORD since Sinai, the acknowledgement that the land and its produce were his gift.

The king will want the same percentage, and he will not be sharing it with God. He will give it to his officers and his servants. Israel is about to run two tithes, and the second one buys a civil service.

'"He will take your male servants and female servants and the best of your young men and your donkeys, and put them to his work. He will take the tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his slaves."'

Takes five and six, and then the destination.

By now every category a family possesses has been named. Sons. Daughters. Fields. Produce. Servants. Livestock. The list is systematic, and it works downward through a household until there is nothing left unlisted.

Then the last four words: and you shall be his slaves.

The Hebrew is 'abadim. It is the word for what Israel was in Egypt. It is the word in the sentence God has repeated to them for four hundred years — I brought you out of the house of slaves — and it is the word Samuel now uses for what they are asking to become.

They came out of a country where the state owned their children and their labour and their time. God broke it open with ten plagues and a sea. And the elders of Israel have come to Ramah to request a return, and God tells them exactly what they are requesting, in the vocabulary of Egypt.

Set the whole speech against the only king who ever came without this verb.

The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Six times a king takes; once a King gives, and what he gives is himself.

Everything in Samuel's warning is about a man moving wealth and people towards the centre. Everything in the gospel is about a King moving in the other direction — who had glory and laid it down, who was rich and became poor, and whose one recorded act of taking was the taking of a cross and a place he did not owe.

'"And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day."'

Here is the sentence that reverses the whole of the previous book.

The engine of Judges was a cry. Israel did evil, God sold them into a hand, and the people of Israel cried out to the LORD — and every single time he answered, because the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning (Judg. 2:18). Five cycles. Five cries. Five deliverers. The cry was the one reliable thing in that entire miserable history.

Samuel says the day is coming when they will cry because of the king, and God will not answer.

The reason is in the middle of the verse and it is not vindictiveness: whom you have chosen for yourselves. The oppressors of the book of Judges were sent; this one is requested. A man may bring his misery to God when it has been done to him. It is a different thing to come complaining about a burden you signed for after reading the terms aloud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — That We Also May Be Like All the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel (v. 19). They repeat the demand and add the reason: that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles (v. 20). Samuel reports it all back to the LORD, and God says: obey their voice and make them a king (vv. 21-22). And Samuel sends them home — go every man to his city.
verseByVerse.theology: The last clause of v. 20 is the whole request. Go out before us and fight our battles was God's job, and one chapter ago he had done it with thunder while Samuel was still at the altar (7:10). They want it transferred to somebody they can see.
verseByVerse.examples: There is no ceremony at the end, no thanksgiving, no covenant. God grants it, Samuel dismisses the assembly, and everybody goes home. The most consequential request in Israel's history is answered and the meeting simply ends.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel. And they said, "No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles." And when Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he repeated them in the ears of the LORD. And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey their voice and make them a king." Samuel then said to the men of Israel, "Go every man to his city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel. And they said, "No! But there shall be a king over us."'

They have heard the whole speech and they say no.

Here is what makes this chapter so sober. This is not a nation stumbling into a mistake, or being deceived, or acting on partial information. God had the terms read out in full — the conscription, the confiscation, the double tithe, the slavery, the unanswered prayer — and the elders of Israel listened to all of it and said no, but there shall be a king over us.

'"that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles."'

Now the reason, in full, and the last clause is the whole of it.

Three things are wanted. To be like all the nations, which is where the request began in verse 5. To have a king who will judge us, which is fair enough and is the thing that has actually broken down. And — go out before us and fight our battles.

Now look back one chapter. Israel was gathered at Mizpah, unarmed, fasting, and the Philistine lords came up to attack. And the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel (7:10).

That was not four hundred years ago. It was within the adult memory of the men making this request. God went out before them and fought their battle, in the open, with the whole nation watching, and the Philistines had not entered Israelite territory since.

They want it done by somebody they can see.

So the sin of this chapter is that, and it explains why God filed it with idolatry in verse 8. Not the office, which he had legislated for. Not the timing, exactly. It is the transfer of a function — taking the one thing God had been doing personally and asking for a man to do it instead, because a man can be looked at, mustered, and counted.

An idol has never mainly been about believing wrong things. It is about relocating a job.

'And when Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he repeated them in the ears of the LORD. And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey their voice and make them a king."'

Samuel takes it back to God a second time, word for word, and gets the same answer he got the first time.

Obey their voice and make them a king. Three times in this chapter God has said it, and every time he has said it after describing the request as a rejection of himself.

'Samuel then said to the men of Israel, "Go every man to his city."'

The assembly is dismissed.

No ceremony marks it. No covenant is cut, no sacrifice offered, no song sung, no thanksgiving made. The most consequential request in Israel's history has been granted, and Samuel tells everybody to go home.

Now hold the long view for a moment, because this chapter is not the end of the argument and the Bible does not treat it as one.

Israel asked for a king to go out before them and fight their battles. They were given Saul, who was a head taller than anyone in the country, and who will spend chapter 17 sitting in his tent while a giant shouts at his army for forty days.

Then they were given David, a man after God's own heart, who fought their battles and won them — and who took another man's wife and had her husband killed, which is precisely the verb of verse 14 applied to a person.

Then, a thousand years later, the King the whole thing was reaching for. He came into the capital on a borrowed donkey rather than a chariot; he had no fields, no vineyards, no officers and nowhere to lay his head; he took nothing from anybody, and gave his life as a ransom for many. He did go out before his people and fight their battle, and he fought it alone, and he won it by dying.

Israel got exactly the king it asked for, and eventually the one it needed. The tragedy of chapter 8 is not that they wanted a king. It is that they wanted one they could look at, and God had been visible at Mizpah in a thunderstorm eighteen months earlier.

8.theology:
Samuel repeats Eli's failure (vv. 1-3). The office was never hereditary; Gideon had refused a dynasty in as many words (Judg. 8:23). The book records it and offers no oracle, no sentence, no comment — and the silence is more damning than a comment. The best man in Israel made precisely the mistake he had been sent as a child to condemn.

The office was not the sin. Deuteronomy 17:14-20 anticipates this request word for word and permits it, with a job description attached. Hannah sang about a king in chapter 2 before anyone thought of asking. What is condemned is like all the nations, and v. 20 says what that means.

They have rejected me (v. 7). Samuel heard a rejection of himself, which is what anyone would hear. God's correction enlarges the wound rather than closing it. For anybody in Christian work who has been passed over or quietly moved aside: the first instinct is always that it is about you, and very often it is not — and the discovery is less flattering than it sounds, because it usually means somebody is refusing God and you were in the way.

Filed with idolatry (v. 8). On the surface the two look nothing alike: nobody here is bowing to an image, and they are asking for a form of government God had legislated for. What makes it the same act is not the object but the transfer. An idol is anything put in the place where God was, to do the job God was doing — and an idol has never mainly been about believing wrong things. It is about relocating a job.

Obey their voice (vv. 7, 9, 22). God grants what he has just called a rejection of himself, having read out the terms in advance and in full. There is a judgment that consists in being told no, and a heavier one that consists in being handed the thing with a receipt: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15); God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28).

He will take, six times (vv. 11-17). Sons, daughters, the best fields, a tenth of the grain, the servants and livestock, a tenth of the flocks — systematically downward through a household until nothing is unlisted. The vineyards and olive orchards are the detail that hurts: neither is a one-year crop, and confiscating them takes three generations of work in an afternoon (cf. Naboth, 1 Kings 21). And 'abadim at v. 17 is the Egypt word. God broke that country open with ten plagues and a sea, and Israel is requesting a return under new management. Set the whole speech against the one King who came without the verb: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

The cry that is not answered (v. 18). The engine of the book of Judges was a cry that was always heard (Judg. 2:18). Here God says the day is coming when they will cry because of the king and he will not answer — and the reason is in the middle of the verse: whom you have chosen for yourselves. The oppressors of Judges were sent. This one is requested.
8.examples:
Then: The elders of Israel heard the full terms read aloud — conscription, confiscation, a second tithe, slavery, and prayers that would go unanswered — and said no, but there shall be a king over us. They wanted somebody to go out before them and fight their battles, eighteen months after God had done it with thunder while the whole nation watched.

Now: Two things. The first is verse 8, and it is the most useful definition of an idol in the Old Testament. Nobody in this chapter worshipped an image; they asked for an ordinary, permitted, sensible arrangement — and God called it what he had called the golden calf, because they were moving a job. Ask what God has actually been doing in your life that you have quietly handed to something you can see and count. The second is verse 18. There is a kind of trouble that is sent, and God always hears the cry about it. And there is a kind we chose after reading the terms, and Samuel is honest that these are not the same conversation.

9.title: Saul the Seeker
9.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of wealth.<sup>2</sup>And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people.<sup>3</sup>Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. So Kish said to Saul his son, "Take one of the young men with you, and arise, go and look for the donkeys."<sup>4</sup>And he passed through the hill country of Ephraim and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. And they passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they passed through the land of Benjamin, but did not find them.<sup>5</sup>When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, "Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us."<sup>6</sup>But he said to him, "Behold, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor; all that he says comes true. So now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us the way we should go."<sup>7</sup>Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we bring the man? For the bread in our sacks is gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?"<sup>8</sup>The servant answered Saul again, "Here, I have with me a quarter of a shekel of silver, and I will give it to the man of God to tell us our way."<sup>9</sup>(Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, "Come, let us go to the seer," for today's "prophet" was formerly called a seer.)<sup>10</sup>And Saul said to his servant, "Well said; come, let us go." So they went to the city where the man of God was.<sup>11</sup>As they went up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water and said to them, "Is the seer here?"<sup>12</sup>They answered, "He is; behold, he is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has come just now to the city, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place.<sup>13</sup>As soon as you enter the city you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat till he comes, since he must bless the sacrifice; afterward those who are invited will eat. Now go up, for you will meet him immediately."<sup>14</sup>So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, they saw Samuel coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.<sup>15</sup>Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel:<sup>16</sup>"Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me."<sup>17</sup>When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people."<sup>18</sup>Then Saul approached Samuel in the gate and said, "Tell me where is the house of the seer?"<sup>19</sup>Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me, and in the morning I will let you go and will tell you all that is on your mind.<sup>20</sup>As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not set your mind on them, for they have been found. And for whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?"<sup>21</sup>Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this way?"<sup>22</sup>Then Samuel took Saul and his young man and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty persons.<sup>23</sup>And Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you, of which I said to you, 'Put it aside.'"<sup>24</sup>So the cook took up the leg and what was on it and set them before Saul. And Samuel said, "See, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the hour appointed, that you might eat with the guests." So Saul ate with Samuel that day.<sup>25</sup>And when they came down from the high place into the city, a bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down to sleep.<sup>26</sup>Then at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Up, that I may send you on your way." So Saul arose, and both he and Samuel went out into the street.<sup>27</sup>As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to pass on before us, and when he has passed on, stop here yourself for a while, that I may make known to you the word of God."
9.overview:
Israel asked for a king like the nations, and two verses into this chapter God introduces the best-looking man in the country, from his shoulders upward taller than any of the people. Every word of the description is about the outside of a person. They are given exactly what they specified, down to the inch — and 16:7 is written against this verse.

Then the monarchy of Israel begins with lost livestock. A farmer's donkeys wander off, his son goes to look for them, and three days and four districts produce nothing. It is the servant who knows there is a man of God in the town, the servant who suggests asking him, and the servant who has a quarter shekel when Saul says they have nothing to bring. Girls at the well give directions at enthusiastic length. And as the two men walk in through the gate, Samuel walks out through it.

Then the narrator steps back a day: now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel. Everything that read as a chain of small accidents was an itinerary. And the reason God gives is the exodus reason — I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me — one chapter after calling the same request a rejection of himself.

Saul asks the seer where the seer lives, is told about his own donkeys before he mentions them, and protests in Gideon's exact words that he is from the least of the tribes. Then he is seated at the head of thirty guests and served the priest's portion, reserved before he arrived: kept for you until the hour appointed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Tallest Man in Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Kish of Benjamin is introduced with a five-generation pedigree and described as a man of wealth (v. 1). His son Saul is a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel asked for a king like the nations. Two verses later God introduces the best-looking and tallest man in the country. They are given precisely what they specified, and the whole description is of the outside of a person.
verseByVerse.examples: And he is a Benjaminite. A reader arriving from the end of Judges knows what that means: the tribe was reduced to six hundred men on a rock in the wilderness, and its women were supplied by a massacre and an abduction (Judg. 20-21). Israel's first king comes from the tribe that nearly ceased to exist.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of wealth. And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of wealth.'

The book opens a new section the way it opened the first one: there was a certain man, with a genealogy and a home town.

Compare 1:1, where Elkanah was introduced with four generations behind him. Same formula, and the reader is meant to hear it. But the last phrase is different: Kish is a man of wealth, which can also be rendered a man of standing. Elkanah was simply a man from Ramah.

The tribe is Benjamin.

If you have come to this book from Judges you cannot read that name neutrally. Benjamin is the tribe that sheltered the men of Gibeah, went to war with the other eleven over it, and was cut down to six hundred survivors hiding on a rock in the wilderness for four months (Judg. 20:47). Its women were replaced by the massacre of Jabesh-gilead and an abduction at a festival.

Israel's first king will come out of the tribe that almost ceased to exist, three generations after it happened.

'And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people.'

Now read that verse against the request that has just been made.

Israel wanted a king like all the nations, one who would go out before us and fight our battles (8:20). What they were asking for was somebody impressive — a figure who would look right at the head of an army, whom the neighbours would take seriously.

Here he is. The best-looking man in the country, by an explicit comparison the narrator takes the trouble to make, and a head taller than everybody else.

Every word of the description is about the outside of a person. There is nothing here about his courage, his judgment, his faith or his character; there is a face and a height. God is giving Israel exactly what it specified, down to the last inch.

Hold the verse. Seven chapters from now, when this man has been rejected and Samuel is sent to Bethlehem to anoint another, he will look at Jesse's eldest and think surely the LORD's anointed is before him — and be told: do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature... for the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (16:7).

That sentence is written against this one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Kish loses his donkeys and sends Saul with a servant to find them (v. 3). They cover four districts and find nothing (v. 4), and Saul proposes going home before his father starts worrying about them instead (v. 5). It is the servant who knows there is a man of God in the town, the servant who suggests asking him, and the servant who has a quarter of a shekel when Saul points out they have nothing to bring (vv. 6-8). Some young women at the well give them directions at length (vv. 11-13), and as they enter the city Samuel is coming out towards them (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The monarchy of Israel begins with a farm errand. Lost livestock, four fruitless districts, an empty food bag, a servant with small change, and a chance conversation at a well — and every step of it puts a particular man through a particular gate at a particular hour.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the servant. He has the information, the idea and the money, and Saul agrees to each of his suggestions in turn. Through the whole episode the future king is the less resourceful of the two men on the road.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. So Kish said to Saul his son, "Take one of the young men with you, and arise, go and look for the donkeys." And he passed through the hill country of Ephraim and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. And they passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they passed through the land of Benjamin, but did not find them. When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, "Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us." But he said to him, "Behold, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor; all that he says comes true. So now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us the way we should go." Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we bring the man? For the bread in our sacks is gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?" The servant answered Saul again, "Here, I have with me a quarter of a shekel of silver, and I will give it to the man of God to tell us our way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. So Kish said to Saul his son, "Take one of the young men with you, and arise, go and look for the donkeys."'

The monarchy of Israel begins with lost livestock.

There is no vision here, no angel, no summons. A wealthy farmer's animals have wandered off and he sends his son out with a farmhand to look for them, which is the least remarkable errand in agricultural life.

'And he passed through the hill country of Ephraim and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. And they passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they passed through the land of Benjamin, but did not find them.'

Four districts, and the sentence is built to feel like the walking.

Passed through... did not find them... passed through... they were not there... passed through... did not find them. Three days of this, we learn later. Two young men working steadily south and finding nothing, in a search that is entirely wasted from their point of view.

Every step of it is taking Saul towards a town he has no intention of visiting.

'When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, "Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us."'

Saul's one contribution so far is a decent instinct, and it deserves noting because there will not be many.

He wants to turn round, and the reason is not that he is tired. It is that his father will start worrying. He can see the moment coming when Kish stops caring about the animals and starts caring about the boy, and he does not want to put him through it.

Zuph, incidentally, is where Elkanah's family came from (1:1). Saul has walked, without knowing it, into Samuel's home district.

'But he said to him, "Behold, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor; all that he says comes true. So now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us the way we should go."'

The servant is the one who knows.

He knows there is a man of God in the town. He knows the man's reputation — all that he says comes true, which is the exact commendation the narrator gave Samuel in 3:19, that God let none of his words fall to the ground. And it is his idea to go.

The future king of Israel is standing in Samuel's own district and does not appear to know he lives there.

'Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we bring the man? For the bread in our sacks is gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?"'

Saul's objection is practical and reasonable: you did not visit a prophet empty-handed, and they have eaten everything.

'The servant answered Saul again, "Here, I have with me a quarter of a shekel of silver, and I will give it to the man of God to tell us our way."'

The servant has money.

A quarter of a shekel is a small coin — not a gift for a great prophet, just what a working man happens to be carrying. He offers it without being asked.

Keep an eye on this servant, because the pattern is set here and holds all the way to the town gate. He has the local knowledge, the initiative and the funds. Every step in this chapter that moves Saul towards his anointing is proposed by the hired man walking beside him.

verseByVerse.quote: (Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, "Come, let us go to the seer," for today's "prophet" was formerly called a seer.) And Saul said to his servant, "Well said; come, let us go." So they went to the city where the man of God was. As they went up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water and said to them, "Is the seer here?" They answered, "He is; behold, he is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has come just now to the city, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place. As soon as you enter the city you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat till he comes, since he must bless the sacrifice; afterward those who are invited will eat. Now go up, for you will meet him immediately." So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, they saw Samuel coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'(Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, "Come, let us go to the seer," for today's "prophet" was formerly called a seer.)'

The narrator interrupts himself to explain an old word, and the aside tells us two things.

The first is that this history was written down long enough after the event for the vocabulary to have shifted. The second is what the older word meant: a seer is one who sees. It is a plain, physical term for a man to whom things are shown.

'As they went up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water and said to them, "Is the seer here?"'

They meet girls going out to the well, which is where you meet people in this part of the Bible. Abraham's servant found Rebekah at a well; Jacob met Rachel at one; Moses met Zipporah at one.

'They answered, "He is; behold, he is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has come just now to the city, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place."'

The answer runs on for three verses and the writer clearly enjoys it.

He is here. He is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has only just arrived himself. There is a sacrifice today. He has to bless it before anyone eats, so the whole town is waiting. Go up now and you will meet him straight away.

It is exactly how people give directions when they are excited to be asked, and it is packed with information that turns out to matter: Samuel is in town today only, has arrived within the hour, and is walking up this street now.

'So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, they saw Samuel coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.'

They walk in through the gate and he walks out through it, and they meet.

Count what had to happen for that sentence to be written. Kish's donkeys had to stray on a particular day. The search had to fail in four districts in a particular order. The servant had to know about the seer, and to be carrying a coin. Saul had to be talked out of turning for home. The women had to be at the well at that hour and to answer at length. And Samuel had to have come to that town, on that morning, for a sacrifice.

None of the people involved is doing anything unusual. A farmer loses animals; a son goes to look for them; a servant makes a sensible suggestion; girls fetch water; a prophet keeps an appointment. And the next verse tells us that God had the whole thing arranged the previous day.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrator steps back a day: now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel that a man of Benjamin would arrive at this hour to be anointed prince over my people Israel — and the reason given is the exodus reason: I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me (vv. 15-16). When Samuel sees him, God says here is the man of whom I spoke to you (v. 17). Saul, not recognising him, asks the way to the seer's house, and is told I am the seer (vv. 18-19). The donkeys are found, says Samuel — and for whom is all that is desirable in Israel? (v. 20). Saul's reply is a protest: am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: God had the appointment in the diary twenty-four hours before Saul knew he was going that way. The donkeys were lost so that a young man would be in a particular street at a particular time.
verseByVerse.examples: The word in v. 16 is nagid, prince or leader-designate, not melek, king. Israel asked for a king; God appoints a leader. And Saul's protest in v. 21 is Gideon's almost exactly — my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house (Judg. 6:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel: "Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me." When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel: "Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel."'

Twenty-four hours in advance, to the hour.

That is the sentence that reorganises the whole chapter. Everything we have just read as a chain of small accidents — the straying donkeys, the fruitless districts, the empty food bag, the servant's coin, the chatty girls at the well — was an itinerary. God had told Samuel the day before what time to expect him.

Note the word for the office: prince. The Hebrew is nagid, a leader or designate, and it is not the word Israel used. They demanded a melek, a king, like all the nations. God appoints a nagid.

It is a smaller word, and a deliberate one. He will be given the crown the people asked for, and God's own title for him is one rank below it.

'"He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me."'

Now listen to where this language comes from.

I have seen my people... their cry has come to me. At a burning bush in the desert God had said: I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry... and I know their sufferings (Ex. 3:7-9).

It is the vocabulary of the exodus, applied here to the appointment of Saul.

That is remarkable, given what God said about this request one chapter ago. He called it a rejection of himself and filed it with four hundred years of idolatry. And now, in the same breath as granting it, he explains it in the words he used when he came down to rescue slaves.

God is genuinely angry about the request and genuinely moved by the people making it, and both are stated in plain Hebrew a chapter apart. He is not being talked into anything. He is giving them a king because they asked wrongly, and giving them a deliverer because he has seen them.

'When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people."'

Samuel does not have to work it out; God identifies him on sight.

The verb in the last clause is unexpected. Not lead, or save, or rule — restrain. It carries the sense of holding in, keeping within bounds, taking charge of something that would otherwise run loose.

That is a fair description of what Israel needed after the book of Judges, where every man did what was right in his own eyes. And it is a strange word to attach to a man whose own reign will end in a medium's house at Endor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul approached Samuel in the gate and said, "Tell me where is the house of the seer?" Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me, and in the morning I will let you go and will tell you all that is on your mind. As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not set your mind on them, for they have been found. And for whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?" Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul approached Samuel in the gate and said, "Tell me where is the house of the seer?"'

He asks the seer where the seer lives.

There is something almost funny about it, and something sad. The most famous man in Israel — a prophet known from Dan to Beersheba, who has judged the nation for a lifetime — is standing in front of the future king, and the future king asks him for directions.

'Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me, and in the morning I will let you go and will tell you all that is on your mind."'

I am the seer. And then, immediately, an invitation, a schedule and a promise.

Eat with me today. In the morning I will send you off. And I will tell you everything on your mind — which is a considerable claim to make to a stranger, and the next verse cashes it.

'"As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not set your mind on them, for they have been found."'

He knows about the donkeys.

Saul has not mentioned them. He has said nothing about his father, the search, or the three days. And the first specific thing the seer says to him is the exact business that brought him here, with the duration attached and the outcome supplied.

Mark the pastoral order, too. Before a word about kingdoms, Samuel deals with the thing actually on the young man's mind. The donkeys are found; stop worrying about the donkeys. Only then does he raise anything else.

'"And for whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?"'

Then the hint, and it is only a hint. Samuel does not say you are to be king. He asks a question about who everything valuable in Israel is for, and lets it hang.

'Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this way?"'

Saul's answer is the best thing he says in the book.

It is also somebody else's, almost word for word. A frightened young man threshing wheat in a winepress once told the angel of the LORD: my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house (Judg. 6:15).

Two men, two calls, the same protest. Gideon and Saul both begin by giving an accurate inventory of their own insignificance, and in both cases the inventory is true.

Here it is exactly true. The least of the tribes of Israel is not modest phrasing; it is arithmetic. Benjamin had been reduced to six hundred men within living memory of Saul's grandfather.

So the chapter has now given us two facts about this man and they do not sit easily together. He is the tallest and best-looking person in Israel, and he comes from the smallest clan of the smallest tribe and knows it. Both are true, and the second is the one that will not last.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Portion That Was Kept
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel seats Saul and his servant at the head of thirty invited guests (v. 22) and tells the cook to bring the portion he had set aside (v. 23). The cook brings the leg, and Samuel says: see, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the hour appointed (v. 24). Saul sleeps on the roof, and at dawn Samuel walks him to the edge of town, sends the servant on ahead, and says stop here yourself for a while, that I may make known to you the word of God (vv. 25-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The leg is the priest's portion under the law (Lev. 7:32-33), and Samuel had ordered it reserved before Saul was anything to him but a sentence God had spoken the previous day.
verseByVerse.examples: Kept for you until the hour appointed. Saul spent three days chasing donkeys through four districts and arrived at a table where his dinner was already waiting under a cloth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took Saul and his young man and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty persons. And Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you, of which I said to you, 'Put it aside.'" So the cook took up the leg and what was on it and set them before Saul. And Samuel said, "See, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the hour appointed, that you might eat with the guests." So Saul ate with Samuel that day. And when they came down from the high place into the city, a bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down to sleep. Then at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Up, that I may send you on your way." So Saul arose, and both he and Samuel went out into the street. As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to pass on before us, and when he has passed on, stop here yourself for a while, that I may make known to you the word of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel took Saul and his young man and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty persons.'

Thirty guests are already seated, and two men who came in off the road looking for donkeys are put at the top of the table.

Note that the servant goes up with him. Samuel seats them both.

'And Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you, of which I said to you, 'Put it aside.'" So the cook took up the leg and what was on it and set them before Saul.'

The instruction to the cook was given earlier — before the meal, before Saul arrived, on the strength of a sentence God had spoken the previous day.

What comes out is the leg. Under the law, the right thigh of a fellowship offering was the priest's portion, given to him by name (Lev. 7:32-33). It was the best cut and it belonged to the man presiding.

Samuel had it put aside for a young man he had never met.

'And Samuel said, "See, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the hour appointed, that you might eat with the guests." So Saul ate with Samuel that day.'

Kept for you until the hour appointed.

Sit with that sentence, because it is the theology of the whole chapter served on a plate. Saul has spent three days walking four districts after animals that were not there, getting hungrier, achieving nothing, and thinking about going home. And he arrives at a table where a portion has been under a cloth since before he came, reserved by name, for an appointment he did not know he had.

Everything that felt like wasted time was the journey to this seat.

Anyone who has spent a season on a search that produced nothing can take that plainly. The donkeys were never the point, and it was not possible to know that while looking for them.

'And when they came down from the high place into the city, a bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down to sleep.'

They make him a bed on the roof, which is where you sleep in that country when the night is warm, and he lies down under the sky on the last ordinary night of his life.

'Then at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Up, that I may send you on your way." So Saul arose, and both he and Samuel went out into the street.'

Early, before the town is awake, the old man calls up to the roof and the two of them walk out into an empty street together.

'As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to pass on before us, and when he has passed on, stop here yourself for a while, that I may make known to you the word of God."'

The servant is sent ahead, and the chapter stops there.

It is a deliberate piece of storytelling. Two men on the edge of a town at first light, one of them about to be told something, and the writer closes the chapter on the sentence before it — that I may make known to you the word of God.

Look back over the twenty-seven verses and count what God used. A herd of donkeys that wandered off. Four districts of fruitless walking. An empty food sack. A servant who happened to know the local prophet's reputation and happened to have a quarter shekel in his pocket. A young man's worry about his father. A group of girls at a well who answered a question at length. A sacrifice scheduled for that day in that town. A cook, and a cut of meat put by.

Not one of those is a miracle. Every one of them is the sort of thing that happens on an ordinary Tuesday, and any of them could have gone differently.

The day before it started, God had told Samuel what time to expect him.

9.theology:
Exactly what they asked for (v. 2). A face and a height, and nothing about courage, judgment or faith. Israel wanted somebody who would look right at the head of an army and be taken seriously by the neighbours, and that is precisely what arrives. Seven chapters on, Samuel will look at Jesse's eldest and be told the LORD sees not as man sees (16:7) — a sentence written against this one.

From the least of the tribes. Benjamin was cut to six hundred men on a rock within living memory (Judg. 20:47), its women supplied by a massacre and an abduction. Saul's protest in v. 21 is not modesty but arithmetic — and it is Gideon's sentence almost word for word (Judg. 6:15). Two men, two calls, the same accurate inventory of their own insignificance. The book will show what each did with it.

Nagid, not melek (v. 16). Israel demanded a king. God appoints a prince — leader, designate — one rank below the word the people used. He will be given the crown they asked for, and God's own title for him is smaller than it.

Anger and pity in the same week. I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me is the language of the burning bush (Ex. 3:7-9), spoken one chapter after God called this request a rejection of himself and filed it with four centuries of idolatry. He is genuinely angry about the request and genuinely moved by the people making it, and he is not being talked into anything.

Providence with no miracle in it. Straying donkeys, four fruitless districts, an empty food sack, a servant who knew the local prophet and happened to be carrying a coin, a son's worry about his father, talkative girls at a well, a sacrifice scheduled for that morning, a cook and a cut of meat put by. Not one of those is supernatural; every one could have gone differently. And God had told Samuel the day before what time to expect him.

Kept for you until the hour appointed (v. 24). The leg is the priest's portion (Lev. 7:32-33), the best cut, belonging to the man presiding — and Samuel had it reserved for a stranger before the stranger existed to him as a person. Saul spent three days failing at a search and arrived at a table where his dinner had been under a cloth all along. Everything that felt like wasted time was the journey to that seat, and it was not possible to know that while looking for the donkeys.
9.examples:
Then: A young man lost three days looking for his father's donkeys, found nothing, wanted to go home so his father would not worry, was talked into asking a local holy man for directions by a servant with a small coin — and walked into a town where a prophet had been told the previous day what time he would arrive and had already ordered his dinner set aside.

Now: Two things. The first is the shape of the whole chapter: God very rarely announces himself in the middle of the arrangement. Every element of Saul's morning was ordinary, reversible and explicable, and the reader only learns it was an appointment because the narrator steps back a day in verse 15. You are unlikely to be given verse 15 at the time. The second is verse 24, and it is for anyone in a season that has produced nothing: the donkeys were never the point, and no amount of looking at them would have revealed that.

10.title: The Spirit of God Came Upon Him
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel? And you shall reign over the people of the LORD and you will save them from the hand of their surrounding enemies. And this shall be the sign to you that the LORD has anointed you to be prince over his heritage.<sup>2</sup>When you depart from me today, you will meet two men by Rachel's tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys that you went to seek are found, and now your father has ceased to care about the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying, "What shall I do about my son?"'<sup>3</sup>Then you shall go on from there farther and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine.<sup>4</sup>And they will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall accept from their hand.<sup>5</sup>After that you shall come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a garrison of the Philistines. And there, as soon as you come to the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, prophesying.<sup>6</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man.<sup>7</sup>Now when these signs meet you, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you.<sup>8</sup>Then go down before me to Gilgal. And behold, I am coming down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do."<sup>9</sup>When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. And all these signs came to pass that day.<sup>10</sup>When they came to Gibeah, behold, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.<sup>11</sup>And when all who knew him previously saw how he prophesied with the prophets, the people said to one another, "What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"<sup>12</sup>And a man of the place answered, "And who is their father?" Therefore it became a proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"<sup>13</sup>When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.<sup>14</sup>Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, "Where did you go?" And he said, "To seek the donkeys. And when we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel."<sup>15</sup>And Saul's uncle said, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you."<sup>16</sup>And Saul said to his uncle, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he did not tell him anything.<sup>17</sup>Now Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And he said to the people of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.'<sup>19</sup>But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and your distresses, and you have said to him, 'Set a king over us.' Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands."<sup>20</sup>Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot.<sup>21</sup>He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found.<sup>22</sup>So they inquired again of the LORD, "Is there a man still to come?" and the LORD said, "Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage."<sup>23</sup>Then they ran and took him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward.<sup>24</sup>And Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? There is none like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"<sup>25</sup>Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and he wrote them in a book and laid it up before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each one to his home.<sup>26</sup>Saul also went to his home at Gibeah, and with him went men of valor whose hearts God had touched.<sup>27</sup>But some worthless fellows said, "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no present. But he held his peace.
10.overview:
It happens on a road at dawn with the one witness sent on ahead: oil, a kiss, and a sentence. Samuel uses God's word for the office — prince — not the people's. And the first confirming sign quotes Saul back to himself: at 9:5 he had worried that his father would stop caring about the donkeys and start worrying about him, and two strangers at Rachel's tomb say it almost word for word. God confirms the anointing with the young man's own private sentence, and settles the worry at the same time.

The third sign is at Gibeath-elohim, the hill of God — which has a Philistine garrison in it, and a band of prophets coming down past it with a tambourine. There the Spirit will rush on him and he will be turned into another man. Then two instructions that pull opposite ways: do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you, and — at Gilgal — seven days you shall wait, until I come to you. Keep the second; chapter 13 is where it breaks.

When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. Not after the signs and not in response to anything he did. He turns to walk away and God changes him on the spot, and the neighbours who have known him all his life ask what has come over the son of Kish.

Then the public lot at Mizpah — where Samuel tells the assembled nation, on coronation day, that asking for a king was a rejection of God, and crowns him anyway. And when the name falls, the king cannot be found. They have to ask God a second question, and the answer is that he is hiding in the luggage.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Flask of Oil and Three Signs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel pours oil on Saul's head, kisses him, and tells him the LORD has anointed him prince over his people Israel (v. 1). Three signs will confirm it: two men at Rachel's tomb with news that the donkeys are found and his father is now anxious about him (v. 2); three men at the oak of Tabor who will give him two loaves (vv. 3-4); and a band of prophets coming down from the high place at Gibeath-elohim, where the Spirit of the LORD will rush on him and he will be turned into another man (vv. 5-6). Then two instructions: do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you (v. 7), and — seven days you shall wait, until I come to you (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The first sign quotes Saul back to himself. At 9:5 he had wanted to turn for home in case his father stopped worrying about the donkeys and started worrying about him. The men at the tomb say it almost word for word. God confirms the anointing with the young man's own sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is the one to keep. Seven days you shall wait. It is the first command Saul is given as king, it is specific, and chapter 13 is where he breaks it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel? And you shall reign over the people of the LORD and you will save them from the hand of their surrounding enemies. And this shall be the sign to you that the LORD has anointed you to be prince over his heritage. When you depart from me today, you will meet two men by Rachel's tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys that you went to seek are found, and now your father has ceased to care about the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying, "What shall I do about my son?"' Then you shall go on from there farther and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. And they will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall accept from their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel?"'

It happens on a road at dawn, with one witness sent on ahead, and it takes three actions.

Oil poured on the head. A kiss. And a sentence, put as a question. There is no crowd, no ceremony and no announcement; the servant has been sent up the road precisely so that nobody sees it.

The word again is prince — nagid, not king. Samuel uses God's word, not the people's, at the moment of the anointing.

The anointing is what gives this book its central title. The anointed one is the mashiach, the messiah; from this morning onward the phrase the LORD's anointed belongs to a man, and David will refuse to lift a hand against it even when its holder is trying to kill him.

'"When you depart from me today, you will meet two men by Rachel's tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys that you went to seek are found, and now your father has ceased to care about the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying, "What shall I do about my son?"'"'

Now go back to 9:5 and read what Saul said on the road three days ago.

Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us.

The sign quotes him. Two strangers at a tomb will say back to him, almost word for word, the sentence he spoke to his servant in a field when nobody was listening.

That is a remarkable piece of pastoral care. God confirms the anointing of a king by having his own private worry repeated to him by men who could not have heard it — and by settling the worry at the same time. The donkeys are found. Your father is anxious. Go home.

The location is chosen too. Rachel's tomb, in the territory of Benjamin: Rachel was Benjamin's mother and died giving birth to him. Israel's first king receives his first confirming sign at the grave of his tribe's ancestress.

'"Then you shall go on from there farther and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. And they will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall accept from their hand."'

The second sign is smaller and stranger, and the detail is exact: three men, three goats, three loaves, one skin of wine, and they will hand over two of the loaves.

These are pilgrims taking offerings up to Bethel. The bread is holy provision, on its way to God, and they will divert some of it to a stranger on the road.

Remember that Saul told his servant three days ago that they had nothing left to eat (9:7).

verseByVerse.quote: After that you shall come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a garrison of the Philistines. And there, as soon as you come to the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, prophesying. Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man. Now when these signs meet you, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you. Then go down before me to Gilgal. And behold, I am coming down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"After that you shall come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a garrison of the Philistines. And there, as soon as you come to the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, prophesying."'

Two things are in that verse and they do not obviously belong together.

The town is Gibeath-elohim, the hill of God. And there is a Philistine garrison in it. The occupying army has a post on the hill of God, which is the political situation of Israel in one place name.

Coming down off that hill is a band of prophets with a small orchestra — harp, tambourine, flute and lyre — making music and prophesying, in a town with foreign troops stationed in it.

Worship did not stop under occupation. It came down the hill past the garrison with a tambourine.

'"Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man."'

The verb rush is the one used of Samson — a sudden seizing, not a gentle settling.

Then the promise that is larger than anything else in the chapter: you will be turned into another man. Not improved, not trained, not promoted. Turned into somebody else.

'"Now when these signs meet you, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you."'

The first instruction is remarkably open. Do what your hand finds to do.
