No orders, no plan, no campaign. He is told to act, on his own judgment, in whatever comes to hand — and given the only thing that makes such freedom safe: for God is with you.

'"Then go down before me to Gilgal. And behold, I am coming down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do."'

The second instruction is the opposite of the first, and it is the one to remember.

Go to Gilgal. Wait. Seven days. Until I come.

Weigh the shape of the two commands together, because a king is being taught something. In most things: use your judgment, God is with you. In this one thing: do nothing until I arrive.

Mark the verse and leave it. It is the first specific order Saul receives as Israel's prince, it has a number of days attached, and three chapters from now he will stand at Gilgal watching his army melt away, wait almost the whole seven days, and offer the burnt offering himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Is Saul Also Among the Prophets?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart, and all the signs happened that day (v. 9). At Gibeah the prophets meet him, the Spirit of God rushes on him, and he prophesies (v. 10). The neighbours are astonished — what has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets? — and it becomes a proverb (vv. 11-12). Then his uncle asks where he has been, and Saul tells him about the donkeys and says nothing at all about the kingdom (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God gave him another heart is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament, and it is said of Saul. Whatever comes later, something real was given here, and it was given before any of the signs happened.
verseByVerse.examples: The proverb bookends his life. It is asked here in wonder, when the Spirit has come on a farmer's son; and it is asked again at 19:24, when he lies stripped and prophesying on the ground at Ramah while the man he is hunting escapes.

verseByVerse.quote: When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. And all these signs came to pass that day. When they came to Gibeah, behold, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them. And when all who knew him previously saw how he prophesied with the prophets, the people said to one another, "What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" And a man of the place answered, "And who is their father?" Therefore it became a proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. And all these signs came to pass that day.'

Six words, and they are among the greatest in the Old Testament: God gave him another heart.

The moment he turns to go, it happens. Not after the signs, not once he has proved himself, not in response to anything he did on the road. He turns his back to walk away and God changes him on the spot.

Take the sentence seriously, because the end of this man's story makes it tempting not to. Whatever else is true of Saul, something real was given to him here. The language is the language the prophets will use for the greatest promise God ever makes to his people: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26).

'When they came to Gibeah, behold, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.'

Sign three arrives, and the Spirit takes hold of a farmer's son in the street.

'And when all who knew him previously saw how he prophesied with the prophets, the people said to one another, "What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"'

The people who react are the ones who have known him all his life.

That is the point of the question. It is not who is this man but what has come over the son of Kish — the neighbours, the people he grew up in front of, watching somebody they thought they had measured do something entirely out of character.

'And a man of the place answered, "And who is their father?" Therefore it became a proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"'

The retort is obscure and has never been settled. The likeliest sense is that prophecy is not a family trade — nobody asks who the prophets' father is, because the gift is not inherited — so there is no reason Kish's boy should be excluded.

What matters more is that the sentence stuck. It became a saying, the kind of thing people in that country said when somebody turned up somewhere he had no business being.

It will be said about him once more. Nine chapters from now Saul will be hunting David, and will send three parties of messengers to Ramah and lose every one of them to the Spirit, and will finally go himself — and end up lying on the ground stripped and prophesying all that day and night while David gets clean away. And the narrator writes: therefore it is said, is Saul also among the prophets? (19:24).

The same proverb opens and closes him. The first time it is wonder. The second time it is a man's public humiliation while the kingdom walks out of his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, "Where did you go?" And he said, "To seek the donkeys. And when we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel." And Saul's uncle said, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you." And Saul said to his uncle, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he did not tell him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, "Where did you go?" And he said, "To seek the donkeys. And when we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel."'

He goes home and a relative asks the ordinary question, and gets an ordinary and accurate answer.

'And Saul's uncle said, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you." And Saul said to his uncle, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he did not tell him anything.'

He tells him about the livestock and nothing about the crown.

The narrator states it flatly and offers no assessment, and readers have taken it both ways for centuries. It may be modesty: a young man who has had oil poured on his head at dawn and does not think it is his to announce. It may be prudence: Samuel had done this in private with the servant sent ahead, and a man who starts telling his uncle he is to be king has not understood the arrangement.

Or it may be the first appearance of something else. This is the man who will shortly be found hiding in the luggage.

The book does not tell us, and it is a mistake to be more certain than the text. What can be said is that Saul is consistently reticent about this kingdom in these early chapters, and that the reticence is attractive, and that it does not last.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel convenes the nation at Mizpah and, on the day of the coronation, restates the charge: today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities (vv. 17-19). The lot narrows to Benjamin, then the Matrites, then Saul son of Kish — but when they sought him, he could not be found (vv. 20-21). They ask God, and are told: behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage (v. 22). They fetch him out, and standing among the people he is taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward (v. 23). Samuel presents him — there is none like him among all the people — and they shout long live the king (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel does not soften the indictment for the occasion. He crowns the man and calls the request a rejection of God in the same speech, and neither statement cancels the other.
verseByVerse.examples: The hiding has been read two ways for as long as people have read it — humility, or fear — and the text refuses to decide. Both fit the man. And what they lead out of the luggage is described in exactly the words of 9:2: he is very tall. That is what Israel asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah. And he said to the people of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.' But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and your distresses, and you have said to him, 'Set a king over us.' Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah. And he said to the people of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.'"'

Mizpah again — the hill where the nation had fasted and confessed and watched God break the Philistines with thunder (7:5-10). Samuel brings them back to the same place to give them a king.

He opens the way God always opens: with the recital. I brought you up. I delivered you from Egypt. I delivered you from every kingdom that oppressed you.

'"But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and your distresses, and you have said to him, 'Set a king over us.'"'

He says it on the day of the coronation.

Stop over that. This is the ceremony. The nation is assembled, the lots are about to be cast, the king is in the crowd, and the presiding prophet uses the occasion to tell them that what they are doing is a rejection of God.

He does not soften it for the day. He does not decide that the decision is made and the mood should be positive. He is going to crown the man — God told him to, three times — and he will not pretend the request was a good one while he does it.

Both things are held together and neither is allowed to cancel the other. God has granted it, and it was a rejection. Samuel obeys the first without withdrawing the second.

'"Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands."'

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot. He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found. So they inquired again of the LORD, "Is there a man still to come?" and the LORD said, "Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage." Then they ran and took him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward. And Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? There is none like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot. He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot.'

The lot narrows from twelve tribes to one clan to one man, and lands where God had already landed a chapter ago.

The procedure matters. Samuel already knows who it is; he anointed him privately on a road at dawn. The lot is not for Samuel's benefit. It is so that the whole nation watches the choice fall publicly, tribe by tribe, and cannot afterwards say the prophet installed his own candidate.

'But when they sought him, he could not be found. So they inquired again of the LORD, "Is there a man still to come?" and the LORD said, "Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage."'

The king of Israel is missing from his own coronation, and God has to tell them where he is.

Picture the scene, because it is genuinely comic and genuinely uncomfortable. The lots have fallen, the nation is assembled, the name has been called — and nobody comes forward. They search. They have to go back and ask God a second question, and the answer is that the man is in among the luggage.

This has been read two ways for as long as it has been read, and the text will not settle it.

It may be humility. He had told Samuel he was from the least clan of the smallest tribe and meant it; he had told his own uncle nothing; and a man who genuinely does not want this might well be found at the back among the packs when they call his name.

It may equally be fear. This is the man who, seven chapters from now, will sit in his tent for forty days while a Philistine shouts at his army, and who will be dismayed and greatly afraid along with everybody else (17:11). Hiding is what he does.

The honest answer is that both fit, that the writer knew both fit, and that he declines to tell us. What can be said is that the same behaviour looks like modesty at a coronation and like paralysis at a battlefield, and that the man never entirely stops doing it.

'Then they ran and took him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward.'

They pull him out of the baggage and stand him up, and the narrator repeats 9:2 word for word.

He is very tall. That is the fact the book keeps giving us about this man, and it is being given again at the exact moment he is presented to the nation, immediately after he has been discovered hiding.

'And Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? There is none like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"'

Samuel's commendation is about how he looks.

Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? The verb is see, and what there is to see is a head and shoulders above the crowd. There is none like him among all the people — which in the context of verse 23 means precisely one thing.

Israel asked in chapter 8 for a king like the nations, someone to go out before them and fight their battles: an impressive figure at the head of an army. They are looking at him and cheering, and everything they can see is exactly what they ordered.

Six chapters from now, God will send Samuel to Bethlehem and refuse him seven sons in a row, and say: do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees (16:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel sets out the rights and duties of the kingship, writes them in a book, and lays it up before the LORD (v. 25). Saul goes home to Gibeah, and with him go men of valor whose hearts God had touched (v. 26). But some worthless fellows say how can this man save us?, despise him, and bring him no present. But he held his peace (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The constitution is written down and deposited at the sanctuary, which is what Deuteronomy 17:18-20 required — a king under a text, with a copy on file that he does not control.
verseByVerse.examples: Worthless fellows is sons of Belial once more (cf. 1:16; 2:12). And Saul's silence is genuinely to his credit; when the people want those men executed after his first victory, he refuses (11:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and he wrote them in a book and laid it up before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each one to his home. Saul also went to his home at Gibeah, and with him went men of valor whose hearts God had touched. But some worthless fellows said, "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no present. But he held his peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and he wrote them in a book and laid it up before the LORD.'

The constitution is written down and filed at the sanctuary.

This is precisely what the law required. Deuteronomy said that when Israel had a king he was to write a copy of the law for himself, keep it with him, and read it every day of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God and that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers (Deut. 17:18-20).

So Israel now has a king who is under a text, and the text is not in his keeping. It is laid up before the LORD, where he cannot amend it.

Here is the crucial difference between this monarchy and every monarchy Israel was asking to imitate. The kings of the nations were the source of law. This one is subject to a document deposited somewhere he does not control.

'Then Samuel sent all the people away, each one to his home. Saul also went to his home at Gibeah, and with him went men of valor whose hearts God had touched.'

Everybody goes home, including the king, who goes back to his father's house in Gibeah and, as the next chapter shows, back to his ploughing.

But some men go with him, and the phrase used of them is lovely: men of valor whose hearts God had touched.

They are not conscripts and there is no army yet. God moved on some men and they attached themselves to the new king voluntarily. It is the first thing that has happened in this whole business that nobody organised.

'But some worthless fellows said, "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no present. But he held his peace.'

Some do not go.

Worthless fellows is, once again, sons of Belial — the phrase Hannah begged Eli not to apply to her, and the narrator's verdict on Eli's sons. It is the standing term in this book for men with nothing in them.

Their question is a fair one on the face of it: how can this man save us? They have just watched him pulled out of a pile of luggage. And they show their contempt in the standard way, by withholding the gift that acknowledged a new ruler.

'But he held his peace.'

Four words, and they are entirely to his credit.

He was publicly insulted on the day of his coronation by men who refused to recognise him, and he let it go. He does not have them seized, or answer them, or remember it out loud. The Hebrew is literally that he was like one deaf.

Nor is this a one-off. When his first victory has been won and the people come demanding that those very men be executed, he refuses: not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel (11:13).

Keep both of those, because they are the high-water mark of the man. Saul begins genuinely humble, genuinely restrained, and genuinely willing to give God the credit. The tragedy of the chapters ahead is not that he was always what he became.

10.theology:
Seven days you shall wait (v. 8). The first specific order Saul is given as prince, with a number attached and a person named. Set beside do what your hand finds to do in the previous verse, a king is being taught the shape of obedience: use your judgment in most things, and in this one thing do nothing until I arrive. Chapter 13 is where he waits almost the whole seven days and then does it himself.

God gave him another heart (v. 9). Among the greatest sentences in the Old Testament, and it is said of Saul — before the signs, at the moment he turned to go, in response to nothing he had done. The end of his story makes it tempting to discount, and it should not be discounted; the language is the language of Ezekiel's greatest promise (Ezek. 36:26).

Crowned and indicted in one speech (vv. 18-19). Samuel calls the request a rejection of God on the day of the coronation, with the king standing in the crowd. He does not soften it for the occasion and does not decide that the mood should be positive. God has granted it, and it was a rejection; obeying the first does not require withdrawing the second.

Hidden among the baggage (v. 22). Humility or fear, and the text will not settle it. Both fit: he had told Samuel he was from the least clan of the smallest tribe and meant it, and he had told his own uncle nothing — and he is also the man who will sit in a tent for forty days while a Philistine shouts at his army (17:11). The same behaviour reads as modesty at a coronation and paralysis at a battlefield, and he never entirely stops doing it.

What Israel could see (vv. 23-24). The narrator repeats 9:2 word for word at the moment of presentation, immediately after the man has been found hiding, and Samuel's commendation is do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? Everything on display is exactly what chapter 8 ordered — and 16:7 is coming.

A king under a text (v. 25). The rights and duties are written in a book and laid up before the LORD, as Deuteronomy 17:18-20 required. The kings of the nations were the source of law; this one is subject to a document deposited where he cannot amend it.

He held his peace (v. 27). Publicly insulted on his coronation day by sons of Belial who withheld the customary gift, and he was like one deaf. It is not a one-off — after his first victory he refuses to let those same men be executed (11:13). Saul begins genuinely humble, genuinely restrained, and genuinely willing to give God the credit. The tragedy ahead is not that he was always what he became.
10.examples:
Then: A man was anointed king of Israel on an empty road at first light, given three signs including one that repeated his own private worry back to him, changed on the spot by God as he turned to walk away — and was then found, on the day of his public coronation, hiding among the luggage.

Now: Two things. Verse 7 and verse 8 belong together and most of Christian obedience lives between them: in the great majority of decisions, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you, and in a few specific ones, wait, because you were told to. Knowing which is which is the whole skill, and Saul got it wrong on the one that had a number attached. And hold verse 9 against the instinct to read a person's end back into their beginning. God gave Saul another heart. Whatever happened afterwards, that sentence was true when it was written.

11.title: Saul's First Victory
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."<sup>2</sup>But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel."<sup>3</sup>The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days' respite that we may send messengers through all the territory of Israel. Then, if there is no one to save us, we will give ourselves up to you."<sup>4</sup>When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, they reported the matter in the ears of the people, and all the people wept aloud.<sup>5</sup>Now, behold, Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. And Saul said, "What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?" So they told him the news of the men of Jabesh.<sup>6</sup>And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled.<sup>7</sup>He took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of the messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!" Then the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.<sup>8</sup>When he mustered them at Bezek, the people of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.<sup>9</sup>And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus shall you say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have salvation.'" When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad.<sup>10</sup>Therefore the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will give ourselves up to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you."<sup>11</sup>And the next day Saul put the people in three companies. And they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. And those who survived were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.<sup>12</sup>Then the people said to Samuel, "Who is it that said, 'Shall Saul reign over us?' Bring the men, that we may put them to death."<sup>13</sup>But Saul said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel."<sup>14</sup>Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom."<sup>15</sup>So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
11.overview:
Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead, and the town offers to surrender. His terms are that he will gouge out every right eye and thus bring disgrace on all Israel — which is a military calculation as much as a cruelty, since the left eye was behind the shield and the right is the one a man fought with. He gives them seven days to look for help, because he does not believe anyone in Israel will come. Given the last three hundred years, that is a reasonable assessment.

And the reader has met this town before. Jabesh-gilead is the place Israel destroyed in the last chapter of Judges to supply wives for the six hundred surviving Benjaminites (Judg. 21:8-12) — and Saul is a Benjaminite. The bond that begins in that blood will close at the end of this book, when the men of Jabesh march all night to take Saul's body off a Philistine wall.

The messengers reach Gibeah and the whole town weeps and does nothing. The king of Israel is coming in from the field behind his oxen and has to ask what the crying is about. And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul... and his anger was greatly kindled. He butchers his own plough team and sends the pieces through the country — the exact summons the Levite used at the end of Judges to raise a civil war, now used to raise a rescue — and the nation comes out as one man.

Three hundred and thirty thousand muster. The promise is kept to the hour. And when the people demand the execution of the men who had despised him, Saul refuses: not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Gouge Out Every Right Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead, and the town offers to submit: make a treaty with us, and we will serve you (v. 1). His terms are that he will gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel (v. 2). The elders ask for seven days to send through Israel for help, and if nobody comes they will surrender (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The right eye is a calculation, not merely cruelty. A man in a battle line held his shield on the left, covering that eye; take the right one and he can never fight again. Nahash is proposing to disarm a town permanently and leave it visible.
verseByVerse.examples: And the reader has met Jabesh-gilead before. It is the town Israel destroyed in the last chapter of Judges — every man and every married woman put to the sword — to supply four hundred wives for the six hundred surviving Benjaminites (Judg. 21:8-12). Saul is a Benjaminite.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you." But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel." The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days' respite that we may send messengers through all the territory of Israel. Then, if there is no one to save us, we will give ourselves up to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."'

The town does not fight. It sues for terms in the first verse.

Jabesh-gilead is east of the Jordan, exposed, a long way from the hill country, and Ammon has arrived in force. The offer is the ordinary one of the ancient world: we will be your vassals, and you will not destroy us.

A reader who has come from Judges has met this town before.

Jabesh-gilead is the place Israel destroyed in the last chapter of that book. When the tribes had almost wiped out Benjamin and then sworn not to give it wives, they found a town that had missed the muster, sent twelve thousand men, and put every male and every married woman to the sword, keeping four hundred girls for the survivors of Benjamin (Judg. 21:8-12).

Saul is a Benjaminite. There are men in that besieged town descended from women taken there in that raid, and there are Benjaminites in Gibeah descended from the same women.

Hold on to the connection, because this book will close with it. Twenty chapters from now, when Saul's headless body is fastened to the wall of Beth-shan, it is the men of Jabesh-gilead who march all night, take it down, and bury it (31:11-13).

'But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel."'

He accepts the surrender and names a price.

The right eye is not chosen for cruelty alone; it is a military calculation. A man standing in a battle line held his shield on his left arm, and it covered the left side of his face. The right eye is the one he fought with. Take it from every man in the town and you have not only humiliated them, you have permanently ended their usefulness as soldiers.

Nahash says exactly what he is doing it for: and thus bring disgrace on all Israel. This is not about Jabesh. It is a message to a nation, written on the faces of one town, and every Israelite who ever passed through would read it.

'The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days' respite that we may send messengers through all the territory of Israel. Then, if there is no one to save us, we will give ourselves up to you."'

They ask for a week, and Nahash gives it to them, which tells you exactly how much he expects from Israel.

He is not worried. He has just been told that runners will go through every territory in the country appealing for help, and he agrees to wait. In his assessment there is nobody in Israel who will come.

Given the last three hundred years, it is a reasonable assessment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — The Spirit Rushed Upon Saul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messengers reach Gibeah and the people weep aloud — and do nothing (v. 4). Saul is coming in from the field behind the oxen and asks what the crying is about (v. 5). And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled (v. 6). He cuts a yoke of oxen in pieces and sends them through Israel with a summons, and the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man (v. 7). Three hundred and thirty thousand muster at Bezek (v. 8). Word goes to Jabesh: by the time the sun is hot tomorrow, you will be delivered (v. 9). And in the morning watch, in three companies, Saul destroys the Ammonites (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The king of Israel is behind a plough. He has been anointed privately and crowned publicly, and he is still working his father's land, and the news has to be explained to him by somebody at the gate.
verseByVerse.examples: The gesture in v. 7 is quoted from the worst page of Judges. A Levite cut up a woman's body and sent the pieces through Israel to summon a war against a brother tribe (Judg. 19:29), and the nation came out as one man (Judg. 20:1). Saul uses the same summons and the same phrase to raise an army that will save a town instead.

verseByVerse.quote: When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, they reported the matter in the ears of the people, and all the people wept aloud. Now, behold, Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. And Saul said, "What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?" So they told him the news of the men of Jabesh. And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled. He took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of the messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!" Then the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, they reported the matter in the ears of the people, and all the people wept aloud.'

The town hears the news and cries, and that is all.

Note what does not happen. Nobody musters. Nobody sends to the king — who lives here, and whose home town this is. There is no meeting of elders and no decision. A whole community weeps about an atrocity two days' march away and goes on standing in the street.

'Now, behold, Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. And Saul said, "What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?" So they told him the news of the men of Jabesh.'

The king of Israel is behind a plough.

He has been anointed privately with oil on a road at dawn. He has been taken by lot in front of the assembled nation at Mizpah and proclaimed with a shout. And he is coming in from a day's work on his father's land, and has to ask why everybody is crying.

He has no court, no palace, no standing army and apparently no intelligence service. Whatever Israel thought it was getting in chapter 8, what it has at this moment is a very tall farmer walking home behind his oxen.

'And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled.'

Then the sentence that changes the afternoon, and both halves of it belong together.

The Spirit of God rushed upon Saul. The same verb as Samson and as chapter 10 — a sudden seizing. And immediately: his anger was greatly kindled.

The anger is not the opposite of the Spirit here; it is what the Spirit produced. A man heard that a town of his countrymen was about to have its eyes cut out to shame the nation, and something took hold of him and he was furious.

Say that plainly, because anger has a poor reputation and this instance is entirely good. There is a way of being calm about atrocity that is not godliness but distance. The whole of Gibeah was weeping and none of them was angry; one man was angry and the town was saved.

'He took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of the messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!"'

He butchers his own plough team and sends the pieces around the country.

The first thing to see is the cost. Those are the oxen he was walking behind ten minutes ago, and they are a farmer's most valuable possession — next year's ploughing, and the year after. He destroys his own livelihood before asking anybody else for anything.

The second thing is where the gesture comes from, and any Israelite would have known.

At the end of the book of Judges a Levite took the body of the woman he had pushed out of a door, cut her limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel (Judg. 19:29). It was the recognised summons to national action, and it worked: the tribes assembled and the result was a civil war that nearly destroyed Benjamin.

Saul uses the identical summons. Same act, same twelve pieces, same distribution — and oxen instead of a woman, and to save a town instead of to destroy a tribe.

A Benjaminite is redeeming the gesture that once destroyed Benjamin.

'Then the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.'

The phrase at the end is from the same passage. When the tribes assembled after the Levite's summons, the congregation assembled as one man (Judg. 20:1) — the only time in that whole book Israel was united, and it was to make war on its own.

Here they come out as one man to rescue.

Note also who gets the credit for the muster: the dread of the LORD fell upon the people. Not Saul's authority and not the horror of the parcels. God moved on the country.

verseByVerse.quote: When he mustered them at Bezek, the people of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand. And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus shall you say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have salvation.'" When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad. Therefore the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will give ourselves up to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you." And the next day Saul put the people in three companies. And they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. And those who survived were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When he mustered them at Bezek, the people of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.'

That is three hundred and thirty thousand men, from a nation that could not raise a company a fortnight ago.

Bezek is the mustering ground, and the numbers are counted in two columns — Israel and Judah separately, which is how they will still be counted in the books of Kings, and which is a crack that will one day become a border.

'And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus shall you say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have salvation.'"'

The message is short and it has a deadline in it.

Not help is coming, which is what frightened people are usually told. By the time the sun is hot tomorrow, it will be over. He names the hour.

'When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad. Therefore the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will give ourselves up to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you."'

The men of Jabesh play their part with some nerve.

They know the relief column is coming at dawn, and they send word to Nahash that they will surrender tomorrow and he may do to them whatever seems good to him. It is entirely true and completely misleading, and it keeps the Ammonites in camp and off their guard on the last night they have.

'And the next day Saul put the people in three companies. And they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. And those who survived were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.'

Three companies, the morning watch, and the enemy camp entered from three sides at once.

It is Gideon's plan — he divided the 300 men into three companies and came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch (Judg. 7:16, 19). Saul is fighting his first battle out of the same book the reader has just finished.

The promise is kept to the hour: they fight until the heat of the day, which is exactly when the messengers said it would be finished.

The last clause is a small masterpiece of reporting. The survivors were scattered so that no two of them were left together. Not a retreat and not a rout — an army that has ceased to exist as an army, its men running singly across country with nobody beside them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–15 — Not a Man Shall Be Put to Death This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people turn on the men who had despised him: who is it that said, shall Saul reign over us? Bring the men, that we may put them to death (v. 12). And Saul refuses: not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel (v. 13). Samuel takes the nation to Gilgal to renew the kingdom, they make Saul king before the LORD, they sacrifice peace offerings, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the high point of Saul's life and the chapter should be allowed to say so. He is magnanimous on the day he could most easily have settled scores, and he gives God the credit in the same breath — the LORD has worked salvation, not Saul.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything from here is decline, and the decline begins two chapters later at this same Gilgal, where he will not wait seven days. The tragedy of Saul is not that he was always what he became. It is that he was once this.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people said to Samuel, "Who is it that said, 'Shall Saul reign over us?' Bring the men, that we may put them to death." But Saul said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel." Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom." So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the people said to Samuel, "Who is it that said, 'Shall Saul reign over us?' Bring the men, that we may put them to death."'

The victory is barely over and the people want a purge.

They are talking about the worthless fellows of 10:27, who asked how can this man save us? and brought no gift. The question has now been answered in front of the whole country, and the crowd wants the men who asked it brought out and killed.

Note that it is the people who demand this, not Saul. The mob is ahead of the king.

'But Saul said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel."'

Here is the best moment of Saul's life.

Take the two halves separately, because each is remarkable.

Not a man shall be put to death this day. He is at the height of his power, on the day of his first victory, with the nation assembled and demanding blood, and the men in question had publicly humiliated him. Every incentive runs one way. He refuses, and he refuses immediately.

Then the reason, and it is the reason that makes the mercy possible: for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.

He does not say I have won a victory and can afford to be generous. He says God did this. And a man who genuinely believes the day was God's work does not treat it as capital to spend on his own grievances.

That is how the two halves of the verse connect, and it holds generally. People who take credit for what God has done are usually the same people who cannot let an insult go, because if the victory is yours then so is the honour, and the honour has been damaged.

'Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom." So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal.'

Gilgal, where the twelve stones came out of the Jordan and the reproach of Egypt was rolled away. They go there to renew the kingdom — not to start it again but to confirm what Mizpah began, now that the doubters have their answer.

'There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.'

Peace offerings, which are the ones eaten in company, and the whole nation rejoicing with its king.

That is the last sentence of Saul's good days, and it deserves a stop.

Look at what this chapter has shown. The Spirit of God rushed on him. He was angry at exactly the right thing when a whole town was weeping and doing nothing. He destroyed his own livelihood to raise an army. He kept his word to the hour. He gave God the credit for the victory in public. And he refused to execute the men who had insulted him, on the day he could have done it with the crowd's blessing.

There is no reading of this chapter in which Saul is not admirable.

Hold that, because it makes the rest of the book harder rather than easier. It would be simpler if he had always been a poor king who was found out. He was not. He began humble, hid from his own coronation, held his peace when insulted, and then rose to this.

Two chapters from now he will be standing at this same Gilgal, watching his army drain away while he waits for Samuel, and on the seventh day he will offer the burnt offering himself. And the prophet will arrive as he finishes and tell him his kingdom will not continue.

Everything after this chapter is decline. Nobody at the peace offerings could have known it.

11.theology:
Anger produced by the Spirit (v. 6). The two halves of the verse belong together: the Spirit rushed on him and his anger was greatly kindled. The anger is not the opposite of the Spirit here; it is what the Spirit produced. There is a way of being calm about atrocity that is not godliness but distance. All Gibeah was weeping and none of them was angry; one man was angry and the town was saved.

The gesture redeemed (v. 7). A Levite once cut a woman into twelve pieces and sent them through Israel, and the tribes assembled as one man to make war on Benjamin (Judg. 19:29; 20:1) — the only time that whole book records Israel united. Saul uses the identical summons and the identical phrase, with oxen instead of a body, to save a town instead of destroy a tribe. A Benjaminite redeems the gesture that once destroyed Benjamin. And the muster is credited to God: the dread of the LORD fell upon the people.

He destroyed his own livelihood first (v. 7). Those were the oxen he had been walking behind ten minutes earlier — a farmer's most valuable possession and next year's ploughing. He wrecks his own before asking anything of anybody.

Mercy and credit come together (v. 13). Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. He is at the height of his power, the crowd is demanding blood, and the men had humiliated him publicly — and he refuses at once. The reason is the mechanism: a man who genuinely believes the day was God's work does not treat it as capital to spend on his own grievances. People who take credit for what God has done are usually the same people who cannot let an insult go, because if the victory is yours then so is the honour, and the honour has been damaged.

Saul was once this. The Spirit rushed on him; he was angry at the right thing when everyone else only wept; he destroyed his own property to raise an army; he kept his word to the hour; he gave God the public credit; and he spared the men who insulted him. There is no reading of this chapter in which he is not admirable, and that makes the rest of the book harder rather than easier. It would be simpler if he had always been a poor king who was found out. Two chapters on he is standing at this same Gilgal, refusing to wait seven days.
11.examples:
Then: An entire town stood in the street weeping about an atrocity two days' march away, and the man who did something about it was the one who came in late from ploughing and had to ask what the noise was. He cut up his own oxen, raised three hundred thousand men, kept his promise to the hour, and then refused to let anybody settle scores on the strength of it.

Now: Two things. Sit with verse 6 in a culture that treats composure as maturity: the Spirit's arrival in this chapter produced fury, and it was the right response, and the weeping crowd was not more spiritual than the angry farmer. Ask what you have grown calm about that ought still to make you angry. And verse 13 gives the test for whether you actually believe a success was God's: not what you say in the thanksgiving, but whether you then spend it on your own grievances.

12.title: Samuel's Farewell Charge
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And Samuel said to all Israel, "Behold, I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you.<sup>2</sup>And now, behold, the king walks before you, and I am old and gray; and behold, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.<sup>3</sup>Here I am; testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it? Testify against me and I will restore it to you."<sup>4</sup>They said, "You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand."<sup>5</sup>And he said to them, "The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand." And they said, "He is witness."<sup>6</sup>And Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore stand still that I may plead with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds of the LORD that he performed for you and for your fathers.<sup>8</sup>When Jacob went into Egypt, and the Egyptians oppressed them, then your fathers cried out to the LORD and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and made them dwell in this place.<sup>9</sup>But they forgot the LORD their God. And he sold them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab. And they fought against them.<sup>10</sup>And they cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, that we may serve you.'<sup>11</sup>And the LORD sent Jerubbaal and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.<sup>12</sup>And when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' when the LORD your God was your king.<sup>13</sup>And now behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the LORD has set a king over you.<sup>14</sup>If you will fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God, it will be well.<sup>15</sup>But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king.<sup>16</sup>Now therefore stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes.<sup>17</sup>Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain. And you shall know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king."<sup>18</sup>So Samuel called upon the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.<sup>19</sup>And all the people said to Samuel, "Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king."<sup>20</sup>And Samuel said to the people, "Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.<sup>21</sup>And do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver, for they are empty.<sup>22</sup>For the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.<sup>23</sup>Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, and I will instruct you in the good and the right way.<sup>24</sup>Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. For consider what great things he has done for you.<sup>25</sup>But if you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king."
12.overview:
Samuel steps back, and he does it by submitting to an audit. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken?... from whose hand have I taken a bribe? The verb is chapter 8's — the word used six times over about the king who was coming — and he applies it to his own forty years and invites the nation to produce one instance. They cannot. And he has already pointed at his own sons standing in the assembly, the men who took bribes and perverted justice. He is clean; his house is not; he does not pretend otherwise.

Then the case, and it is a history: cried out, delivered, forgot, sold, cried out, delivered. Four deliverers named, the fourth being himself. And the charge, with a date on it — when you saw that Nahash... came against you, you said, no, but a king shall reign over us, when the LORD your God was your king. The office was not vacant.

The terms he then sets out are the theological heart of the chapter, and what has changed in them is nothing. Fear the LORD, serve him, obey his voice — the conditions of Sinai, unaltered, with one addition: both you and the king who reigns over you. The king stands inside the covenant, not above it, and is named in both the promise and the threat. There was never a mechanism to be had.

Then thunder and rain on the wheat harvest — a sign that costs the nation part of its year's food, because a sign that costs nothing proves nothing. And when they beg him to pray, Samuel answers with two things that most people cannot hold together: do not be afraid; you have done all this evil.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Whose Ox Have I Taken?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel opens by acknowledging that he has done exactly what they asked: I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you (v. 1). He is old and grey, his sons are among them, and he has walked before them since his youth (v. 2). Then he submits to an audit: whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I taken a bribe? — and offers restitution for anything they can name (v. 3). They acquit him, and he calls the LORD and his anointed as witnesses (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb is chapter 8's. Samuel takes the word God used six times over about the coming king — he will take — and applies it to his own forty years, in question form, in public, with an offer to repay.
verseByVerse.examples: And the audit has a shadow over it. His sons turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice (8:3), and he says in v. 2 that they are standing there. He is clean; his house is not; and he does not pretend otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to all Israel, "Behold, I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you. And now, behold, the king walks before you, and I am old and gray; and behold, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day. Here I am; testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it? Testify against me and I will restore it to you." They said, "You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand." And he said to them, "The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand." And they said, "He is witness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel said to all Israel, "Behold, I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you."'

He begins by stating that he did what he was asked, and the phrase he chooses is God's.

I have obeyed your voice. Three times in chapter 8 God told him obey their voice (8:7, 9, 22), and Samuel now reports back to the assembly in exactly those words. He is not claiming to have approved; he is stating that the instruction was carried out.

'"And now, behold, the king walks before you, and I am old and gray; and behold, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day."'

Three beholds, and the middle one is painful.

The king walks before you — the office is filled, the transition is done. I am old and grey. And behold, my sons are with you.

He puts them in front of the assembly. These are the men whose corruption gave the elders their occasion in chapter 8: they turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice (8:3). Samuel does not defend them, explain them or leave them out. He says they are here.

'"Here I am; testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it? Testify against me and I will restore it to you."'

Now listen to the verb, because it is the verb of chapter 8.

When Samuel warned them what a king would do, the speech was built on one word used six times in seven verses: he will take your sons, your daughters, your fields, your grain, your servants, your flocks (8:11-17).

Here he applies it to himself, and puts it as a question. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? From whose hand have I taken a bribe?

The contrast is the whole point of the paragraph. The man who has led Israel for a lifetime is inviting the nation to name one thing he ever took from them — and the king they have just been given will take, as a matter of policy, from everybody.

Note also the two animals he names. An ox and a donkey are the working stock of a small farm: the plough team and the transport, the two things a poor family cannot manage without. He does not ask whether he has taken anybody's silver. He asks about the things whose loss would actually ruin somebody.

He does not merely deny it. He submits to a public audit before two named witnesses, God and the king, and offers restitution for anything they can produce. That is not a defence; it is an invitation to prosecute.

'They said, "You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand."'

They acquit him, and the acquittal is unanimous and complete.

Take the measure of that. He has judged this nation on circuit for a working lifetime — every dispute, every verdict, every property claim, at Bethel and Gilgal and Mizpah and Ramah — and standing in front of everyone he ever ruled against, he asks for a single complaint, and there is not one.

'And he said to them, "The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand." And they said, "He is witness."'

He has it formally attested, which is a lawyer's instinct and a wise one.

You have not found anything in my hand. That is the record, sworn to, on the day he steps back — and a life that can end like this is a considerable achievement, and that Samuel plainly wanted it on the record precisely because his sons had made the family name a byword.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — The LORD Your God Was Your King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel pleads the case, and the case is a history: your fathers cried out in Egypt and God sent Moses and Aaron; they forgot him and were sold into hands; they cried out and confessed and he sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah and Samuel, and they lived in safety (vv. 6-11). Then the charge, with a date on it: when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, no, but a king shall reign over us — when the LORD your God was your king (v. 12). And then the terms: if you and the king fear the LORD, it will be well; if you rebel, the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The cycle he recites is the book of Judges in six verses, and its engine is a cry that was always answered. Verse 12 says what broke it: this time they did not cry, they asked for somebody else.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 14-15 are the theological heart of the chapter. The king changes nothing. The same covenant, the same conditions, the same consequences — only now the king stands inside them with everybody else, and is named in both halves.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. Now therefore stand still that I may plead with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds of the LORD that he performed for you and for your fathers. When Jacob went into Egypt, and the Egyptians oppressed them, then your fathers cried out to the LORD and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and made them dwell in this place. But they forgot the LORD their God. And he sold them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab. And they fought against them. And they cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, that we may serve you.' And the LORD sent Jerubbaal and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. Now therefore stand still that I may plead with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds of the LORD that he performed for you and for your fathers."'

The word is a legal one. He is going to plead with them, and the case he will argue is not their record but God's.

All the righteous deeds of the LORD — the evidence in this trial is what God has done, and Israel is in the dock.

'"When Jacob went into Egypt, and the Egyptians oppressed them, then your fathers cried out to the LORD and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and made them dwell in this place."'

The pattern is stated once, cleanly: oppression, a cry, a man sent, deliverance.

'"But they forgot the LORD their God. And he sold them into the hand of Sisera... and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab. And they fought against them."'

Then the same pattern in reverse, and the verb is the one the book of Judges used constantly. They forgot. Not rejected, not renounced — mislaid.

The three hands he names are three of that book's oppressors: Sisera at the Kishon, the Philistines, Eglon of Moab. And he sold them is the exact word Judges used, twice (Judg. 2:14; 4:2).

'"And they cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, that we may serve you.'"'

The cry, and this time with the confession in it — which is what chapter 10 of Judges finally produced after five cycles of wordless groaning.

'"And the LORD sent Jerubbaal and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety."'

Four names, and the fourth is his own.

Jerubbaal is Gideon — called by the nickname his father gave him, let Baal contend (Judg. 6:32). Barak, from the Kishon. Jephthah, from Gilead. And Samuel, who is standing in front of them saying it.

He includes himself without embarrassment, and he is entitled to: the last time this nation was delivered, it was at Mizpah under his prayers and God's thunder, and the men listening were there.

The point of the whole recital is in the last clause. You lived in safety. The system they have just replaced worked. Every time they cried, somebody came.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' when the LORD your God was your king. And now behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the LORD has set a king over you. If you will fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God, it will be well. But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"And when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' when the LORD your God was your king."'

Here is the charge, and it comes with a date attached.

Samuel says the demand was made when you saw that Nahash... came against you. It was not a considered constitutional reform; it was a reaction to a threat on the border. They looked east, saw an Ammonite army, and asked for a man.

The closing clause is the whole indictment in six words: when the LORD your God was your king.

That office was not vacant, and it is what makes the request what God called it in 8:7. They did not choose a king instead of anarchy; they chose one instead of him.

There is a bitter irony in the timing too, and Samuel does not spell it out. They asked because they were frightened of Nahash. And when Nahash actually came, in chapter 11, what saved Jabesh-gilead was not the institution of monarchy but the Spirit of God rushing on a farmer who was still behind his oxen.

'"And now behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the LORD has set a king over you."'

Both halves of that sentence are true and they are held together without any attempt to resolve them.

The king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked — this was your doing. And the LORD has set a king over you — and it was his.

'"If you will fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God, it will be well."'

Now the terms, which are the theological centre of the chapter.

Read what has changed in the covenant: nothing. Fear the LORD, serve him, obey his voice, do not rebel. Those are the conditions of Sinai and of Deuteronomy, unaltered.

The only new element is the phrase both you and the king who reigns over you. The king does not stand outside the arrangement administering it. He stands inside it, subject to the same terms as the farmers, and he is named in the sentence.

'"But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king."'

The same in the negative, with the king named again.

This is the answer to everything chapter 8 was about. Israel wanted a king so that things would be different — somebody to go out before them and fight their battles, an arrangement like the nations had. Samuel tells them, on the day of the inauguration, that the arrangement changes nothing whatever.

Obedience will still be the condition of blessing. Rebellion will still bring the hand of the LORD. The king is one more Israelite standing under the same covenant, and if the nation rebels he goes down with them.

There was never a mechanism to be had. That is what Israel had actually been shopping for since chapter 4, when they sent for the ark; and it is what Micah wanted when he hired a Levite; and it is what the elders wanted when they asked for a crown. Something in place of a relationship. And every time, God gives them the thing and tells them plainly that it will not do what they want it to do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Thunder in the Wheat Harvest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now therefore stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes (v. 16). Samuel asks a question with an edge in it: is it not wheat harvest today? He will call on the LORD for thunder and rain, so that they will know their wickedness in asking for a king (v. 17). It comes, and the people greatly fear the LORD and Samuel (v. 18). And they beg him: pray for your servants... that we may not die, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Wheat harvest is May or June, the dry months. Rain then is not merely unusual; it flattens the standing crop and ruins what has been cut. Samuel asks for a sign that will cost the nation part of its year's food.
verseByVerse.examples: It is the third thunder in the book. Hannah sang that God would thunder against his adversaries when there was no war and nobody listening (2:10); he did it at Mizpah while Samuel was still at the altar (7:10); and here Samuel asks for it against Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain. And you shall know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king." So Samuel called upon the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel. And all the people said to Samuel, "Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Now therefore stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today?"'

The question is not conversational. It is the sign.

Wheat harvest in that country is May or June, and it falls in the dry season. Rain does not come then. It is not that rain is unlikely at wheat harvest; it is that everybody plans the year around its not happening, because rain on cut grain spoils it and rain on standing grain flattens it.

'"I will call upon the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain. And you shall know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king."'

He asks for a storm on the harvest, so that the nation will understand what it has done.

The sign is not free. It will damage the year's food, and it is chosen for exactly that reason: a sign that costs nothing proves nothing. Israel is going to be told that its request was wicked, and the telling will be written across the crop.

'So Samuel called upon the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.'

It is the third thunder in this book, and the three belong together.

Hannah sang it first, in a corrupt sanctuary, with no war on and nobody listening: the adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven (2:10). Then it happened at Mizpah, against the Philistines, while Samuel was still at the altar and Israel had nothing but a lamb and a confession (7:10).

Now it is called down on Israel, on their own harvest, at their own coronation, to tell them their king was a sin.

'And all the people said to Samuel, "Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king."'

It works. They ask for prayer and they name the offence.

Weigh how they put it: we have added to all our sins this evil. They are not pretending it was their only fault, or that they were misled. They place it on top of a pile they acknowledge is already there.

Mark what they ask for: pray for your servants to the LORD your God. Not for the storm to stop and not for the king to be taken away. They ask the man they have just replaced to intercede for them, and they call the LORD your God while doing it — which is frightened, and honest, and exactly wrong, and Samuel is about to correct it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Far Be It From Me That I Should Cease to Pray
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel's answer to a terrified nation holds two things together: do not be afraid; you have done all this evil (v. 20). Do not turn aside from the LORD, and do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver (vv. 20-21). The ground is God himself: the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself (v. 22). Then his own commitment: far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you (v. 23). And the last word is both halves again — fear him and serve him and consider what great things he has done (v. 24); and if you still do wickedly you will be swept away, you and your king (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not deny the sin in order to calm them, and he does not let the sin drive them away. Do not be afraid and you have done all this evil are in the same sentence, and neither is softened to make room for the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 is the sentence to take out of the chapter. He has just been publicly replaced by these people, and he calls not praying for them a sin against God. Not a failure of kindness or of duty — a sin.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to the people, "Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart. And do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver, for they are empty. For the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself. Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, and I will instruct you in the good and the right way. Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. For consider what great things he has done for you. But if you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel said to the people, "Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil."'

Hold the two halves of that sentence together, because everything pastoral in this chapter is in them.

Do not be afraid. And, in the same breath, you have done all this evil.

The sin is not denied in order to comfort them. That is the cheap way, and it is the common one: tell frightened people that it was not as bad as they think, that they were only doing their best, that anybody would have done the same. Samuel says none of it. The thing they did was evil and he says so while they are still shaking.

Nor will he let the evil drive them away. He does not use their terror to extract anything, or leave them in it a while for their own good.

Both at once. You did it, and do not be afraid.

'"Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart."'

The instruction that follows is the one nobody expects: keep going.

The danger for a person who has just discovered the size of his sin is not usually that he will take it lightly. It is that he will conclude he has forfeited the right to serve, and quietly withdraw. Samuel heads it off in one clause. Do not turn aside. Serve the LORD with all your heart, starting now, as the people who did this.

'"And do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver, for they are empty."'

Their name is tohu — formlessness, waste, nothing. It is the word for the state of the earth before God spoke in Genesis 1:2.

The sentence is almost a joke at the expense of idols. Do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver — for they are empty. There is no argument offered. The reason not to follow them is simply what they are.

'"For the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself."'

Now the ground of the whole thing, and look carefully at where it is placed.

The LORD will not forsake his people. Why? Two reasons are given, and neither of them is Israel.

For his great name's sake — because his own reputation is bound up with them, and he will not have it said among the nations that he brought a people out and abandoned them. And because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself — because he wanted to.

That is the entire security of Israel, stated on the day they have just been told their most recent decision was wicked. Not their record, which is a disgrace. Not their promises, which they have broken continuously since Sinai. His name, and his pleasure.

Paul reaches for the same ground when he wants to say why God's choice of a people cannot fail: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Rom. 11:29). And it is the answer to every anxious believer who has worked out that God has every reason to be finished with him. He does have every reason. He has also given two of his own, and they are not about you.

'"Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, and I will instruct you in the good and the right way."'

Now the sentence to carry out of this chapter.

Take in who is speaking and to whom. This is the man they told to his face he was too old and his sons were no good. He has been publicly superseded; the king walks before them and Samuel has just said so himself. Every human reason to withdraw is available to him, and several of them are respectable.

He says that not praying for them would be a sin against the LORD.

Not a failure of duty. Not unkindness, or a shame, or a thing beneath him. A sin, and against God rather than against them.

That is a category most of us have never put prayerlessness in. We think of intercession as something offered when we have the energy and the affection for it, and its absence as a shortfall. Samuel treats the people who have hurt him as a charge laid on him by God, so that to stop praying would be to disobey.

Then, in the same breath, the second half of his job: I will instruct you in the good and the right way. He will go on teaching them as well. Prayer and instruction, both continued, for the people who replaced him.

'"Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. For consider what great things he has done for you."'

The motive he leaves them with is not fear of the storm. It is memory.

Consider what great things he has done for you. That is the same argument he made with the stone at Ebenezer — till now the LORD has helped us — and the same one he has made in this chapter with the recital of the judges. Look at the record and serve accordingly.

'"But if you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king."'

The last words of his farewell are a warning with the king in them again.

He has said it three times now: you and your king (vv. 14, 15, 25). The new arrangement will not save them, will not exempt them, and will not survive them if they go on. Israel asked for something that would change the terms, and Samuel ends his public ministry by telling them for the third time that nothing has changed at all.

12.theology:
The verb turned on himself (v. 3). He will take six times over in 8:11-17; whose ox have I taken? here. And the two animals are chosen with care: an ox and a donkey are a small farm's plough team and transport, the things whose loss actually ruins a family. He does not merely deny it — he submits to a public audit before two named witnesses and offers restitution, which is not a defence but an invitation to prosecute.
