The office was not vacant (v. 12). They did not choose a king instead of anarchy; they chose one when the LORD your God was your king. And the timing is bitter: they asked because they feared Nahash, and when Nahash actually came what saved Jabesh-gilead was not the monarchy but the Spirit of God rushing on a farmer who was still behind his oxen.

Nothing has changed (vv. 14-15, 25). The covenant terms are Sinai's, unaltered, with the king inserted inside them — named in the promise and named in the threat, three times over. Israel had been shopping for a mechanism since chapter 4, when they sent for the ark; Micah wanted one when he hired a Levite; the elders wanted one when they asked for a crown. Something in place of a relationship. Every time God grants the thing and says plainly that it will not do what they want it to do.

The costly sign (vv. 17-18). Rain at wheat harvest flattens standing grain and spoils what is cut. Samuel asks for a sign that will damage the year's food, because a sign that costs nothing proves nothing. It is the third thunder in the book — sung by Hannah when there was no war and nobody listening (2:10), given at Mizpah against the Philistines (7:10), and now called down on Israel's own harvest.

Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil (v. 20). He refuses the cheap comfort of denying the sin, and refuses to let the sin drive them off, and does both in one sentence. Then the instruction nobody expects: keep going. The danger for someone who has just seen the size of his sin is rarely that he will take it lightly; it is that he will conclude he has forfeited the right to serve and quietly withdraw.

His name and his pleasure (v. 22). The security of Israel is stated on the day they are told their latest decision was wicked, and neither reason is Israel. For his great name's sake, and because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself. Paul reaches for the same ground: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Rom. 11:29). To the anxious believer who has worked out that God has every reason to be finished with him: he does have every reason, and he has given two of his own, and they are not about you.

Prayerlessness as sin (v. 23). Said by a man they had just told to his face that he was old and his sons were no good, about the people who replaced him. Not a failure of duty, not unkindness — a sin against the LORD. Most of us have never put it in that category; we treat intercession as something offered when we have the energy for it. Samuel treats these people as a charge laid on him by God.
12.examples:
Then: An old man who had judged a nation for a working lifetime stood in front of everyone he had ever ruled against, asked whether he had taken so much as one donkey, offered to repay anything they could name — and was acquitted unanimously. Then he called down a storm on their harvest to tell them their new king was a sin, and promised to go on praying for them.

Now: Three things. Verse 3 is a standard for anyone in any kind of trust: could you invite the people you have led to name one thing you took? Verse 20 is the model for how to speak to somebody who has just realised what they have done — both halves, neither softened, and then keep serving. And verse 23 is the sharpest. Think of the person who has most recently passed you over, replaced you, or made it clear they would rather have somebody else. Samuel calls ceasing to pray for such people a sin against God, and he is not exaggerating for effect.

13.title: Saul's Presumptuous Sacrifice
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Saul lived for one year and then became king, and when he had reigned for two years over Israel,<sup>2</sup>Saul chose three thousand men of Israel. Two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, every man to his tent.<sup>3</sup>Jonathan defeated the garrison of the Philistines that was at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear."<sup>4</sup>And all Israel heard it said that Saul had defeated the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel had become a stench to the Philistines. And the people were called out to join Saul at Gilgal.<sup>5</sup>And the Philistines mustered to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore in multitude. They came up and encamped in Michmash, to the east of Beth-aven.<sup>6</sup>When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were hard pressed), the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns,<sup>7</sup>and some Hebrews crossed the fords of the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.<sup>8</sup>He waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him.<sup>9</sup>So Saul said, "Bring the burnt offering here to me, and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.<sup>10</sup>As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. And Saul went out to meet him and greet him.<sup>11</sup>Samuel said, "What have you done?" And Saul said, "When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines had mustered at Michmash,<sup>12</sup>I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering."<sup>13</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, "You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you. For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.<sup>14</sup>But now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."<sup>15</sup>And Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal. The rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the army; they went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people who were present with him, about six hundred men.<sup>16</sup>And Saul and Jonathan his son and the people who were present with them stayed in Geba of Benjamin, but the Philistines encamped in Michmash.<sup>17</sup>And raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies. One company turned toward Ophrah, to the land of Shual;<sup>18</sup>another company turned toward Beth-horon; and another company turned toward the border that looks down on the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.<sup>19</sup>Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, "Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears."<sup>20</sup>But every one of the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle,<sup>21</sup>and the charge was two-thirds of a shekel for the plowshares and for the mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and for setting the goads.<sup>22</sup>So on the day of the battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, but Saul and Jonathan his son had them.<sup>23</sup>And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.
13.overview:
Israel has a standing army for the first time — three thousand men — and Jonathan enters the book with a command and no introduction. He attacks the Philistine garrison at Geba, and Saul blows the trumpet, and the country hears that Saul defeated it. Nobody lies. The credit simply moves, and the man who two chapters ago refused all of it and said today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel does not correct it. Most collapses begin at about that size.

The Philistines come up in force, and Israel goes to ground in caves, holes, rocks, tombs and cisterns — five hiding places in one verse — while some cross the Jordan altogether. This is the nation that asked for a king to go out before them and fight their battles, on the first day a battle came.

And Saul is at Gilgal, where he was told on the day of his anointing to wait seven days. He waited seven days. He did wait. And the prophet did not come, and the army drained away by the hour, and on the last day he offered the burnt offering himself — and as soon as he had finished, behold, Samuel came.

Every reason Saul gives is true. The people were scattering, Samuel had not come, the Philistines had mustered. And then one sentence gives him away: so I forced myself. A man who believed it was permitted would not have needed to. The kingdom is taken from his line, and the LORD has already sought out a man after his own heart — a boy in Bethlehem, three chapters away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul keeps three thousand men and sends the rest home (vv. 1-2). Jonathan defeats the Philistine garrison at Geba — and the trumpet goes out through the land announcing that Saul had defeated it (vv. 3-4). The Philistines muster in overwhelming force, chariots and horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore, and camp at Michmash (v. 5). Israel goes to ground: the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns, and some cross the Jordan altogether (vv. 6-7). And Saul is at Gilgal, with the people following him trembling.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 is the first crack in Saul and nobody in it tells a lie. Jonathan struck the garrison; the proclamation says Saul did. The credit simply moves, and the man who once said today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel does not correct it.
verseByVerse.examples: Five hiding places are listed in one verse — caves, holes, rocks, tombs, cisterns. This is the army Israel asked for a king to lead, on the day it was needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul lived for one year and then became king, and when he had reigned for two years over Israel, Saul chose three thousand men of Israel. Two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, every man to his tent. Jonathan defeated the garrison of the Philistines that was at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear." And all Israel heard it said that Saul had defeated the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel had become a stench to the Philistines. And the people were called out to join Saul at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Saul lived for one year and then became king, and when he had reigned for two years over Israel, Saul chose three thousand men of Israel.'

The first verse of this chapter is damaged, and the honest thing is to say so once and move on.

In the Hebrew it runs, literally, Saul was ___ years old when he began to reign, and he reigned ___ and two years over Israel — with the numbers missing. It is the standard formula used for every king in Samuel and Kings, and in this one instance the figures have dropped out of the text. Translations handle the gap differently and the ESV footnote says plainly that the number is lacking. Paul gives the length of the reign as forty years (Acts 13:21).

Nothing in the chapter depends on it.

'Two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, every man to his tent.'

For the first time Israel has a standing army, and it is three thousand men.

This is what a monarchy buys: not a levy raised in a crisis and sent home afterwards, but soldiers kept under arms. Two thousand under the king, and a thousand under his son — and Jonathan enters the book here, with a command, and no introduction.

'Jonathan defeated the garrison of the Philistines that was at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear."'

Jonathan attacks and Saul announces it.

'And all Israel heard it said that Saul had defeated the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel had become a stench to the Philistines.'

Now read those two verses together, because this is the first crack in the man and there is not a lie anywhere in it.

Verse 3: Jonathan defeated the garrison. Verse 4: all Israel heard it said that Saul had defeated the garrison.

Nobody has said anything false. Saul blew the trumpet; the message went out; the country drew the obvious conclusion from who was doing the announcing. The credit simply moved, in the ordinary way credit moves, and the man it moved to did not correct it.

Hold that against chapter 11. Two chapters ago, on the day of his greatest victory, with the crowd demanding blood, he said today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel and refused to take anything for himself. He is now taking his son's.

It is a small thing and the narrator gives it one clause. Most collapses begin at about this size.

Note the last phrase too: Israel had become a stench to the Philistines. That is not a victory report; it is a warning. Jonathan's raid has provoked the occupying power, and everybody in the country knows what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistines mustered to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore in multitude. They came up and encamped in Michmash, to the east of Beth-aven. When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were hard pressed), the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns, and some Hebrews crossed the fords of the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the Philistines mustered to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore in multitude. They came up and encamped in Michmash, to the east of Beth-aven.'

The Philistines come, and the numbers are enormous.

Chariots and horsemen are what Israel does not have and cannot answer; the phrase like the sand on the seashore is the one used of the Midianite camels and of Abraham's descendants, and it means uncountable.

The chariot figure is very large and some manuscripts read three thousand, which fits the horsemen better. The point of the verse survives either reading: a first-class army has arrived and Israel has three thousand men and, as verse 22 will tell us, almost no weapons.

'When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were hard pressed), the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns.'

Five hiding places, listed one after another, and the writer takes his time over them.

Caves. Holes. Rocks. Tombs. Cisterns. A cistern is a bell-shaped pit cut in rock for water, and a man who climbs into one cannot get out without help; a tomb is a hole full of the dead. These are not defensive positions. They are places to be not-found.

Read it against chapter 8. This is the nation that asked for a king so that he might go out before us and fight our battles, on the first day the battle actually comes. They have the king, and they are in the cisterns.

'and some Hebrews crossed the fords of the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead.'

Some leave the country altogether.

The term used for them is Hebrews, which is the word foreigners use about Israel in this book, and it is used here of men going over the river to sit out the war on the other side.

'Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.'

Gilgal, and the reader should hear the name.

This is where Samuel told him, on the morning he was anointed, to go and wait: then go down before me to Gilgal... seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do (10:8). It is also where the nation renewed the kingdom and rejoiced greatly after Jabesh (11:14-15).

He is in the right place, doing the right thing, with an army that is trembling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel — and Samuel did not come, and the army was draining away (v. 8). So Saul called for the burnt offering and offered it (v. 9). As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came (v. 10). Asked what he has done, Saul gives three reasons, all of them true, and one sentence that gives him away: so I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering (vv. 11-12). Samuel's verdict: you have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God... but now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: He waited almost the whole of it. That is what makes this chapter so uncomfortable: this is not defiance, it is obedience that failed in the last hour, with the enemy massed and the army melting and every excuse available and true.
verseByVerse.examples: The sin is not that a king offered sacrifice; kings did (2 Sam. 6:17). It is that he was given one order with a number of days on it back in 10:8, and Samuel calls it the command of the LORD your God. And I forced myself is the confession hidden inside the defence.

verseByVerse.quote: He waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him. So Saul said, "Bring the burnt offering here to me, and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering. As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. And Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him.'

Read the first four words carefully, because a great deal of what follows depends on them.

He waited seven days.

He did wait. This is not a man who ignored the instruction, or forgot it, or decided it did not apply. He held his position for the whole appointed period with a first-class army massed at Michmash and his own force draining away into the hills by the hour.

Try to feel the seventh day. The prophet has not come. The Philistines are eight miles off with chariots. Every hour another handful of men slips away, and the king can watch it happening; by verse 15 he will have six hundred left out of three thousand. He has done everything he was told to do and it has produced nothing but a smaller army.

'So Saul said, "Bring the burnt offering here to me, and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.'

On the last day, he does it himself.

Be precise about what the offence is, because the obvious answer is not quite right. The sin is not simply that a king performed a sacrifice. David will offer burnt offerings and peace offerings when he brings up the ark, and Solomon will sacrifice at the dedication of the temple, and neither is condemned for it (2 Sam. 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62-63).

The offence is that Saul had one specific standing order — wait at Gilgal, seven days, until I come — and on the seventh day he stopped waiting.

'As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came.'

That is the most painful sentence in the chapter.

As soon as he had finished. Not an hour later, not the next morning. Samuel walks into Gilgal at the moment the fire is lit.

He was coming. He had always been coming. The seven days were nearly up and the prophet was on the road, and Saul missed him by the length of a sacrifice.

There is nothing to be added to that, and the writer adds nothing. He simply puts the two clauses side by side and lets the reader do the arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel said, "What have you done?" And Saul said, "When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines had mustered at Michmash, I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering." And Samuel said to Saul, "You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you. For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Samuel said, "What have you done?"'

The same question God asked in the garden, and the angel asked at Bochim (Gen. 3:13; Judg. 2:2). It is never a request for information.

'And Saul said, "When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines had mustered at Michmash..."'

Three reasons, and here is the difficulty with this chapter: every one of them is true.

The people were scattering; the narrator said so in verse 8 before Saul says it here. Samuel had not come within the days appointed — on the seventh day he was still absent. The Philistines had mustered at Michmash, and the numbers are in verse 5.

Saul is not making excuses in the sense of inventing them. He is giving an accurate account of his situation, and any officer in that position would have given the same one.

'"I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering."'

Now the sentence that gives him away, and it is his own.

So I forced myself.

He is describing an act he had to compel himself to perform. Not a decision he came to, not a judgment call he was at peace with — something he had to push himself over the edge into doing.

So he knew. The whole defence collapses on those three words, because a man who believed the sacrifice was permitted would not have needed to force himself into it. Saul is telling the prophet, without meaning to, that his conscience was against him at the time and he overrode it.

Note also the reason he gives for the anxiety: I have not sought the favour of the LORD. He was worried about going into battle unblessed. That is a real concern and a pious one, and it is exactly what the seven-day instruction was designed to provide — Samuel was coming to offer those sacrifices himself.

So the shape of it is this. He disobeyed a direct command in order to obtain the very thing obedience would have given him, one sacrifice-length before it arrived.

'And Samuel said to Saul, "You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you."'

Two things in the verdict, and the second is the important one.

You have done foolishly. The word in Hebrew is not about low intelligence; folly in these books is a moral category, the condition of a man who will not reckon with God.

Then: you have not kept the command of the LORD your God.

That is how the seven days at Gilgal are classified. Not Samuel's scheduling, not a piece of protocol between a prophet and a king — the command of God. It had been given three chapters ago in a single sentence at the end of a private conversation on a road (10:8), and it was binding.

'"For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall not continue."'

There is the cost, and it is enormous.

Forever. A dynasty, of the kind that will be promised to David in 2 Samuel 7. That was available to Saul, and it is gone, and it went in the time it took to burn one animal.

Readers reasonably feel the sentence is severe here, and it should be faced rather than softened. He waited six days and most of a seventh, under real pressure, with true reasons, in a crisis, and the kingdom is taken from his line for it.

Two things can be said, and neither of them makes it comfortable.

The first is that a king in Israel was under a text, and this was the test of it. Israel had asked for a king like the nations, and the whole difference between that king and theirs was that theirs took orders. The first specific order was wait. Everything about the office turned on whether he would.

The second is I forced myself. It was not a misunderstanding. The chapter records a man overriding his own conscience under pressure, and pressure is precisely the condition under which obedience actually counts for something. Waiting when Samuel had arrived on day two would have proved nothing.

'"The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."'

Here, unnamed, is David.

He is at this moment a boy in Bethlehem looking after sheep, and it will be three chapters before Samuel is sent to find him. The phrase attached to him is among the best known in Scripture, and Paul quotes it in a synagogue in Pisidian Antioch when he tells Israel's story: I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22).

Mark what the phrase means, because it is often heard as a compliment about David's feelings. The contrast in this chapter is with a man who did not keep what he was commanded, and the second half of Paul's quotation supplies the sense: who will do all my will. A man after God's own heart is a man who does what God says.

The title used is prince again — nagid, the word God used of Saul on the road (9:16; 10:1). The office is not being abolished. It is being given to somebody else.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel leaves, and Saul numbers what is left: about six hundred men (v. 15). Philistine raiders go out in three companies (vv. 17-18). And the narrator explains the strategic position: there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had forbidden it, so every Israelite went down to them to have his plough or axe sharpened, at a price (vv. 19-21). So on the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, but Saul and Jonathan his son had them (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Two swords in the whole army, and a monopoly on iron that reached into every farm in the country. Israel was not merely occupied; it was disarmed by an industrial policy, and paid the occupier to sharpen its own tools.
verseByVerse.examples: Six hundred men is the number of Benjamin's survivors on the rock of Rimmon (Judg. 20:47), and Hannah's line is about to be tested: not by might shall a man prevail (2:9). Chapter 14 opens with one of the two swordsmen walking off alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal. The rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the army; they went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people who were present with him, about six hundred men. And Saul and Jonathan his son and the people who were present with them stayed in Geba of Benjamin, but the Philistines encamped in Michmash. And raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies. One company turned toward Ophrah, to the land of Shual; another company turned toward Beth-horon; and another company turned toward the border that looks down on the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal.'

He delivers the sentence and leaves.

There is no discussion, no appeal, and no comfort. The prophet who came to offer the sacrifices does not offer them; he says what he came to say and walks out of the camp.

'The rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the army; they went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people who were present with him, about six hundred men.'

He counts what is left, and it is six hundred.

Three thousand men at the start of the chapter. Six hundred now. Four out of every five have gone into the caves or over the Jordan, and the number he is left with is one that any Israelite would recognise.

Six hundred is what remained of the tribe of Benjamin after the civil war — the survivors who fled to the rock of Rimmon and sat there four months while their tribe was destroyed behind them (Judg. 20:47). Saul is a Benjaminite, and he is standing in Gibeah, which is the town the war was fought over, with six hundred men.

'And Saul and Jonathan his son and the people who were present with them stayed in Geba of Benjamin, but the Philistines encamped in Michmash. And raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies.'

The Philistines do not even bother to attack.

They send raiding parties out in three directions — north to Ophrah, west to Beth-horon, east towards the wilderness — and simply strip the country while the king of Israel sits in Geba with six hundred men and watches.

Three companies is Gideon's number, and it was Saul's own at Jabesh (Judg. 7:16; 11:11). The formation that won Israel's battles is being used by the enemy on Israel's farms.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, "Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears." But every one of the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle, and the charge was two-thirds of a shekel for the plowshares and for the mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and for setting the goads. So on the day of the battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, but Saul and Jonathan his son had them. And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, "Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears."'

Now the strategic situation, and the writer has held it back until now.

There is not one blacksmith in the country. Not restricted, not licensed — none. The Philistines had a monopoly on ironworking and they enforced it as policy, and the policy is quoted: lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears.

This is disarmament by industry rather than by conquest. You do not need to take a nation's weapons if you own the only forge.

'But every one of the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle, and the charge was two-thirds of a shekel for the plowshares and for the mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and for setting the goads.'

They charged for it, and the narrator knows the prices.

Two thirds of a shekel for a ploughshare, a third for an axe. Every farmer in Israel walked down to a Philistine town once a season to have his own tools sharpened by the people occupying his country, and paid over the odds for it.

That is a humiliation administered a hundred times a year in every village, and it is quiet enough that nobody would call it a war.

'So on the day of the battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, but Saul and Jonathan his son had them.'

Two swords.

Six hundred men, and two weapons between them, both in the hands of the royal family. The rest are carrying farm tools that a Philistine smith sharpened for them and charged them for.

Now set that beside what Israel asked for in chapter 8. They wanted a king to go out before us and fight our battles, like all the nations — and the nations' armies were exactly what the Philistines have at Michmash: chariots, horsemen, iron, and a professional smith.

Here is the army the request produced. Six hundred frightened men with agricultural implements.

'And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.'

The chapter ends with the enemy taking up position in the pass, and everything in it pointing one way. The king has lost his dynasty. The army has lost four fifths of its men. The country has no weapons and no blacksmith. And a garrison holds the high ground at Michmash.

Now remember what Hannah sang in the second chapter of this book, in a corrupt sanctuary, with nothing to go on: the bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength... not by might shall a man prevail (2:4, 9).

The very next verse of the story has one man and his armour-bearer getting up and walking towards that pass.

13.theology:
The first crack (vv. 3-4). Jonathan struck the garrison; the proclamation says Saul did; nobody says anything false. Credit moves in the ordinary way credit moves, and it is not corrected. Set it against 11:13, where at the height of his power he refused to take anything for himself.

The sin was not the sacrifice. Kings did offer sacrifices — David when the ark came up, Solomon at the dedication (2 Sam. 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62-63) — and neither is condemned. Saul had one specific standing order with a number of days on it (10:8), and Samuel classifies it as the command of the LORD your God, not as a prophet's scheduling.

He waited almost all of it (v. 8). That is what makes this hard. Not defiance, but obedience that failed in the last hour, under real pressure, with true reasons. And the answer is in his own defence: so I forced myself (v. 12). He describes an act he had to compel himself into — which means his conscience was against him and he overrode it. The whole defence collapses on those three words.

He disobeyed to get what obedience was bringing. His stated anxiety was that he had not sought the LORD's favour — which is a real and pious concern, and precisely what the seven days existed to supply. Samuel was on the road with those sacrifices. Saul missed him by the length of one offering: as soon as he had finished... behold, Samuel came.

Why so severe? Two things, and neither makes it comfortable. A king in Israel was a king under a text, and the whole difference between him and the kings of the nations was that he took orders; the first specific order was wait, and everything about the office turned on it. And pressure is exactly the condition under which obedience counts for anything — waiting when the prophet arrived on day two would have proved nothing.

A man after his own heart (v. 14). The first appearance of David, unnamed, a boy with sheep. The phrase is often heard as a compliment about his feelings; the contrast here is with a man who did not keep what the LORD commanded, and Paul's quotation supplies the sense: a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22).

Two swords (v. 22). No blacksmith in the land, by Philistine policy — disarmament by industry rather than conquest — and every farmer walking down to the occupier once a season to have his own tools sharpened, at a price the narrator knows. Six hundred men with agricultural implements: the army Israel's request produced. And Hannah's line is about to be tested — not by might shall a man prevail (2:9) — because the next verse has one of the two swordsmen getting up and walking toward the pass.
13.examples:
Then: A king held his position for seven days as ordered, watched four fifths of his army disappear into caves and cisterns while he did it, gave way in the last hour with every reason on his side — and the prophet walked into camp as the fire was still burning.

Now: Two things. The first is I forced myself, and it is the most useful diagnostic in the chapter. When a course of action requires you to override something in yourself before you can take it, that resistance is usually information rather than weakness, and Saul's own word for it convicted him faster than any of Samuel's. The second is the timing. He was one sacrifice short. There is no way to know, in the seventh hour of waiting, how close the answer is — which is exactly why the instruction had a number on it and not a condition.

14.title: Jonathan's Faith and Saul's Folly
14.text: <sup>1</sup>One day Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine garrison on the other side." But he did not tell his father.<sup>2</sup>Saul was staying in the outskirts of Gibeah in the pomegranate cave at Migron. The people who were with him were about six hundred men,<sup>3</sup>including Ahijah the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people did not know that Jonathan had gone.<sup>4</sup>Within the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.<sup>5</sup>The one crag rose on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.<sup>6</sup>Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few."<sup>7</sup>And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do all that is in your heart. Do as you wish. Behold, I am with you heart and soul."<sup>8</sup>Then Jonathan said, "Behold, we will cross over to the men, and we will show ourselves to them.<sup>9</sup>If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stand still in our place, and we will not go up to them.<sup>10</sup>But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for the LORD has given them into our hand. And this shall be the sign to us."<sup>11</sup>So both of them showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines. And the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have hidden themselves."<sup>12</sup>And the men of the garrison hailed Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come up to us, and we will show you a thing." And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come up after me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel."<sup>13</sup>Then Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer after him. And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them after him.<sup>14</sup>And that first strike, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made, killed about twenty men within as it were half a furrow's length in an acre of land.<sup>15</sup>And there was a panic in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The garrison and even the raiders trembled, the earth quaked, and it became a very great panic.<sup>16</sup>And the watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude was dispersing here and there.<sup>17</sup>Then Saul said to the people who were with him, "Count and see who has gone from us." And when they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.<sup>18</sup>So Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." For the ark of God went at that time with the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>Now while Saul was talking to the priest, the tumult in the camp of the Philistines increased more and more. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."<sup>20</sup>Then Saul and all the people who were with him rallied and went into the battle. And behold, every Philistine's sword was against his fellow, and there was very great confusion.<sup>21</sup>Now the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before that time and who had gone up with them into the camp, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.<sup>22</sup>Likewise, when all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle.<sup>23</sup>So the LORD saved Israel that day. And the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.<sup>24</sup>And the men of Israel had been hard pressed that day, so Saul had laid an oath on the people, saying, "Cursed be the man who eats food until it is evening and I am avenged on my enemies." So none of the people had tasted food.<sup>25</sup>Now when all the people came to the forest, behold, there was honey on the ground.<sup>26</sup>And when the people entered the forest, behold, the honey was dropping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.<sup>27</sup>But Jonathan had not heard his father charge the people with the oath, so he put out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright.<sup>28</sup>Then one of the people said, "Your father strictly charged the people with an oath, saying, 'Cursed be the man who eats food this day.'" And the people were faint.<sup>29</sup>Then Jonathan said, "My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have become bright because I tasted a little of this honey.<sup>30</sup>How much better if the people had eaten freely today of the spoil of their enemies that they found. For now the defeat among the Philistines has not been great."<sup>31</sup>They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. And the people were very faint.<sup>32</sup>The people pounced on the spoil and took sheep and oxen and calves and slaughtered them on the ground. And the people ate them with the blood.<sup>33</sup>Then they told Saul, "Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood." And he said, "You have dealt treacherously; roll a great stone to me here."<sup>34</sup>And Saul said, "Disperse yourselves among the people and say to them, 'Let every man bring his ox or his sheep and slaughter them here and eat, and do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.'" So every one of the people brought his ox with him that night and they slaughtered them there.<sup>35</sup>And Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar that he built to the LORD.<sup>36</sup>Then Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light; let us not leave a man of them." And they said, "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said, "Let us draw near to God here."<sup>37</sup>And Saul inquired of God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into the hand of Israel?" But he did not answer him that day.<sup>38</sup>And Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and know and see how this sin has arisen today.<sup>39</sup>For as the LORD lives who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die." But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.<sup>40</sup>Then he said to all Israel, "You shall be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side." And the people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you."<sup>41</sup>Therefore Saul said, "O LORD God of Israel, why have you not answered your servant this day? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, O LORD, God of Israel, give Urim. But if this guilt is in your people Israel, give Thummim." And Jonathan and Saul were taken, but the people escaped.<sup>42</sup>Then Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken.<sup>43</sup>Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." And Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff that was in my hand. Here I am; I will die."<sup>44</sup>And Saul said, "God do so to me and more also; you shall surely die, Jonathan."<sup>45</sup>Then the people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As the LORD lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day." So the people ransomed Jonathan, so that he did not die.<sup>46</sup>Then Saul went up from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.<sup>47</sup>When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, against the Ammonites, against Edom, against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned he routed them.<sup>48</sup>And he did valiantly and struck the Amalekites and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them.<sup>49</sup>Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua. And the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn was Merab, and the name of the younger Michal.<sup>50</sup>And the name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. And the name of the commander of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle.<sup>51</sup>Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.<sup>52</sup>There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. And when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he attached him to himself.
14.overview:
The chapter is built as a contrast and every scene keeps it. Jonathan takes his armour-bearer and climbs into a pass towards a Philistine garrison, and the sentence he goes on is the theology of the whole book: it may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few. Read it against the end of chapter 13 — no blacksmith in Israel, two swords in the army, chariots on the other side. Jonathan says the arithmetic is not the relevant category.

Weigh the first two words, because they make the sentence. It may be. He has no promise, no prophet and no sign. He acts on what God is like rather than on a guarantee that God will act — a harder faith than certainty, and a better one. The sign he chooses is the dangerous option, and he goes up on hands and feet, arriving unable to hold a weapon.

Twenty men fall in the space of half a furrow, and an army comes apart in a panic the Hebrew calls a panic of God. Saul, meanwhile, orders a roll call, begins to consult God, and cancels it mid-sentence because events are moving — withdraw your hand, which is the Gilgal instinct exactly. And the verdict names nobody: so the LORD saved Israel that day.

Then the oath. Saul had cursed anyone who ate until I am avenged on my enemies, and the army walks through a forest running with honey and does not touch it. Jonathan, who had not heard, eats and says his father has troubled the land — Achan's word. The starving men eat meat with the blood at nightfall, and Saul rebukes the sin he manufactured. God goes silent. Saul hunts for a culprit, swears to kill whoever it is, and names his own son — and the army refuses and ransoms him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Did Not Tell His Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan says to his armour-bearer, come, let us go over to the Philistine garrison on the other side — but he did not tell his father (v. 1). Saul is sitting under a pomegranate tree at the edge of Gibeah with six hundred men and a priest in an ephod (vv. 2-3). The ground between is described: two rocky crags facing each other across a pass, named Bozez and Seneh (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The priest is given a pedigree: Ahijah son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli. The house God sentenced in chapter 2 is still wearing the ephod, three generations on.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men are described in these five verses. One is sitting under a tree with an army, and one is climbing into a pass with a servant. Neither knows what the other is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: One day Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine garrison on the other side." But he did not tell his father. Saul was staying in the outskirts of Gibeah in the pomegranate cave at Migron. The people who were with him were about six hundred men, including Ahijah the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people did not know that Jonathan had gone. Within the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh. The one crag rose on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'One day Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine garrison on the other side." But he did not tell his father.'

The last clause is the one the chapter will keep coming back to.

But he did not tell his father. It is not presented as rebellion and Jonathan is nowhere criticised for it; it is simply a fact, and it tells us something about the household. The king's son is going out to do something that matters and does not think it worth mentioning to the king.

'Saul was staying in the outskirts of Gibeah in the pomegranate cave at Migron. The people who were with him were about six hundred men.'

Here is his father, under a pomegranate tree on the edge of town with six hundred men.

The detail is not flattering and it is not meant to be. Israel is occupied, raiding parties are stripping the country in three directions, and the king is sitting at the outskirts.

'including Ahijah the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people did not know that Jonathan had gone.'

The priest is given four generations, and the third name should stop the reader.

Ichabod's brother. This is the family of Eli: Phinehas who died on the day the ark was taken, his son born as his mother died naming him the glory has departed, and now Phinehas's other son's son, standing beside Saul in an ephod.

The house God sentenced in chapter 2 — no old man in your house, forever — is still serving. God's judgments in Scripture are frequently slower than readers expect, and the house of Eli holds the priesthood for a long time yet; Saul will destroy most of it at Nob, and Solomon will finish it (22:18-19; 1 Kings 2:27).

'Within the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.'

The writer gives us the ground, and he gives the crags their names.

Two cliffs facing each other across a narrow pass, with a garrison on the far one. The names mean something like shining and thorny, and the fact that they had names at all means people knew this place.

It is the hardest possible approach: a defended height reached by climbing a rock face in full view. That is the route Jonathan has chosen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — By Many or by Few
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan's proposal contains the theology of the whole book: it may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (v. 6). His armour-bearer answers I am with you heart and soul (v. 7). They agree a sign — if the garrison says come up to us, that is God giving them over (vv. 8-10). The Philistines see them and jeer about Hebrews coming out of their holes, and then call them up (vv. 11-12). Jonathan climbs on his hands and feet and about twenty men fall in the space of half a furrow (vv. 13-14). And a panic spreads through the camp and the raiders, and the earth quaked (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Note what Jonathan does not claim. It may be — he has been given no promise and does not pretend to one. He acts on what God is like, not on a guarantee that God will act, and that is a harder and better faith than certainty.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign he chooses is the difficult option. If the garrison comes down, they stand still; if it calls them up, they climb a cliff into it. And he goes up on hands and feet, which means he arrives unable to hold a weapon.

verseByVerse.quote: Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few." And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do all that is in your heart. Do as you wish. Behold, I am with you heart and soul." Then Jonathan said, "Behold, we will cross over to the men, and we will show ourselves to them. If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stand still in our place, and we will not go up to them. But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for the LORD has given them into our hand. And this shall be the sign to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few."'

Here is the sentence the whole book has been building towards, and it is spoken by a young man about to climb a cliff with one servant.

Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.

Read it against the end of the last chapter. There is no blacksmith in Israel; there are two swords in the entire army, and both belong to Saul and Jonathan; the Philistines have chariots and horsemen and a garrison in the pass. The arithmetic could not be worse.

Jonathan says the arithmetic is not the relevant category. God is not working with a percentage. Many or few is a distinction that matters to generals and does not constrain him at all.

It is Hannah's line, thirteen chapters later and in prose: the bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength... not by might shall a man prevail (2:4, 9). She sang it in a sanctuary with nothing to go on; her son's generation is about to see it in a pass.

Now weigh the two words at the front, because they are the making of the sentence: it may be.

Jonathan does not claim a promise. He has had no word from God, no prophet, no sign; Samuel is not here and nobody has told him to do this. He does not say the LORD will work for us. He says it may be that he will, for this is the kind of God he is.

That is a harder faith than certainty and a better one. Certainty about the outcome is comfortable and is usually unavailable. What Jonathan has is confidence about God's character and a willingness to act on it without knowing how it will go — which is precisely what the three men in Babylon had when they said God was able to deliver them from the furnace, but if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Dan. 3:17-18).

'And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do all that is in your heart. Do as you wish. Behold, I am with you heart and soul."'

The armour-bearer is not named and gets one of the best lines in the book.

Literally, behold, I am with you according to your heart. He is not being told the plan; he is agreeing to a man. And he knows exactly what he is agreeing to, because he is going up the same cliff.

'Then Jonathan said, "Behold, we will cross over to the men, and we will show ourselves to them. If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stand still in our place, and we will not go up to them. But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for the LORD has given them into our hand. And this shall be the sign to us."'

He proposes a test, and mark which way round he has set it.

If the garrison offers to come down — the safer outcome, fighting on level ground — they will stand still and do nothing. If the garrison tells them to come up, they will climb into a defended position under the eyes of the men holding it.

Whichever answer sends them forward is the more dangerous one. He has arranged a test in which God's yes costs him considerably more than God's no.

verseByVerse.quote: So both of them showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines. And the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have hidden themselves." And the men of the garrison hailed Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come up to us, and we will show you a thing." And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come up after me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel." Then Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer after him. And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them after him. And that first strike, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made, killed about twenty men within as it were half a furrow's length in an acre of land. And there was a panic in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The garrison and even the raiders trembled, the earth quaked, and it became a very great panic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So both of them showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines. And the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have hidden themselves."'

They stand up in the open and let themselves be seen, and the enemy laughs at them.

The jeer is precise and it stings, because it is true. Chapter 13 said the men of Israel hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns (13:6). The Philistines know it. Everybody knows it.

'And the men of the garrison hailed Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come up to us, and we will show you a thing." And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come up after me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel."'

Come up to us, and we will show you a thing. It is a taunt with a threat inside it, and it is the exact sentence Jonathan asked for.

The sign arrives out of the mouths of men who have no idea they are giving it. They are mocking, and they are also, without knowing, telling a man that God has handed them over.

'Then Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer after him. And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them after him.'

He goes up a cliff on hands and knees.

Consider what that means for a soldier. Climbing on all fours, he cannot hold a weapon or a shield; he arrives at the top winded, unarmed in his hands, in front of a garrison that has been watching him come the whole way. There is no worse way to enter a fight.

They fall before him. The armour-bearer, coming up behind, finishes them.

'And that first strike, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made, killed about twenty men within as it were half a furrow's length in an acre of land.'

Twenty men in a space the size of half a furrow.

That is a farmer's measurement — the length a plough team covers in a short run — and it tells us the fight happened in a very small area. This was not a battle. It was two men in a confined space at the top of a rock.

'And there was a panic in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The garrison and even the raiders trembled, the earth quaked, and it became a very great panic.'

Then it spreads, and the writer widens the frame in three steps: the camp, the field, all the people.

The raiding parties that had gone out in three directions in chapter 13 are shaking. The ground itself moves. And the phrase at the end is, in Hebrew, a panic of God — a terror that is not accounted for by anything on the ground.

Twenty men died at the top of a crag, and an army came apart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul's watchmen see the enemy dispersing, and Saul orders a roll call to find who is missing — Jonathan and his armour-bearer (vv. 16-17). He tells the priest to bring the ark, and then, as the tumult grows, withdraw your hand (vv. 18-19). Israel goes in, and finds every Philistine's sword against his fellow (v. 20). The Hebrews who had gone over to the Philistines change sides, and the men hiding in the hill country come out and join the pursuit (vv. 21-22). So the LORD saved Israel that day (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul starts to enquire of God and cancels it mid-sentence because the situation is moving. It is the same instinct as Gilgal: the pressure of events overrules the consultation, and the consultation is the thing that was commanded.
verseByVerse.examples: The deserters come back and the men in the caves come out, and neither group is criticised for it. Verse 23 gives the credit where the chapter has been pointing all along, and it is not to the six hundred and not to the two men in the pass.

verseByVerse.quote: And the watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude was dispersing here and there. Then Saul said to the people who were with him, "Count and see who has gone from us." And when they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there. So Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." For the ark of God went at that time with the people of Israel. Now while Saul was talking to the priest, the tumult in the camp of the Philistines increased more and more. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand." Then Saul and all the people who were with him rallied and went into the battle. And behold, every Philistine's sword was against his fellow, and there was very great confusion. Now the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before that time and who had gone up with them into the camp, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. Likewise, when all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle. So the LORD saved Israel that day. And the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude was dispersing here and there.'

The first Saul knows of it is that the enemy army is falling to pieces in front of his watchmen.

'Then Saul said to the people who were with him, "Count and see who has gone from us." And when they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.'

His first action is a roll call.

An enemy army is disintegrating on the hillside opposite, and the king of Israel orders a head count. It is not unreasonable — he wants to know what has happened — and it is a very long way from the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul and his anger was greatly kindled.

'So Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." For the ark of God went at that time with the people of Israel.'

He sends for the ark, or, on another reading of the text, for the ephod, which was the instrument for enquiring of God.

Either way the intention is right: before committing, ask.

'Now while Saul was talking to the priest, the tumult in the camp of the Philistines increased more and more. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."'

Then he cancels it in the middle.

Withdraw your hand. The consultation is stopped halfway because events are moving and the opportunity looks like it is opening. The noise from the enemy camp is increasing, and Saul decides there is no longer time to ask God anything.

Put that beside Gilgal. There, he waited almost seven days and gave way in the last hour because the army was scattering. Here, he begins to enquire and breaks it off because the battle is starting. Twice now the pressure of the moment has overruled the thing he was supposed to do, and both times he was very close.

'Then Saul and all the people who were with him rallied and went into the battle. And behold, every Philistine's sword was against his fellow, and there was very great confusion.'

They arrive to find the enemy killing each other.

It is Gideon's valley again, exactly: the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade (Judg. 7:22). Israel's part in both battles is to turn up after God has done it.

'Now the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before that time and who had gone up with them into the camp, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.'

The collaborators change sides.

There were Israelites serving in the Philistine army — conscripts, mercenaries, men who had made an arrangement — and when the tide turns they turn with it. The narrator reports it without comment.

'Likewise, when all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle.'

The men in the caves come out.

These are the ones from 13:6, in the holes and the tombs and the cisterns. They hear the enemy is running and they come out and join the chase.

It would be easy to be sour about that, and the writer is not. They came out. The nation that was hiding in the ground at the start of the chapter is pursuing a beaten army by the end of it, and it began with one man saying it may be that the LORD will work for us.

'So the LORD saved Israel that day.'

There is the verdict, and it names nobody.

Not Jonathan, who went up the cliff. Not the armour-bearer. Not Saul, and not the six hundred, and not the returning deserters. The LORD saved Israel that day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–35 — Cursed Be the Man Who Eats
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul had laid an oath on the army: cursed be the man who eats food until it is evening and I am avenged on my enemies (v. 24). They come into a forest running with honey and nobody touches it (vv. 25-26). Jonathan, who had not heard, dips his staff and eats, and his eyes became bright (v. 27). Told of the oath, he answers: my father has troubled the land, and the victory has been the smaller for it (vv. 28-30). By evening the people are so famished that they slaughter the spoil on the ground and eat it with the blood (vv. 31-32). Saul stops it, rolls up a great stone, and builds an altar — it was the first altar that he built to the LORD (vv. 33-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The oath is sworn for my enemies and my vengeance, and the word Jonathan uses for its effect is Achan's word: he has troubled the land (cf. Josh. 7:25). A king's rash vow has done to Israel what a thief's sin did at Ai.
verseByVerse.examples: And it manufactured the sin it then punished. Men who have fought all day without food eventually eat meat with the blood in it, which the law forbids (Lev. 17:10-14) — and Saul, who starved them, rebukes them for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel had been hard pressed that day, so Saul had laid an oath on the people, saying, "Cursed be the man who eats food until it is evening and I am avenged on my enemies." So none of the people had tasted food. Now when all the people came to the forest, behold, there was honey on the ground. And when the people entered the forest, behold, the honey was dropping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath. But Jonathan had not heard his father charge the people with the oath, so he put out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright. Then one of the people said, "Your father strictly charged the people with an oath, saying, 'Cursed be the man who eats food this day.'" And the people were faint. Then Jonathan said, "My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have become bright because I tasted a little of this honey. How much better if the people had eaten freely today of the spoil of their enemies that they found. For now the defeat among the Philistines has not been great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the men of Israel had been hard pressed that day, so Saul had laid an oath on the people, saying, "Cursed be the man who eats food until it is evening and I am avenged on my enemies." So none of the people had tasted food.'

The narrator goes back to fill in what Saul had been doing while Jonathan was climbing.

He had put the army under a curse. No food until evening, on pain of being cursed, and the reason given is in the last five words: until... I am avenged on my enemies.

Read the pronouns. My vengeance. My enemies. There is no mention of God in the oath at all, and the men who will go hungry all day are fighting for the king's satisfaction.

Set it beside what his son said an hour earlier at the top of the crag: the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel (v. 12). Two men, the same battle, and one of them is thinking about the LORD and Israel while the other is thinking about his enemies and himself.

'Now when all the people came to the forest, behold, there was honey on the ground. And when the people entered the forest, behold, the honey was dropping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.'

God puts food in their path and the oath stops them eating it.

The picture is deliberate and almost unbearable. Wild honey running on the ground in front of an exhausted army, free, provided, requiring nothing but a hand — and not a man touches it.

'But Jonathan had not heard his father charge the people with the oath, so he put out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright.'

He had not heard it. He was in the pass at the time.

The detail the narrator chooses is physical: his eyes became bright. That is what food does to a man who has been fighting since dawn on an empty stomach. It is the visible difference between an army that has eaten and one that has not, recorded in one man's face.

'Then one of the people said, "Your father strictly charged the people with an oath, saying, 'Cursed be the man who eats food this day.'" And the people were faint.'

Somebody tells him, and the narrator adds four words of his own: and the people were faint.

'Then Jonathan said, "My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have become bright because I tasted a little of this honey."'

Jonathan's verdict is a single verb, and it is a heavy one.

My father has troubled the land. The word is 'akar, and every Israelite knew where it came from. When Achan's theft brought defeat on the army at Ai, Joshua said to him why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today, and the place was called the Valley of Achor, the valley of trouble (Josh. 7:25-26).

Jonathan is saying that his father's oath has done to Israel what a thief's sin did at Ai.

'"How much better if the people had eaten freely today of the spoil of their enemies that they found. For now the defeat among the Philistines has not been great."'

Here is the cost, stated plainly by the man who won the battle.

The victory was smaller than it should have been. An army that had eaten would have pursued further and struck harder; a starving one stopped early. The oath did not merely inconvenience the men. It let the Philistines get away.

That is the mark of the rash vow throughout Scripture. It sounds serious, it is made in God's presence, it costs the people who did not make it, and it damages the very thing it was meant to protect. Jephthah's vow was the same shape, and it cost him a daughter (Judg. 11:35).

verseByVerse.quote: They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. And the people were very faint. The people pounced on the spoil and took sheep and oxen and calves and slaughtered them on the ground. And the people ate them with the blood. Then they told Saul, "Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood." And he said, "You have dealt treacherously; roll a great stone to me here." And Saul said, "Disperse yourselves among the people and say to them, 'Let every man bring his ox or his sheep and slaughter them here and eat, and do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.'" So every one of the people brought his ox with him that night and they slaughtered them there. And Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar that he built to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. And the people were very faint.'

A day's fighting across fifteen miles of country on nothing at all.

'The people pounced on the spoil and took sheep and oxen and calves and slaughtered them on the ground. And the people ate them with the blood.'

At sunset, when the oath expires, they fall on the animals like men who have not eaten in a day, because that is what they are.

The verb is violent — they pounced. They butcher the beasts where they stand and eat the meat with the blood still in it.

It is a real offence, and it is not a technicality. The prohibition on blood is one of the oldest and most repeated in the law: you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood (Gen. 9:4); the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls (Lev. 17:11, 14). Blood belonged to God and to the altar.

'Then they told Saul, "Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood." And he said, "You have dealt treacherously; roll a great stone to me here."'

Saul is told, and he is properly appalled, and he acts at once and correctly.

He calls it treachery, has a great stone rolled up as a slaughtering block so that the animals can be bled properly, and sends word through the camp that every man must bring his beast there. It is the right response and it is efficiently done.

He seems not to notice that he caused it.

Follow the chain. Saul swore the oath. The oath starved the army. The starving army, released at nightfall, ate meat with the blood. Saul then rebukes them for sinning against the LORD.

The king manufactured the sin he is now condemning, and there is no sign anywhere in the passage that the connection occurred to him.

'So every one of the people brought his ox with him that night and they slaughtered them there. And Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar that he built to the LORD.'

That last clause is quiet and it lands hard.

It was the first altar that he built to the LORD.

He is well into his reign. He has been anointed, crowned, confirmed at Gilgal, given a victory at Jabesh, and rejected at Gilgal. And this is the first altar he ever built.

Gideon built one and named it before he fought anybody. Samuel built one at Ramah when he went home. Saul builds his first in a field at night, to fix a problem he created.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–46 — Though It Be in Jonathan My Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul proposes a night pursuit and the people agree, but the priest says let us draw near to God here (v. 36). So Saul enquires — but he did not answer him that day (v. 37). Saul's response to the silence is to hunt for the guilty man, and to swear that though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die; and nobody in the army says a word (vv. 38-39). The lot is cast by Urim and Thummim and falls on Jonathan, who answers plainly: I tasted a little honey... here I am; I will die (vv. 41-43). Saul confirms the sentence (v. 44). And the people refuse: shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel?... he has worked with God this day. So they ransom him (v. 45).
verseByVerse.theology: Set verse 44 beside 11:13. On the day of his first victory Saul refused to execute the men who had publicly despised him, because today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. Here, on the day of another victory, he insists on executing his own son — and the people use his own sentence back at him.
verseByVerse.examples: The army overrules the king to save the man God used. It is the only thing that stands between Jonathan and a sentence pronounced in the name of the LORD, and the writer records it without a word of criticism for anybody but Saul.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light; let us not leave a man of them." And they said, "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said, "Let us draw near to God here." And Saul inquired of God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into the hand of Israel?" But he did not answer him that day. And Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and know and see how this sin has arisen today. For as the LORD lives who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die." But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light; let us not leave a man of them." And they said, "Do whatever seems good to you."'

A night pursuit is proposed, and the army agrees, and the phrase they use should be familiar by now.

Do whatever seems good to you. It is the sentence the book of Judges ends on, in substance — every man doing what was right in his own eyes — and it is what the men of Gibeah said in that book's worst chapter (Judg. 19:24). An army that says this to its king is not offering counsel.

'But the priest said, "Let us draw near to God here."'

The priest has to interrupt.

Nobody in the command tent has suggested asking God about the plan, and it takes a clergyman to raise it — and the way he raises it is a rebuke wrapped in a suggestion.

'And Saul inquired of God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into the hand of Israel?" But he did not answer him that day.'

God says nothing.

That last clause is left standing with nothing attached to it. But he did not answer him that day. No refusal, no rebuke, no explanation. Silence.

It will happen again, at the very end. On the night before Gilboa, Saul will enquire of the LORD and the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets — and he will go looking for a medium at Endor (28:6).

The silence begins here.

'And Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and know and see how this sin has arisen today. For as the LORD lives who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die."'

Saul's response to God's silence is to look for somebody to blame.

It is not an unreasonable inference; unanswered enquiry could indicate unconfessed sin in the camp, as at Ai. But watch what he does with it. He swears another oath — the second in one day — and this one commits him in advance to executing whoever is found, and he names his own son in it before there is any evidence.

As the LORD lives who saves Israel. He invokes God as the God who saves, in the act of promising to kill the man God used to save them that morning.

'But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.'

The army says nothing.

They know. Somebody had told Jonathan about the oath in the forest, which means the story has been round the camp all day. The whole army knows what happened and not one man will say it, and their silence in front of the king is its own comment on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to all Israel, "You shall be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side." And the people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you." Therefore Saul said, "O LORD God of Israel, why have you not answered your servant this day? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, O LORD, God of Israel, give Urim. But if this guilt is in your people Israel, give Thummim." And Jonathan and Saul were taken, but the people escaped. Then Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken. Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." And Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff that was in my hand.
