Here I am; I will die." And Saul said, "God do so to me and more also; you shall surely die, Jonathan." Then the people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As the LORD lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day." So the people ransomed Jonathan, so that he did not die. Then Saul went up from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then he said to all Israel, "You shall be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side." And the people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you."'

He divides the nation from his own household, which means he already suspects.

'Therefore Saul said, "O LORD God of Israel, why have you not answered your servant this day? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, O LORD, God of Israel, give Urim. But if this guilt is in your people Israel, give Thummim." And Jonathan and Saul were taken, but the people escaped.'

This is the one place in Scripture where we watch a question actually being framed for the Urim and Thummim.

They were kept in the breastpiece of the high priest and used for enquiry, and everywhere else Scripture simply names them. (The fuller wording of v. 41, which names both, follows the Greek; the Hebrew here is shorter.) Here we watch a question being framed for them: two alternatives, assigned in advance, one to each object. It is a sacred lot with a binary answer, and the whole nation is standing there while it is cast.

The lot falls on the king's side of the field.

'Then Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken.'

'Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." And Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff that was in my hand. Here I am; I will die."'

Jonathan's answer is one of the most dignified speeches in the Old Testament, and it is seventeen words long.

He does not plead that he had not heard the oath, which is true and is stated in verse 27 and would be a complete defence. He does not point out that he won the battle. He does not appeal to the army, who are plainly on his side. He states exactly what he did — a little honey, on the tip of a staff — and submits.

Here I am; I will die. It is the same here I am that Samuel said in the dark at Shiloh.

'And Saul said, "God do so to me and more also; you shall surely die, Jonathan."'

His father confirms it with a third oath.

Now set this verse beside 11:13, because the writer has built the whole of Saul's story so that we would.

On the day of his first victory, when the people came demanding the execution of men who had publicly despised him, Saul said: not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.

On the day of this victory, he says: you shall surely die, Jonathan.

The same king, the same kind of day, and the reverse in every particular. Then he spared his enemies because God had saved Israel. Now he will kill his son, and God had saved Israel through the son.

'Then the people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As the LORD lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day." So the people ransomed Jonathan, so that he did not die.'

The army stops him.

Look at the argument they use, because it is Saul's own. Who has worked this great salvation in Israel is the language he used at Jabesh, and they are quoting the principle back at him: you do not execute men on a day God has saved Israel. You said so yourself.

They swear an oath of their own to cancel his — as the LORD lives — and they give the reason in five words that settle it: he has worked with God this day.

Then: so the people ransomed Jonathan. The text does not say what the ransom was, and guessing is a distraction. What it says is that a man who had been condemned under an oath sworn in God's name was not executed, because somebody else paid.

Note the shape without pressing it into an allegory the text does not make. One man went alone into the pass and worked a great salvation for a nation that was hiding in caves. That nation then found him under sentence of death, and would not have it, and ransomed him.

The gospel runs the other way round, and that is the point of the comparison. Jonathan was ransomed by the people he had saved. Christ ransomed the people who condemned him — and there was no army to intervene, and no substitute offered, because he was the substitute.

'Then Saul went up from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.'

The pursuit is abandoned.

The night attack Saul proposed never happens. The enemy walks home. A day that began with two men routing an army ends with the king of Israel having starved his troops, manufactured a national sin, tried to kill his own son, been overruled by his own army, and let the Philistines go.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with a summary of the reign, and it is favourable. Saul fought on every front — Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, the Philistines — and wherever he turned he routed them (v. 47). And he did valiantly and struck the Amalekites and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them (v. 48). Then the household: three sons, two daughters, his wife Ahinoam, and Abner his cousin commanding the army (vv. 49-51). And a last note: there was hard fighting with the Philistines all his days, and when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he attached him to himself (v. 52).
verseByVerse.theology: This is a real assessment and it should be allowed to stand. Saul was not a failure as a soldier. He secured the borders on every side and broke the raiders who had been eating Israel's harvests since the book of Judges.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause is how the rest of the book begins. A king who recruited every strong man he saw is going to see a shepherd from Bethlehem come up out of a valley carrying a giant's head.

verseByVerse.quote: When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, against the Ammonites, against Edom, against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned he routed them. And he did valiantly and struck the Amalekites and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them. Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua. And the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn was Merab, and the name of the younger Michal. And the name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. And the name of the commander of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle. Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel. There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. And when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he attached him to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, against the Ammonites, against Edom, against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned he routed them.'

The chapter ends with a summary of the reign, and it is favourable.

This needs saying clearly, because a reader who has just watched the honey and the oath will not expect it. Saul was a successful soldier. Five enemies are named on every frontier — Moab east, Ammon east, Edom south, Zobah far north, the Philistines west — and the verdict is wherever he turned he routed them.

'And he did valiantly and struck the Amalekites and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them.'

He did valiantly. The narrator says it in his own voice.

The phrase delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them is the language of the judges — the thing Israel had needed since Midian camped on the harvests. Saul did it. The raids stopped.

The Amalekites are mentioned here in passing, and the next chapter is about them.

'Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua. And the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn was Merab, and the name of the younger Michal. And the name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. And the name of the commander of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle.'

The household is listed, and almost everybody in it will matter.

Jonathan will love David and die beside his father on Gilboa. Malchi-shua will die on the same day. Merab will be promised to David and given to somebody else. Michal will love David, be given to him, be taken away, be given back, and despise him at the end. And Abner — the king's cousin and general — will hold Saul's house together for years after Gilboa and then be murdered in a gateway.

'There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. And when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he attached him to himself.'

The last sentence of the chapter is how the rest of the book gets started.

For a king with no standing army it is sensible policy with no standing army worth the name: recruit every capable man you meet. It is also, exactly, how a shepherd from Bethlehem ends up at court.

Two chapters from now Saul will see a young man come up out of a valley with a giant's head in his hand, and he will do what this verse says he always did. He will attach him to himself.

That will be the beginning of the end of him.

14.theology:
By many or by few (v. 6). Hannah sang it in prose form thirteen chapters earlier with nothing to go on (2:4, 9); chapter 13 supplied the arithmetic; Jonathan says the arithmetic does not constrain God. And it may be is the making of it: no promise, no prophet, no sign, and no claim to certainty — confidence about God's character and a willingness to act without knowing the outcome. It is the faith of the three men at the furnace: he is able to deliver us, but if not (Dan. 3:17-18).

The sign that costs more (vv. 9-10). If the garrison comes down they do nothing; if it calls them up they climb a cliff into it. Jonathan arranged a test in which God's yes is far more expensive than God's no.

Withdraw your hand (v. 19). Saul begins to enquire and stops halfway because the opportunity looks like it is opening. At Gilgal he waited almost seven days and gave way in the last hour. Twice the pressure of the moment overruled the thing he was told to do, and both times he was very close.

The rash vow (vv. 24, 29-30). Sworn for my vengeance and my enemies, with God nowhere in it, while his son at the top of the crag was saying the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel. It starved the army, and Jonathan's verb for its effect is Achan's — his father has troubled the land (cf. Josh. 7:25). It also manufactured the sin Saul then condemned: men who fight all day without food eventually eat meat with the blood (Lev. 17:11, 14), and there is no sign the connection occurred to him. That is the shape of the rash vow everywhere in Scripture — it sounds serious, it is made in God's presence, it costs the people who did not make it, and it damages the thing it meant to protect.

He did not answer him that day (v. 37). No refusal, no rebuke, no explanation. It happens again on the last night of his life, when the LORD answers neither by dreams nor Urim nor prophets and he goes to Endor (28:6). The silence begins here.

The exact reversal of 11:13. On the day of his first victory the people demanded the execution of men who had despised him, and Saul refused — not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. Here he insists on executing his own son, and the army stops him by quoting his own principle back: shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Then he spared enemies because God had saved; now he would kill the son through whom God saved.

Ransomed (v. 45). The text does not say what the ransom was and guessing is a distraction. Note the shape without forcing it: one man went alone into the pass and worked a great salvation for a nation hiding in caves, and that nation found him under a death sentence and paid. The gospel runs the other way, and that is the point of the comparison. Jonathan was ransomed by the people he saved. Christ ransomed the people who condemned him, and no army intervened and no substitute was offered, because he was the substitute.

He did valiantly (vv. 47-48). Give this its full weight. Five frontiers, wherever he turned he routed them, and the language of the judges: he delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them. Saul was not a failure as a soldier, and the book says so in its own voice.
14.examples:
Then: Two men climbed a cliff on their hands and knees towards a garrison that had just jeered at them, killed twenty in the space of half a furrow, and broke an army — while the king sat under a pomegranate tree, ordered a head count, cancelled his consultation of God halfway through, and had already sworn an oath that would starve his troops past a forest floor running with honey.

Now: Three things. Verse 6 is the model for acting without certainty: it may be is not weak faith but honest faith, and it is built on what God is like rather than on a guarantee nobody gave you. Verse 19 is the warning — the moment when consulting God starts to feel like a delay you cannot afford is precisely the moment the consultation matters. And verses 24 to 33 are the anatomy of a rash commitment: made in God's name, costing people who never agreed to it, forcing them into the very failure it was supposed to prevent, and leaving the man who made it genuinely unable to see that he caused it.

15.title: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel; now therefore listen to the words of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, 'I have noted what Amalek did to Israel in opposing them on the way when they came up out of Egypt.<sup>3</sup>Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.'"<sup>4</sup>So Saul summoned the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand men on foot, and ten thousand men of Judah.<sup>5</sup>And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley.<sup>6</sup>Then Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, depart; go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.<sup>7</sup>And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt.<sup>8</sup>And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive and devoted to destruction all the people with the edge of the sword.<sup>9</sup>But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.<sup>10</sup>The word of the LORD came to Samuel:<sup>11</sup>"I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not performed my commandments." And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the LORD all night.<sup>12</sup>And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. And it was told Samuel, "Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself and turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."<sup>13</sup>And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD."<sup>14</sup>And Samuel said, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?"<sup>15</sup>Saul said, "They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God, and the rest we have devoted to destruction."<sup>16</sup>Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! I will tell you what the LORD said to me this night." And he said to him, "Speak."<sup>17</sup>And Samuel said, "Though you are little in your own eyes, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go, devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.'<sup>19</sup>Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD?"<sup>20</sup>And Saul said to Samuel, "I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have devoted the Amalekites to destruction.<sup>21</sup>But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the things devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal."<sup>22</sup>And Samuel said, "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.<sup>23</sup>For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king."<sup>24</sup>Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore, please pardon my sin and return with me that I may bow before the LORD."<sup>26</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel."<sup>27</sup>As Samuel turned to go away, Saul seized the skirt of his robe, and it tore.<sup>28</sup>And Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you.<sup>29</sup>And also the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man, that he should have regret."<sup>30</sup>Then he said, "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow before the LORD your God."<sup>31</sup>So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed before the LORD.<sup>32</sup>Then Samuel said, "Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalekites." And Agag came to him cheerfully. Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."<sup>33</sup>And Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.<sup>34</sup>Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul.<sup>35</sup>And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.
15.overview:
The commission opens with a reason, and the reason is a specific historical act: what Amalek did to Israel... on the way when they came up out of Egypt. They attacked the back of the column — those who were lagging behind you, the faint and weary, three weeks out of slavery (Deut. 25:17-18) — and God swore that day to have war with Amalek from generation to generation. Four hundred years lie between the crime and this sentence, and in the interval Amalek kept coming. That is the case Scripture makes, and it does not make child and infant a comfortable sentence; pretending otherwise would be dishonest.

Saul does the military work well, and before the attack he warns the Kenites clear — because they showed kindness to Israel on the same journey Amalek attacked it. His reasoning there is exactly right, which is what makes verse 9 what it is. They spared all that was good and destroyed all that was despised and worthless. Not squeamishness, not mercy: a valuation, carried out with care, with the obedience stopping precisely where the value began.

Then a monument — the man who once hid among the baggage puts up a stone to himself on the road home. He greets Samuel with I have performed the commandment of the LORD, and Samuel answers with a question that needs no argument: what then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears? The evidence has been making a noise in the background the whole time.

And the oracle: to obey is better than sacrifice... for rebellion is as the sin of divination. Saul's confession, when it comes, is exactly accurate — I feared the people and obeyed their voice — and the request attached to it is honour me now before the elders. The chapter ends on two griefs, and neither is his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel comes with a commission, and it begins by establishing authority: the LORD sent me to anoint you, now therefore listen to the words of the LORD (v. 1). The charge is historical: I have noted what Amalek did to Israel in opposing them on the way when they came up out of Egypt (v. 2). And the order is total — devote them to destruction, man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The ground is stated and it is not ethnic. Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim, and Deuteronomy records how: he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you... and he did not fear God (Deut. 25:17-18). They came at the stragglers. God swore that day to have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Ex. 17:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Four hundred years stand between the crime and this sentence, and in the interval Amalek kept coming — with Eglon, with Midian, camped on Israel's harvests like locusts (Judg. 3:13; 6:3; 7:12). That is the case Scripture makes. It does not remove the difficulty of child and infant, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel; now therefore listen to the words of the LORD. Thus says the LORD of hosts, 'I have noted what Amalek did to Israel in opposing them on the way when they came up out of Egypt. Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel; now therefore listen to the words of the LORD."'

He establishes the chain of authority before he says anything else.

The LORD sent me. I anointed you. Now listen. Every clause is a reminder that Saul holds the office at somebody's pleasure, and that the man standing in front of him is the one through whom the orders come.

'"Thus says the LORD of hosts, 'I have noted what Amalek did to Israel in opposing them on the way when they came up out of Egypt.'"'

The commission opens with a reason, and the reason is a specific historical act.

Not that Amalek are Amalekites. Not that they occupy land Israel wants. What Amalek did to Israel... on the way when they came up out of Egypt, which is a reference every hearer would have caught.

It happened at Rephidim, a few weeks out of Egypt (Ex. 17:8-16). And Deuteronomy records what kind of attack it was, in a passage that reads like a charge sheet: he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God (Deut. 25:17-18).

They came at the back of the column. Not the armed men at the front — the stragglers, the exhausted, the ones who could not keep up: a nation of freed slaves three weeks out of slavery, with children and old people at the rear. That is who Amalek attacked, and that is what God noted.

He swore about it at the time, and Moses built an altar and named it: the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Ex. 17:16).

'"Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey."'

There is the order, and it must be read as it stands.

The phrase devote to destruction is the herem, the ban: a thing placed entirely under God's judgment, not to be taken as plunder, not to be profited from. And the list is comprehensive and includes the words no reader gets past easily. Child and infant.

Set out what Scripture itself says about this, and then be honest about what it does not settle.

The ground is stated and it is moral rather than ethnic: an act, named, with the manner of it on record. Four hundred years lie between the crime and the sentence, which is a very long "note" and not a hot temper. In the interval Amalek did not stop; they came with Eglon of Moab against Israel, and they came with Midian year after year to camp on the harvests like locusts, and they are named in three separate campaigns in the book of Judges alone (Judg. 3:13; 6:3; 7:12). This is a standing, repeated, four-century aggression.

The ban means nobody profits. That is the point of it and it is the point Saul misses: the whole arrangement exists so that this cannot become a raid for cattle.

Now the honest half. None of that makes child and infant a comfortable sentence, and it is not faithlessness to feel the weight of it. Scripture does not ask readers to pretend. What it does is refuse to let the reader think the judgment was arbitrary, or racial, or hasty, and it insists throughout that Israel deserved no better and was told so plainly (Deut. 9:4-6).

One thing more, and it is not a template. This is a specific command, to one king, at one moment, about one nation under a sworn judgment. Nothing in the New Testament permits a Christian to reason from it to anything, and Paul closes the door explicitly: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul musters two hundred and ten thousand men and lies in wait in the valley (vv. 4-5). First he sends a warning to the Kenites to get clear, for you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt (v. 6). Then he defeats Amalek from Havilah to Shur (v. 7), takes Agag alive, and devotes the people to destruction (v. 8). But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The Kenites are Jethro's people, and Saul's reasoning about them is exactly right: the judgment is for what Amalek did, and the Kenites did the opposite. He understood the principle perfectly on the morning of the battle.
verseByVerse.examples: Which makes verse 9 what it is. Read the two halves: they kept everything good and destroyed everything worthless. That is not squeamishness about killing and it is not mercy. It is a valuation, carried out with care, and the obedience stopped exactly where the value began.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul summoned the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand men on foot, and ten thousand men of Judah. And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley. Then Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, depart; go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Saul summoned the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand men on foot, and ten thousand men of Judah. And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley.'

Two hundred and ten thousand men, and Judah counted separately again.

He does the military work properly: musters, moves, and sets an ambush in the valley. Whatever else this chapter shows, Saul was competent at this.

'Then Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, depart; go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.'

Before the attack, he clears the innocent out of the way.

The Kenites are Jethro's people — Moses' father-in-law's clan, who came up with Judah into the wilderness and settled among Israel (Judg. 1:16). Jael, who put a tent peg through Sisera's head, was a Kenite.

Look at Saul's reasoning, because it is exactly right. The Amalekites are under judgment for what they did to Israel on the way when they came up out of Egypt. The Kenites showed kindness to Israel when they came up out of Egypt. Same period, same journey, opposite conduct, opposite treatment.

He has understood the principle perfectly. The judgment is not about who these people are but about what they did, and a clan living among Amalek who behaved differently is not to be touched. He sends a warning ahead so they can get clear.

Nothing in this book shows Saul thinking more clearly than he does in verse 6. Which is exactly why the next three verses are what they are.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt. And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive and devoted to destruction all the people with the edge of the sword. But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt.'

The campaign is a success across a great sweep of desert country.

'And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive and devoted to destruction all the people with the edge of the sword.'

All the people, and the king alive.

'But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.'

Read the two halves of that verse against each other, because the whole chapter is in the comparison.

Spared: Agag, the best sheep, the best oxen, the fattened calves, the lambs — and the summary, all that was good.

Destroyed: all that was despised and worthless.

That is not a man who found the order too hard to carry out. It is not squeamishness about killing; he killed everything without economic value, and the text says he did it thoroughly. It is a valuation. Somebody went through the herds picking out the fat calves and the good breeding stock, and put the sword through the scrawny ones.

The word for what he would not do is utterly destroy — the ban again, and the whole purpose of the ban was that nobody should profit from the judgment. Saul kept the profit and executed the rubbish.

Note also who is named first: Saul and the people. In a few verses he will put the people first and himself nowhere.

Note what obedience looked like here. He went where he was sent, he fought whom he was told to fight, he won, he spared the Kenites correctly, he destroyed the Amalekites as commanded, and he kept the good livestock. On any ordinary reckoning that is ninety-five per cent of the instruction.

The chapter is about the five per cent, and about what selecting it reveals.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — The Bleating of the Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not performed my commandments — and Samuel is angry and cries to the LORD all night (vv. 10-11). In the morning he learns that Saul has gone to Carmel and set up a monument for himself before going down to Gilgal (v. 12). Saul greets him: blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD (v. 13). And Samuel answers with a question that needs no argument: what then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear? (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The monument is the tell. The man who was found hiding among the baggage on the day of his coronation has put up a stone to himself on the way home from a battle he did not finish.
verseByVerse.examples: And Saul's defence has three moves in one sentence (v. 15): they brought them, the people spared them, and it was to sacrifice to the LORD your God. Blame shifted, a religious motive supplied, and a small distance opened between himself and God.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Samuel: "I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not performed my commandments." And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the LORD all night. And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. And it was told Samuel, "Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself and turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The word of the LORD came to Samuel: "I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not performed my commandments."'

God says he regrets it, and the sentence has troubled readers for a long time. Verse 29 will appear to deny it in the same chapter, and both are dealt with there.

What matters here is the reason given, and it is put in two clauses. Saul has turned back from following me, and he has not performed my commandments. A direction and a duty: he has faced round, and he has not done what he was told.

'And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the LORD all night.'

The prophet does not receive the news calmly.

He is angry — and the text does not say with whom. And he spends the night crying out to God, which suggests he spent it pleading for the man.

Remember that Samuel had opposed the monarchy from the start, was personally rejected in the asking of it, and had told the nation on coronation day that the whole thing was a sin. He has every reason to feel vindicated by this news. Instead he is up all night about it.

The last verse of the chapter tells us this never stopped: Samuel grieved over Saul.

'And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. And it was told Samuel, "Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself and turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."'

Now the detail that tells us where the man has got to.

He set up a monument for himself.

The Hebrew is literally a hand — a standing stone, a marker, the kind of thing raised to keep a name alive. Absalom will put one up for the same reason and the writer will say so plainly: I have no son to keep my name in remembrance (2 Sam. 18:18).

Now put it beside chapter 10. On the day of his coronation this man could not be found, and God had to tell the assembly that he was hiding among the baggage. He told his own uncle nothing about the kingdom. He held his peace when men publicly insulted him.

He is now erecting a monument to himself on the road home from a battle he did not finish.

The stones in this book have all been about God up to now. Samuel set one up at Mizpah and called it till now the LORD has helped us (7:12). There is a great stone in a wheatfield at Beth-shemesh that marks where the ark came home. Saul's stone has his own name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD." And Samuel said, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?" Saul said, "They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God, and the rest we have devoted to destruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD."'

He greets the prophet with a blessing and a report, and the report is false.

The question is whether he knows it. He has just built a monument to a victory, the campaign went well, the Amalekites are destroyed, and the livestock in the pens behind him has been earmarked for sacrifice. It is entirely possible that Saul believed this sentence when he said it.

That is what makes the next verse so devastating.

'And Samuel said, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?"'

The line requires no argument whatever.

Samuel does not dispute the claim, or produce a witness, or reason from the law. He simply mentions what can be heard from where they are standing. The evidence is making a noise in the background of the conversation, and it has been the whole time.

There is a warning in the shape of it for anybody who has ever given an account of himself that was technically constructed. Some things cannot be argued away because they are audible.

'Saul said, "They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God, and the rest we have devoted to destruction."'

The defence has three moves in a single sentence, and each one matters.

First: they have brought them, the people spared them. Verse 9 said Saul and the people. The king has removed himself from his own sentence.

Second: to sacrifice to the LORD. The disobedience is re-described as piety. He does not say the animals were valuable; he says they were for worship, which makes the whole thing sound like an excess of devotion rather than a failure of obedience.

Third, and quietest: the LORD your God.

Not our God, and not the LORD my God. Talking to the prophet who anointed him, about a command he was given directly, he refers to God as Samuel's. It is the smallest movement in the sentence and it is the most revealing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stop! says Samuel, and delivers what God said in the night (v. 16). The diagnosis comes first: though you are little in your own eyes, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? (v. 17). Then the charge — why did you not obey, why did you pounce on the spoil (vv. 18-19)? Saul insists I have obeyed the voice of the LORD and describes the disobedience in the next breath (vv. 20-21). And then the oracle: has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice... for rebellion is as the sin of divination... because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 17 is the diagnosis of the whole man. The smallness was real once — the least clan of the smallest tribe, hiding in the luggage — and it has become the excuse. He will say so himself in v. 24: I feared the people.
verseByVerse.examples: Rebellion is as the sin of divination. The comparison is exact, because divination is the attempt to get an outcome out of God without submitting to him — and so is keeping the best of the flock for an offering. And Saul will end his life consulting a medium at Endor (ch. 28), doing literally what Samuel here says he is already doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! I will tell you what the LORD said to me this night." And he said to him, "Speak." And Samuel said, "Though you are little in your own eyes, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel. And the LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go, devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.' Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! I will tell you what the LORD said to me this night." And he said to him, "Speak."'

One word, and it cuts the defence off.

Stop. Samuel will not let the explanation run any further, and what he has to say is not his own assessment: what the LORD said to me this night. The verdict was reached before the conversation started.

'And Samuel said, "Though you are little in your own eyes, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel."'

Here is the diagnosis of the whole man, in one question.

Though you are little in your own eyes.

It was true, and it was once his best quality. He told Samuel he was from the least clan of the smallest tribe (9:21). He hid among the baggage (10:22). He said nothing to his uncle about the kingdom, and nothing to the men who insulted him.

Samuel is not praising it here. He is naming it as the problem.

Because the smallness has stopped being humility and started being an excuse. A man who thinks of himself as little does not have to answer for what happens on his watch; the people wanted the sheep, and who is he to stop them? Verse 24 will have Saul say it in his own words: I feared the people.

There is the danger in a self-image of insignificance, and it is not usually seen as a danger at all. It looks like modesty and it functions as an exemption. Are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? You are not little. You were made responsible, and being frightened of the people you are responsible for is not humility.

'"And the LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go, devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.' Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD?"'

The order is quoted back to him and then two questions are put.

Note the verb in the second one: why did you pounce on the spoil? It is the word used one chapter ago of the starving army at the end of the day of the oath — the people pounced on the spoil and ate the meat with the blood (14:32).

Saul had rebuked them for that. Samuel now uses the same verb of the king, and there is no excuse of hunger this time.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul said to Samuel, "I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have devoted the Amalekites to destruction. But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the things devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Saul said to Samuel, "I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have devoted the Amalekites to destruction."'

He says it again, and this time he lists the evidence.

I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. Four first-person claims in two sentences: I have obeyed, I have gone, I have brought, I have devoted. And one of the four is the disobedience itself — I have brought Agag — offered as proof of compliance.

He has been told he did not obey. He answers by asserting that he did, in more detail.

'"But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the things devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal."'

Then but, and the exception describes exactly what he was just accused of.

He says the best of the things devoted to destruction. He knows they were under the ban; he uses the technical term. And the same three moves come round again: the people did it, it was for sacrifice, and it is the LORD your God.

This is the state the chapter is diagnosing, and it is worse than lying. A man who lies knows what he is covering. Saul appears able to say I have obeyed and then narrate the disobedience without the two colliding, because the exception has been filed under something else — the people's doing, and a religious purpose — and once filed there it does not count against the claim.

Anyone who has ever given a completely honest account of a matter and left one thing in a different category will recognise the mechanism.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said, "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samuel said, "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams."'

Now the summit of the chapter, and one of the great sentences of the Old Testament.

Take first what it is not saying. It is not a rejection of sacrifice. Samuel is a man who has offered burnt offerings all his life, at Mizpah and Gilgal and Ramah; the whole system was God's own arrangement. The form is not being attacked.

What is being attacked is the idea that the form can be used to buy off the substance.

Saul's plan was to take what God had placed under the ban and put it on God's altar. He was going to disobey and then worship with the proceeds. And Samuel asks the question that destroys it: does the LORD delight in offerings as much as in being obeyed?

The prophets will say this for the next four hundred years and they will keep saying it because it keeps being needed. I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (Hos. 6:6). What does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? (Mic. 6:8). You will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it... the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit (Ps. 51:16-17). And Jesus quotes Hosea twice into arguments with the Pharisees (Matt. 9:13; 12:7).

The reason it keeps being needed is that religion is the most convenient thing in the world to substitute for obedience. It is measurable, it is public, it feels like devotion, and it can be increased. A man who will not do the thing God has actually said can always do something else for God instead, and can generally do it generously.

'"For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry."'

Then a comparison that ought to stop anybody.

Rebellion — not idolatry, not blasphemy, but declining to do what God said — is as the sin of divination.

The comparison is exact, and it is not rhetorical exaggeration. Divination is the attempt to get something out of the spiritual world on your own terms: to secure an outcome, obtain information or manage a god, without submitting to him. It treats the divine as a resource.

That is precisely what Saul has done. He kept what God put under the ban and proposed to hand some of it back as an offering — God as a party to be managed, with a share.

A terrible thing is waiting at the end of this book. The man being told here that rebellion is like divination will finish his life, thirteen chapters from now, in a house at Endor after dark, asking a medium to bring up a dead prophet, because the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets (28:6). Samuel names the character of his sin here. Saul eventually performs it literally.

'"Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king."'

Then the sentence, and it is built as an exchange.

You rejected. He has rejected. The same verb both ways, and the second follows the first.

Hear it against chapter 8, where God said of the nation's demand for a king, they have rejected me from being king over them (8:7). Israel rejected God as king and asked for a man; the man has now rejected God's word and is himself rejected. The whole experiment has come round in seven chapters.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul confesses, and the confession is accurate: I have sinned... because I feared the people and obeyed their voice (v. 24). But the request attached to it is about appearances — pardon my sin and return with me (v. 25). Samuel refuses (v. 26). As he turns to go, Saul grabs at his robe and the hem tears, and Samuel makes the accident the sign: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (vv. 27-28). And then: the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man, that he should have regret (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: He was told to obey the voice of the LORD and he obeyed the voice of the people. That is the exact inversion of the office, and it is his own account of himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 29 stands eighteen verses after I regret that I have made Saul king, in the same chapter, from the same prophet. The two are not an oversight. God genuinely grieves and genuinely turns in response to what people do; what he is not is fickle, or a man who can be talked round.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice. Now therefore, please pardon my sin and return with me that I may bow before the LORD." And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice."'

Now he says it, and the analysis is exactly right.

I have sinned. No qualification this time, no the people took, no your God. And then the reason, which is the truest sentence Saul speaks in the chapter: because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.

Read that against the office he held. He was told at the outset to listen to the words of the LORD (v. 1). He obeyed the voice of the people instead. It is the precise inversion of the job.

There is an irony in the phrase that the writer surely intends. In chapter 8, three times, God told Samuel to obey their voice and give them a king. Now the king they were given explains his ruin with the same words.

Fear of people is the most respectable of the ruling passions, because it can always be described as consideration. Saul is not accused of arrogance here or of cruelty. He was frightened of the men he was supposed to lead, and it cost him a kingdom.

'"Now therefore, please pardon my sin and return with me that I may bow before the LORD."'

Two requests, and the second one is the trouble.

Pardon my sin is right. Return with me is about being seen. He wants the prophet standing beside him when he bows, and verse 30 will say why in as many words.

'And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel."'

Samuel refuses, and repeats the verdict without softening a word of it.

verseByVerse.quote: As Samuel turned to go away, Saul seized the skirt of his robe, and it tore. And Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you. And also the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man, that he should have regret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As Samuel turned to go away, Saul seized the skirt of his robe, and it tore.'

He grabs at the old man's coat as he walks off, and a piece comes away in his hand.

It is an accident, and it is the desperate physical action of somebody who cannot let a conversation end. And Samuel turns it into the sign.

'And Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you."'

Torn, and the word is the one that just happened in the air between them.

Keep this scene, because the robe comes back. Nine chapters from now Saul will be hunting David through the wilderness and will go into a cave to relieve himself, and David will creep up and cut off the skirt of Saul's robe — and then his heart will strike him for even doing that much to the LORD's anointed (24:4-5).

The same garment, the same gesture, and the two men the opposite way round.

Mark a neighbour of yours, who is better than you. Not named, not described, and already living somewhere in the same country. Saul will spend the rest of his life trying to find out who.

'"And also the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man, that he should have regret."'

Now the difficulty, and it should be faced rather than managed.

Eighteen verses ago God said I regret that I have made Saul king (v. 11). The last verse of the chapter will say it again: the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel (v. 35). And here, in the middle, the same prophet says God does not have regret because he is not a man.

The word is the same in all three places. This is not a slip; the writer has put the contradiction inside a single chapter deliberately, and it means the two statements are answering different questions.

Verse 29 denies that God is like a man. Men change their minds because they were misinformed, or because they were talked round, or because they are inconsistent; men make promises and then wish they had not. God is none of that. He cannot be argued out of a position or surprised into one, and what he has sworn stands.

Verses 11 and 35 say something else: that God is not indifferent to what happens. He is not a mechanism running a plan with nothing in it. Something in him turns when a man he raised up turns away. The word for it is grief.

Both are true and Scripture will not let go of either. Take one alone and you get a God who is either fickle or frozen, and the Bible presents neither.

Note where each sits in the chapter. The unchangeableness is applied to the verdict — the kingdom is gone and there is no point asking again. The regret is applied to the person. God's sentence on Saul is settled, and God's sorrow over Saul is real, and the chapter ends on the sorrow.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people (v. 30). Samuel goes back with him, and Saul bows (v. 31). Then Agag is brought, walking cheerfully, saying surely the bitterness of death is past — and Samuel answers him and hacks him to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal (vv. 32-33). The two men part, Samuel to Ramah and Saul to Gibeah, and do not meet again (v. 34). But Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 30 is the whole man in one sentence. He has just admitted the sin, and what he asks for next is to be honoured in front of the elders. The confession is real and the concern underneath it has not moved.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends on two griefs and neither is Saul's. The prophet mourned him, and God regretted him — and the man himself went home to Gibeah. Note also that the one Amalekite Saul spared has a descendant: Haman the Agagite (Esth. 3:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow before the LORD your God." So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed before the LORD. Then Samuel said, "Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalekites." And Agag came to him cheerfully. Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past." And Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then he said, "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow before the LORD your God."'

Here is the whole man in one sentence.

He begins with a real confession — I have sinned, said for the second time and with nothing attached to soften it. And then yet, and what follows the yet is what he actually wants.

Honour me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.

Not help me, not pray for me, not what shall I do. He has just been told the kingdom is torn from him, and his concern is that the prophet should not be seen walking away from him in front of the leadership.

Once more, the LORD your God, in the same breath as the request to be allowed to bow before him.

It would be easy to conclude that the confession was therefore false, and that is probably too quick. Both things are in him. He knows he has sinned and says so twice, and he cannot stop thinking about how it looks. Most people are that mixture; Saul is simply a man whose version of it was recorded.

'So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed before the LORD.'

Samuel goes with him, which is the last kindness he does him.

He had refused twice. He goes anyway, and stands beside a rejected king in front of the elders while the man worships. He does not withdraw the verdict, and he does not humiliate him in public.

'Then Samuel said, "Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalekites." And Agag came to him cheerfully. Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."'

Then the prophet finishes the job the king would not.

Agag comes in confidently — he has been alive for days now, a captive king kept back from the slaughter, and he has evidently concluded that he is going to live. Surely the bitterness of death is past.

'And Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.'

The sentence Samuel pronounces is exact and it is judicial: as your sword has made women childless. This is not the execution of a prisoner of war for being on the losing side. It is the last act of a four-hundred-year case, and the charge is what Agag's own sword did.

The verb for what Samuel does is brutal and the text does not soften it. An old prophet butchers a king in pieces at a sanctuary, and the writer says it happened before the LORD.

It is hard reading and it is meant to be. What it establishes is that the ban was not a formality that could be quietly dropped once the fighting was over — Saul had treated it as one, and somebody had to do what he would not.

A long shadow falls here. Centuries later, in a Persian palace, a man is promoted above all the officials of the empire and sets out to exterminate every Jew in a hundred and twenty-seven provinces. The writer of that book gives his name with a label attached: Haman the Agagite (Esth. 3:1).

The one Amalekite Saul kept alive has a descendant, and the descendant nearly finishes what Rephidim started.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul. And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul.'

Two old men go home in opposite directions, and the working relationship between prophet and king is over.

Note the town's name as the writer gives it: Gibeah of Saul. Not Gibeah of Benjamin, as it was in chapter 13. The place has taken his name now, like the monument at Carmel.

'And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul.'

They never meet again.

The phrase needs a word of explanation, because Saul does appear before Samuel at Ramah in chapter 19, and something of Samuel appears to Saul at Endor in chapter 28. The sense is that Samuel never again sought him out, and there was no further dealing between them as prophet and king. The formal relationship ends here.

Then three words that change the tone of the whole chapter: Samuel grieved over Saul.

Sit with them for a moment. This is the man Saul replaced, who was rejected by the nation in Saul's favour, who warned against the monarchy from the beginning and was proved right in every particular. He had every human ground for satisfaction.

He mourned him instead, and went on mourning until God had to tell him to stop: how long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? (16:1).

Samuel had said at his farewell that ceasing to pray for these people would be a sin against the LORD (12:23). This is what that looks like when the person concerned has failed beyond recovery.

'And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.'

The last sentence of the chapter is God's grief, not his anger.

The verdict was delivered in verse 23 and it does not move. But the chapter does not end on the verdict. It ends on the same word it used in verse 11, and it is the word for something turning inside a person: God was sorry.

That is the last thing said about the rejection of Saul, and it should govern how the rest of his story is read. He is not written off with contempt by the God who rejected him. He is grieved over.

Now take the great sentence of this chapter and follow it to the end of the Bible, because it has one.

To obey is better than sacrifice. Israel's tragedy, restated by prophet after prophet, is that the two kept coming apart — a nation offering rams while doing as it pleased, and kings building monuments to themselves on the way home from half-finished obedience.

They came together once. The letter to the Hebrews puts Psalm 40 into the mouth of Christ at his coming into the world: sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me... Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. And then the writer draws the conclusion himself: he does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb. 10:5-10).

Obedience and sacrifice, which Saul tried to trade against each other, turn out in the end to be the same act, performed by one person, once.

15.theology:
The ban, honestly. The ground is moral and not ethnic, an act named with the manner of it on record; four centuries stand between the crime and the sentence; and Amalek did not stop, appearing in three separate campaigns in Judges alone (3:13; 6:3; 7:12). The whole point of the herem is that nobody profits — which is exactly what Saul missed. None of that makes child and infant comfortable, and it is not faithlessness to feel it. And it is not a template: a specific command, to one king, at one moment, about one nation under a sworn judgment. The weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4).

Verse 9 is a valuation. Kept: the best sheep, the best oxen, the fattened calves, all that was good. Destroyed: all that was despised and worthless. He killed everything without economic value and did it thoroughly. On any ordinary reckoning he obeyed ninety-five per cent of the instruction, and the chapter is about the five per cent and about what selecting it reveals.

Little in your own eyes (v. 17). It was true and it was once his best quality — the least clan, the baggage, the silence under insult. Samuel names it as the problem, because it has stopped being humility and become an exemption. A man who thinks of himself as little need not answer for what happens on his watch. I feared the people (v. 24) is his own word for it, and fear of people is the most respectable of the ruling passions because it can always be described as consideration.

To obey is better than sacrifice (v. 22). Not a rejection of sacrifice — Samuel offered them all his life and the system was God's own arrangement. What is attacked is using the form to buy off the substance: Saul meant to disobey and then worship with the proceeds. The prophets say it for four hundred years because it keeps being needed (Hos. 6:6; Mic. 6:8; Ps. 51:16-17), and Jesus quotes Hosea into two arguments (Matt. 9:13; 12:7). Religion is the most convenient thing in the world to substitute for obedience: measurable, public, felt as devotion, and capable of being increased.

Rebellion as divination (v. 23). The comparison is exact and not rhetorical. Divination is the attempt to get something from the spiritual world on your own terms without submitting — treating the divine as a resource — which is precisely what keeping the banned livestock and offering God a share amounts to. And thirteen chapters later Saul is in a house at Endor after dark asking a medium to raise a dead prophet (28:6). Samuel names the character of his sin; Saul eventually performs it literally.

Regret, and no regret (vv. 11, 29, 35). The same word three times in one chapter, and the contradiction is deliberate. Verse 29 denies that God is like a man: he cannot be misinformed, talked round, or surprised, and what he has sworn stands. Verses 11 and 35 deny that he is indifferent: something in him turns when a man he raised up turns away, and the word for it is grief. Take either alone and you get a God who is fickle or frozen, and Scripture presents neither. Note where each sits: the unchangeableness is applied to the verdict, the regret to the person.

Where it ends. The chapter closes not on the sentence but on two griefs, and neither is Saul's — Samuel grieved over Saul, until God had to tell him to stop (16:1), and the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king. He is not written off with contempt by the God who rejected him. And the great sentence has an end in the New Testament: obedience and sacrifice, which Saul tried to trade against each other, turn out to be the same act, performed by one person, once. Behold, I have come to do your will, O God... and by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb. 10:5-10).
15.examples:
Then: A king carried out a four-hundred-year-old judgment carefully, warned the innocent clear beforehand on exactly the right principle, destroyed everything that had no resale value, kept the good breeding stock for a sacrifice, put up a monument to himself on the way home, and greeted the prophet with I have performed the commandment of the LORD while the sheep were bleating behind him.

Now: Three things. Verse 14 is the test for any account of yourself that has been carefully constructed: some things cannot be argued away because they are audible. Verse 17 is the uncomfortable one — a low view of yourself can function as an exemption from responsibility, and being frightened of the people you are answerable for is not humility. And verse 22 is the standing danger of a religious life: when God has said something you will not do, there is always something else you can do for him instead, and you can generally do it generously.

16.title: The LORD Looks on the Heart
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons."<sup>2</sup>And Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me." And the LORD said, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.'<sup>3</sup>And invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. And you shall anoint for me him whom I declare to you."<sup>4</sup>Samuel did what the LORD commanded and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, "Do you come peaceably?"<sup>5</sup>And he said, "Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice." And he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.<sup>6</sup>When they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed is before him."<sup>7</sup>But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."<sup>8</sup>Then Jesse called Abinadab and made him pass before Samuel. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one."<sup>9</sup>Then Jesse made Shammah pass by. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one."<sup>10</sup>And Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel. And Samuel said to Jesse, "The LORD has not chosen these."<sup>11</sup>Then Samuel said to Jesse, "Are all your sons here?" And he said, "There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep." And Samuel said to Jesse, "Send and get him, for we will not sit down till he comes here."<sup>12</sup>And he sent and brought him in. Now he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome. And the LORD said, "Arise, anoint him, for this is he."<sup>13</sup>Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. And Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.<sup>14</sup>Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him.<sup>15</sup>And Saul's servants said to him, "Behold now, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you.<sup>16</sup>Let our lord now command your servants who are before you to seek out a man who is skillful in playing the lyre, and when the harmful spirit from God is upon you, he will play it, and you will be well."<sup>17</sup>So Saul said to his servants, "Provide for me a man who can play well and bring him to me."<sup>18</sup>One of the young men answered, "Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, who is skillful in playing, a man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a man of good presence, and the LORD is with him."<sup>19</sup>Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me David your son, who is with the sheep."<sup>20</sup>And Jesse took a donkey laden with bread and a skin of wine and a young goat and sent them by David his son to Saul.<sup>21</sup>And David came to Saul and entered his service. And Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer.<sup>22</sup>And Saul sent to Jesse, saying, "Let David remain in my service, for he has found favor in my sight."<sup>23</sup>And whenever the harmful spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand. So Saul was refreshed and was well, and the harmful spirit departed from him.
16.overview:
God has to tell Samuel to stop mourning — the grief was right, and it has outlasted its usefulness — and the cure is an errand: fill your horn and go to Bethlehem, for I have provided for myself a king, which in Hebrew is I have seen for myself a king. Seeing is what this chapter is about, and God has already done it before Samuel sets out. Two details show the state of the country: the prophet is afraid the king will murder him, and a town's elders come out trembling when he arrives.

Then the prophet makes exactly the mistake the nation made. He sees Eliab and is certain — and God stops him with a phrase that is a quotation: do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature. That is Saul's description, twice over (9:2; 10:23). This is not a general remark about human vanity; it is a correction of the criterion that produced the last king, delivered to the man who anointed him.

Seven sons pass and none is chosen. And the answer to are all your sons here? is the most revealing sentence in the chapter: there remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep. Jesse did not bring him. He was not consecrated, not invited, and not mentioned until the prophet asked directly. Then a prophet, a town's elders and seven grown men stood and waited while somebody fetched him.

The Spirit rushes on David from that day forward — and the very next sentence says the Spirit departed from Saul. The same Spirit, opposite directions, consecutive verses, and neither man knows. The chapter ends with the rejected king kept well by the music of his replacement, whom he has made his armour-bearer, and whom Saul loved greatly.
16.theology:
The LORD looks on the heart (v. 7). Two things follow and they pull opposite ways. The comfort is enormous: God is not assessing you on what everybody else assesses you on — height, looks, presence, birth order, all of which were working for Eliab and none of which counted. The discomfort is that if God looks on the heart, he is looking at the one part of you nobody has ever seen, and a reputation can be managed where a heart cannot be tidied for a visit. David, chosen by this standard, will fail catastrophically by it and write the only prayer that answers it (Ps. 51:10). And note that Samuel does not acquire the ability: told the principle in v. 7, he still has to be given the answer in v. 12. Seeing the heart is God's work, not a skill.

A different criterion, not the opposite one (v. 12). The narrator describes David's looks five verses after saying looks are not the instrument, and the tension should be named. God does not prefer unattractive people and David was not chosen despite being handsome. Appearance simply is not the measure — Eliab was probably handsome too, and was refused on a ground nobody in the room could see.

Jesse did not bring him (v. 11). Seven sons consecrated and invited, and the eighth left with the sheep, unmentioned until the prophet asked whether that was everybody. The reason given is true and is the kind of true reason that gets given about the member of a family nobody considers a candidate for anything.

From that day forward (v. 13). The verb is Samson's and Saul's — a sudden seizing — but the phrase is new in this book. The Spirit rushed on Samson repeatedly and left; it clothed Gideon for a campaign; it came on Saul in bursts. Here it comes and stays.

A harmful spirit from the LORD (v. 14). Scripture speaks this way more than once — the lying spirit sent against Ahab (1 Kings 22:19-23), Satan afflicting Job within stated limits (Job 1:12; 2:6) — and never says God is the author of evil (Jas. 1:13). It holds a sovereign who governs what opposes him without being implicated, and does not explain the mechanism. What the verse does make plain is the order: the Spirit left, and something occupied the space (cf. Matt. 12:43-45). ⚠️ And this text must not be used to read depression or mental illness as demonic oppression. It is a specific judgment on a specific man after a prophetic rejection; a great deal of harm has been done by people who thought otherwise. Note too that the remedy is not exorcism. It is music.

Saul loved him greatly (v. 21). It is easy to read the coming chapters as though Saul were an enemy from the start. He was not. He met this young man, liked him, loved him, and gave him the position of closest personal trust in the army. Everything that follows — the spear, the daughter used as a trap, the three thousand men in the wilderness, the priests of Nob, Endor — begins here.

Where verse 7 ends up. God looked past seven consecrated sons and sent for the one nobody had invited: God chose what is low and despised in the world (1 Cor. 1:28). A thousand years later the birth of the true King was announced in the fields outside this same town, to shepherds. And the King himself was somebody the eye would pass over — he had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isa. 53:2). Man looks on the outward appearance. Everybody did, and missed him.
16.examples:
Then: A father consecrated seven sons for a sacrifice conducted by the most important man in Israel and did not send for the eighth, because somebody had to mind the sheep. The prophet worked through the whole family, found nobody, and then refused to sit down until the boy who had not been invited was fetched in from the field.

Now: Three things. Verse 7 cuts both ways and both should be felt: God is not using the instrument the world uses on you, and he is using one you cannot manage. Verse 11 is for anyone who has been the person not sent for — and note that David was not sulking about it; he was doing the job he had been left with, which is where the messenger found him. And verse 21 is the warning: Saul's ruin did not begin in hatred. It began with a man he genuinely loved doing well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — How Long Will You Grieve?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has to tell Samuel to stop mourning: how long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn and go to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons (v. 1). Samuel's objection is startling: how can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me (v. 2). God gives him a sacrifice to conduct and tells him he will be shown what to do (vv. 2-3). And when he reaches Bethlehem the elders come out trembling, asking whether he comes peaceably (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb provided in v. 1 is literally seen: I have seen for myself a king. Seeing is what this chapter is about, and God has already done it before anybody sets out.
verseByVerse.examples: Two details tell you the state of the country. The prophet of Israel is afraid the king will murder him, and the elders of a small town tremble when he arrives, because a prophet turning up unannounced generally meant somebody was in trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons." And Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me." And the LORD said, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.' And invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. And you shall anoint for me him whom I declare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel?"'

The prophet has to be told to stop mourning.

The last verse of the previous chapter said Samuel grieved over Saul, and enough time has now passed that God interrupts it. Not to rebuke him for having a heart — the grief was right, and God's own regret is recorded in the same verse — but because there is work to do and Samuel has stopped.

Grief has a proper length and it can outlast its usefulness. The man had every reason for his, and the question how long is put to him kindly and firmly, and it is followed immediately by an errand.

'"Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons."'

The cure for the grieving is a journey, and the last clause is the sentence to watch.

I have provided for myself a king — and the Hebrew verb is see. I have seen for myself a king among his sons.

Keep that, because seeing is what this chapter is about. God has already looked at Jesse's household and made his choice before Samuel has filled the horn, and by verse 7 the difference between God's looking and everybody else's will be the point of the whole passage.

Note also for myself. The last king was provided for Israel, because Israel asked. This one God has seen for his own purposes.
