'And Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me."'

The prophet is frightened of the king.

Take in what that tells us. Samuel anointed this man, crowned him, rebuked him twice and pronounced his rejection to his face. He is the most senior figure in Israel. And he now says plainly that if Saul learns of this journey he will be murdered.

He is not being cowardly; he is being accurate. The man who will shortly throw a spear at a boy playing the lyre, and who will one day order the slaughter of eighty-five priests and their whole town, is entirely capable of it.

'And the LORD said, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.' And invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. And you shall anoint for me him whom I declare to you."'

God gives him a way to travel safely, and it needs saying straight what it is.

It is not a lie. Samuel really does take a heifer, really does sacrifice, and really does invite Jesse; when the elders ask why he has come he tells them the truth and the sacrifice happens. What he does not do is announce the second purpose to a hostile court.

There is a difference between deceiving a man and declining to brief him, and Scripture is comfortable with it in a way that anxious readers sometimes are not. The midwives in Egypt, Rahab on the wall, and here a prophet under a king who kills people: none of them is required to publish his itinerary to those who mean harm.

Mark how little Samuel is told. Go to Jesse. One of his sons. I will show you what you shall do, and him whom I declare to you. He sets out knowing the town and the family and nothing else, and he will get the name only when the boy is standing in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel did what the LORD commanded and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, "Do you come peaceably?" And he said, "Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice." And he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Samuel did what the LORD commanded and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, "Do you come peaceably?"'

A whole town's leadership comes out shaking.

Here is the other half of the picture in verse 2. The prophet is afraid of the king, and the elders of a small country town are afraid of the prophet — because a man like Samuel arriving unannounced usually meant that somebody was in trouble and there was about to be a reckoning.

He has, after all, recently hacked a king to pieces at Gilgal.

'And he said, "Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice." And he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.'

He reassures them and gives them something to do.

Consecrate yourselves is a real instruction with real content — washing, clean clothes, abstinence, the ordinary preparation for coming near holy things. And then he consecrates Jesse and his sons personally and invites them.

Note the phrase, because the next paragraphs turn on a name that is missing from it: Jesse and his sons.

Bethlehem, incidentally, has appeared in this history before. It is where the Levite's concubine came from, and where Ruth the Moabite came to glean, and where her great-grandson is at this moment out with the sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Man Looks on the Outward Appearance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel sees Eliab and thinks surely the LORD's anointed is before him (v. 6). And God stops him: do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (v. 7). Seven sons pass and none is chosen (vv. 8-10). Are all your sons here? — there remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep (v. 11). They send for him and will not sit down till he comes. Samuel anoints him among his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet makes exactly the mistake the nation made. The height of his stature is the phrase used twice of Saul (9:2; 10:23), and God is not making a general observation — he is correcting the criterion that produced the last king, to the man who anointed him.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesse did not bring him. Seven sons were consecrated and invited and the eighth was left with the sheep, and his own father did not think him worth mentioning until asked directly. Then a prophet, a town's elders and a family stood and waited for a boy to be fetched in from a field.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed is before him." But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed is before him."'

The prophet takes one look at the eldest and is certain.

It is not a foolish conclusion. Eliab is the firstborn, which counted for a great deal; he is evidently impressive; and Samuel has spent his adult life around the business of choosing and anointing. He is the best-qualified man in Israel to make this judgment.

He is also making, in this verse, exactly the mistake the whole nation made in chapter 8.

'But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him."'

Read the phrase God chooses, because it is a quotation.

The height of his stature. When Saul was introduced: from his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people (9:2). When Saul was presented to the nation at his coronation, the narrator repeated it word for word (10:23). Height is the one physical fact this book keeps giving us about the king who has just been rejected.

So God is not offering a general reflection on human vanity. He is correcting the specific criterion that produced Saul, and he is correcting it to the man who anointed Saul, about Saul's replacement, using Saul's own description.

The verb is the verb of chapter 15. I have rejected him is what was said of Saul twice in the rejection oracle (15:23, 26). Eliab is turned down in the same words.

'"For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."'

Here is the verse, and it is one of the load-bearing sentences of the Old Testament.

Take the two halves. Man looks on the outward appearance — and the Hebrew is literally to the eyes, to what is available to the eyes. That is not presented as a wickedness peculiar to Israel in the eleventh century. It is a description of how human assessment works, and the man it is being said to is a prophet who has just done it.

Then the LORD looks on the heart.

Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions, and both are in the verse.

The first is comfort, and it is enormous. God is not assessing you on the things everybody else assesses you on. Not height, not looks, not presence, not the impression you make in a room, not the order you were born in — all of which were working powerfully in Eliab's favour and none of which counted. The people the world does not look at twice are not overlooked by God, because he was never using that instrument.

The second is not comfortable at all. If God looks on the heart, then he is looking at the one part of you that nobody else has ever seen, and the assessment is being made there. A reputation can be managed; the heart cannot be tidied for a visit.

David, who is about to be chosen by this standard, will later fail catastrophically by it, and will write the psalm that asks for the only remedy: create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me (Ps. 51:10).

The chapter is quietly honest that Samuel does not acquire this ability. He is told the principle in verse 7 and still has to be told the answer in verse 12. Seeing the heart is God's work, not a skill a spiritual man develops.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesse called Abinadab and made him pass before Samuel. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one." Then Jesse made Shammah pass by. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one." And Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel. And Samuel said to Jesse, "The LORD has not chosen these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jesse called Abinadab and made him pass before Samuel. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one." Then Jesse made Shammah pass by. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one."'

Two more, and two refusals, and the writer gives them the same sentence twice.

The repetition is doing something. This is not a swift divine selection; it is a slow, public, increasingly awkward procession in front of the whole town, with a prophet saying no to one promising young man after another.

'And Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel. And Samuel said to Jesse, "The LORD has not chosen these."'

Seven, and none.

Seven is the number of completeness in this literature, and that is the point of counting them. Jesse has produced the full set — everybody he considers a possibility, every son he thought worth consecrating and bringing — and the answer is no to all of them.

Put yourself in the room. The sacrifice has been made, the family is standing there, the prophet has worked through the entire family line, and there is nobody left. By any ordinary reckoning the errand has failed and somebody has misheard God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said to Jesse, "Are all your sons here?" And he said, "There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep." And Samuel said to Jesse, "Send and get him, for we will not sit down till he comes here." And he sent and brought him in. Now he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome. And the LORD said, "Arise, anoint him, for this is he." Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. And Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel said to Jesse, "Are all your sons here?" And he said, "There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep."'

The question has to be asked, and the answer is the most revealing sentence in the chapter.

There remains yet the youngest. There is another one.

Jesse was told to consecrate himself and his sons and come to a sacrifice conducted by the most important man in Israel, and he did not send for this one. The boy was not brought, not consecrated, not invited, and not mentioned until the prophet asked directly whether that was everybody.

The word rendered youngest also carries the sense of smallest, least. And the reason given is that somebody has to mind the sheep, which is true, and is the kind of true reason that gets given about the member of a family nobody thinks of as a candidate for anything.

Take it as it stands. David's own father did not consider him worth including in the shortlist of his own sons.

'And Samuel said to Jesse, "Send and get him, for we will not sit down till he comes here."'

The whole gathering waits.

The prophet, the elders of Bethlehem, Jesse, and seven grown men stand about in a field or a courtyard while somebody runs to fetch the boy who was not asked. Nobody sits down. Nobody eats. The sacrifice is on hold.

'And he sent and brought him in. Now he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome. And the LORD said, "Arise, anoint him, for this is he."'

He arrives, and the narrator immediately describes his appearance, five verses after telling us that appearance is not the criterion.

The tension is real and it should be named rather than smoothed over. What the chapter is not saying is that God prefers unattractive people, or that David was chosen despite being good-looking, or that there is virtue in being unimpressive.

What it is saying is that appearance is not the instrument. David happened also to be handsome. It was not why. Eliab was probably handsome too, and it was not why he was refused; he was refused on a ground nobody in the room could see.

The point of verse 7 is not that God uses the opposite criterion from us. It is that he uses a different one altogether.

'Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers.'

Note the vessel, because it is not the one used last time.

Saul was anointed from a flask of oil (10:1) — a small pottery jar. David is anointed from the horn of oil. A horn is the picture of strength all through this book, from the first line of Hannah's song to its last: my horn is exalted in the LORD... he will exalt the horn of his anointed (2:1, 10). The oil comes out of the thing she sang about.

In the midst of his brothers. The seven who were consecrated and invited stand and watch the one who was left with the sheep have oil poured on his head.

Eliab is there. He will be in the army at the valley of Elah in the next chapter, and when his little brother turns up with provisions he will lose his temper with him in front of everyone (17:28). This scene is presumably somewhere behind that.

'And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. And Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.'

The verb is the one used of Samson and of Saul: a sudden seizing.

But the phrase attached to it has not been used before in this book, and it changes everything: from that day forward.

The Spirit rushed on Samson repeatedly and left him; it clothed itself with Gideon for a campaign; it came on Saul at Gibeah and again at Jabesh, in bursts, for occasions. Here it comes and stays.

That is the phrase John the Baptist reaches for when he explains how he knew who Jesus was: I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him... he on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (John 1:32-33). The sign was not the descending. Everybody's Spirit descended. The sign was that it stayed.

Then the last clause, and it is very flat: Samuel rose up and went to Ramah. No ceremony, no proclamation, no announcement to the town. He anoints a shepherd boy in a Bethlehem courtyard and goes home, and David goes back to the sheep.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him (v. 14). His servants propose music, and Saul agrees (vv. 15-17). One of the young men knows exactly who to fetch, and describes him in six phrases: skilful with the lyre, a man of valour, a man of war, prudent in speech, a man of good presence, and the LORD is with him (v. 18). So Saul sends to Jesse for David your son, who is with the sheep (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is the exact mirror of verse 13, and the two stand side by side on purpose. The Spirit rushed upon David from that day forward; the Spirit departed from Saul. One sentence each, in opposite directions, in consecutive verses.
verseByVerse.examples: The servant's list ends where it matters. Five of the six items are accomplishments; the last is the LORD is with him, which is the highest thing this book says about anybody and the only thing on the list nobody can acquire.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him. And Saul's servants said to him, "Behold now, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you. Let our lord now command your servants who are before you to seek out a man who is skillful in playing the lyre, and when the harmful spirit from God is upon you, he will play it, and you will be well."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him.'

Read this verse against the one before it, because they are a matched pair and the writer has put them side by side deliberately.

Verse 13: the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward.

Verse 14: the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul.

Two sentences, consecutive, the same Spirit, opposite directions. The kingdom changes hands in the space between them, and neither man knows it: David has gone back to the flock and Saul is on his throne.

Now the second clause, which is one of the hardest in the book: a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him.

Several things need saying, and none of them makes it easy.

Scripture is willing to speak this way and does so more than once. Micaiah sees the LORD ask who will entice Ahab, and a spirit volunteering to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets, and God saying you are to entice him, and you shall succeed (1 Kings 22:19-23). Satan afflicts Job only within limits God sets and states (Job 1:12; 2:6). The Bible is not embarrassed to say that such things operate under God's hand.

What it never says is that God is the author of evil, or that he does wrong. God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one (Jas. 1:13). The consistent picture is of a sovereign who governs even what opposes him and is never implicated in it, and Scripture holds that without explaining the mechanism.

What the verse does make plain is the order of events. The Spirit left, and then something else occupied the space. Saul is not tormented instead of being abandoned; he is tormented because the place is empty. Jesus describes the same shape in a parable about a house swept and put in order and left unoccupied (Matt. 12:43-45).

One more thing, and it matters pastorally. This verse should not be used to read depression or mental illness as demonic oppression. Saul's case is a specific judgment on a specific man following a specific rejection, announced by a prophet; nothing here licenses a general diagnosis of anybody's darkness, and a good deal of harm has been done by people who thought it did.

Note what the remedy turns out to be. Not an exorcism. Music.

'And Saul's servants said to him, "Behold now, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you. Let our lord now command your servants who are before you to seek out a man who is skillful in playing the lyre, and when the harmful spirit from God is upon you, he will play it, and you will be well."'

His household understands what is happening to him and proposes something practical.

They are not dismissive; they name the trouble accurately, in the same terms the narrator has used. And their suggestion is that a man with a lyre should be found and kept at hand.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul said to his servants, "Provide for me a man who can play well and bring him to me." One of the young men answered, "Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, who is skillful in playing, a man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a man of good presence, and the LORD is with him." Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me David your son, who is with the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Saul said to his servants, "Provide for me a man who can play well and bring him to me."'

The king agrees, and the word he uses is the word from verse 1.

Provide for me a man — the same verb God used when he said I have provided for myself a king, which is literally seen. God saw a king for himself; Saul asks his servants to see him a musician; and it is the same person.

'One of the young men answered, "Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, who is skillful in playing, a man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a man of good presence, and the LORD is with him."'

A servant answers with six phrases, and the last one is not like the others.

Skilful with the lyre; a man of valour; a man of war; prudent in speech; a man of good presence. Five accomplishments, and any recruiting officer would be pleased with the list.

Then: and the LORD is with him.

That is the highest thing this book ever says about anybody. It was said of Samuel when he grew up (3:19), and it will be said of David repeatedly from here to the end of his story. It is also the only item on the list that nobody can acquire, train for or fake, and a servant somewhere in the household had noticed it about a teenager who looked after sheep.

A word about a man of war, because it sits oddly before the next chapter, where David arrives at the army as a boy bringing bread and Saul asks whose son he is.

The likeliest explanation is the simplest: these narratives are arranged by theme as much as by clock, and chapter 16 introduces David to the reader as the man he is going to be. It is also worth noting that what Saul asks in 17:55-58 is not who is this but whose son is this — a question about family, asked because the young man's father is about to be exempted from tax (17:25). Nothing in either chapter needs forcing.

'Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me David your son, who is with the sheep."'

There is the phrase again: who is with the sheep.

It is how his father described him when the prophet asked (v. 11), and it is now how the king of Israel identifies him in an official summons. That is what David is known as. The anointing has happened, the Spirit has come, and to everybody who writes about him he is still the one out with the flock.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — And Saul Loved Him Greatly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesse loads a donkey with bread, wine and a young goat and sends it with David (v. 20). And David came to Saul and entered his service. And Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer (v. 21). Saul asks Jesse to let him stay, for he has found favor in my sight (v. 22). And whenever the harmful spirit came, David played, and Saul was refreshed and was well (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul loved him greatly. Everything that follows — the spear, the pursuit, the three thousand men in the wilderness, the cave, the medium at Endor — begins here, with a king who loved the boy who would replace him and did not know it.
verseByVerse.examples: The last verse is the position at the end of the chapter: the rejected king is being kept well by the music of his successor, who has been made his armour-bearer and stands close enough to be run through.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesse took a donkey laden with bread and a skin of wine and a young goat and sent them by David his son to Saul. And David came to Saul and entered his service. And Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer. And Saul sent to Jesse, saying, "Let David remain in my service, for he has found favor in my sight." And whenever the harmful spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand. So Saul was refreshed and was well, and the harmful spirit departed from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Jesse took a donkey laden with bread and a skin of wine and a young goat and sent them by David his son to Saul.'

The father sends a present with the boy, and the contents are worth a glance.

Bread, wine and a young goat — which is almost exactly what the three pilgrims were carrying at the oak of Tabor on the day of Saul's anointing: three young goats, three loaves of bread, and a skin of wine (10:3).

'And David came to Saul and entered his service. And Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer.'

Four words in the middle of that verse govern the whole rest of the book: Saul loved him greatly.

Stop there before going on, because it is easy to read the coming chapters as though Saul were an enemy from the start. He was not. The king met this young man, and liked him, and loved him, and promoted him to the position of closest personal trust in the army.

An armour-bearer carried a man's weapons, stood beside him in battle, and slept near him. Saul gave David the job Jonathan's unnamed servant had at Michmash: the man at your shoulder.

Everything that follows — the spear at the wall, the daughter used as a trap, the three thousand men combing the wilderness, the priests of Nob, the witch at Endor — begins with a king who loved him.

'And Saul sent to Jesse, saying, "Let David remain in my service, for he has found favor in my sight."'

He writes to the father to keep him permanently, and the phrase is warm: he has found favour in my sight.

Note the last two words, given what the chapter has been about. In my sight — in Saul's eyes. The man whose eyes were the problem has looked at David and approved of him, and he is right, and he does not know what he is looking at.

'And whenever the harmful spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand. So Saul was refreshed and was well, and the harmful spirit departed from him.'

Here is the position at the close of the chapter, and it is one of the strangest in Scripture.

A rejected king, tormented in the empty place where the Spirit used to be, is being kept well by the music of the boy who has been anointed to replace him — who plays for him whenever it comes on, and it works, and the king is refreshed.

Weigh what David is doing here, because it is the pattern of his whole life. He has been anointed king by the prophet of Israel. He could say so. Instead he carries another man's weapons, plays for him when the darkness comes, and waits — holding a right he does not grasp at, in the form of a servant (cf. Phil. 2:6-7).

Neither of them can see the whole picture. Saul does not know who this is. David has been anointed and is a servant. And for a while — and it is not a short while — the two of them live like this: the man who has lost everything soothed nightly by the man who is going to receive it.

Now stand back from the chapter, because its great verse has an end that is not in this book.

God looked past seven consecrated sons standing in a row and sent for a boy nobody had invited, who was out with the sheep, whose own father had not thought to mention him. That is the criterion of verse 7 in action, and it is entirely characteristic. God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are (1 Cor. 1:28).

A thousand years later, in the fields outside this same town, the announcement that the true King had been born was made to shepherds — not to the priesthood, or the court, or anybody who had been invited to anything.

The King himself, when he came, was somebody the eye would have passed over: he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isa. 53:2). Man looks on the outward appearance. Everybody did, and missed him.

17.title: The Battle Is the LORD's
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines gathered their armies for battle. And they were gathered at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.<sup>2</sup>And Saul and the men of Israel were gathered, and encamped in the Valley of Elah, and drew up in line of battle against the Philistines.<sup>3</sup>And the Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with a valley between them.<sup>4</sup>And there came out from the camp of the Philistines a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.<sup>5</sup>He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail, and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze.<sup>6</sup>And he had bronze armor on his legs, and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders.<sup>7</sup>The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. And his shield-bearer went before him.<sup>8</sup>He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.<sup>9</sup>If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us."<sup>10</sup>And the Philistine said, "I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, that we may fight together."<sup>11</sup>When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.<sup>12</sup>Now David was the son of an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, named Jesse, who had eight sons. In the days of Saul the man was already old and advanced in years.<sup>13</sup>The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the battle. And the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah.<sup>14</sup>David was the youngest. The three eldest followed Saul,<sup>15</sup>but David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem.<sup>16</sup>For forty days the Philistine came forward and took his stand, morning and evening.<sup>17</sup>And Jesse said to David his son, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers.<sup>18</sup>Also take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them."<sup>19</sup>Now Saul and they and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.<sup>20</sup>And David rose early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper and took the provisions and went, as Jesse had commanded him. And he came to the encampment as the host was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.<sup>21</sup>And Israel and the Philistines drew up for battle, army against army.<sup>22</sup>And David left the things in charge of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the ranks and went and greeted his brothers.<sup>23</sup>As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same words as before. And David heard him.<sup>24</sup>All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid.<sup>25</sup>And the men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. And the king will enrich the man who kills him with great riches and will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel."<sup>26</sup>And David said to the men who stood by him, "What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?"<sup>27</sup>And the people answered him in the same way, "So shall it be done to the man who kills him."<sup>28</sup>Now Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spoke to the men. And Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, "Why have you come down? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle."<sup>29</sup>And David said, "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?"<sup>30</sup>And he turned away from him toward another, and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him again as before.<sup>31</sup>When the words that David spoke were heard, they repeated them before Saul, and he sent for him.<sup>32</sup>And David said to Saul, "Let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine."<sup>33</sup>And Saul said to David, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth."<sup>34</sup>But David said to Saul, "Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. And when there came a lion, or a bear, and took a lamb from the flock,<sup>35</sup>I went after him and struck him and delivered it out of his mouth. And if he arose against me, I caught him by his beard and struck him and killed him.<sup>36</sup>Your servant has struck down both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God."<sup>37</sup>And David said, "The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you!"<sup>38</sup>Then Saul clothed David with his armor. He put a helmet of bronze on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail,<sup>39</sup>and David strapped his sword over his armor. And he tried in vain to go, for he had not tested them. Then David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them." So David put them off.<sup>40</sup>Then he took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his shepherd's pouch. His sling was in his hand, and he approached the Philistine.<sup>41</sup>And the Philistine moved forward and came near to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him.<sup>42</sup>And when the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance.<sup>43</sup>And the Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.<sup>44</sup>The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."<sup>45</sup>Then David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.<sup>46</sup>This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. And I will give the dead bodies of the host of the Philistines this day to the birds of the air and to the wild beasts of the earth, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,<sup>47</sup>and that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand."<sup>48</sup>When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.<sup>49</sup>And David put his hand in his bag and took out a stone and slung it and struck the Philistine on his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground.<sup>50</sup>So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him. There was no sword in the hand of David.<sup>51</sup>Then David ran and stood over the Philistine and took his sword and drew it out of its sheath and killed him and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.<sup>52</sup>And the men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron, so that the wounded Philistines fell on the way from Shaaraim as far as Gath and Ekron.<sup>53</sup>And the people of Israel came back from chasing the Philistines, and they plundered their camp.<sup>54</sup>And David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.<sup>55</sup>As soon as Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" And Abner said, "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know."<sup>56</sup>And the king said, "Inquire whose son the boy is."<sup>57</sup>And as soon as David returned from the striking down of the Philistine, Abner took him, and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand.<sup>58</sup>And Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
17.overview:
Two armies on two hills with a valley between, and neither will come down. Out of the Philistine camp comes a champion, itemised like a quartermaster's inventory — bronze five times over, an iron spearhead of fifteen pounds, and a man walking in front to carry his shield. Israel has no blacksmith and two swords in the whole army (13:19-22). He proposes single combat: one man each, and the loser's nation serves. And the first name in the list of the frightened is Saul — the man Israel asked for because he was a head taller than anybody, so that he might go out before them and fight their battles.

Twice a day for forty days. Eighty appearances, long enough for fear to become a routine and an army to organise its day around a humiliation. Then a supply runner arrives on his father's errand, having left the sheep with a keeper and the parcels with the baggage-keeper, and asks two questions. The first is about the reward, and he is not criticised for it. The second changes the chapter: who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?

Everyone else has been doing arithmetic for six weeks. David does a different sum. And everyone who looks at him gets him wrong — Eliab sees presumption and claims to know his heart, which is the one thing 16:7 says only God can see; Saul sees a youth who is not able; Goliath sees somebody ruddy and handsome in appearance, which is 16:12 word for word.

His argument to Saul is not I killed a lion, so I can kill a Philistine. It is the LORD who delivered me... will deliver me — the logic of the stone at Ebenezer. He refuses the king's armour because he has not tested it, takes stones out of a brook, and runs at the giant. And there was no sword in his hand.
17.theology:
The spine of the book, completed. Hannah sang not by might shall a man prevail (2:9) in a corrupt sanctuary with no war on and nobody listening. Jonathan said nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (14:6) at the foot of a cliff with one servant. David says the LORD saves not with sword and spear (17:47) in a valley in front of two armies. Three people, none of them in authority, saying the same thing across sixteen chapters while the nation asks for a king to fight its battles.

The living God (v. 26). Not our God or the God of Israel but the God who is alive — a loaded word in this book, where the last god mentioned had to be picked up off his own temple floor by his own priests and was found the next morning with his head and hands on the doorstep (5:3-4). The question was never whether a boy can beat a giant. It is whether the God whose armies these are is alive.

Everyone judges by the eyes and everyone is wrong. Eliab claims to know the evil of your heart — the one thing 16:7 reserves to God — and his stated grounds are false, since v. 20 says David left the sheep with a keeper. It is a form of attack that is unanswerable by design: not you are wrong, which can be discussed, but I know why you are really doing this. And anger of that kind usually has shame behind it — Eliab has stood in this valley for forty days and not gone down.

Arguing from the record (v. 37). Look at the subject of the verb: the LORD who delivered me... will deliver me. The lion and the bear are not evidence about David's strength but about God's track record, which is exactly what Samuel's stone was for — till now the LORD has helped us (7:12). That reasoning is available to anybody. It requires no special temperament, only a memory and the honesty to keep the record.

Untested armour (v. 39). The objection is not size but unfamiliarity, and David says it twice. The best equipment in the kingdom, offered kindly, would have killed him; his weapons come out of the brook rather than the armoury, and they are the ones he has actually used.

He fell on his face (v. 49). Which is what Dagon did, twice, in front of the ark at Ashdod — and the second time his head was off (5:3-4). Philistia's god and Philistia's champion go down the same way. And there was no sword in the hand of David, so he finishes it with Goliath's own: the weapon that was to take his head takes the giant's. It is a shape the New Testament reaches for at the end — that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).

The champion, and how to read this chapter. Two nations, one representative each, and whatever happens to him happens to everybody. Israel had no answer and stood paralysed for forty days by a perfectly fair arrangement. Then somebody came who was not part of the army, down from the hill on his father's errand, unrecognised, despised by his brother, assessed as inadequate by the king and laughed at by the enemy — and fought alone, without the equipment the situation appeared to require. And the people who contributed nothing rose with a shout and took the plunder home. The usual reading, in which we are David and our problems are Goliath, is exactly backwards. In this valley one person can fight and everybody else is on the hill. The good news of the chapter is not that you can be David; it is that somebody has been.
17.examples:
Then: An army stood on a hillside for six weeks while one man walked out twice a day and shouted at it, and the prize for dealing with him — money, the king's daughter, and permanent tax exemption for a whole household — was common knowledge in the ranks and eighty times a day everybody decided it was not enough.

Now: Three things. First, verse 37 is the most transferable sentence in the chapter, and it is not about courage: David reasoned from what God had actually done, in private, years earlier, with nobody watching. Keep the record; you will want it. Second, verse 39 — when somebody offers you their armour, the question is not whether it is good but whether you have ever moved in it. And third, verse 28. Eliab's attack was a claim to know a motive, and it was confident and false, and David did not argue with it, correct it, or produce the one fact that would have ended it. He turned and asked somebody else the same question.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two armies face each other across the valley of Elah, each on its own hill (vv. 1-3). And out of the Philistine camp comes a champion, itemised like an inventory: height, bronze helmet, coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, bronze greaves, a bronze javelin, a spear shaft like a weaver's beam with a fifteen-pound iron head — and a man walking in front to carry his shield (vv. 4-7). His challenge is single combat, winner takes the nation: I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man (vv. 8-10). When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The height is textually contested — the Hebrew has six cubits and a span, about nine feet nine; the old Greek and a Dead Sea scroll have four cubits and a span, about six feet nine. Nothing turns on it. Either way he towers over men who averaged around five feet three.
verseByVerse.examples: Note who is named first in v. 11. Saul. The man Israel asked for because he was a head taller than anybody else, so that he might go out before us and fight our battles (8:20), is the first person listed as afraid.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines gathered their armies for battle. And they were gathered at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim. And Saul and the men of Israel were gathered, and encamped in the Valley of Elah, and drew up in line of battle against the Philistines. And the Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with a valley between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the Philistines gathered their armies for battle... And the Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with a valley between them.'

Two armies face each other from two hills, and neither will come down.

There is the whole military situation in one sentence, and it is why nothing happens for six weeks. Whoever descends into the valley of Elah gives up the high ground and attacks uphill. Neither commander will do it, so the two forces sit and look at each other across a few hundred yards of open ground.

The place names are real and the country is still there. Socoh and Azekah are on the western edge of the Judean hills, where the highlands drop towards the Philistine plain, and the valley of Elah is one of the roads into Judah. This is a fight about a doorway.

verseByVerse.quote: And there came out from the camp of the Philistines a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span. He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail, and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze. And he had bronze armor on his legs, and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. And his shield-bearer went before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And there came out from the camp of the Philistines a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.'

A word about the number, once, and then it can be left alone.

Six cubits and a span is about nine feet nine inches, and that is what the Hebrew text has. The oldest Greek translation, a Dead Sea scroll of Samuel and Josephus all read four cubits and a span, which is about six feet nine. The ESV prints six, and the difference does not affect anything in the chapter: the average man of that time and place stood around five feet three, so either figure describes somebody who towers over every soldier on the field.

'He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail, and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze. And he had bronze armor on his legs, and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. And his shield-bearer went before him.'

The narrator takes an inventory, and he does it like a quartermaster.

Helmet, bronze. Coat of mail, five thousand shekels — something over a hundred and twenty pounds of metal, worn. Greaves on the legs, bronze. A javelin slung across his back, bronze. A spear with a shaft the thickness of a weaver's beam and a head of fifteen pounds of iron.

Count the material. Bronze five times, and iron once — and iron is the point of the spear. Israel, we were told four chapters ago, has no blacksmith in the entire country, and two swords in its whole army (13:19-22). The man coming down the hill is carrying more metal on his body than Israel's army possesses.

The last item on the list is a person. His shield-bearer went before him. The giant does not carry his own shield; a man walks in front of him holding it.

The description is designed to do to the reader exactly what the sight of him did to the army, and it works. By the end of verse 7 there is no sensible answer to this man.

verseByVerse.quote: He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me. If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us." And the Philistine said, "I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, that we may fight together." When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me."'

He proposes single combat, which was a recognised way of settling a war.

Rather than two armies destroying each other, each side puts up a champion and the nations abide by the result. It saved lives, and it worked because both sides believed the outcome expressed something more than muscle.

Note how he describes Israel: are you not servants of Saul? Not servants of the LORD. He defines them by their king, which is precisely what they asked to be defined by in chapter 8, and it is exactly the wrong description — as David will point out in eighteen verses.

'"If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us."'

The stakes are the nation. One man's fight, and the loser's people go into slavery.

Keep the shape of it, because it is the shape of the whole story: a single representative stands for everybody, and what happens to him happens to them.

'And the Philistine said, "I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, that we may fight together."'

The verb is the one to follow through the chapter: I defy.

It means to taunt, to reproach, to hold up to contempt. It comes back in verse 25, twice on David's lips in verses 26 and 36, and finally in his speech to Goliath himself: the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied (v. 45). Everybody uses the word. The question of the chapter is who is being defied.

'When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.'

Here is the answer to chapter 8, and the name at the front of the sentence is the point.

Saul and all Israel. The man they asked for. The one who was from his shoulders upward taller than any of the people (9:2), whose height was the reason they cheered him, and who was requested specifically so that he might go out before us and fight our battles (8:20).

There is a man in this army closer to Goliath's size than anybody else in the country, and he is listed first among the frightened.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrator turns aside to reintroduce David: Jesse's eighth son, the three eldest at the war, David going back and forth between the court and his father's sheep (vv. 12-15). And the Philistine came out morning and evening for forty days (v. 16). Jesse sends David with grain, ten loaves and ten cheeses, to see how his brothers are and bring back some token (vv. 17-18). David rises early, left the sheep with a keeper, and arrives as the army is going out shouting the war cry (vv. 19-20). He leaves the provisions with the baggage-keeper and runs to the ranks to greet his brothers (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Eighty appearances of the giant, twice a day for forty days, and nobody goes down. Forty is the number of testing in this literature, and Israel is failing the examination in public.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything about David's arrival is ordinary and obedient. He is a supply runner on his father's errand, and he makes arrangements for the flock before he goes and for the provisions when he gets there. Nobody in the chapter is less obviously a hero.

verseByVerse.quote: Now David was the son of an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, named Jesse, who had eight sons. In the days of Saul the man was already old and advanced in years. The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the battle. And the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah. David was the youngest. The three eldest followed Saul, but David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem. For forty days the Philistine came forward and took his stand, morning and evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now David was the son of an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, named Jesse, who had eight sons. In the days of Saul the man was already old and advanced in years.'

Now the narrator stops the battle and reintroduces David from the beginning, as though we had not met him.

He does this deliberately. Chapter 16 showed us the anointing and the court; this chapter starts him again from the village, because the whole point of what follows is that nobody at the valley of Elah knows who he is.

'The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the battle... David was the youngest. The three eldest followed Saul, but David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem.'

Verse 15 is the sentence that holds the two chapters together.

David is not a permanent fixture at court. He went back and forth — up to Gibeah when the king needed music, home to Bethlehem when he did not. He is a part-time musician and a full-time shepherd, and at this moment he is at home.

'For forty days the Philistine came forward and took his stand, morning and evening.'

Twice a day, for forty days. Eighty times.

Sit with the arithmetic. Every morning the army of Israel forms up, and the giant walks out and shouts, and they go back to their tents. Every evening the same. For nearly six weeks.

Forty is the number of testing in this literature — forty days of rain, forty years in the wilderness, forty days on the mountain, and forty days in another wilderness a thousand years later. This is Israel's examination, conducted twice daily in public, and the nation is failing it.

There is something worse in the repetition than in the threat. A crisis that lasts an afternoon can be survived by nerve. Eighty appearances is long enough for fear to become a routine — for a whole army to organise its day around a humiliation and simply live with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesse said to David his son, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers. Also take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them." Now Saul and they and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines. And David rose early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper and took the provisions and went, as Jesse had commanded him. And he came to the encampment as the host was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry. And Israel and the Philistines drew up for battle, army against army. And David left the things in charge of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the ranks and went and greeted his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Jesse said to David his son, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers. Also take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them."'

An old man sends food to the front and wants news.

Everything in the errand is ordinary. Twenty pounds of roasted grain and ten loaves for the boys, ten cheeses for their commanding officer — which is a father sweetening the man his sons serve under. And then the real request, which is why he is sending anybody at all: see if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them.

He wants proof they are alive. Three sons have been at a stand-off for six weeks and he has heard nothing.

'And David rose early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper and took the provisions and went, as Jesse had commanded him.'

Three details, and each is worth a moment.

He rose early. He left the sheep with a keeper — he does not simply walk off and leave them, and this fact will matter in eight verses when his brother accuses him of exactly that. And he went as Jesse had commanded him.

The young man who has been anointed king of Israel is running an errand for his father and doing it properly.

'And he came to the encampment as the host was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry. And Israel and the Philistines drew up for battle, army against army.'

He arrives at the best possible moment: the army is forming up and shouting.

Mark the war cry, because it is the same noise Israel made when the ark arrived at Aphek — a shout that made the earth resound, from an army that lost thirty thousand men that afternoon (4:5). Israel is good at the shouting.

'And David left the things in charge of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the ranks and went and greeted his brothers.'

He hands over the supplies to the man whose job it is, and runs.

It is the second time in three verses that he has made proper arrangements for something in his care before doing the next thing. And there is a small irony in the location: the last person this book found among the baggage was Saul, hiding from his own coronation (10:22). David drops his parcels there and goes forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–30 — The Armies of the Living God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David hears the challenge, and sees what everybody else does: all the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid (vv. 23-24). The soldiers tell him the reward — riches, the king's daughter, and tax exemption for the man's father's house (v. 25). And David asks two questions in one breath: what will be done for the man who kills him, and who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God? (v. 26). Eliab's anger flares: with whom have you left those few sheep... I know your presumption and the evil of your heart (v. 28). David answers mildly and turns to somebody else (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: These are David's first recorded words in the Bible, and they contain both a practical question and a theological one. Everyone else has been doing arithmetic — nine feet, forty days, a hundred and twenty-five pounds of bronze. David does a different sum: whose armies are these?
verseByVerse.examples: And Eliab does the one thing chapter 16 said nobody can do. I know... the evil of your heart — from the brother God passed over, about the brother God chose, on the ground that only God can see. His accusation is also false: v. 20 says David left the sheep with a keeper.

verseByVerse.quote: As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same words as before. And David heard him. All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid. And the men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. And the king will enrich the man who kills him with great riches and will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel." And David said to the men who stood by him, "What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" And the people answered him in the same way, "So shall it be done to the man who kills him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same words as before. And David heard him.'

He is in the middle of a conversation with his brothers when the show starts.

'All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid.'

The whole army runs, with David standing there watching it happen.

The verse is important because it establishes that David sees exactly what everybody else sees. He is not spared the sight, and he is not too young to understand it. The giant comes out, the army of Israel breaks and runs, and a teenager with a bag of cheeses watches his nation flee for the eightieth time.

'And the men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. And the king will enrich the man who kills him with great riches and will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel."'

The soldiers explain the reward, and the reward is substantial: money, the king's daughter, and permanent tax exemption for the man's whole household.

Note that it is common knowledge in the ranks and nobody has taken it. The prize has been on offer for weeks and eighty times a day men have decided it is not enough.

'And David said to the men who stood by him, "What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?"'

These are the first words David speaks in the Bible, and there are two questions in them.

The first is practical: what does the man get? Note that David asks it, and asks it first, and that the narrator does not criticise him for it. He is interested in the reward. He asks about it twice more in the next few verses.

Before going on, deal with the thing readers notice and commentators often hurry past. He asks about the money. He asks again in verse 27 and again in verse 30, and he is standing there with a sack of cheeses while an army is too frightened to move.

Was he in it for the prize?

The narrator does not say so, does not criticise him, and that silence is the answer. The reward had been publicly offered by the king; wanting it was not shameful, and a young man from a family that had just been described as needing tax relief might reasonably be interested. What the chapter shows is that the prize was on offer to every soldier in Israel for six weeks and not one of them took it, which means the reward was never what was lacking.

Scripture is generally more relaxed about mixed motives than we are. Moses looked to the reward (Heb. 11:26), and the Lord himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Heb. 12:2). Wanting what God has attached to obedience is not mercenary. It becomes mercenary when it is the only thing in the sentence, and here it is followed at once by something nobody in that valley had said aloud in forty days.

The second question is the one that changes the chapter.

Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?

Everybody at the valley of Elah has been doing arithmetic for six weeks. Nine feet tall. A hundred and twenty-five pounds of bronze. A fifteen-pound spearhead. Forty days. Two armies. The sums have been done and re-done and they come out the same way every time.

David does a different sum entirely, and it has two terms in it that nobody else has been using. The man is uncircumcised — outside the covenant, with no claim on anybody. And the army he is shouting at belongs to the living God.

That phrase is the hinge. Not our God, or the God of Israel, but the God who is alive — which in this book is a loaded word. The last god to be mentioned in these pages had to be picked up off the floor of his own temple by his own priests, and then his head and hands were found on the doorstep (5:3-4).

So the question is not whether a boy can beat a giant. It is whether the God whose armies these are is alive. David has framed it correctly and everybody else has framed it wrongly, and that is the whole difference between him and the army.

'And the people answered him in the same way, "So shall it be done to the man who kills him."'

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spoke to the men. And Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, "Why have you come down? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle." And David said, "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?" And he turned away from him toward another, and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him again as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spoke to the men. And Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, "Why have you come down? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle."'

His eldest brother turns on him, and every part of the attack repays taking apart.

First, who is speaking. Eliab is the son Samuel looked at and thought surely the LORD's anointed is before him, and God said no, and gave the reason (16:6-7). He was in the room when the oil was poured on his youngest brother's head.

Second, the sneer: those few sheep in the wilderness. It is contempt for the job, and through the job for the boy. And it is inaccurate as well as unkind — David left the flock with a keeper before he came (v. 20). The accusation is simply false.

Third, and this is the extraordinary part: I know your presumption and the evil of your heart.

Read that against 16:7. The LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart. Eliab claims to have done the one thing the chapter said belongs to God alone, and he claims it about the brother God actually chose, having himself been passed over on exactly that ground.

It is a very common form of attack and it is unanswerable by design. Not you are wrong, which can be discussed, but I know why you are really doing this — a claim about motive, made confidently, by somebody who cannot possibly know.

Something else is probably underneath it. Eliab is a soldier who has stood in this valley for forty days and not gone down. His little brother has been here twenty minutes and is asking why nobody has dealt with the Philistine. Anger of that kind usually has shame somewhere behind it.

'And David said, "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?"'

The answer is mild, and the small word in the middle of it tells a story.

What have I done now? That is the sentence of a younger brother with some history — somebody used to being the one at fault, who knows this tone of voice.

There is no self-defence, no correction of the falsehood about the sheep, or mention the anointing, which would have ended the argument permanently. He says he only asked a question.

'And he turned away from him toward another, and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him again as before.'

Then he turns round and asks somebody else the same thing.

Nothing in the paragraph is more instructive. He does not win the argument with Eliab, and he does not leave. He simply declines to be diverted by it and goes back to the question that matters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–40 — I Cannot Go With These
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul sends for him, and David's offer is simple: let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine (vv. 31-32). Saul assesses him and refuses — you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth (v. 33). David answers with his job: a lion came, and a bear, and he went after them and took the lamb out of the mouth (vv. 34-36). And then the argument itself: the LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine (v. 37). Saul dresses him in his own armour, and David cannot walk in it: I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them (vv. 38-39). So he takes a staff, five smooth stones from the brook, a pouch and a sling (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 37 is the logic of Ebenezer. Samuel set up a stone and said till now the LORD has helped us (7:12), and this is what such a stone is for: when the next trouble arrives you have something in the record to argue from. David is not being brave about the future. He is reasoning from the past.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's armour is the tallest man in Israel's armour, and it is untested, and David says so twice. He goes down to the brook instead. His weapons come out of the stream rather than the armoury, and they are the ones he has actually used.

verseByVerse.quote: When the words that David spoke were heard, they repeated them before Saul, and he sent for him. And David said to Saul, "Let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the words that David spoke were heard, they repeated them before Saul, and he sent for him.'

Word travels up. Somebody in the ranks has been struck by what the boy said and it reaches the king.

'And David said to Saul, "Let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine."'

Two sentences, and the first is about everybody else.

Let no man's heart fail because of him. Before he volunteers, he addresses the morale of the army — which is a strange thing for a teenage supply runner to say to a king, and it is the sentence of somebody who has been watching men be afraid and thinks it unnecessary.

'And Saul said to David, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth."'

Saul makes exactly the assessment chapter 16 warned about.

He looks at David and measures him: too young, insufficiently experienced, physically outmatched by a professional. Every word of it is true, and it is the same instrument that had approved of Saul himself — height, bearing, obvious capacity — and that God had refused to use at Bethlehem.

Note also the phrase he ends on: a man of war from his youth. It is a soldier's verdict, and it is being pronounced by a king who has not gone down into that valley either.

verseByVerse.quote: But David said to Saul, "Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. And when there came a lion, or a bear, and took a lamb from the flock, I went after him and struck him and delivered it out of his mouth. And if he arose against me, I caught him by his beard and struck him and killed him. Your servant has struck down both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God." And David said, "The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But David said to Saul, "Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. And when there came a lion, or a bear, and took a lamb from the flock, I went after him and struck him and delivered it out of his mouth. And if he arose against me, I caught him by his beard and struck him and killed him."'

He answers the objection with his job.

Saul has said he is a shepherd rather than a soldier, as though those were opposites, and David explains what shepherding actually involved. A predator takes a lamb; the shepherd goes after it, strikes it, and takes the animal out of its mouth. If it turns on him, he catches it by the beard and kills it.

Read that slowly, because familiarity has flattened it. He put his hand into a lion's mouth for one sheep, and he did it more than once, and he did it for animals that were not his — your servant used to keep sheep for his father.

This is the first thing the Bible tells us about how David treated something in his care, and it is the answer to those few sheep in the wilderness. He went into the mouth of a lion for one of them.

The man who will write the LORD is my shepherd learned the trade at the sharp end.

'"Your servant has struck down both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God."'

The reason he gives for putting the giant in the same category as an animal is not that he is confident. It is the defying.

'And David said, "The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine."'

Weigh what kind of argument that is.

He does not say I killed a lion, therefore I can kill a Philistine. Look at the subject of the verb. The LORD who delivered me... will deliver me. The lion and the bear are not evidence about David's strength; they are evidence about God's record.

That is the logic of the stone at Ebenezer. Samuel set one up between Mizpah and Shen and called it till now the LORD has helped us (7:12) — not a prediction, but a fact placed in the landscape so that the next time trouble came there would be something to argue from.

David is arguing from his stones. Two of them, in a field, with nobody watching, years ago.

Take that personally, because it is available to anybody. The reasoning does not require a special temperament or a great deal of faith; it requires a memory and the honesty to keep the record. What has God actually done? Start there, and reason forward.

'And Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you!"'

The king lets him go, with a blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul clothed David with his armor. He put a helmet of bronze on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail, and David strapped his sword over his armor. And he tried in vain to go, for he had not tested them. Then David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them." So David put them off. Then he took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his shepherd's pouch. His sling was in his hand, and he approached the Philistine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul clothed David with his armor. He put a helmet of bronze on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail, and David strapped his sword over his armor.'

Saul dresses him in his own equipment, and it is meant kindly.

Look at it, though, and it is absurd. Saul is the tallest man in Israel. The armour is built for a body a head and shoulders above everybody else, and it is being fastened onto a teenager.

Note the detail: David strapped his sword over his armor. A sword — one of the two in the entire army (13:22).

'And he tried in vain to go, for he had not tested them. Then David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them." So David put them off.'

He cannot walk in it, and the reason he gives twice is not that it is too big.

I have not tested them. The objection is not size but unfamiliarity. Whatever the protection is worth, he has never moved in it, and a man about to fight for his life is not going to learn a new set of equipment on the way down the hill.

A small scene, with a large principle in it. David has just argued from what God has done through him before, with what he knows how to use. Saul offers him the best equipment in the kingdom and it would have killed him.

'Then he took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his shepherd's pouch. His sling was in his hand, and he approached the Philistine.'

He goes to the streambed and picks up stones.

Every item is a shepherd's: staff, pouch, sling, and ammunition out of the water. His weapons come from the brook rather than the armoury.

Something should be said about the sling, because a modern reader hears something a child plays with. It was a serious military weapon and every army had specialists in it. This book has already described some: Benjamin fielded seven hundred picked left-handed slingers who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (Judg. 20:16). A stone from a practised sling travels at something like the speed of a modern handgun bullet, and it is the one weapon on that field that works at a distance — which means the only man in the valley who does not have to get within reach of a fifteen-pound spearhead is the boy with no armour.

A last word about the five, since people ask. The text does not say why. The suggestion that Goliath had four brothers is a guess built on a much later verse (2 Sam. 21:22), and the simplest answer is that a slinger carries spares. Nothing in the chapter turns on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–47 — The Battle Is the LORD's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Goliath comes on with his shield-bearer in front, sees David, and he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance (vv. 41-42). He curses him by his gods and promises his flesh to the birds (vv. 43-44). And David answers: you come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied (v. 45). The purpose is stated twice — that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's (vv. 46-47).
verseByVerse.theology: Goliath commits chapter 16's exact error. Ruddy and handsome in appearance is word for word what the narrator said when David was brought in from the sheep (16:12). Every man in this chapter who looks at David misjudges him — Eliab, Saul, and now the Philistine.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 47 completes a set. Hannah sang not by might shall a man prevail (2:9) in a corrupt sanctuary with nothing to go on. Jonathan said nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (14:6) at the foot of a cliff. David says it in a valley in front of two armies. It is the spine of the book.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistine moved forward and came near to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him. And when the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance. And the Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the Philistine moved forward and came near to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him.'

The shield-bearer is mentioned again, and by now it is almost comic. Even at the moment of single combat the champion has a man walking ahead of him holding a screen.

'And when the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance.'

Now hear the words.

Ruddy and handsome in appearance is what the narrator wrote when the boy was brought in from the sheep for Samuel to look at: he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome (16:12).

Goliath looks at David and sees exactly what the text told us was there — and draws the wrong conclusion, because he is reading appearance.

Three men in one chapter, then. Eliab looked at him and saw presumption. Saul looked at him and saw a youth who was not able. Goliath looks at him and sees somebody not worth the trouble. Every assessment in this chapter is made by the eyes, and every one is wrong, and the reader has been told why since 16:7.

'And the Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.'

He sees the staff and not the sling.

That is a real detail and a telling one. David is carrying a shepherd's staff in one hand and a sling in the other, and the giant registers the stick. A man in a hundred and twenty-five pounds of bronze, looking down at what he assumes is a boy come to shoo him like an animal.

Then he curses him by his gods — Dagon among them, presumably, whose statue could not stand up in his own temple.

'The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."'

Remember the threat, because David is about to hand it back with the plural changed.
