verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. And I will give the dead bodies of the host of the Philistines this day to the birds of the air and to the wild beasts of the earth, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied."'

Now the great speech, and it is built on a single contrast: three weapons against one name.

Goliath's inventory is recited back to him — sword, spear, javelin — and set against the name of the LORD of hosts.

That title has a history in this book, and this is where it arrives at its destination. It appeared for the first time in the whole Bible in a sentence about an ordinary man walking up to Shiloh once a year (1:3). The first person recorded praying by it was a childless woman asking for a baby (1:11). And now it is a war cry in a valley, shouted by her great-grandson's generation at an armoured champion.

LORD of hosts means the LORD of armies — of every army there is, in heaven and on earth. David is telling a professional soldier that he has miscounted the forces present.

The last clause identifies the actual offence: the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. Not whom you have insulted us by defying. The forty days of taunting were not aimed at Israel's honour, whatever Goliath thought he was doing.

'"This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. And I will give the dead bodies of the host of the Philistines this day to the birds of the air and to the wild beasts of the earth."'

He returns the threat, and enlarges it from one body to an army.

Note the order of the verbs, though, because it is the theology of the whole speech in miniature. The LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down. God does the delivering; the boy does the striking. Both are in the sentence and neither swallows the other.

'"that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear."'

Two purposes, and two audiences, and the second is the surprising one.

One is what you would expect: that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. The nations are watching, and the question raised by forty days of unanswered blasphemy is whether Israel's God is real.

Then: that all this assembly may know. Israel. His own side. The army standing behind him on the hill needs to learn something too, and what it needs to learn is stated in the next clause.

'"For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand."'

The LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's.

With that, a set of three is complete, and the three sentences are the spine of this book.

Hannah sang the first, in a corrupt sanctuary, with no war on and nobody listening, having just handed over a toddler: the bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength... not by might shall a man prevail (2:4, 9).

Jonathan said the second at the bottom of a cliff with one servant and no promise: nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (14:6).

David says the third in a valley, in front of two armies, to a man in armour: the LORD saves not with sword and spear.

Three people, none of them in authority — a countrywoman, a king's son acting without orders, and a shepherd on an errand — and between them they say the same thing three times across sixteen chapters while the nation asks for a king to fight its battles.

The last clause turns the whole thing round: he will give you into our hand. Not mine. David is about to fight alone, and he says the victory belongs to everybody on the hill behind him.

Ask what the battle is the LORD's actually meant that afternoon, because it is a sentence Christians say about situations in which nothing then happens.

It did not mean David could stay on the hill. Three verses from now he runs at an armoured man with a leather strap and a stone, and if the stone misses he dies. Nothing about the LORD's ownership of the battle removed one step of the walk down into that valley.

What it meant was that the outcome was not being decided by the inventory in verses 5 to 7. David still had to sling; God decided where the stone went. It is not an alternative to acting but a statement about who determines what the acting produces — which is why it could be said by a man about to run at a giant and could not be said by an army standing still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 48–54 — There Was No Sword in the Hand of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine (v. 48). The stone sinks into his forehead and he falls on his face (v. 49). So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone... There was no sword in the hand of David (v. 50). Then David takes Goliath's own sword and cuts off his head with it, and the Philistines run (v. 51). Israel and Judah pursue as far as Gath and Ekron and plunder the camp (vv. 52-53). David takes the head to Jerusalem and puts the armour in his tent (v. 54).
verseByVerse.theology: He runs at him. Everybody else has been retreating from this man twice a day for forty days, and the shepherd's first movement is forward and fast.
verseByVerse.examples: The giant falls on his face to the ground, which is exactly what Dagon did in front of the ark at Ashdod, twice (5:3-4). And he dies by his own weapon — the sword that was to take David's head takes his.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine. And David put his hand in his bag and took out a stone and slung it and struck the Philistine on his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground. So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him. There was no sword in the hand of David. Then David ran and stood over the Philistine and took his sword and drew it out of its sheath and killed him and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.'

He runs at him.

Hold that sentence. For forty days, twice a day, the men of Israel have looked at this man and gone backwards; verse 24 says they fled from him. The first movement David makes is forward, and it is fast.

Tactically it is also right. A slinger needs distance and needs to be moving; the last thing he wants is to let an armoured man close on him slowly. But the writer is not reporting tactics. He is reporting that one person on that field advanced.

'And David put his hand in his bag and took out a stone and slung it and struck the Philistine on his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground.'

Five verbs and it is over: put, took, slung, struck, sank.

The forehead is the one place the bronze does not cover. Helmet above, coat of mail below, shield in front of him held by another man — and a gap.

Then the last clause: he fell on his face to the ground.

The reader of this book has seen that before. Twice, in the temple at Ashdod, the Philistines came in the morning and found Dagon fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD (5:3-4). The second time his head was off.

Philistia's god went down on his face in front of the LORD, and lost his head. Philistia's champion goes down on his face in front of the LORD's anointed, and loses his.

'So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him. There was no sword in the hand of David.'

The narrator stops to say it explicitly, and he did not have to: there was no sword in the hand of David.

Chapter 13 ended by telling us there were exactly two swords in Israel's army, and both belonged to the royal family. One of them was strapped on David's hip fifteen verses ago and he took it off with the armour.

The nation that had no blacksmith did not need one.

'Then David ran and stood over the Philistine and took his sword and drew it out of its sheath and killed him and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.'

He finishes it with Goliath's own sword.

The weapon that was going to take David's head takes Goliath's. The man had promised to give the boy's flesh to the birds, and the instrument of that promise is drawn out of its sheath by the boy and used on him.

The Bible comes back to that shape at the very end. The last enemy is destroyed by his own weapon — that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Heb. 2:14). Death was the thing held over everybody's head, and it was death that finished the one holding it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron, so that the wounded Philistines fell on the way from Shaaraim as far as Gath and Ekron. And the people of Israel came back from chasing the Philistines, and they plundered their camp. And David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron.'

Now the army moves.

They have been standing on that hill for six weeks. One man went down and won, and the whole force rises with a shout and chases a beaten enemy fifteen miles to the gates of their own cities.

The text carries no criticism of them, and there should not be much in the reading either. This is how it works: the champion fights, and the people enter into what he won. They did nothing to earn the victory and they share in it entirely, and the pursuit is real work and theirs to do.

'And the people of Israel came back from chasing the Philistines, and they plundered their camp.'

They take the spoil, which none of them fought for.

'And David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.'

Two objects, two destinations, and one of them is a surprise.

Jerusalem at this moment is not Israelite. It is a Jebusite town that Benjamin failed to take in the first chapter of Judges and that will not be captured for another generation, when this same man walks up and takes it and makes it his capital (2 Sam. 5:6-9).

The armour he keeps. And the sword goes to the sanctuary at Nob, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod, where David will collect it years later when he is running for his life from Saul — and where asking for it will cost eighty-five priests their lives (21:8-9; 22:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 55–58 — Whose Son Is This Youth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As David goes out, Saul asks Abner whose son he is, and Abner does not know (v. 55). The king repeats it: inquire whose son the boy is (v. 56). When David comes back with the head still in his hand, Saul asks him directly, and David answers: I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite (vv. 57-58).
verseByVerse.theology: The question is about parentage, not identity, and there is a reason for it in this chapter: v. 25 promised that the man who killed Goliath would have his father's house made free in Israel. Saul needs to know which household to exempt.
verseByVerse.examples: So the scene ends with a boy standing in front of a king holding a severed head, naming his father. The last verse of the chapter is the name of a village and a family, which is where the whole line to Bethlehem runs.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" And Abner said, "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know." And the king said, "Inquire whose son the boy is." And as soon as David returned from the striking down of the Philistine, Abner took him, and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand. And Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" And Abner said, "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know."'

The king asks his general who the boy's father is, and the general does not know.

Readers have long noticed that Saul appears not to recognise a young man who was his own armour-bearer in the previous chapter, and it is worth a sentence rather than an argument. The question asked here, three times, is not who is this but whose son is this — and there is a reason for it in verse 25, which promised that the man who killed Goliath would have his father's house made free in Israel. Saul needs to know which household to exempt, and Abner, who has not met the family, cannot tell him.

'And as soon as David returned from the striking down of the Philistine, Abner took him, and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand.'

Hold the picture as the chapter closes.

A teenager is walked into the presence of the king of Israel by the commander of the army, and he is carrying a severed head.

'And Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."'

The last words of the chapter are a village and a family.

Jesse the Bethlehemite. Not the anointing, which he does not mention. Not the lion or the bear. A father's name and a small town in Judah.

Now stand back from the whole chapter, because its shape is the reason it has never been forgotten, and the shape is older and larger than a story about courage.

Two nations stood on two hills, and between them a single man offered terms: one champion each, and whatever happens to him happens to everybody. Israel had no answer. For forty days the whole people stood paralysed by one enemy they could not face, and the arrangement was entirely fair and entirely hopeless.

Then somebody came who was not part of the army. He came down from the hill on his father's errand. Nobody recognised him; his own brother despised him; the king assessed him and found him inadequate; the enemy looked at him and laughed. He went out with none of the equipment the situation appeared to require, alone, in front of everybody, and he fought the battle in the name of the LORD and not with a sword. And when he had won it, the people who had contributed nothing rose with a shout and entered into it, and took the plunder home.

That is not an illustration somebody has imposed on the passage. It is how the passage is built, and it is why the New Testament can speak the way it does about a representative who partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).

The usual way of reading this chapter is that we are David and our problems are Goliath, and that is exactly backwards. In this valley there is only one person who can fight, and everybody else is on the hill. The good news of the passage is not that you can be David. It is that somebody has been.

18.title: Jonathan's Covenant and Saul's Jealousy
18.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.<sup>2</sup>And Saul took him that day and would not let him return to his father's house.<sup>3</sup>Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul.<sup>4</sup>And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt.<sup>5</sup>And David went out and was successful wherever Saul sent him, so that Saul set him over the men of war. And this was good in the sight of all the people and also in the sight of Saul's servants.<sup>6</sup>As they were coming home, when David returned from striking down the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with songs of joy, and with musical instruments.<sup>7</sup>And the women sang to one another as they celebrated, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands."<sup>8</sup>And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?"<sup>9</sup>And Saul eyed David from that day on.<sup>10</sup>The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand.<sup>11</sup>And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, "I will pin David to the wall." But David evaded him twice.<sup>12</sup>Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.<sup>13</sup>So Saul removed him from his presence and made him a commander of a thousand. And he went out and came in before the people.<sup>14</sup>And David had success in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him.<sup>15</sup>And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in fearful awe of him.<sup>16</sup>But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.<sup>17</sup>Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you for a wife. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him."<sup>18</sup>And David said to Saul, "Who am I, and who are my relatives, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?"<sup>19</sup>But at the time when Merab, Saul's daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite for a wife.<sup>20</sup>Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David. And they told Saul, and the thing pleased him.<sup>21</sup>Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him." Therefore Saul said to David a second time, "You shall now be my son-in-law."<sup>22</sup>And Saul commanded his servants, "Speak to David in private and say, 'Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now then become the king's son-in-law.'"<sup>23</sup>And Saul's servants spoke those words in the ears of David. And David said, "Does it seem to you a little thing to become the king's son-in-law, since I am a poor man and have no reputation?"<sup>24</sup>And the servants of Saul told him, "Thus and so did David speak."<sup>25</sup>Then Saul said, "Thus shall you say to David, 'The king desires no bride-price except a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, that he may be avenged of the king's enemies.'" Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.<sup>26</sup>And when his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king's son-in-law. Before the time had expired,<sup>27</sup>David arose and went, along with his men, and killed two hundred of the Philistines. And David brought their foreskins, which were given in full number to the king, that he might become the king's son-in-law. And Saul gave him his daughter Michal for a wife.<sup>28</sup>But when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal, Saul's daughter, loved him,<sup>29</sup>Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually.<sup>30</sup>Then the commanders of the Philistines came out to battle, and as often as they came out David had more success than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.
18.overview:
The chapter opens in the room where the last one ended, with the head still in David's hand, and the first thing that happens is that the crown prince loves him. Jonathan makes a covenant, and then does something the narrator refuses to explain: he stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt. The robe is the mark of the heir — Saul tore Samuel's and was told the kingdom was torn from him. And there were two swords in the whole army of Israel, both in the royal family, and David had none at Elah. Jonathan hands him one.

Then the women sing. It is a victory song for Saul, with David named second, and Saul hears only the arithmetic — and reaches, out of jealousy rather than revelation, the exactly correct conclusion: what more can he have but the kingdom? From that day he watches him.

The spear comes the next day, while David is playing as he did day by day, and David evades it twice — which means he came back and sat down again. And verse 12 gives the diagnosis of everything that follows: Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.

After that, every device backfires. Promotion makes the country love him; a daughter offered as a snare becomes a wife who saves his life; a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, designed to kill him, is paid double and early. And when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, the effect of knowing it was more fear.
18.theology:
Jonathan's robe (v. 4). The heir strips off the mark of his own succession, his armour, his belt, his bow, and one of the nation's two swords, and gives them to the man who will take his throne — unasked, out of love, and without a word of explanation from the narrator. The robe runs right through the book: torn from Saul (15:27-28), given away by Jonathan here, and cut in a cave by David, whose heart then struck him for it (24:4-5). Everyone else in this story fights over the kingdom; Jonathan takes his coat off. He is the only person who does gladly the thing the others destroy themselves resisting.

Hearing an insult in a compliment (vv. 7-8). The women came out to meet King Saul; he is named first and credited with thousands; and Hebrew verse escalates in pairs rather than scoring. Saul reduces a national celebration to a comparison of two numbers. That is not a failure of hearing but a condition of the man doing it — and the conclusion he draws from jealousy happens to be true.

The verb rushed (v. 10). The book's word for God suddenly taking hold of a man — Samson, Saul at Gibeah, Saul at Jabesh, David at his anointing — is here used of what fills the space the Spirit left. And David goes on playing as he did day by day, and after the first spear he comes back.

Verse 12 is the whole diagnosis. It was not David's ambition that frightened Saul; David had done nothing but win his battles, marry into his family, and play for him when he was ill. What frightened him was that the LORD was with the young man, and he could see it. He is not afraid of the wrong thing — he has correctly identified the most important fact in the situation — and it produces a spear rather than repentance. A man can be entirely right about where God is at work and find the knowledge yields nothing but fear, because what he wants is not God but the position.

Piety as a murder weapon (v. 17). Fight the LORD's battles is this book's highest language, put into a marriage contract to get a man killed. And the calculation is a coward's: not I will not kill him but my hand must not be the one — which is precisely what David will one day arrange for Uriah (2 Sam. 11:15). This book spares nobody.

A snare (v. 21). The word God used at Bochim of the gods Israel would not drive out (Judg. 2:3), and of what Gideon's ephod became (Judg. 8:27). Saul applies it to his own daughter, about the man she loves — and the narrator states her love for him, which he almost never does of a woman in these histories.

Saw and knew, and feared more (v. 28). The evidence that should have stopped him is what drove him on, because he was never asking whether God was with David. He was asking whether the throne was safe. And the chapter closes with David highly esteemed — the exact reverse of the lightly esteemed he called himself in v. 23, and a quiet working-out of 2:30.
18.examples:
Then: The heir to the throne of Israel took off his robe, his armour and one of the country's only two swords and gave them to the shepherd who was going to replace him — while his father, in the same week, worked out that the same young man would have the kingdom and began watching him with a spear in his hand.

Now: Three things. Jonathan is the model nobody imitates: he had everything to lose and handed it over gladly, before being asked, to the person whose rise meant his own eclipse. Ask what you would have to take off. Second, verse 8 is a warning about a habit of hearing rather than an occasion of it — a man who can extract an insult from a compliment will never run short of insults. And third, verse 28 is the sobering one: it is entirely possible to see clearly that God is blessing someone and to find that the clarity makes it worse, and the test of which you are doing is what the evidence produces in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Stripped Himself of the Robe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The moment David finishes speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul (v. 1). Saul keeps him at court (v. 2). Jonathan makes a covenant with him (v. 3), and then does something extraordinary: he stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt (v. 4). And David succeeds wherever he is sent, and it pleases everybody — the people, the servants, and Saul (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan is the crown prince, and the robe is the mark of the heir. He takes off the succession and hands it to the man who is going to have it, and the narrator does not say a word about what it means. He does not need to.
verseByVerse.examples: Note the sword in that list. There were two swords in the entire army of Israel and they belonged to Saul and Jonathan (13:22). David had none at the valley of Elah — the narrator said so explicitly (17:50). The king's son gives him one of the nation's two.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. And Saul took him that day and would not let him return to his father's house. Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt. And David went out and was successful wherever Saul sent him, so that Saul set him over the men of war. And this was good in the sight of all the people and also in the sight of Saul's servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.'

It happens in the room where the last chapter ended, with the head still in David's hand.

Their souls were knit — bound, tied together, the word used of Jacob's life being bound up with Benjamin's (Gen. 44:30). And the measure given twice in five verses is as his own soul: Jonathan loved David the way he loved himself, which is the standard the law sets for loving a neighbour and which almost nobody meets.

Consider who this is. Jonathan is the king's eldest son and the heir to the throne. He is also the man who went up a cliff with one servant and broke a Philistine army while his father sat under a tree. He has every reason to resent the boy who has just done in one afternoon what he did at Michmash, and to see him as a rival for a throne that is his.

'And Saul took him that day and would not let him return to his father's house.'

The part-time musician becomes a permanent fixture. He does not go home to Bethlehem again.

'Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul.'

A covenant, which in this world is a formal, sworn, binding thing — not a friendship but a treaty. Jonathan initiates it.

'And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt.'

Now read this verse slowly, because it is one of the great acts in the Old Testament and it is performed without a word of explanation.

The robe comes first. In this book a robe is not a garment; it is an office. Samuel wore one and Saul tore it and was told the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (15:27-28). The heir's robe is the visible mark of the succession.

Jonathan takes it off and puts it on David.

Then the rest of the list, and the writer builds it: his armour, and even his sword and his bow and his belt. The even is the narrator's, and it points at the sword.

There were two swords in the entire army of Israel, because the Philistines allowed no blacksmith in the country, and both belonged to the royal family (13:22). One chapter ago the narrator went out of his way to say there was no sword in the hand of David (17:50).

Jonathan hands him one of the two.

Put the whole gesture together. The crown prince strips off the mark of his succession, his protection, and half the nation's edged weapons, and gives them to the young man everybody in the room can see is going to replace him — and he does it out of love, before anybody has asked him for anything.

Everyone else in this book fights over the kingdom. Israel demands it, Saul clings to it and throws spears to keep it, and Jonathan takes his coat off and hands it over. He is the only person in the story who does gladly the thing the others will destroy themselves resisting.

'And David went out and was successful wherever Saul sent him, so that Saul set him over the men of war. And this was good in the sight of all the people and also in the sight of Saul's servants.'

For one verse everybody is pleased, and the writer lists them: the people, the servants, and by implication the king who did the promoting.

It is the last time in this book that everybody is on the same side.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The women come out singing: Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands (vv. 6-7). Saul is furious — what more can he have but the kingdom? — and eyed David from that day on (vv. 8-9). The next day the harmful spirit rushes on him and he hurls a spear at David twice while David is playing, as he did day by day (vv. 10-11). Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul (v. 12). So he removes him from court and promotes him — and David succeeds in everything, and all Israel and Judah loved David (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The song is a victory song for the king, with David named second. Saul hears only the comparison. And his conclusion — what more can he have but the kingdom? — happens to be exactly right, which he does not know.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 is the diagnosis of everything that follows. His fear of David rises in precise proportion to the evidence that God is with him, and every promotion designed to remove the threat makes it larger.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were coming home, when David returned from striking down the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with songs of joy, and with musical instruments. And the women sang to one another as they celebrated, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands." And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" And Saul eyed David from that day on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As they were coming home, when David returned from striking down the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with songs of joy, and with musical instruments.'

The women come out to meet the king, and they come out of every town.

This is what Israel did after a victory: Miriam at the sea, Deborah after the Kishon, Jephthah's daughter at the door. Tambourines and dancing and a song made up for the occasion.

'And the women sang to one another as they celebrated, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands."'

Now look carefully at the song, because everything depends on how it is heard.

It is a victory song for Saul. The women came out to meet King Saul; he is named first; he is credited with thousands. It is, on any ordinary reading, a compliment to the king with a nice line about the young man who killed the champion.

Hebrew poetry also works in pairs that escalate — thousands, then ten thousands — and the second line is often simply a heightening of the first rather than a comparison. The women are not conducting an assessment. They are singing.

'And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?"'

Saul hears only the arithmetic.

He reduces a national celebration to a comparison between two numbers, and he gets the numbers the right way round, and he is right that his is the smaller. That is the whole of what he takes from the day.

There is a way of listening that can extract an insult from a compliment, and it is not a failure of hearing. It is a condition of the man doing it.

Then his conclusion, which is a genuine piece of political insight: what more can he have but the kingdom?

He is correct. That is exactly what David is going to have, and it was decided in a Bethlehem courtyard two chapters ago and Saul has no idea. He has arrived at the truth by the wrong road, from jealousy rather than revelation, and it will govern the rest of his life.

'And Saul eyed David from that day on.'

One clause, and it is the beginning of everything.

The verb means to watch with suspicion, to keep under observation. And in a book that has made so much of eyes — the LORD looks on the heart, man looks on the outward appearance — the king's contribution is a sidelong look that never stops.

From that day on. Not an outburst; a settled practice, beginning on the afternoon of a national celebration and running until the day he dies on Gilboa.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand. And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, "I will pin David to the wall." But David evaded him twice. Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand.'

The verb is the terrible one.

Rushed. It is the word used when the Spirit of the LORD came on Samson, and on Saul at Gibeah, and on Saul at Jabesh when his anger was kindled for a town about to lose its eyes, and on David at his anointing. It is this book's word for God taking hold of a man suddenly.

Here it is used of what fills the space the Spirit left.

Then the detail that says everything about David in this period: he is playing the lyre as he did day by day. This is routine. Every day, the king is tormented, and every day the young man he is watching with suspicion sits down and plays for him.

The last clause is put at the end of the sentence like a loaded gun on a table. Saul had his spear in his hand.

A king's spear was his sceptre — the thing he held while sitting, the mark of office. It is also, at close range, a weapon.

'And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, "I will pin David to the wall." But David evaded him twice.'

He throws it, and the intention is recorded: to pin a man to a wall like an insect.

The last word is the one to notice. Twice.

David evaded him twice, which means that after the first spear he came back. He picked up the lyre, sat down in the same room as the man who had just tried to kill him, and went on playing.

'Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.'

Here is the diagnosis of the entire rest of the book, in one sentence.

Three things are stated. Saul was afraid of David. The LORD was with David. The LORD had departed from Saul.

The middle clause is the cause of the first. It was not David's ambition that frightened him — David has done nothing but win his battles, marry into his family and play for him when he was ill. What frightened Saul was that God was with the young man, and he could see it.

That is a terrible position to be in and it should be named exactly. He is not afraid of the wrong thing. He has correctly identified the most important fact in the situation, which is that the LORD is with David. And the evidence that ought to have brought him to his knees drives him to a spear instead.

A man can be entirely right about where God is at work and find that the knowledge produces nothing in him but fear, because the thing he actually wants is not God but the position.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul removed him from his presence and made him a commander of a thousand. And he went out and came in before the people. And David had success in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him. And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in fearful awe of him. But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Saul removed him from his presence and made him a commander of a thousand. And he went out and came in before the people.'

He solves the problem by promoting him, which is what frightened men in authority generally do.

Removing David from court gets him out of the room. Making him a field commander sends him where Philistines are, which is the same calculation Saul will make explicitly in four verses. And he went out and came in before the people is the standard phrase for leading an army in public.

'And David had success in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him. And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in fearful awe of him.'

Every measure backfires in the same way, and the narrator gives the reason each time: for the LORD was with him.

Saul now stands in fearful awe of a young officer in his own army. The word is stronger than nervousness; it is dread.

'But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.'

The promotion meant to remove him makes the whole country love him.

Note the two names, kept separate: all Israel and Judah. The book counts them apart at musters and it counts them apart here, and one day the crack will become a border. For the moment both halves love the same man.

Everything Saul does to reduce David enlarges him. He is not being outmanoeuvred by a clever rival; David has made no move at all. He is being defeated by the fact stated in verse 12.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul offers his elder daughter Merab, with a condition: only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles — and a private calculation: let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him (v. 17). David's answer is a self-assessment: who am I, and who are my relatives, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king? (v. 18). And when the time came, Merab was given to somebody else (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Read what Saul does with the phrase. Fight the LORD's battles is the language of this whole book, and he uses it as a murder weapon — sending a man to the front in the hope that the enemy will do what he does not want on his own hands.
verseByVerse.examples: David's reply is Saul's own sentence from the beginning. Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? (9:21). Two men, the same protest — and one of them is now arranging a death.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you for a wife. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him." And David said to Saul, "Who am I, and who are my relatives, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?" But at the time when Merab, Saul's daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite for a wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you for a wife. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles."'

The offer is the reward promised at the valley of Elah, and the condition attached to it is a piece of blasphemy.

Fight the LORD's battles. That is the language of this book at its highest — the battle is the LORD's, said in a valley in front of two armies four chapters ago. Saul puts it in a marriage contract as a way of getting a man killed.

'For Saul thought, "Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him."'

The narrator opens the king's head and shows us what is in it.

The calculation is precise and it is the calculation of a coward: not I will not kill him but my hand must not be the one. He wants the outcome and not the responsibility.

It is exactly what David will one day be told to arrange for Uriah, and he will do it, and it will be the ruin of his house (2 Sam. 11:15). This book does not spare anybody.

'And David said to Saul, "Who am I, and who are my relatives, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?"'

David's answer is Saul's own sentence.

When Samuel first hinted at the kingdom, the young man from Gibeah said: am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? (9:21).

Family, clan, insignificance. The same protest, from the same kind of young man — and the one who made it first is now sitting on the other side of the room calculating how to have him killed.

'But at the time when Merab, Saul's daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite for a wife.'

Then the promise is simply broken, publicly, at the appointed time.

There is no explanation. The girl who was promised to the national hero in front of the army is married to somebody else on the day, and David says nothing about it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Michal loves David, and the news pleased Saul: let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him (vv. 20-21). He has his servants work on David privately, and David objects that he is a poor man and have no reputation (vv. 22-23). So Saul names a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, thinking to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines (v. 25). David brings two hundred and marries Michal (vv. 26-27). But when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal loved him, Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually (vv. 28-29). And David goes on succeeding (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The word for what a daughter is to be is a snare — and it is the word God used at Bochim about the gods of the nations, and the word for what Gideon's ephod became (Judg. 2:3; 8:27). A father is deploying his own child as one.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 28 is the mechanism of Saul's ruin stated in a sentence. He saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and the effect of knowing it was more fear. The evidence that should have ended the campaign is what escalated it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David. And they told Saul, and the thing pleased him. Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him." Therefore Saul said to David a second time, "You shall now be my son-in-law." And Saul commanded his servants, "Speak to David in private and say, 'Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now then become the king's son-in-law.'" And Saul's servants spoke those words in the ears of David. And David said, "Does it seem to you a little thing to become the king's son-in-law, since I am a poor man and have no reputation?" And the servants of Saul told him, "Thus and so did David speak." Then Saul said, "Thus shall you say to David, 'The king desires no bride-price except a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, that he may be avenged of the king's enemies.'" Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David. And they told Saul, and the thing pleased him.'

Two sentences, and everything wrong with this household is between them.

Michal loved David. The phrase is small and it is unusual: the narrator states a woman's love for a man, which he almost never does in these histories. He puts it down plainly and without decoration.

Her father is pleased — not because his daughter is happy, but for the reason the next verse gives.

'Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him."'

The word is snare.

It is a loaded word in these books. God used it at Bochim about the gods Israel refused to drive out — their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3). It is what Gideon's golden ephod became to him and his family (Judg. 8:27). It is the word for the thing that catches you.

Saul applies it to his own daughter, in his own thoughts, about the man she loves.

'And Saul commanded his servants, "Speak to David in private and say, 'Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now then become the king's son-in-law.'"'

He runs it through intermediaries, with a script, and the script is all warmth.

The king delights in you. All his servants love you. Neither statement is true of the man who wrote it, and both are being said by employees who have been told what to say.

'And Saul's servants spoke those words in the ears of David. And David said, "Does it seem to you a little thing to become the king's son-in-law, since I am a poor man and have no reputation?"'

David's objection is money and standing.

A marriage required a bride-price, and a royal marriage required a considerable one. He says he is poor and — literally — lightly esteemed, which is a striking thing for the most celebrated soldier in Israel to say about himself, and it uses the same root as the word in Samuel's oracle for those who despise God and are lightly esteemed in return (2:30).

'Then Saul said, "Thus shall you say to David, 'The king desires no bride-price except a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, that he may be avenged of the king's enemies.'" Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.'

Saul names a price designed to be fatal.

The demand is grotesque and it is meant to be. A hundred Philistine foreskins cannot be collected at a distance; every one requires a man dead at close quarters and then handled. It is a hundred separate opportunities to be killed, and the narrator states the purpose in the last sentence so that nobody misses it.

Note the pretext: that he may be avenged of the king's enemies. He is dressing an assassination as patriotism, exactly as he dressed it as piety in verse 17.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king's son-in-law. Before the time had expired, David arose and went, along with his men, and killed two hundred of the Philistines. And David brought their foreskins, which were given in full number to the king, that he might become the king's son-in-law. And Saul gave him his daughter Michal for a wife. But when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal, Saul's daughter, loved him, Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually. Then the commanders of the Philistines came out to battle, and as often as they came out David had more success than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king's son-in-law. Before the time had expired, David arose and went, along with his men, and killed two hundred of the Philistines.'

He brings double, and early.

A hundred was the price. David delivers two hundred and does it before the deadline, which tells us something about the young man and also removes any possibility of dispute over the count.

Note along with his men. David has men now. The commander of a thousand has a following of his own, and that fact will matter for the next twelve chapters.

'And David brought their foreskins, which were given in full number to the king, that he might become the king's son-in-law. And Saul gave him his daughter Michal for a wife.'

Given in full number to the king. They are counted out in front of him.

The scene is deliberately grim. A king who wanted a young man dead has to sit and watch two hundred proofs that he is not, counted onto the floor, and then hand over his daughter.

'But when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal, Saul's daughter, loved him, Saul was even more afraid of David.'

Here is the mechanism of his ruin, stated as plainly as it can be.

He saw and knew that the LORD was with David — and the effect of knowing it was more fear.

Sit with that, because it is the strangest thing about Saul and it is not rare. The evidence that ought to have stopped him is the thing that drove him on. Every proof that God was with David — the giant, the campaigns, the two hundred, his own daughter's love — made him more determined, because he was not asking whether God was with David. He was asking whether the throne was safe.

A man who wants the position more than he wants God will find that the clearest evidence of God's hand becomes his worst news.

'So Saul was David's enemy continually.'

There is the settled state, in five words.

Not angry, not suspicious, not watchful. Continually. It has stopped being an episode and become the shape of his life, and it will remain so through fourteen chapters, three thousand men, two caves and a witch, until the day the Philistines find him on Mount Gilboa.

'Then the commanders of the Philistines came out to battle, and as often as they came out David had more success than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.'

The chapter ends where it began: David succeeding, and everybody noticing.

The last phrase is highly esteemed — and it is the exact opposite of what David called himself in verse 23, when he said he was lightly esteemed. The book that told us those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed (2:30) is quietly showing the promise working itself out in two men at the same court.

19.title: The Hunter and the Hunted
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David.<sup>2</sup>And Jonathan told David, "Saul my father seeks to kill you. Therefore be on your guard in the morning. Stay in a secret place and hide yourself.<sup>3</sup>And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to my father about you. And if I learn anything I will tell you."<sup>4</sup>And Jonathan spoke well of David to Saul his father and said to him, "Let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have brought good to you.<sup>5</sup>For he took his life in his hand and he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?"<sup>6</sup>And Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan. Saul swore, "As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death."<sup>7</sup>And Jonathan called David, and Jonathan reported to him all these things. And Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.<sup>8</sup>And there was war again. And David went out and fought with the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, so that they fled before him.<sup>9</sup>Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. And David was playing the lyre.<sup>10</sup>And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.<sup>11</sup>Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him, that he might kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, told him, "If you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed."<sup>12</sup>So Michal let David down through the window, and he fled away and escaped.<sup>13</sup>Michal took an image and laid it on the bed and put a pillow of goats' hair at its head and covered it with the clothes.<sup>14</sup>And when Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, "He is sick."<sup>15</sup>Then Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him."<sup>16</sup>And when the messengers came in, behold, the image was in the bed, with the pillow of goats' hair at its head.<sup>17</sup>Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me thus and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?" And Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"<sup>18</sup>Now David fled and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and lived at Naioth.<sup>19</sup>And it was told Saul, "Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah."<sup>20</sup>Then Saul sent messengers to take David, and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied.<sup>21</sup>When it was told Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. And Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied.<sup>22</sup>Then he himself went to Ramah and came to the great well that is in Secu. And he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" And one said, "Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah."<sup>23</sup>And he went there to Naioth in Ramah. And the Spirit of God came upon him also, and as he went he prophesied until he came to Naioth in Ramah.<sup>24</sup>And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
19.overview:
The killing of David becomes official policy, given to the household as an instruction — and Jonathan warns him, hides him, and then argues for him in four moves worth copying: the proposal named as sin; the facts (he has not sinned against you); the benefit to the accuser (his deeds have brought good to you); and the accuser's own remembered gladness (you saw it, and rejoiced). He even quotes his father's best sentence back to him — the LORD worked a great salvation (cf. 11:13). And it works. Saul listens and swears in the name of the LORD.

The oath lasts one campaign. The trigger is a victory: David beats the Philistines, and that evening the spear goes into the wall. He had come back and played the lyre after every previous attempt; this is the night he leaves and never lives at that court again.

Then the daughter Saul gave as a snare lowers him out of a window and puts a household idol in the bed to buy him the night — and when she is caught, saves herself by telling her father that David had threatened to kill her. Both things are true of her, and the narrator lets both stand.

And the chapter ends in the strangest scene in the book. Three arrest parties walk into a company of prophets and are absorbed into it; the king goes himself and is seized on the road; and he lies stripped on the ground for a day and a night while the man he came for walks away. Is Saul also among the prophets? — the same words that were spoken in wonder on the day he became king.
19.theology:
How to speak for somebody who is not in the room (vv. 4-5). Jonathan names the proposal as sin in his opening clause, states that there is no charge, argues the accuser's own interest, and then makes him look at his own past joy. And he uses the moral word twice — innocent blood, without cause. Learn it as a pattern; and it worked: Saul heard it and swore. He was not beyond reach.

One campaign (vv. 6-10). The gap between the oath and the spear is a single victory, and the victory is the trigger. Nothing had changed in David except that he had won again.

Leaving is not a failure of grace (v. 10). David absorbed three attempts and returned to the lyre each time. The fourth ended it, and the narrator nowhere suggests he should have stayed for a fifth. What changed was not his patience but a spear standing in the plaster where his chest had been.

The snare that saved him (v. 12). Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare (18:21) — and she is the reason he is alive. Note also the window: Rahab lowered the spies through one, and Damascus lowered Paul over a wall in a basket (Josh. 2:15; Acts 9:25).

The teraphim in the bed (v. 13). A household idol, life-sized, in the house of the LORD's anointed — the same kind of object Rachel stole and Micah kept (Gen. 31:19; Judg. 17:5). The narrator reports it and says nothing, and a reader is left to notice.

Michal, both things at once (v. 17). She risked her life for her husband, and when the risk arrived she got out from under it by inventing a threat he never made, leaving in her father's mind a David who would murder his own wife. She was in an impossible position, and people in impossible positions do this. It is also the start of a distance that never closes: the last we hear of her, when the ark comes into Jerusalem, is that she despised him in her heart (2 Sam. 6:16).

The proverb turned round (v. 24). At 10:11-12 the neighbours asked it in astonishment, when the Spirit came on a young farmer on the day he was made king: God had done something unaccountable with an ordinary man. Here the same words are said over a king lying stripped on the ground, and the Spirit that once made him another man simply immobilises him. Between the two askings lies everything.

Four hunts, no rescue anybody would have designed. There is no battle in this chapter, no miracle performed for David, no angel and no fire. A brother-in-law argues, a wife lowers a rope, and three arrest parties and a king are stopped by being made to worship. The manhunt is defeated without a blow, and the man at the centre does nothing but run — which is what he does for the next twelve chapters.
19.examples:
Then: A king sent three separate arrest parties after one fugitive and lost every one of them to a prayer meeting, went himself, was seized by the Spirit on the road, and spent a day and a night lying stripped on the ground in front of the prophet who had told him his kingdom was gone — while the man he came for walked quietly out of town.

Now: Two things. Jonathan's speech is the best model in Scripture for defending an absent person to someone determined against them: name the thing honestly, state the facts, argue their own interest, and make them remember what they themselves once felt. It is not manipulation; every element of it is true, and it worked. And verse 10 is for anyone who has been told that staying is always the godlier option. David went back four times. Then he left, and the book does not criticise him for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Why Will You Sin Against Innocent Blood?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul tells Jonathan and all his servants to kill David — but Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David (v. 1). Jonathan warns him, hides him, and goes out to plead his case (vv. 2-3). And the plea is a model: let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have brought good to you. For he took his life in his hand and he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause? (vv. 4-5). Saul listens and swears: as the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death (v. 6). So Jonathan brings him back (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Four moves in two verses, and every one repays copying. The facts of the case; the benefit to the man he is talking to; that man's own remembered joy on the day; and the plain moral name for what is proposed — innocent blood.
verseByVerse.examples: And it works. Saul hears it, agrees, and swears in the name of the LORD. Whatever else is true of him, he can still be reached by an argument; the tragedy of the next four verses is how long the agreement lasts.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David. And Jonathan told David, "Saul my father seeks to kill you. Therefore be on your guard in the morning. Stay in a secret place and hide yourself. And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to my father about you. And if I learn anything I will tell you." And Jonathan spoke well of David to Saul his father and said to him, "Let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have brought good to you. For he took his life in his hand and he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?" And Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan. Saul swore, "As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death." And Jonathan called David, and Jonathan reported to him all these things. And Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David.'

It is now official policy, given to the household as an instruction.

Up to this point the attempts have been private — a spear in a room, a bride-price designed to be fatal — and deniable. Saul now tells his court, including his son, to kill the man.

The writer names the obstacle in the same verse, twice identifying whose son he is: but Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David.

'And Jonathan told David, "Saul my father seeks to kill you. Therefore be on your guard in the morning. Stay in a secret place and hide yourself."'

He warns him first and argues afterwards, which is the right order.

'"And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to my father about you. And if I learn anything I will tell you."'

The arrangement is careful. He will stand in the field where David is hiding, so that David can hear the conversation, and he undertakes to report whatever he learns.

'And Jonathan spoke well of David to Saul his father and said to him, "Let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have brought good to you."'

Now the plea, and it is a model of how to speak for somebody who is not in the room.

He opens with the category. Let not the king sin. Not do not make a mistake, not you will regret this — the proposal is named as sin, to the man's face, in the first clause.

Then the facts: he has not sinned against you. There is no charge. Nothing David has done constitutes an offence, and Jonathan says so flatly.

Then the benefit to the accuser: his deeds have brought good to you. He argues Saul's own interest, which is not flattery but relevance.

'"For he took his life in his hand and he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?"'

Then the four best words in the speech: you saw it, and rejoiced.

He reminds his father of his own gladness. There was a day when Saul stood on that hillside and watched a boy come back with a head in his hand, and he was delighted, and the whole country sang. Jonathan makes him look at it.

Note also how he describes the victory: the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. That is Saul's own sentence from his best day — today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel (11:13), spoken when he refused to execute men who had insulted him. His son is quoting him back to himself.

Last, the moral name for the proposal, twice: sin against innocent blood, and without cause.

'And Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan. Saul swore, "As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death."'

It works.

That should be said before anything else. Saul hears the argument, accepts it, and swears an oath in the name of the LORD that David will not be killed. He is not beyond reach; a son speaking plainly to him about sin got through.

'And Jonathan called David, and Jonathan reported to him all these things. And Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.'

David comes back to court on his brother-in-law's word, and everything is as it was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Spear in the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is war again, and David strikes the Philistines with a great blow (v. 8). Then the harmful spirit comes on Saul as he sits in his house with his spear in his hand, and David is playing the lyre (v. 9). Saul tries to pin him to the wall and misses; the spear goes into the plaster; and David fled and escaped that night (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The oath of verse 6 lasted exactly one campaign. Between the swearing and the spear there is one victory, and the trigger is the victory.
verseByVerse.examples: And David is at the lyre again. After the two throws of 18:11 he came back and played; after the oath he came back and played; and this is where it ends. The spear in the wall is the last night he ever spends under that roof.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was war again. And David went out and fought with the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, so that they fled before him. Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. And David was playing the lyre. And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And there was war again. And David went out and fought with the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, so that they fled before him.'

One campaign. That is how long the oath lasts, and the thing that breaks it is a victory.

'Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. And David was playing the lyre.'

The scene is 18:10 again, staged identically: the house, the spirit, the spear in the hand, the young man playing.

David is at the lyre again. After two spears he had come back and played; after the plot with the bride-price he had come back and played; after his father-in-law's oath he came back and played. The narrator does not comment on it and the repetition is the comment.

'And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.'

This time the spear goes into the plaster.

Picture the room afterwards: an overturned lyre, a king, and a spear standing in the wall where a man's chest had been a second earlier.

Then David fled and escaped that night. That is the end of it. He has absorbed three attempts and gone on serving; the fourth ends the arrangement, and he never lives at that court again.

There is a point at which a person has to leave, and it is not a failure of patience or of grace. David had endured this repeatedly and returned each time. What ended it was not a change in his character but a spear in the wall, and the writer does not suggest he should have stayed for a fifth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Let Down Through the Window
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul posts watchers on the house to kill him in the morning, and Michal tells him: if you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed (v. 11). She lets him down through the window (v. 12), puts a household image in the bed with a goats'-hair pillow at its head, and tells the messengers he is ill (vv. 13-14). Saul sends them back to bring the bed itself, and they find the image (vv. 15-16). Confronted, Michal answers her father: he said to me, let me go. Why should I kill you? (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The daughter Saul gave as a snare (18:21) is the reason David is alive. The trap married the man and then lowered him out of a window while her father's men watched the front door.
verseByVerse.examples: Two things are true of her and the narrator states both without comment. She risked her life for her husband. And when caught, she protected herself by inventing a threat he never made — and left David in her father's mind as a man who would kill his own wife.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him, that he might kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, told him, "If you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed." So Michal let David down through the window, and he fled away and escaped. Michal took an image and laid it on the bed and put a pillow of goats' hair at its head and covered it with the clothes. And when Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, "He is sick." Then Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him." And when the messengers came in, behold, the image was in the bed, with the pillow of goats' hair at its head. Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me thus and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?" And Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him, that he might kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, told him, "If you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed."'

The house is watched, and the person who sees it is the king's daughter.

Remember what her father said when he arranged this marriage: let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him (18:21). The trap married David, found out what her father was doing, and warned him.

'So Michal let David down through the window, and he fled away and escaped.'

Out of a window, at night, past men posted at the door.

It is a small escape with a long history in Scripture: Rahab let the spies down through a window in the wall of Jericho on a scarlet cord, and centuries later the disciples in Damascus lowered Paul over the wall in a basket when the gates were being watched (Josh. 2:15; Acts 9:25). God's people have quite often left a city by the window.

'Michal took an image and laid it on the bed and put a pillow of goats' hair at its head and covered it with the clothes.'

She makes a dummy, and the material she makes it out of is worth a sentence.

The word is teraphim — a household idol, of the kind Rachel stole from her father's house and sat on (Gen. 31:19, 34), and of the kind Micah kept in his shrine in the hills of Ephraim (Judg. 17:5). There is one in David's house, and it is life-sized enough to pass for a man under bedclothes at a distance.

The narrator says nothing about it. He reports it, and moves on, and a reader is left to notice what is standing in the bedroom of the LORD's anointed.

'And when Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, "He is sick." Then Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him."'

Her father's answer to the news that his son-in-law is ill is that they should carry the bed to him so that he can kill the man in it.

Take in what that sentence is. A king has been told that a sick man is lying in his daughter's house, and his instruction is that the bed be brought so that he can do it himself. There is no pretence left in him now.

'And when the messengers came in, behold, the image was in the bed, with the pillow of goats' hair at its head.'

'Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me thus and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?" And Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"'

Here Michal says something that is not true, and the shape of it matters.

She tells her father that David threatened her — that he said, in effect, help me or I will kill you. Nothing in the account suggests it. She warned him and she lowered him and she made the dummy, and the whole plan appears to have been hers.

Both things are true of her, and the narrator lets both stand. She risked her life to save her husband. And when the risk arrived, she got out from under it by putting the blame on him, and she left in her father's mind a picture of David as a man who would threaten to murder his own wife.

She was in an impossible position and that people in impossible positions do this. It is also the beginning of a distance between these two that never closes. David is given another wife within a chapter; Michal is given away by her father to another man; and the last we ever hear of her, years later when the ark comes into Jerusalem, is that she despised him in her heart (2 Sam. 6:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–24 — Is Saul Also Among the Prophets?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David runs to Samuel at Ramah and they stay at Naioth (v. 18). Saul sends messengers, and when they see the prophets prophesying with Samuel at their head, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied (v. 20). A second party goes, and prophesies; a third, and prophesies (v. 21). So Saul goes himself — and the Spirit comes on him too, and he prophesies all the way (vv. 22-23). And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Three arrest parties are disarmed without a blow, and then the king. God stops a manhunt four times over by putting his Spirit on the men sent to conduct it, and David simply walks away.
verseByVerse.examples: The proverb is the one from 10:12, and it has turned completely round. There it was spoken in wonder, when the Spirit came on a farmer's son on the day he was made king. Here it is said over a king lying stripped on the ground for a day and a night while the kingdom walks out of his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Now David fled and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and lived at Naioth. And it was told Saul, "Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah." Then Saul sent messengers to take David, and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied. When it was told Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. And Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied. Then he himself went to Ramah and came to the great well that is in Secu. And he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" And one said, "Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah." And he went there to Naioth in Ramah. And the Spirit of God came upon him also, and as he went he prophesied until he came to Naioth in Ramah. And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now David fled and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and lived at Naioth.'

He runs to the old man who anointed him.

It is the first thing David does as a fugitive, and it is a good instinct: he goes to the prophet and tells him all that Saul had done to him. The two of them then go and live at Naioth, which appears to be the prophets' settlement at Ramah.

This is also, as far as the book records, the last time these two are ever together. Samuel dies in chapter 25.

'And it was told Saul, "Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah." Then Saul sent messengers to take David, and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied.'

The arrest party walks into a prayer meeting and never makes the arrest.

They see the prophets and Samuel at their head, and the Spirit of God comes on them, and they join in. No blow is struck. Nobody argues with them or bars the door.

'When it was told Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. And Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied.'

He sends a second party, and the same thing happens. He sends a third.

There is something close to comedy in the repetition, and it is entirely at the king's expense. Three times he despatches men to bring back a fugitive, and three times they arrive and are absorbed into a company of worshippers.

'Then he himself went to Ramah... And he went there to Naioth in Ramah. And the Spirit of God came upon him also, and as he went he prophesied until he came to Naioth in Ramah.'

So he goes himself, and it happens to him before he even arrives.

As he went he prophesied — the Spirit takes him on the road, and he comes into Naioth already prophesying, which is not what he set out to do.

'And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"'

He ends on the floor.

The stripping is probably the removal of his outer robes and armour rather than nakedness as we would mean it; the point is that a king is lying on the ground without the marks of his office, in front of the prophet who told him the kingdom was torn from him, for a day and a night, while the man he came to arrest walks away.

Then the proverb, and it is the bookend of Saul's life.
