The first time it was asked, the Spirit had just come on a young farmer from Gibeah on the day he was anointed, and the neighbours who had known him all his life said in astonishment: what has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets? (10:11-12). It was wonder. It meant that God had done something unaccountable with an ordinary man.

Here the same words are said over a king stripped on the ground, and they mean the opposite. The Spirit that once made him another man now simply immobilises him.

Between the two askings lies everything: the waiting at Gilgal, the oath at Michmash, the Amalekite livestock, the monument at Carmel, the spear, and the arrest parties.

Now stand back and see what God has done in this chapter, because it is easily missed in the strangeness of the ending.

David is hunted four times, and he is not defended once. There is no battle here, no miracle performed for him, no angel and no fire. What happens is that a brother-in-law argues, a wife lowers a rope, and three arrest parties and a king are stopped by being made to worship.

The manhunt is defeated without a single blow, and the man at the centre of it does nothing but run and keep running. Which is what he will be doing for the next twelve chapters, and hold on to it as they begin: the LORD's anointed spends a third of this book as a fugitive, and at no point is he abandoned, and at almost no point is he rescued in a way anybody would have designed in advance.

20.title: Covenant Friendship
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?"<sup>2</sup>And he said to him, "Far from it! You shall not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. And why should my father hide this from me? It is not so."<sup>3</sup>But David vowed again, saying, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death."<sup>4</sup>Then Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."<sup>5</sup>David said to Jonathan, "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to sit at table with the king. But let me go, that I may hide myself in the field till the third day at evening.<sup>6</sup>If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.'<sup>7</sup>If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him.<sup>8</sup>Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you. But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself, for why should you bring me to your father?"<sup>9</sup>And Jonathan said, "Far be it from you! If I knew that it was determined by my father that harm should come to you, would I not tell you?"<sup>10</sup>Then David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?"<sup>11</sup>And Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.<sup>12</sup>And Jonathan said to David, "The LORD, the God of Israel, be witness! When I have sounded out my father, about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if he is well disposed toward David, shall I not then send and disclose it to you?<sup>13</sup>But should it please my father to do you harm, the LORD do so to Jonathan and more also if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in safety. May the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father.<sup>14</sup>If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die;<sup>15</sup>and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth."<sup>16</sup>And Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies."<sup>17</sup>And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul.<sup>18</sup>Then Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.<sup>19</sup>On the third day go down quickly to the place where you hid yourself when the matter was in hand, and remain beside the stone heap.<sup>20</sup>And I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I shot at a mark.<sup>21</sup>And behold, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you, take them,' then you are to come, for, as the LORD lives, it is safe for you and there is no danger.<sup>22</sup>But if I say to the youth, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away.<sup>23</sup>And as for the matter of which you and I have spoken, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever."<sup>24</sup>So David hid himself in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat food.<sup>25</sup>The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat by Saul's side, but David's place was empty.<sup>26</sup>Yet Saul did not say anything that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him. He is not clean; surely he is not clean."<sup>27</sup>But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"<sup>28</sup>Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem.<sup>29</sup>He said, 'Let me go, for our clan holds a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away and see my brothers.' For this reason he has not come to the king's table."<sup>30</sup>Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman, do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?<sup>31</sup>For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die."<sup>32</sup>Then Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"<sup>33</sup>But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.<sup>34</sup>And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.<sup>35</sup>In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointment with David, and with him a little boy.<sup>36</sup>And he said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.<sup>37</sup>And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?"<sup>38</sup>And Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stay!" So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master.<sup>39</sup>But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.<sup>40</sup>And Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go and carry them to the city."<sup>41</sup>And as soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the stone heap and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. And they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most.<sup>42</sup>Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'" And he rose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
20.overview:
David arrives with three questions that have no answer: what have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin? He is not protesting his innocence in general; he is asking to be shown the charge, and there is not one. The reader knows what David does not — it is not anything he has done, but that the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul (18:12). That is the hard thing about this kind of hatred: there is no fault to correct, so there is no way to fix it.

Jonathan will not believe it, on a ground that was true a fortnight ago — my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. Saul had indeed told him openly (19:1); he has since learned not to. So David says it plainly: there is but a step between me and death — and asks that if there really is guilt in him, Jonathan should kill him personally rather than hand him over.

Then the field, and the covenant, and the sentence that shows how much Jonathan understands: may the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father. Past tense, about a man still on the throne. And the most remarkable request in the book: show kindness to my children when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David — not if. The heir asks the fugitive for mercy in the kingdom he knows is coming.

At the feast Saul talks himself into an explanation for one day, and on the second he asks — and never uses the name. The son of Jesse, from here to the end. When Jonathan repeats David's question back to him, his father throws a spear at him, and that is what finally convinces him. They meet in the field, and David bows three times to the man who gave up a throne for him, and they weep, David weeping the most.
20.theology:
No charge to answer (v. 1). David asks to be shown his guilt and cannot find any, and neither can the reader. Being hated for a reason can be addressed; being hated because God is with you cannot, and 18:12 has already named it.

As he has been with my father (v. 13). Future blessing, past tense about a reigning king, in one sentence, with no bitterness and no announcement. Jonathan has understood what Saul has spent five chapters refusing to.

Mercy negotiated in advance (vv. 14-15). When the LORD cuts off every one of David's enemies — and his father is chief among them and he is the heir. He can see the whole thing: the throne is going, his line will be at David's mercy, his father's resistance is futile. And his response is to ask for kindness rather than to fight. It was kept. Years later David asks whether anyone is left of the house of Saul that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake, and seats a man lame in both feet at the king's table for life (2 Sam. 9:1-13). A promise made in a field by two young men in trouble was honoured decades later to a crippled grandson of the man hunting them.

Fighting for an inheritance nobody wants (v. 31). Neither you nor your kingdom shall be established — Saul's whole campaign is, in his own account, for his son. And the son gave it away two chapters earlier, with his own robe (18:4). There is a particular grief in a man destroying himself on behalf of somebody who does not want what he is fighting for.

The name goes first (v. 27). The son of Jesse, and it is settled habit from here on (22:7-13; 25:10). It is what people do with somebody they have decided to destroy.

What finally convinced Jonathan (v. 33). Not David's argument, and not the evidence. A spear thrown at his own head across a festival table. So Jonathan knew. And he left in fierce anger, grieved — for David.

The LORD between them (vv. 23, 42). The basis of the covenant is not affection, which cools, but a third party who does not. Jonathan promises nothing he cannot deliver: not that they will meet again, not that he can protect him. He states what has been sworn and who guarantees it. They meet once more, in the woods at Ziph, where he says the thing his father never could — you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you (23:17).
20.examples:
Then: Two young men arranged a signal with three arrows and a boy who would never know what he was carrying — and when it came to it the signal was unnecessary, and they met in the open and wept, and the heir to the throne asked the fugitive to spare his children when the kingdom changed hands.

Now: Three things. Verse 1 is for anyone who has looked hard for the offence and cannot find it — sometimes there is not one, and the search for a fault to correct is itself the trap. Verse 4 is Jonathan's: he committed himself to David before he was persuaded, which is what this kind of loyalty looks like from the inside. And verses 14-15 are the hardest and best. He could see that his family's future depended entirely on the mercy of the man his father was hunting, and he asked for mercy instead of fighting — and a lame grandson ate at a king's table because he did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Is But a Step Between Me and Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David comes to Jonathan with three questions: what have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life? (v. 1). Jonathan will not have it — my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me (v. 2). David answers that Saul knows exactly how close they are and is keeping it from him, and then says it plainly: there is but a step between me and death (v. 3). Whatever you say, I will do for you (v. 4). So David proposes a test at the new moon feast, and asks for one thing: if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan's confidence that his father hides nothing from him is loyalty, and it is out of date. Saul had told him openly to kill David in 19:1; he has since learned not to.
verseByVerse.examples: And David's request in v. 8 is the measure of what these two are to each other. He would rather be executed by Jonathan than handed to Saul — not because he expects it, but because he is willing to put the possibility in his friend's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?" And he said to him, "Far from it! You shall not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. And why should my father hide this from me? It is not so." But David vowed again, saying, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death." Then Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?"'

Three questions, and they are the questions of a man who genuinely cannot account for what is happening to him.

What have I done. What is my guilt. What is my sin. He is not protesting his general innocence; he is asking to be shown the charge, because he has looked for it and cannot find one.

He cannot, because there is not one. He killed the giant, won the campaigns, married into the family, played the lyre through the bad nights and came back after the spears. The reader knows the answer and David does not: it is not anything he has done. It is that the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul (18:12).

That is one of the harder things about being on the receiving end of this kind of hatred. There is no fault to correct, so there is no way to fix it.

'And he said to him, "Far from it! You shall not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. And why should my father hide this from me? It is not so."'

His friend will not believe it, and the reason is touching and out of date.

My father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. It had been true. In chapter 19 Saul told Jonathan openly to kill David, which is how Jonathan came to warn him in the first place (19:1-2).

What Jonathan does not yet know is that his father has learned from that. The openness he is appealing to was withdrawn the day it cost Saul an assassination.

There is something else in the denial as well, and anybody who has had to hear hard truth about a parent will recognise it. It is not so. He is not weighing evidence. He is refusing a picture of his father that he cannot yet hold.

'But David vowed again, saying, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved.'"'

David has read the situation exactly, including Saul's motive for the concealment.

Mark what he says about it: Saul is keeping it quiet lest he be grieved. Even here, David credits the man with wanting to spare his son pain. He does not say because your father knows you would stop him, which is also true and would be the sharper reading.

'"But truly, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death."'

One of the great sentences of the book, and it is nine words in English.

There is but a step between me and death. It is a picture of a man walking along an edge, and it is the settled condition of the next twelve chapters of his life.

He is not being dramatic. He has been speared at four times, escaped through a window, and been hunted by three arrest parties in a fortnight.

'Then Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."'

Jonathan hands him a blank cheque.

He has not accepted the argument — he still thinks his father is not capable of this. He puts himself at David's disposal anyway, before he is convinced, which is what friendship of this kind looks like from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: David said to Jonathan, "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to sit at table with the king. But let me go, that I may hide myself in the field till the third day at evening. If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.' If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him. Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you. But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself, for why should you bring me to your father?" And Jonathan said, "Far be it from you! If I knew that it was determined by my father that harm should come to you, would I not tell you?" Then David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?" And Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'David said to Jonathan, "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to sit at table with the king. But let me go, that I may hide myself in the field till the third day at evening."'

The new moon was a monthly festival with a sacrifice and a meal, and attendance at the king's table was expected of his officers and family.

So David's absence will be conspicuous by design. That is the point of choosing this occasion: it forces a reaction.

'"If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.'"'

The cover story, and it should be reported honestly rather than defended.

Part of it is true: David has just asked leave of Jonathan, in verse 5, in those very words. The annual clan sacrifice at Bethlehem is probably also real. What is untrue is the implication that David has gone there, and the whole thing is arranged to produce a false impression in Saul's mind.

The narrator does not comment, and neither should a reader go much beyond him. Scripture records a good many people concealing things from men who intend murder — the midwives in Egypt, Rahab on the wall, Samuel with his heifer on the Bethlehem road (16:2) — and it does not stop to lecture any of them.

'"If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him."'

The test is well designed: one absence, two possible reactions, and the reaction is the verdict.

'"Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you."'

He appeals to the covenant of chapter 18, and to the word hesed — the loyal love that keeps its promises when it does not have to. It will be used four times in this chapter.

Note also who initiated that covenant. You have brought your servant into a covenant. David did not ask for it; Jonathan made it, in the room where the giant's head was still in his hand.

'"But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself, for why should you bring me to your father?"'

Here is the measure of the two men.

David tells Jonathan that if there really is a charge against him, Jonathan should execute him personally rather than hand him over. He is not expecting it — the first four verses have established that he cannot find any guilt in himself. He is putting his life in his friend's hands in the plainest form available, and doing it as an argument: you can have it if it is owed.

'And Jonathan said, "Far be it from you!... Come, let us go out into the field."'

They leave the buildings. Everything that follows in this chapter happens in the open, away from the house, and that is a comment on the house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — The LORD Be With You, As He Has Been With My Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan swears: he will sound his father out and report either way, and if there is harm determined he will send David away in safety (vv. 12-13). Then the sentence that shows how much he understands: may the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father. And then his request — show me the steadfast love of the LORD that I may not die, and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth (vv. 14-15). He makes a covenant with the house of David and has him swear again by his love (vv. 16-17). Then the practical arrangement: a stone heap, three arrows, and a boy sent to fetch them (vv. 18-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Read v. 13 again. As he has been with my father — in the past tense, about a man still on the throne. Jonathan has understood what his father cannot admit.
verseByVerse.examples: And vv. 14-15 are extraordinary. The crown prince states as a settled fact that David will have the kingdom and all his enemies removed, and asks only that his own children be spared in it. David keeps it: years later he sends for a lame man named Mephibosheth and seats him at the king's table (2 Sam. 9:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jonathan said to David, "The LORD, the God of Israel, be witness! When I have sounded out my father, about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if he is well disposed toward David, shall I not then send and disclose it to you? But should it please my father to do you harm, the LORD do so to Jonathan and more also if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in safety. May the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father. If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die; and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth." And Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies." And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Jonathan said to David, "The LORD, the God of Israel, be witness! When I have sounded out my father... if he is well disposed toward David, shall I not then send and disclose it to you?"'

He swears with God as witness, and the undertaking is exact: either way, David will be told.

'"But should it please my father to do you harm, the LORD do so to Jonathan and more also if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in safety."'

He calls down a curse on himself if he fails to warn the man his father wants dead.

Consider what he is undertaking. If the verdict is harm, Jonathan will actively assist the escape of the person his father has identified as the obstacle to Jonathan's own throne. He is swearing, under oath, to work against his family's interest.

'"May the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father."'

Read the tenses.

May the LORD be with you — future, a blessing. As he has been with my father — past, and finished.

Saul is alive and reigning. His son says, in a single sentence, that the LORD was with him and prays that he will be with David instead. There is no bitterness in it and no announcement; it is simply what Jonathan has understood and his father has spent five chapters refusing to.

'"If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die; and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth."'

Now the most remarkable request in the chapter, and possibly in the friendship.

Take the assumption inside it first. When the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth — not if. Jonathan states the future as settled: David will have the kingdom, and everyone opposing him will be removed.

His father is at this moment the chief of those enemies, and Jonathan is his heir.

So what he asks for is mercy. Show me hesed while I live, and do not cut it off from my house forever. He is negotiating, in advance, for the survival of his children under the regime that will replace his own.

That is an act of extraordinary clear sight and extraordinary humility together. He can see the whole thing — that the throne is going, that his line will be at the mercy of the man he loves, that his father's resistance is futile — and his response is to ask for kindness rather than to fight.

It was kept. Years later, when David is secure in Jerusalem and every rival house would normally be destroyed, he asks: is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? They bring him a man lame in both feet, Jonathan's son, and David seats him at the king's table for the rest of his life (2 Sam. 9:1-13).

A promise made in a field by two young men in trouble was honoured decades later to a crippled grandson of the man who had been hunting them.

'And Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies." And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul.'

He makes the covenant not with David but with the house of David — a dynasty that does not exist yet, in a family with no throne, on behalf of his own descendants.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty. On the third day go down quickly to the place where you hid yourself when the matter was in hand, and remain beside the stone heap. And I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I shot at a mark. And behold, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you, take them,' then you are to come, for, as the LORD lives, it is safe for you and there is no danger. But if I say to the youth, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away. And as for the matter of which you and I have spoken, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty."'

The practical arrangements begin, and they are careful and unhurried.

'"On the third day go down quickly to the place where you hid yourself when the matter was in hand, and remain beside the stone heap. And I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I shot at a mark."'

A hiding place they have used before, a stone heap for a landmark, and an archery practice that will look entirely ordinary to anyone watching from the town.

'"And behold, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you, take them,' then you are to come... But if I say to the youth, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away."'

The signal is spoken to a child who will have no idea what he is carrying.

The plan is a good one. Two men who cannot be seen speaking to each other arrange to have their message delivered in public, at volume, to somebody else.

Note the phrasing of the bad outcome: then go, for the LORD has sent you away. Not my father has driven you out. If David has to run, Jonathan has already decided how to describe it.

'"And as for the matter of which you and I have spoken, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever."'

The LORD is between you and me forever. It is the sentence he will repeat as his farewell in verse 42, and it is the whole basis of the arrangement: not affection, which can cool, but a third party who does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–34 — Why Has Not the Son of Jesse Come?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David hides. At the feast the king takes his usual seat and David's place is empty, and Saul says nothing on the first day, assuming ritual uncleanness (vv. 24-26). On the second he asks: why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal? (v. 27). Jonathan gives the agreed answer (vv. 28-29), and Saul erupts — insulting his son through his mother, and naming the real issue: as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established (vv. 30-31). Jonathan asks David's question back — why should he be put to death? What has he done? — and his father throws a spear at him (vv. 32-33). Jonathan leaves the table in fierce anger and eats nothing (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul does not use David's name. The son of Jesse, here and for the rest of the book — a man he once loved greatly, reduced to somebody's son.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 31 shows what he thinks he is defending: neither you nor your kingdom. He is fighting for Jonathan's inheritance, and Jonathan gave it away two chapters ago, of his own accord, with his own robe (18:4).

verseByVerse.quote: So David hid himself in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat food. The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat by Saul's side, but David's place was empty. Yet Saul did not say anything that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him. He is not clean; surely he is not clean." But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?" Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem. He said, 'Let me go, for our clan holds a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away and see my brothers.' For this reason he has not come to the king's table."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So David hid himself in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat food. The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat by Saul's side, but David's place was empty.'

The narrator seats everybody and then shows us the gap.

Saul is on his usual seat by the wall — and this is the man who threw a spear at a wall with David in front of it. Jonathan opposite. Abner beside the king. And an empty place.

'Yet Saul did not say anything that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him. He is not clean; surely he is not clean."'

He says nothing, and the narrator lets us hear him talking himself into an explanation.

The repetition is the giveaway: he is not clean; surely he is not clean. A man who was genuinely unconcerned would think it once. Saul is working at it.

Ritual uncleanness would be a real and sufficient reason to miss a sacrificial meal, so the explanation is a good one. It lasts a day.

'But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"'

Here is a small thing that runs to the end of the book: he does not use the name.

The son of Jesse. Not David, whom he loved greatly and made his armour-bearer and his son-in-law. From here on it is almost always this: the son of Jesse, to Jonathan, to his officers at Gibeah, to Ahimelech at Nob. Nabal will use it too, as an insult, and he will get it from the court (22:7-13; 25:10).

It is what people do with somebody they have decided to destroy. The name goes first.

'Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem..."'

Jonathan gives the agreed answer, and adds a detail of his own — my brother has commanded me to be there — which was not in the script.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman, do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness? For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die." Then Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?" But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death. And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman, do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?"'

He goes for his son through his son's mother, and it is the sentence of a man with nothing left to lose.

The insult is aimed at Jonathan and lands on Ahinoam, Saul's own wife, who has done nothing and is not present. It is a common enough move and it is always the same move: hurt the person in front of you by defiling somebody they love.

The charge itself is that Jonathan has chosen David. Which is exactly right. He chose him in chapter 18 and took off his robe to prove it.

'"For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die."'

Now read what Saul thinks he is fighting for.

Neither you nor your kingdom. He is arguing for Jonathan's inheritance. Everything — the spears, the arrest parties, the manhunt about to consume the rest of his life — is being done, in his own account of it, for his son.

His son gave the kingdom away two chapters ago, voluntarily, with his own robe and his own sword, to the man his father wants killed.

There is a particular grief in that, and it is not rare. A man destroying himself on behalf of somebody who does not want what he is fighting for, and cannot say so in a way that will be heard.

'Then Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"'

Jonathan asks David's question.

It is verse 1 almost word for word: what have I done? What is my guilt? The friend puts the innocent man's question to the king, and there is no answer to it, because there is no charge.

He also asked it in chapter 19 and it worked; Saul listened and swore an oath. He tries it again.

'But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.'

The answer is a spear.

Count them. Two throws at David in 18:11, one more in 19:10, and now one at his own son across a festival table in front of Abner and the court.

Note what the spear finally accomplishes: so Jonathan knew. The argument had not convinced him. His father's own weapon, thrown at his own head, did.

It took an attempt on his life to make Jonathan believe what David had told him in verse 3.

'And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.'

He leaves the table furious and does not eat.

The anger is right, and it is the second time in this book that a son of Kish has been angry at the correct thing — the Spirit of God rushed on Saul at Jabesh and his anger was greatly kindled for a town about to lose its eyes (11:6). The father was capable of this once.

The grief is for the other man. Jonathan has just been called a whore's son and had a spear thrown at him, and the narrator says he was grieved for David.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the morning Jonathan goes out with a boy and shoots beyond him, calling the agreed words — is not the arrow beyond you? — and then, hurry, be quick, do not stay (vv. 35-38). But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter (v. 39). He sends the boy home with his weapons (v. 40), and David comes out from behind the stone heap, bows three times to the ground, and they kiss and weep together, David weeping the most (v. 41). And Jonathan's farewell: go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD... the LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever (v. 42).
verseByVerse.theology: The elaborate signal turns out to be unnecessary. Once the boy is gone they simply meet, which is what they wanted all along, and the whole apparatus of arrows was to buy them five minutes.
verseByVerse.examples: David bows three times to the ground — the anointed king of Israel, prostrate before the heir who took off his robe for him. And David weeping the most is the narrator's own note. He is losing the only person at that court who was ever safe.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointment with David, and with him a little boy. And he said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him. And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?" And Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stay!" So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master. But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter. And Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go and carry them to the city." And as soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the stone heap and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. And they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most. Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'" And he rose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointment with David, and with him a little boy. And he said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.'

He keeps the appointment, and he shoots the arrow that means run.

'And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?" And Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stay!"'

The agreed words, shouted across a field to a child, and then three more that were not in the plan.

Hurry. Be quick. Do not stay. On the face of it he is chivvying a boy after an arrow. Behind a stone heap a man is listening to his friend telling him to run.

'But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.'

The narrator points at it so that we do not miss the double meaning.

'And Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go and carry them to the city."'

Then he sends the child home, and the whole elaborate system becomes unnecessary.

'And as soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the stone heap and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times.'

He comes out, and the first thing he does is put his face in the dirt.

Three times, which is the full formal obeisance offered to a king. And it is being offered by the man God has anointed to be king, to the heir who has just given up the throne for him.

'And they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most.'

Two men in a field, kissing and weeping, and the narrator adds three words nobody asked him for.

David weeping the most.

It is a strange, small, entirely human observation, and it is the kind of detail that gets into a story only because somebody was there. And it is a fair question why it was David.

Jonathan is losing a friend and going back to a house where his father throws spears at him. David is losing everything at once: his position, his wife, his home, his standing, the court where he was loved, and the only man in it who was ever safe. He is walking into the wilderness with nothing, and he will not have a settled address for a decade.

'Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'"'

The farewell is a covenant, not a goodbye.

Go in peace is what you say to somebody you may not see again. And then he gives the reason it can be said: they have sworn, in God's name, and the LORD is between them, and it extends to their children, and it is forever.

He does not promise to see David again. He does not promise to protect him, which is beyond his power. He states what has been sworn and who guarantees it.

'And he rose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.'

One goes out into the country and one goes back into the town, and the sentence is as bare as that.

They will meet once more. In three chapters, in the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan will come out and find David in the woods and strengthen his hand in God, and say the thing his father could never say: you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you (23:16-17). That is the last conversation they ever have.

After that, Jonathan appears once more in this book, dead on Mount Gilboa beside his father (31:2). And David will say over him the words that end their story: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me (2 Sam. 1:26).

The covenant made in this field outlived both of them. It is why a crippled man who could not walk was carried into the palace years later and given a permanent place at the king's table — because two young men in serious trouble swore something to each other in the open air, with God between them, and one of them remembered.

21.title: David at Nob
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?"<sup>2</sup>And David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I send you, and with which I have charged you.' I have made an appointment with the young men for such and such a place.<sup>3</sup>Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is here."<sup>4</sup>And the priest answered David, "I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread— if the young men have kept themselves from women."<sup>5</sup>And David answered the priest, "Truly women have been kept from us as always when I go on an expedition. The vessels of the young men are holy even when it is an ordinary journey. How much more today will their vessels be holy?"<sup>6</sup>So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away.<sup>7</sup>Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen.<sup>8</sup>Then David said to Ahimelech, "Then have you not here a spear or a sword at hand? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste."<sup>9</sup>And the priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, behold, it is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you will take that, take it, for there is none but that here." And David said, "There is none like that; give it to me."<sup>10</sup>And David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath.<sup>11</sup>And the servants of Achish said to him, "Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"<sup>12</sup>And David took these words to heart and was much afraid of Achish the king of Gath.<sup>13</sup>So he changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands and made marks on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down his beard.<sup>14</sup>Then Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see the man is mad. Why then have you brought him to me?<sup>15</sup>Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to behave as a madman in my presence? Shall this fellow come into my house?"
21.overview:
A priest at Nob comes out trembling to meet a man walking up the road alone, and his question goes straight to the trouble: why are you alone? Men in David's position do not travel by themselves. And David lies to him — there is no secret royal errand — and the lie is what puts the priest in danger, because a man told he is helping the king helps freely and asks nothing further. David himself names it in the next chapter: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house.

There is no ordinary bread in the building, only the twelve loaves of the Presence that the law reserves for Aaron's sons in a holy place. Ahimelech weighs it and hands them over — and a thousand years later the Son of God cites him approvingly in an argument with the most careful rule-keepers of his generation, admits the irregularity outright (it was not lawful), and draws the conclusion from Hosea: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.

Then one verse dropped in with no comment: an Edomite called Doeg, Saul's chief herdsman, was at the sanctuary that day. Everything in chapter 22 comes out of it. And Goliath's sword, wrapped behind the ephod ever since Elah, is handed back to David on the day he has nothing at all.

So he runs to Gath, which is Goliath's home town, carrying Goliath's sword — is recognised at once by the song that started all his trouble, is much afraid, and saves his life by drooling into his beard in the gateway. Two psalms carry headings pointing to that day, and one of them is oh, taste and see that the LORD is good.
21.theology:
The lie, named by David himself (v. 2). The narrator offers no defence and neither should a reader. What makes it worse than a private falsehood is its effect: a priest who believed he was assisting the king assisted freely, and eighty-five men died for it. David says so at 22:22 without excusing himself.

Mercy and not sacrifice (vv. 4-6). Jesus takes this incident up in all three Synoptics (Matt. 12:3-7; Mark 2:25-26; Luke 6:3-4) and does not argue that the rule did not apply — he says plainly it was not lawful. The irregularity is admitted, and the conclusion drawn is Hosea 6:6, which is Samuel's principle at 15:22 in another key. God is not indifferent to his own arrangements, and he is not served by a use of them that leaves a hungry man hungry. Ahimelech got it right, and the Lord said so.

Doeg, planted (v. 7). The narrator interrupts a conversation about bread to say somebody else was in the building, gives his nationality, employer and trade, and goes straight back to the bread. The whole of the next chapter is in that verse, and it is left entirely unremarked.

The trophy of his best day (v. 9). Goliath's sword has lain wrapped behind the ephod since Elah, a memorial of the day God saved Israel by a boy with a sling, and it is handed back to David on the worst day of his life — who takes it to the dead man's home town.

Where Psalm 34 came from. He was much afraid, and the narrator says so of the man who ran at a giant. He scratched at a gate and let saliva run into his beard because it was the only thing he could think of. And the headings of Psalms 56 and 34 point at that day — when I am afraid, I put my trust in you, and oh, taste and see that the LORD is good. The psalm did not come from the throne. It came from the gate at Gath, which anybody should hold on to whose own worst day would not look like a testimony from outside.
21.examples:
Then: The most famous soldier in Israel walked into a country priest's yard alone and hungry, told him a lie to get bread, took the sword he had captured as a boy off a hook behind the ephod, and carried it into the home town of the man he had killed with it — where he saved his life by pretending to be insane.

Now: Two things, and they pull against each other, which is why the chapter needs both. Ahimelech is the model for what to do when a rule and a hungry person meet in the same room, and the Lord Jesus said so. And David is the warning about what a convenient falsehood costs when other people are standing in the room while you tell it. The same chapter holds both, and so does most of life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Bread of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David arrives alone at Nob, and Ahimelech the priest comes to meet him trembling, asking why he is on his own (v. 1). David tells him the king has sent him on a secret errand, which is untrue, and asks for five loaves (vv. 2-3). There is no ordinary bread, only the holy bread — and the priest gives it, on the understanding that the men are ceremonially clean (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD and replaced weekly, and the law says plainly that it belonged to Aaron and his sons and was to be eaten in a holy place (Lev. 24:5-9). Ahimelech hands it to a fugitive and his men.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus takes this incident up in all three Synoptic Gospels when the Pharisees object to his disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, and his conclusion is Hosea's: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice (Matt. 12:3-7). It is Samuel's principle at 15:22, applied by the Lord to a hungry man and a rule.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?" And David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I send you, and with which I have charged you.' I have made an appointment with the young men for such and such a place. Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is here." And the priest answered David, "I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread— if the young men have kept themselves from women." And David answered the priest, "Truly women have been kept from us as always when I go on an expedition. The vessels of the young men are holy even when it is an ordinary journey. How much more today will their vessels be holy?" So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?"'

The priest is frightened before a word is said.

Nob was where the tabernacle had been re-established after Shiloh fell, and the man in charge is a great-grandson of Eli. What he sees coming up the road is the king's son-in-law, the captain of the bodyguard, the most famous soldier in Israel — on foot, unarmed, and by himself.

His question is the right one and it goes straight to the trouble: why are you alone? Men in David's position do not travel alone. Something has gone very wrong, and Ahimelech can see it.

'And David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I send you.'"'

David lies to him.

It should be said plainly, because David himself will say it plainly in the next chapter. There is no secret royal errand. He is running for his life, and he invents a commission to explain himself, and the invention is what puts the priest in danger — because a man who has been told he is helping the king will help freely and without asking further questions.

Twenty-two verses from now, when eighty-five priests are dead, David will say: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house (22:22). The narrator offers no defence of him here and neither should a reader.

'"Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is here."'

He is hungry, and that is the whole of the request.

'And the priest answered David, "I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread — if the young men have kept themselves from women."'

There is nothing in the building but the bread of the Presence.

The law is specific about it. Twelve loaves in two rows on a table of pure gold before the LORD, replaced every Sabbath, and the old loaves shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion (Lev. 24:5-9).

Ahimelech knows this perfectly well; he is the priest. And he weighs it, attaches the one condition that seems to him to matter, and hands it over.

'And David answered the priest, "Truly women have been kept from us as always when I go on an expedition..." So the priest gave him the holy bread.'

Now the reason this small transaction is famous.

A thousand years later, on a Sabbath, some Pharisees watch Jesus' disciples pulling heads of grain as they walk through a field, and object. And he answers them with this chapter.

Have you not read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God... and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him? (Mark 2:25-26).

Note what he does not say. He does not say the bread was not holy, or that the rule did not apply, or that David was technically within his rights. He says it was not lawful. The irregularity is admitted.

Then, in Matthew's account, he draws the conclusion out of the prophets: if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the guiltless (Matt. 12:7).

That is Hosea 6:6, and it is Samuel's principle at Gilgal six chapters ago: to obey is better than sacrifice (15:22). The same order of things. God is not indifferent to his own arrangements, and he is not served by a use of them that leaves a hungry man hungry.

Ahimelech got it right. Faced with a starving man and twelve consecrated loaves that were about to be replaced anyway, he fed him — and the Son of God cited him approvingly in an argument with the most careful rule-keepers of his generation.

One footnote, since readers meet it. Mark's version says this happened in the days of Abiathar the high priest, and the priest here is Ahimelech, Abiathar's father. Abiathar is the man who escapes the massacre in the next chapter and becomes the well-known high priest of the period, so the phrase reads naturally as locating the incident in his era, or in the section of Scripture associated with his name. Nothing in either account depends on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrator drops in a name and moves on: a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen (v. 7). David then asks for a weapon, having come away with nothing, and Ahimelech tells him what is in the building: the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah... wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod (vv. 8-9). There is none like that; give it to me.
verseByVerse.theology: Doeg is placed in the room with no comment whatever. He is Saul's chief herdsman, he is an Edomite, and he is at the sanctuary for some religious reason of his own. The next chapter is what he does with what he saw.
verseByVerse.examples: The sword David took from the giant has been at the sanctuary ever since, wrapped up behind the ephod as a memorial. It comes back to him on the day he has nothing at all — and in the very next verse he carries it to Gath, which is the town Goliath came from.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen. Then David said to Ahimelech, "Then have you not here a spear or a sword at hand? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste." And the priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, behold, it is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you will take that, take it, for there is none but that here." And David said, "There is none like that; give it to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen.'

One verse, dropped in, with no comment at all.

The narrator interrupts a conversation about bread to tell us that somebody else was in the building, and then goes straight back to the bread. He gives us the man's nationality, his employer, and his job, and says nothing about what he is doing there beyond a phrase that probably means he was fulfilling some religious obligation.

An Edomite — a foreigner, from Esau's people — who is Saul's chief herdsman, at the sanctuary, watching the king's fugitive son-in-law take holy bread and a weapon from the high priest.

Everything in the next chapter comes out of this verse, and the writer plants it without underlining.

'Then David said to Ahimelech, "Then have you not here a spear or a sword at hand? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste."'

The lie continues, and he asks for a weapon.

The detail is true even if the reason is not: he has nothing. He left the court through a window at night with what he stood up in.

'And the priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, behold, it is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod."'

There it is.

The last thing the narrator told us about that sword was that David took it off the giant's body and used it to cut off his head (17:51), and that he put the armour in his tent. The sword itself came here, to the sanctuary, and has been lying wrapped in cloth behind the ephod ever since — a relic of the day God saved Israel by a boy with a sling.

It is handed back to him on the worst day of his life so far.

'And David said, "There is none like that; give it to me."'

Four words, and they can be read two ways at once.

Practically, it is the only weapon in the building and he takes it. But he says more than that: there is none like that. He is holding the sword he took when he had none, given by a God who saves not with sword and spear, on a day when he has nothing else at all.

His best day's trophy is the equipment of his worst.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David flees to Achish king of Gath, and is recognised at once: is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing... Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands? (vv. 10-11). He is much afraid (v. 12), so he feigns madness — scratching at the doors of the gate and letting his spittle run down his beard (v. 13). Achish is contemptuous: do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to behave as a madman in my presence? (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: He has run to the enemy's capital carrying the enemy champion's sword, and the first thing the courtiers do is quote the song that started all his trouble. There is nowhere left for him inside Israel and nowhere safe outside it.
verseByVerse.examples: Two psalms carry titles pointing to this episode. Psalm 56 — when the Philistines seized him in Gath — and Psalm 34, whose heading names the day he changed his behavior before Abimelech. That psalm contains oh, taste and see that the LORD is good, and it was written about a man drooling into his beard in a foreign gateway.

verseByVerse.quote: And David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath. And the servants of Achish said to him, "Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?" And David took these words to heart and was much afraid of Achish the king of Gath. So he changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands and made marks on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down his beard. Then Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see the man is mad. Why then have you brought him to me? Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to behave as a madman in my presence? Shall this fellow come into my house?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath.'

Read that sentence and then remember what he is carrying.

Gath is Goliath's town. It is named as his in the first description of him — a champion named Goliath of Gath (17:4) — and David is walking into it with the man's sword on his hip.

It is either the boldest thing in the book or the most desperate, and verse 12 tells us which.

'And the servants of Achish said to him, "Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"'

They know him at once, and they quote the song.

That song has now followed him everywhere. It made Saul watch him with suspicion, it was in Saul's mouth when he raged at Jonathan, and here it is in a Philistine court, sung back at him by the servants of the king whose champion he killed. Everybody in that room can recite it.

They also call him the king of the land, which is not his title and is a shrewd guess by men who have been keeping an eye on Israel.

'And David took these words to heart and was much afraid of Achish the king of Gath.'

The narrator says it without any softening: much afraid.

This is the man who ran at a giant. He is now standing in that giant's home town, recognised, in a foreign court, with no army and no plan, and he is frightened.

'So he changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands and made marks on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down his beard.'

So the anointed king of Israel scratches at a gate and drools into his beard.

Nothing here can be made dignified and the writer does not try. Madness was one of the few conditions that afforded a man protection in that world — the mad were thought to be under a god's hand, and were left alone — so it is a calculated performance and it works. It is also the lowest point of his life so far, and it is recorded in detail.

'Then Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see the man is mad. Why then have you brought him to me? Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to behave as a madman in my presence?"'

The king's irritation is entirely about the inconvenience, and the contempt is total.

Do I lack madmen? He is not even worth a decision. They throw him out.

Now here is what makes this chapter worth reading twice, and it is not in the chapter.

Two psalms carry headings that point to this day. The first is Psalm 56 — when the Philistines seized him in Gath — and it says: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you... in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me? (Ps. 56:3-4). He was much afraid, verse 12 says so, and the psalm does not pretend otherwise; it puts the fear and the trust in the same sentence.

The second is Psalm 34, whose heading names the day when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out. And that psalm is one of the most-loved in the book. I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears... this poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles... oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! (Ps. 34:4-8).

Somebody wrote taste and see that the LORD is good about the afternoon he stood in an enemy gateway with saliva running into his beard because it was the only thing he could think of to stay alive.

Hold that, if your own worst day would not look like a testimony from the outside. The psalm did not come from the throne. It came from the gate at Gath.

22.title: The Massacre at Nob
22.text: <sup>1</sup>David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all his father's house heard it, they went down there to him.<sup>2</sup>And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about four hundred men.<sup>3</sup>And David went from there to Mizpeh of Moab. And he said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me."<sup>4</sup>And he left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in the stronghold.<sup>5</sup>Then the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not remain in the stronghold; depart, and go into the land of Judah." So David departed and went into the forest of Hereth.<sup>6</sup>Now Saul heard that David was discovered, and the men who were with him. Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing about him.<sup>7</sup>And Saul said to his servants who stood about him, "Hear now, people of Benjamin; will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards, will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds,<sup>8</sup>that all of you have conspired against me? No one discloses to me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day."<sup>9</sup>Then answered Doeg the Edomite, who stood by the servants of Saul, "I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub,<sup>10</sup>and he inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."<sup>11</sup>Then the king sent to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests who were at Nob, and all of them came to the king.<sup>12</sup>And Saul said, "Hear now, son of Ahitub." And he answered, "Here I am, my lord."<sup>13</sup>And Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread and a sword and have inquired of God for him, so that he has risen against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?"<sup>14</sup>Then Ahimelech answered the king, "And who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king's son-in-law, and captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house?<sup>15</sup>Is today the first time that I have inquired of God for him? No! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all the house of my father, for your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little."<sup>16</sup>And the king said, "You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house."<sup>17</sup>And the king said to the guard who stood about him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and they knew that he fled and did not disclose it to me." But the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the LORD.<sup>18</sup>Then the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five persons who wore the linen ephod.<sup>19</sup>And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword.<sup>20</sup>But one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David.<sup>21</sup>And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And David said to Abiathar, "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house.<sup>23</sup>Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping."
22.overview:
David reaches a cave, and the muster roll that gathers to him is one of the least promising in Scripture: everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul. Four hundred of them, and not one word about courage, ability or faith. These are the men who become the mighty men of 2 Samuel 23. He puts his parents in Moab — his great-grandmother Ruth's country — till I know what God will do for me.

Meanwhile Saul sits under a tamarisk with his spear, appeals to his own tribe, and offers them fields and vineyards and commands of thousands: which is precisely the confiscation Samuel warned a king would take (8:14), now offered as the currency of loyalty. The rest of the speech is self-pity, four mes in two verses. And Doeg the Edomite steps forward with a report in which every fact is true and the one exculpating fact — that David told the priest he was on the king's business — is left out.

Ahimelech's defence is honest and it is the worst thing he could have said: he lists David's faithfulness, his place as son-in-law, his command of the bodyguard, his honour in the house — every one of which is the reason Saul wants him dead. And the bodyguard refuses the order. Ordinary soldiers, in silence, decline to strike the priests of the LORD, and the narrator records it without a word of praise.

So Doeg does it. Eighty-five men in linen ephods, and then the town: both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep. That is the wording of the command about Amalek which Saul would not obey (15:3). He would not do it to the enemies of God. He does it to a town of God's priests.
22.theology:
The distressed, the indebted, the bitter (v. 2). Not patriots and not veterans — the failed, the insolvent and the aggrieved, gathering round a man with no position and a price on his head. Within a generation they are the corps listed by name, the men who broke a Philistine garrison to fetch him water from Bethlehem's well (2 Sam. 23:8-17). The making of them happens in caves, under a commander who is himself being hunted.

Doeg's kind of lie (vv. 9-10). Every fact he reports is accurate. He simply omits the sentence that makes it innocent — and he was standing there when it was said. That is how the most damaging falsehood is usually told: not by inventing anything, but by reporting true things with the exculpating fact removed.

An honest man answering the wrong charge (v. 14). Ahimelech thinks he is refuting treason and is in fact producing character evidence for the man the king cannot bear. He does not know he is standing in front of somebody who has thrown four spears, and he does not know David lied to him. He dies for a deception he was never party to.

The refusal (v. 17). The one clean thing in the chapter, and it comes from nobody in particular — not Abner, the commander and the king's cousin, who is standing right there, but the men without names. No speech, no argument; they simply do not move. The narrator offers no praise, and the absence of comment is the comment.

Verse 19 against 15:3. Both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep is the command Saul was given about a nation under a four-century sentence, and would not carry out; he kept the best of the flock and lost the kingdom for it. Here he executes it in full, on his own initiative, against an Israelite town, down to the infants and the donkeys. He would not do it to God's enemies. He does it to God's priests, and the writer states the two lists seven chapters apart and adds nothing.

Both held at once. This is also the fulfilment of the oracle against Eli — no old man in the house, the descendants dying by the sword of men (2:31-33), and Ahimelech was Eli's great-grandson. God's word stands, and it makes Saul and Doeg not one degree less guilty of what they chose. Scripture holds both without offering to resolve them, exactly as at Acts 2:23.

I have occasioned the death (v. 22). Every excuse was available and true — Saul ordered it, Doeg did it, David was running for his life — and he uses none of them. He owns the lie of chapter 21 and the decision to go on with it in front of a man he had already worked out. And then he offers the only thing he has: not safety, which he does not possess, but company. He who seeks my life seeks your life. Saul destroyed the priesthood to protect his crown, and the last priest walked out of the ruins carrying the ephod to David (23:6).
22.examples:
Then: A king's own bodyguard stood in a ring around him and refused, without a word, to kill the priests of the LORD — so he handed the sword to a foreigner, who killed eighty-five men in their vestments and then destroyed their town down to the livestock, using the exact terms of a command from God that the same king had refused to obey against an enemy.

Now: Three things. Doeg's report is the model of the damaging truth — nothing invented, one thing left out — so ask whether any account you have given lately was accurate in that way. The guards are the model of the other kind of courage: no speech, no confrontation, simply not moving when told to do what should not be done. And David's I have occasioned the death is the hardest. He had four true things he could have said instead, and said none of them, to the one man in the world with a right to hear it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Everyone Who Was in Distress
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David escapes to the cave of Adullam, and his family come down to him (v. 1). And then others: everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about four hundred men (v. 2). He takes his parents to the king of Moab for safety till I know what God will do for me (vv. 3-4). And the prophet Gad tells him to leave the stronghold for Judah, and he goes (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Read the muster roll. Not veterans and not volunteers with a cause: the distressed, the indebted and the bitter. These are the men nobody else wanted, and they become the core of the army that will one day be listed by name as David's mighty men (2 Sam. 23).
verseByVerse.examples: He puts his parents in Moab, which is not random. His great-grandmother was Ruth the Moabitess, who came from that country to Bethlehem and would not go back (Ruth 1:16). David sends his father and mother the other way along the same road.

verseByVerse.quote: David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all his father's house heard it, they went down there to him. And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about four hundred men. And David went from there to Mizpeh of Moab. And he said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me." And he left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in the stronghold. Then the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not remain in the stronghold; depart, and go into the land of Judah." So David departed and went into the forest of Hereth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all his father's house heard it, they went down there to him.'

He gets out of Philistine territory and into a cave, and the first people to arrive are his family.

Including Eliab, presumably, who told him in front of the army that he knew the evil of your heart. Whatever was between those brothers, when David was a hunted man his father's whole house came down and joined him in a hole in the ground.

'And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about four hundred men.'

Then the rest, and the roll rewards a slow reading.

Everyone in distress — men under pressure, in trouble of some kind. Everyone in debt — men who could not pay, which in that world meant men facing slavery for themselves and their children. And everyone bitter in soul — the aggrieved, the disappointed, men with a grudge against how things had gone for them.

Four hundred of them, and there is not one word in the list about courage or ability or faith.

This is the beginning of David's army. Not a militia of patriots, and not veterans: the failed, the indebted and the embittered, gathering in a cave around a man with no position and a price on his head. The Hebrew for what they are is not flattering and the writer does not flatter them.

Within twenty years these men, or their sons, are the corps listed by name at the end of 2 Samuel — the thirty and the three, the men who broke through a Philistine garrison to bring David a drink of water from the well at Bethlehem (2 Sam. 23:8-17). The distressed and the debtors became the mighty men.

The making of them is what the next ten chapters are about, and it happens in caves and wildernesses under a commander who is himself being hunted.

'And David went from there to Mizpeh of Moab. And he said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me."'
