He gets his parents out of the country, and the country he chooses is Moab.

That is not a random choice. Jesse's grandmother was Ruth the Moabitess, who left Moab for Bethlehem and would not go back (Ruth 1:16). David is sending his elderly father and mother to his own family's other side, along a road his great-grandmother walked in the opposite direction.

Note the phrase he uses for his situation: till I know what God will do for me. Not until things settle, or until Saul dies, or until I have an army. He does not know what is coming and says so, and he expects God to do something.

'Then the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not remain in the stronghold; depart, and go into the land of Judah." So David departed and went into the forest of Hereth.'

A prophet appears with no introduction, and David obeys immediately.

Gad turns up here as though we know him, and he stays with David for the rest of his life; he is the one who brings him the choice of three judgments after the census, forty years later (2 Sam. 24:11-14). From this point the fugitive has a prophet, and shortly he will have a priest with an ephod as well.

The instruction itself is counter-intuitive: leave the stronghold, go back into Judah, which is where Saul is looking. He goes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — Hear Now, People of Benjamin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul is under a tamarisk tree at Gibeah with his spear in his hand, and his speech is one long complaint: will the son of Jesse give you fields and vineyards and make you commanders? — none of you is sorry for me (vv. 6-8). Doeg the Edomite volunteers what he saw at Nob (vv. 9-10). Ahimelech is summoned with his whole father's house and answers with dignity: who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king's son-in-law, and captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house? Is today the first time that I have inquired of God for him? (vv. 11-15). Saul's reply is four words: you shall surely die (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The bribe Saul dangles is the exact list Samuel gave when he warned what a king would take: he will take the best of your fields and vineyards... and give them to his servants (8:14). He is buying loyalty with other people's confiscated land, and saying so out loud.
verseByVerse.examples: Ahimelech's defence is entirely true and it is the wrong defence, because the charge is not really about him. He testifies to David's faithfulness — son-in-law, captain of the bodyguard, honoured in the house — to a king for whom every one of those facts is the problem.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Saul heard that David was discovered, and the men who were with him. Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing about him. And Saul said to his servants who stood about him, "Hear now, people of Benjamin; will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards, will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, that all of you have conspired against me? No one discloses to me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day." Then answered Doeg the Edomite, who stood by the servants of Saul, "I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, and he inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Saul heard that David was discovered, and the men who were with him. Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing about him.'

Everybody is standing and the king is sitting under a tree with a spear.

The narrator has now placed that spear in Saul's hand four times, and it has been thrown three. It is the thing he holds.

'And Saul said to his servants who stood about him, "Hear now, people of Benjamin; will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards, will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?"'

He opens with the tribe.

Hear now, people of Benjamin. His court is staffed with his own clansmen, and his first argument is that David is from Judah and they are not. It is the oldest appeal in politics and it is being made by a man who was anointed to lead all twelve tribes.

Then the bribe, which should be set beside the warning it echoes.

Samuel had told the nation what a king would do: he will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants (8:14). That is the confiscation Israel was warned about, and here is the king naming it as the currency of loyalty — and implying, quite openly, that this is what he does for them.

'"that all of you have conspired against me? No one discloses to me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me."'

The rest of the speech is self-pity, and the pronouns run one way.

Conspired against me. Discloses to me. Sorry for me. My son against me. Four times in two verses, from a king to his own household, complaining that nobody feels for him.

Note also that he knows about the covenant. When my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse — he has worked out what happened in the field, and his complaint is not that it happened but that nobody told him.

'Then answered Doeg the Edomite, who stood by the servants of Saul, "I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, and he inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."'

Then the Edomite speaks.

He has been waiting for this. A king has just told a room full of Benjaminites that nobody cares about him and that he is surrounded by conspirators, and the one foreigner in the room steps forward with information.

Everything he says is factually accurate and the whole report is a lie in its effect. He describes a priest giving bread, a weapon and an oracle to a fugitive, and leaves out the one thing that makes it innocent: that Ahimelech had been told David was on the king's own business.

Doeg was standing there. He heard it. He omits it.

That is how the most damaging kind of falsehood is usually told — not by inventing anything, but by reporting true things with the exculpating fact removed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests who were at Nob, and all of them came to the king. And Saul said, "Hear now, son of Ahitub." And he answered, "Here I am, my lord." And Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread and a sword and have inquired of God for him, so that he has risen against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?" Then Ahimelech answered the king, "And who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king's son-in-law, and captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house? Is today the first time that I have inquired of God for him? No! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all the house of my father, for your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little." And the king said, "You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king sent to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests who were at Nob, and all of them came to the king.'

He summons not one priest but the whole family, which tells us what he has decided before anybody arrives.

And they come. Every one of them walks to Gibeah at the king's word, because that is what you do when the king sends.

'And Saul said, "Hear now, son of Ahitub." And he answered, "Here I am, my lord."'

He is addressed by his father's name, not his own — the same trick Saul uses on David — and he answers here I am, which is the word Samuel said in the dark at Shiloh and Jonathan's sentence in the field.

'And Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread and a sword and have inquired of God for him, so that he has risen against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?"'

The charge is conspiracy, and Doeg's three items are recited as the evidence: bread, a sword, an oracle.

'Then Ahimelech answered the king, "And who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king's son-in-law, and captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house?"'

The priest's defence is the truth, delivered straight, and it is the worst thing he could possibly have said.

Every clause of it is accurate. David is the most faithful servant Saul has. He is the king's son-in-law. He is captain of the bodyguard. He is honoured in the house.

And every one of those facts is precisely what Saul cannot bear. The man is defending himself by listing the reasons the king wants David dead.

It is what happens when an honest man is questioned by somebody whose real motive he has not grasped. Ahimelech thinks he is answering a charge of treason and is producing character evidence. He has no idea he is standing in front of a man who has thrown four spears.

'"Is today the first time that I have inquired of God for him? No! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all the house of my father, for your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little."'

This is his real answer, and it is unanswerable: this was routine.

He has enquired of God for David before, more than once. Of course he has — David is the captain of the bodyguard, and consulting the LORD before an operation is what the priesthood is for. Nothing that happened at Nob was unusual in any way.

Then the plea: your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little. He is telling the truth, and he does not know that David lied to him, and he is about to die for a deception he was never party to.

'And the king said, "You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house."'

Four words of verdict, and no engagement with the defence at all.

Saul does use his name here, which he has not done since the summons. And the sentence extends to the whole family, which is why they were all summoned.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — The Servants of the King Would Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul orders his guard to kill the priests, because their hand also is with David — but the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the LORD (v. 17). So he turns to Doeg, who kills eighty-five men wearing the linen ephod (v. 18). And then Nob itself: both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The refusal in v. 17 is the one clean thing in the chapter. Ordinary soldiers, standing in front of their king, decline an unlawful order about the priests of the LORD — and the narrator states it without a word of praise, which is its own kind of praise.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 19 is the sentence to read twice. Both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep is the wording of the command Saul was given about Amalek and would not obey (15:3). He would not do it to the enemies of God. He does it to a town of God's priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to the guard who stood about him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and they knew that he fled and did not disclose it to me." But the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the LORD. Then the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five persons who wore the linen ephod. And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king said to the guard who stood about him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and they knew that he fled and did not disclose it to me."'

He gives the order to his own bodyguard, and he calls them what they are while doing it: the priests of the LORD.

He is not confused about who these men are. He knows.

'But the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the LORD.'

Here is the one clean thing in the chapter.

They refuse. Ordinary soldiers, standing in a ring around a king who has already killed for less, decline to carry out a direct royal order, and they decline it in silence — the text records no speech, no argument and no plea. They simply do not move.

The narrator does not praise them, which is his way, and the absence of comment is the comment. Somewhere in the guard of a man like Saul there were men who had worked out that there are orders you do not obey.

Sit with that, because this is the only recorded refusal in the chapter and it comes from nobody in particular. Not Abner, the commander and the king's cousin, who is standing there. Not any of the servants named. The men without names.

'Then the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five persons who wore the linen ephod.'

So he turns to the foreigner, and the foreigner does it.

Eighty-five men in priestly dress, killed by one man on the orders of the king of Israel, in front of a bodyguard who had just refused.

The detail who wore the linen ephod is put there so that nobody can pretend these were combatants. They were dressed for the altar when they were summoned and they were dressed for the altar when they died.

'And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword.'

Now read that list, and then turn back seven chapters.

Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey (15:3).

It is the same sentence. Man and woman, child and infant, and the livestock enumerated after them.

Saul was given that command by God about a nation under a four-hundred-year sentence for attacking the weak at the back of Israel's column, and he did not carry it out. He kept the best of the sheep and the oxen and the fattened calves and the king, and told Samuel it was for sacrifice, and lost the kingdom for it.

And here, of his own initiative, with no command from anybody, he executes it in full — against an Israelite town, the town of the priests of the LORD, down to the infants and the donkeys.

He would not do it to God's enemies. He does it to God's priests.

There is nothing to add to that and the writer adds nothing. He states the two lists seven chapters apart and lets anyone who is reading carefully put them together.

One more thing, and it is not a consolation but it is the truth. This is the fulfilment of a sentence passed forty years earlier. The man of God told Eli that God would cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house, and that all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men (2:31-33). Ahimelech was Eli's great-grandson.

God's word stands, and it does not make Saul or Doeg one degree less guilty of what they chose to do. Scripture holds both of those at once, as it does at Acts 2:23, and it does not offer to resolve them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — With Me You Shall Be in Safekeeping
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One son of Ahimelech escapes and runs to David: Abiathar (v. 20). He tells him what has happened (v. 21). And David answers without a word of excuse: I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house (v. 22). Then: stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not say he could not have known, or that Saul is responsible, or that Doeg did it. Both are true and he says neither. I have occasioned the death — and he had seen Doeg standing there and gone ahead anyway.
verseByVerse.examples: Abiathar is the survivor promised in the oracle against Eli's house: the only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out (2:33). He serves David for forty years and is finally removed by Solomon, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27).

verseByVerse.quote: But one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David. And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD. And David said to Abiathar, "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house. Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David.'

One man gets out.

He is the survivor the oracle promised. The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart (2:33). Abiathar will serve David for forty years, and Solomon will finally remove him from the priesthood — and the historian stops to say why: thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27).

He runs to David, which is the only direction left.

'And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD.'

'And David said to Abiathar, "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house."'

David takes it, without one word of qualification.

Look at what he does not say, because every one of these was available to him and every one is true. He does not say that Saul gave the order. He does not say that Doeg swung the sword. He does not say that he had no way of knowing, or that he was running for his life, or that a hungry man must eat.

He says two things. I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. He saw the man. He understood what he was, and what he would do with what he had seen, and he asked for the bread and the sword anyway.

And then: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house.

That is a confession of the kind almost nobody makes, and it is made to the one surviving son of the family, on the day he arrives with the news. There is no attempt to share the weight out.

It does not make him the murderer; Saul gave the order and Doeg carried it out and both will answer for it. What David is owning is the lie in chapter 21 and the decision to go on with it in front of a man he knew was watching.

'"Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping."'

Then he offers the only thing he has, which is a place beside him in a cave.

The honesty of it is the striking part: he who seeks my life seeks your life. He does not promise safety, because he has none to promise. He is a hunted man offering a hunted man company, and the guarantee amounts to whatever happens to me will happen to you.

And that turns out to be worth having. Abiathar brought the ephod down with him (23:6), and from the next chapter onward the fugitive can enquire of God directly — which is precisely what Saul, sitting on his throne under his tamarisk tree, can no longer do at all.

Saul destroyed the priesthood to protect his crown, and the last priest of Israel walked out of the ruins carrying the ephod to David.

23.title: David Strengthens Himself in the LORD
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Now they told David, "Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are robbing the threshing floors."<sup>2</sup>Therefore David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go and attack these Philistines?" And the LORD said to David, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."<sup>3</sup>But David's men said to him, "Behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?"<sup>4</sup>Then David inquired of the LORD again. And the LORD answered him, "Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will give the Philistines into your hand."<sup>5</sup>And David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines and brought away their livestock and struck them with a great blow. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.<sup>6</sup>When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech had fled to David to Keilah, he had come down with an ephod in his hand.<sup>7</sup>Now it was told Saul that David had come to Keilah. And Saul said, "God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars."<sup>8</sup>And Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men.<sup>9</sup>David knew that Saul was plotting harm against him. And he said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here."<sup>10</sup>Then David said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city on my account.<sup>11</sup>Will the men of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? O LORD, the God of Israel, please tell your servant." And the LORD said, "He will come down."<sup>12</sup>Then David said, "Will the men of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" And the LORD said, "They will surrender you."<sup>13</sup>Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed from Keilah, and they went wherever they could go. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up the expedition.<sup>14</sup>And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.<sup>15</sup>David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.<sup>16</sup>And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God.<sup>17</sup>And he said to him, "Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this."<sup>18</sup>And the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.<sup>19</sup>Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, which is south of Jeshimon?<sup>20</sup>Now come down, O king, according to all your heart's desire to come down, and our part shall be to surrender him into the king's hand."<sup>21</sup>And Saul said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me.<sup>22</sup>Go, make yet more sure. Know and see the place where his foot is, and who has seen him there, for it is told me that he is very cunning.<sup>23</sup>See therefore and take note of all the lurking places where he hides, and come back to me with sure information. Then I will go with you. And if he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah."<sup>24</sup>And they arose and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah to the south of Jeshimon.<sup>25</sup>And Saul and his men went to seek him. And David was told, so he went down to the rock and lived in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon.<sup>26</sup>Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other side of the mountain. And David was hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them,<sup>27</sup>a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land."<sup>28</sup>So Saul returned from pursuing after David and went against the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape.<sup>29</sup>And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of Engedi.
23.overview:
The Philistines are robbing the threshing floors at Keilah — stealing the year's food from a town of Judah — and David asks God whether to go. His men, quite reasonably, say it is a terrible idea; so he asks again, and God answers again, this time with a promise attached. He saves the town. A fugitive with six hundred men spends his only asset defending people who cannot pay him and will not shelter him, while the king with a standing army uses it to hunt him.

A single verse explains how he can ask at all: Abiathar came down from the ruins of Nob with an ephod in his hand. Four times in this chapter David asks God a question and gets an answer. Saul, who destroyed the priesthood to secure his crown, has nobody left to ask — so he infers instead: God has given him into my hand. Seven verses later the narrator answers him in his own words: God did not give him into his hand.

Then Jonathan walks into a wilderness his father's army is searching, for no purpose but one, and the text names it exactly: he strengthened his hand in God. He tells David the hunt will fail, that David will be king, that he himself will stand next to him — the one thing in the speech that never comes true — and then: Saul my father also knows this. Saul knows. The pursuit is not a mistake about a rival; it is a man fighting a verdict he has understood.

The Ziphites inform, the chase closes round a hill in the Wilderness of Maon with David running out of ground, and a messenger arrives with news of a Philistine raid. Saul breaks off. There is no angel and no recorded prayer — just bad news from somewhere else, arriving at the only minute it could have helped. They named the rock.
23.theology:
Asking, and asking again (vv. 2-4). The obvious course was to go, and he asked anyway; then his frightened men objected and he went back and asked a second time. God does not rebuke the second asking — he answers it with more than he gave the first, adding I will give the Philistines into your hand. Anyone who has been told that asking again is a failure of faith should look at verse 4.

The ephod, and the door Saul shut himself (v. 6). This reads like an aside and it is the engine of the chapter. The massacre at Nob put the priest and the ephod in the fugitive's camp, so David can enquire and the king cannot. Saul had already stopped hearing from God (28:6 will say so); Nob was him closing the last door with his own hand.

Reading providence backwards (v. 7). Saul is not a secularist — he reads events as God's doing, and hunts the LORD's anointed sincerely believing the LORD is helping him. That is a more frightening thing to be than an unbeliever. His method is the one to watch: he wants something, he sees a circumstance that serves it, and he names the circumstance God's will. Favourable circumstances prove nothing on their own, and the man who most needs to hear it is always the one whose plan is going well.

A warning is given so that it need not happen (vv. 11-12). God says the men of Keilah will surrender him; David leaves; they never do. That is not God being mistaken about the future — it is God telling a man what lies down a road so that he does not walk it, which is what nearly every warning in Scripture is for. A father who says that branch will break is not refuted when the child climbs down.

He strengthened his hand in God (v. 16). Not encouraged, not resupplied — the image is of a grip going slack, and Jonathan closing David's fingers back round what he already had. Nothing new was given; Samuel had poured the oil years before. What a hunted man loses is not information but hold. That is the whole ministry of encouragement in five words, and it requires no gift anybody lacks: say out loud, in the wilderness, the thing your friend already knows and can no longer feel.

Saul my father also knows this (v. 17). The pursuit is not paranoia and not a misjudgment of a rival. Saul has heard the verdict of God, understood it, and committed the rest of his reign and his army to fighting it. There is a kind of sin that continues precisely because it knows. And Jonathan's I shall be next to you is the one false line in a true speech: this is their last meeting, and he dies on Gilboa beside the father he went home to serve.

How rescue usually arrives (v. 27). No angel, no earthquake, no oracle, no recorded prayer — a messenger with bad news from elsewhere, at the only minute it could have mattered. That is verse 14 seen from the ground: God did not give him into his hand. And they marked the spot, as Samuel marked Ebenezer (7:12), because they knew they would forget by next year.
23.examples:
Then: Two armed forces went round one hill in opposite directions, yards apart and out of sight, with the smaller one running out of ground — until a rider reached the larger one with news of a raid three days' march away, and it turned and left. They called the hill the Rock of Escape.

Now: Two things to take. Jonathan is the pattern for what to do about a discouraged Christian, and it is simpler than most people think: you do not need a new word for them, you need to say the old one out loud where they are. Go to them, and strengthen their hand in God. And Saul at verse 7 is the pattern to avoid — the habit of taking a convenient circumstance as divine endorsement of what you already wanted. He was doing theology, and he was hunting God's anointed while he did it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Word comes that the Philistines are robbing the threshing floors at Keilah, and David asks the LORD whether to go (v. 1-2). The answer is yes. His men object — behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah — so he asks again, and gets the same answer with a promise attached (vv. 3-4). He saves the town (v. 5). And a note explains how he is able to ask: Abiathar came down with the ephod in his hand (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: He is a fugitive with four hundred frightened men and no standing, and the first thing he does with the little he has is spend it defending a town that is not his and cannot protect him. Saul, meanwhile, has an army and is using it to hunt one man.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 6 is the hinge of the whole chapter. The massacre at Nob put an ephod in David's camp, so the hunted man can ask God questions and the king on the throne cannot ask anybody anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they told David, "Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are robbing the threshing floors." Therefore David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go and attack these Philistines?" And the LORD said to David, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah." But David's men said to him, "Behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?" Then David inquired of the LORD again. And the LORD answered him, "Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will give the Philistines into your hand." And David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines and brought away their livestock and struck them with a great blow. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah. When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech had fled to David to Keilah, he had come down with an ephod in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now they told David, "Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are robbing the threshing floors."'

Note what is being robbed, because it is not treasure.

The threshing floors are where the grain harvest is separated and stored. Raiding them at harvest time is the cheapest way to make war on a farming town: you let them do the work and then take the year's food. Keilah is not facing a siege; it is facing a winter with nothing in the barn.

Keilah is a town of Judah, David's own tribe, about three miles from where he is hiding. And nobody from the government is coming, because the government's army is out looking for him.

'Therefore David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go and attack these Philistines?" And the LORD said to David, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."'

He asks first.

Keep that in view for the whole chapter, because it happens four times in twenty-nine verses and it is the thing that distinguishes him from the man hunting him. The obvious course is to go; his tribe is being robbed and he has four hundred armed men. He asks anyway.

'But David's men said to him, "Behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?"'

His men say no, and they are not being cowardly — they are being accurate.

They are wanted men in their own country. They are frightened where they are. Marching into open ground to fight the Philistine army, with Saul's forces somewhere behind them, is a plainly terrible idea, and any competent soldier would say so.

'Then David inquired of the LORD again. And the LORD answered him, "Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will give the Philistines into your hand."'

So he asks a second time, and God answers a second time, and adds something.

The first answer was an instruction. The second is an instruction with a promise inside it: I will give the Philistines into your hand. God does not rebuke him for asking twice. He gives the frightened men something to hold.

Anybody who has been told that asking again is a failure of faith should sit with that. David had a clear word and his men were afraid, so he went back and asked again, and God met the second asking with more than he gave the first.

'And David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines and brought away their livestock and struck them with a great blow. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.'

David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.

Look at what he is doing and what it costs him. He is a hunted man with no title, no supply line, and a price on his head, and he spends the one asset he has — four hundred men — on a town that cannot pay him, cannot shelter him, and as we are about to discover would hand him over within the week.

And Saul, who has a throne, a standing army and a commander-in-chief, is using all of it to chase one man round the hills while the Philistines rob his people's grain.

The narrator does not say which of them is behaving like a king. He does not need to.

'When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech had fled to David to Keilah, he came down with an ephod in his hand.'

Here is the note that explains the whole chapter.

It reads like an aside and it is the engine of everything that follows. Abiathar, the one survivor of Nob, arrived carrying the ephod — the priestly vestment used for enquiring of the LORD.

So David can ask God questions. Four times in this chapter he does, and four times he gets an answer.

Saul cannot ask anybody anything, because he killed the men who could have told him. He destroyed the priesthood at Nob to secure his crown, and the effect of it is that the priest and the ephod are now in the cave with his rival, and the king of Israel is left guessing.

He had already stopped hearing from God before that — the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets, as it will be put at 28:6. Nob was him closing the last door himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — God Has Given Him Into My Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul hears David is shut up in a walled town and concludes: God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars (v. 7). David calls for the ephod and asks two questions — will Saul come down, and will the men of Keilah surrender me? The answers are yes and yes (vv. 9-12). So he leaves, and Saul gives up the expedition (v. 13). The section closes: and Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul reads a providence and reads it exactly backwards. The narrator lets his sentence stand for seven verses and then answers it in the same words: God did not give him into his hand. A circumstance that looks like God's endorsement is not evidence of anything on its own.
verseByVerse.examples: The men of Keilah would have handed over the man who had just saved their harvest, and God says so before they can. Note what the answer does: because David is told what would happen, it never happens. The warning is given so that the thing warned of is avoided.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was told Saul that David had come to Keilah. And Saul said, "God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars." And Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men. David knew that Saul was plotting harm against him. And he said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here." Then David said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city on my account. Will the men of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? O LORD, the God of Israel, please tell your servant." And the LORD said, "He will come down." Then David said, "Will the men of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" And the LORD said, "They will surrender you." Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed from Keilah, and they went wherever they could go. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up the expedition. And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now it was told Saul that David had come to Keilah. And Saul said, "God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars."'

Read that sentence carefully, because it is one of the most instructive mistakes in Scripture.

Saul looks at a circumstance — his enemy is inside a walled town with gates — and he draws a theological conclusion from it: God has given him into my hand. The reasoning is not stupid. A man in a walled town is trapped; you can besiege him; that is simply true.

It is completely wrong, and the narrator will say so in his own words seven verses later. For the moment he lets it stand.

Two things in it repay attention.

The first is that Saul is doing theology. He is not a secularist; he reads events as God's providence, and he is at this moment hunting the LORD's anointed while sincerely believing the LORD is helping him do it. That is a more frightening thing to be than an atheist.

The second is the method. He has a desire, he sees a circumstance that serves it, and he calls the circumstance God's will. There is no asking involved, and there is nobody left to ask. Favourable circumstances are not, by themselves, evidence of anything at all — and the man who most needs to hear that is always the one whose plan is going well.

'And David knew that Saul was plotting harm against him. And he said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here."'

David's response to the same news is four words: bring the ephod here.

That is the contrast the chapter is built on, and it is put in consecutive verses. Saul infers. David asks.

'"O LORD, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city on my account. Will the men of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? O LORD, the God of Israel, please tell your servant."'

Notice the shape of the prayer before the questions in it.

To destroy the city on my account. His first thought is not his own neck but what his presence will cost the town he has just saved. That is the man; it is the same instinct as I have occasioned the death in the previous chapter.

'And the LORD said, "He will come down." Then David said, "Will the men of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" And the LORD said, "They will surrender you."'

Two questions, two answers, and the second one is bitter.

They will hand him over. The men whose harvest he saved last week, at the risk of every life he commands, will open the gates and give him to Saul rather than take the consequences of keeping him.

It should be said that they are not monsters. Saul had just destroyed an entire town for sheltering David — the news from Nob would have reached Keilah — and these are farmers with families inside walls that will not hold against an army. Fear does this to ordinary decent people. It does not make it less of a betrayal, and God tells David it is coming.

There is a question readers rightly ask here: if they never actually did it, in what sense was the answer true? The answer is that God told him what would happen, and the telling is why it did not. This is not God being mistaken about the future. It is God warning a man about a road so that the man does not walk down it — which is what almost every warning in Scripture is for. A father who says that branch will break is not proved wrong when the child comes down.

'Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed from Keilah, and they went wherever they could go. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up the expedition.'

Six hundred now, up from four hundred. Men keep coming.

And the phrase they went wherever they could go is as bleak as it sounds. No destination, no plan; out of the town and into the hills, because staying was the one thing they knew would kill them.

'And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.'

But God did not give him into his hand.

There is the answer to verse 7, in Saul's own vocabulary. He said God has given him into my hand. The narrator waits seven verses and then writes the sentence with the word not in it.

And note the rest of it: Saul sought him every day. Every day. This is a king spending the whole of his reign, day after day, on one man — and the reason he never finds him is not that David is clever, though he is. The reason is stated: God did not hand him over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — He Strengthened His Hand in God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David is at Horesh in the Wilderness of Ziph, and saw that Saul had come out to seek his life (v. 15). And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God (v. 16). He says: do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this (v. 17). They make a covenant, and part (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's son walks into a wilderness where his father's army is searching, for no purpose except to encourage his friend, and the text names the purpose precisely: not cheered him up, not brought supplies — strengthened his hand in God. He put David's grip back on the thing David already knew.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul my father also knows this. The pursuit is not a mistake about a rival. Saul knows who will be king and is hunting him anyway. And Jonathan's I shall be next to you never comes true: this is the last time these two men meet, and the next mention of Jonathan is his body on Mount Gilboa.

verseByVerse.quote: David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh. And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God. And he said to him, "Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this." And the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the Wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.'

This is where the chapter turns, and it turns on a visit.

The verse establishes what David can see: the king is out, personally, hunting him. He is in scrub country with six hundred men and nowhere to be.

'And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God.'

One sentence. Read it again slowly.

Jonathan is the crown prince. His father's army is combing that wilderness at that moment for the man he is going to see. Every step of the journey is a risk, and there is no political purpose to it, no message to carry, no negotiation to conduct.

He goes because his friend is frightened.

Then the phrase, which is one of the great phrases of the Old Testament: he strengthened his hand in God.

The writer could have said he encouraged him. He could have said he brought supplies, or news, or men. He says something more exact than any of those. Jonathan took hold of David's hand — the image is of a grip going slack — and put it back on God.

He did not give him anything new. David already knew he was anointed; Samuel had poured the oil over him in his father's house. What a hunted man loses is not information but grip, and what Jonathan did was close his fingers round what he already had.

That is the whole ministry of encouragement in five words, and anyone can do it. You do not need a new revelation for a discouraged believer. You need to say, out loud, in the wilderness, the thing they already know and can no longer feel.

'And he said to him, "Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this."'

Now take that speech apart, because there are four things in it and each one costs him something.

Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. He is telling his own father's hunted enemy that the hunt will fail — and he is right, and he lives in that man's house.

You shall be king over Israel. The heir to the throne of Israel says to a fugitive, in a wilderness, that the fugitive will have his crown. He has said it before, in the field at Gibeah, and he says it again here without a flicker.

And I shall be next to you. This is the only thing he says that is not true, and it is the saddest line in the book. He pictures a future in which David reigns and Jonathan stands at his right hand, the two of them together, the friendship surviving into the kingdom. It never happens. He dies on Mount Gilboa beside his father, and David tears his clothes and sings very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary (2 Sam. 1:26).

Saul my father also knows this.

And that is the sentence to sit with.

Saul knows. His own son says so, plainly, as a settled fact: the king of Israel is aware that David will be king, and is hunting him anyway. He has known since the day he shouted at Jonathan that as long as the son of Jesse lives upon the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established (20:31), and probably since the song at the city gates.

So this is not a tragic misunderstanding, and it is not paranoia about a rival he cannot assess. It is a man who has heard the verdict of God, understood it, and decided to spend the rest of his life fighting it with an army. There is a kind of sin that goes on precisely because it knows.

'And the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.'

And Jonathan went home.

Home is his father's house. He walks back to Gibeah, to the table where the spear was thrown at him, and takes his place as the king's son.

He has just told a man in a wood that that man will have his throne, and now he goes back to serve the father who will die trying to prevent it, and to die with him. Jonathan is loyal to two people who cannot both be served, and he does not solve it; he carries it.

This is the last time these two ever meet. The next we hear of Jonathan, the Philistines have overtaken Saul and his sons on Mount Gilboa and killed them (31:2).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ziphites go up to Saul and offer to hand David over (vv. 19-20). Saul blesses them — may you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me — and sends them to search out every hiding place, for it is told me that he is very cunning (vv. 21-23). The chase closes on a mountain in the Wilderness of Maon: Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other side... and David was hurrying to get away, for Saul and his men were closing in (vv. 24-26). Then a messenger reaches Saul: hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land (v. 27). He breaks off. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul invokes the LORD's blessing on informers and calls their betrayal compassion — for him. Everything in his mouth is still about himself, and he is now using the divine name to bless it.
verseByVerse.examples: The rescue arrives as a Philistine raid: the enemy Saul was anointed to fight pulls him off the mountain at the moment the circle closes. It is not a miracle and nobody prays for it. It is a piece of bad news arriving at the right minute, and Israel named the rock after it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, which is south of Jeshimon? Now come down, O king, according to all your heart's desire to come down, and our part shall be to surrender him into the king's hand." And Saul said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me. Go, make yet more sure. Know and see the place where his foot is, and who has seen him there, for it is told me that he is very cunning. See therefore and take note of all the lurking places where he hides, and come back to me with sure information. Then I will go with you. And if he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah." And they arose and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah to the south of Jeshimon. And Saul and his men went to seek him. And David was told, so he went down to the rock and lived in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon. Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other side of the mountain. And David was hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them, a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land." So Saul returned from pursuing after David and went against the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape. And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of Engedi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, which is south of Jeshimon?"'

The Ziphites are men of Judah. David's own tribe informs on him, twice — they do it again in chapter 26 — and they travel to Gibeah to do it.

Nobody is paying them. Nobody has threatened them. They simply calculate which way the power runs and act accordingly.

'"Now come down, O king, according to all your heart's desire to come down, and our part shall be to surrender him into the king's hand."'

According to all your heart's desire. They have taken the measure of the man exactly. They know what he wants more than anything in the world, and they say so to his face as a courtesy.

'And Saul said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me."'

Saul pronounces a blessing in the name of the LORD on a pair of informers.

He also calls what they have done compassion — compassion on him. That pronoun again. The man has been sorry for himself since the tamarisk tree, and here he describes the betrayal of a fugitive by his own tribesmen as an act of pity toward the king.

Everything he touches gets bent round to face him, including the divine name.

'"Go, make yet more sure. Know and see the place where his foot is, and who has seen him there, for it is told me that he is very cunning."'

Note the last clause, and note who says it. It is told me that he is very cunning.

David has never once acted against Saul. He played the harp, killed the giant, led the army, married the daughter, obeyed the orders, and ran. There is no cunning to report. But Saul is being told there is, by someone, and he believes it — because a man who has decided on a conclusion attracts the evidence he needs.

'And Saul and his men went to seek him. And David was told, so he went down to the rock and lived in the Wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the Wilderness of Maon.'

'Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other side of the mountain. And David was hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them,'

The sentence is left hanging in mid-air, and that is deliberate.

Picture it. One hill, and two forces going round it in opposite directions, out of sight of each other by a matter of yards. David is running out of mountain. Saul's men are extending the line to come round both sides at once, which is the classic way to take a hill, and it works.

There is nothing David can do about it. He has no clever move left. Everything in the chapter up to now has depended on his asking God and getting an answer, and here there is no time to ask anything.

'a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land."'

A man on a horse arrives with bad news from somewhere else.

Consider how the rescue comes. There is no angel, no earthquake, no answer from the ephod, and no record that anybody prayed. What happens is that the Philistines — the enemy Saul was anointed to save Israel from, and has been ignoring in order to hunt one of his own officers — choose that week to raid, and the raid pulls him off the hill at the exact moment the line was closing.

It is a piece of ordinary bad news, arriving at the only minute it could have helped. And it is the answer to God did not give him into his hand in verse 14: this is what that sentence looks like on the ground.

Most deliverance is like this. Not the parting of a sea, but a message arriving, a meeting being cancelled, a job falling through, somebody else's crisis pulling a threat away — and only afterwards does anyone see what it was.

'So Saul returned from pursuing after David and went against the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape.'

They named the rock.

Somebody in that party understood what had just happened well enough to give the hill a name, so that the story could be told at it afterwards. Sela-hammahlekoth — the Rock of Escape, or of Divisions, since the mountain divided the two forces.

Israel had a long habit of doing this. Ebenezer, the stone Samuel set up after Mizpah, was another (7:12): till now the LORD has helped us. They put a marker on the ground at the place where God did something, because they knew perfectly well that they would forget it by next year otherwise.

Anyone reading this could stand to have a few. Not stones, but named days, written down — the ones where the messenger arrived in time.

'And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of Engedi.'

He moves on, to a place of springs and caves above the Dead Sea. And Saul, having dealt with the Philistines, comes straight back — which is where the next chapter begins, with the king walking alone into a cave.

24.title: David Spares Saul at En-gedi
24.text: <sup>1</sup>When Saul returned from following the Philistines, he was told, "Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi."<sup>2</sup>Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel and went to seek David and his men in front of the Wildgoats' Rocks.<sup>3</sup>And he came to the sheepfolds by the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting in the innermost parts of the cave.<sup>4</sup>And the men of David said to him, "Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, 'Behold, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.'" Then David arose and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul's robe.<sup>5</sup>And afterward David's heart struck him, because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe.<sup>6</sup>He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed."<sup>7</sup>So David persuaded his men with these words and did not permit them to attack Saul. And Saul rose up and left the cave and went on his way.<sup>8</sup>Afterward David also arose and went out of the cave, and called after Saul, "My lord the king!" And when Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth and paid homage.<sup>9</sup>And David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Behold, David seeks your harm'?<sup>10</sup>Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD gave you today into my hand in the cave. And some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD's anointed.'<sup>11</sup>See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand. For by the fact that I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you, you may know and see that there is no wrong or treason in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life to take it.<sup>12</sup>May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you.<sup>13</sup>As the proverb of the ancients says, 'Out of the wicked comes wickedness.' But my hand shall not be against you.<sup>14</sup>After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea!<sup>15</sup>May the LORD therefore be judge and give sentence between me and you, and see to it and plead my cause and deliver me from your hand."<sup>16</sup>As soon as David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul lifted up his voice and wept.<sup>17</sup>He said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil.<sup>18</sup>And you have declared this day how you have dealt well with me, in that you did not kill me when the LORD put me into your hands.<sup>19</sup>For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe? So may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day.<sup>20</sup>And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand.<sup>21</sup>Swear to me therefore by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father's house."<sup>22</sup>And David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
24.overview:
Saul takes three thousand picked men to Engedi after six hundred fugitives, steps into a cave to relieve himself, and does not know that the men he is hunting are sitting in the dark at the back of it. His own men tell David this is the day of which the LORD said... I will give your enemy into your hand — and there is no such promise anywhere in the book. God never said it. They have manufactured a divine word out of a convenient circumstance, which is exactly what Saul did one chapter earlier about this same man, and the narrator sets the two sentences side by side and says nothing.

David cuts the corner off Saul's robe instead, and his conscience hits him for it — because Samuel's robe tore at Gilgal and the tearing was the sign: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day. He has just made that gesture himself, with a knife, on the king's own coat.

Then he walks out into the daylight in front of three thousand soldiers, calls the king my father, holds up the cloth, and hands the case to a court he cannot corrupt: may the LORD judge between me and you... but my hand shall not be against you. Three thousand chosen men of Israel, he says, out in the wilderness after a dead dog and a single flea.

Saul weeps, and the tears are real. You are more righteous than I. If a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe? I know that you shall surely be king. He asks for an oath about his children, gets it — and it is kept, in the person of a lame grandson at David's own table a generation later. Then he goes home. And David does not go with him.
24.theology:
The promise that does not exist (v. 4). Search the book: God never said he would give David's enemy into his hand. Samuel did not say it, Jonathan did not say it, no oracle records it. Exhausted, frightened men saw their enemy at his most helpless and could not imagine what else it could be. And the tell is in the second half of their sentence — you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you. A word from God that ends by handing you unlimited discretion is generally your own word. Saul had made the identical move at 23:7, and the writer puts both in consecutive chapters without comment.

The providence and the conclusion are two things (v. 10). David does not deny that the LORD gave Saul into his hand — he says so himself. He denies what his men inferred from it. God arranging an opportunity is not God licensing what you want to do with it, and that single distinction is the whole difference between David in this cave and Saul on his throne.

Why a scrap of cloth (v. 5). Saul tore Samuel's robe at Gilgal and the tear was the sign of the kingdom torn away (15:27-28). Cutting the king's robe is that sign performed by hand — the transfer enacted instead of waited for. Saul reads it the same way: he is looking at the piece of his robe when he says I know that you shall surely be king (v. 20).

The LORD's anointed (v. 6). The argument does not claim Saul is a good king, and does not claim the throne is not David's; he has been anointed for it himself. It claims that oil was poured on that head at God's command, and no reading of circumstances gives a private man the right to undo it with a knife. What God gave, God can take.

Judgment handed over, not abandoned (v. 12). He asks the LORD to avenge him. He believes he has been wronged and wants it answered; what he gives up is doing the answering. That is not pretending not to mind — it is moving the case to a court that cannot be corrupted and whose judge is not a party to it. Paul stands on this ground at Romans 12:19. A Christian can let a grievance go, not because it does not matter, but because it is being handled.

Feeling is not repentance (vv. 16-22). Saul's confession is accurate and complete: good for evil, and he names who did which. He concedes the throne. He weeps. And he is out with three thousand men again two chapters later. A man can mean every word while he says it, weep honestly, be exactly right about his own sin, and be back at the same behaviour within the month, because nothing underneath moved. The proof is the last clause of the chapter: Saul went home, and David went up to the stronghold. He believed the tears. He did not trust them.
24.examples:
Then: Six hundred men watched their enemy walk unarmed into their own hiding place, and their commander crawled up behind him, cut a piece off his coat, came back, and then had to argue them out of killing him — before walking into the open in front of the man's army to show him the cloth.

Now: The chapter is for anybody holding a justified grievance and the power to act on it. Two things in it are practical. First, the test David's men failed: when a circumstance lines up perfectly with what you already wanted, and you find yourself calling it God's leading, check whether God ever actually said it — and be suspicious of any leading that ends with and then do as seems good to you. Second, what David did instead: he did not swallow the wrong, deny it, or minimise it. He named it, asked God to judge it, and took his own hand off it. Those are not the same as letting it go, and it is the second that a person can actually do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Day of Which the LORD Said
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul comes back from the Philistines with three thousand chosen men to the Wildgoats' Rocks, and goes into a cave to relieve himself — the cave where David and his men are sitting in the innermost parts (vv. 1-3). His men tell him this is the day the LORD promised: behold, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you (v. 4). David cuts off the corner of Saul's robe instead — and afterward David's heart struck him (vv. 4-5). He will not touch the LORD's anointed, and he stops his men (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no such promise anywhere in this book. God never said it. The men are reading a convenient circumstance and calling it a word from God — which is precisely what Saul did one chapter earlier about this same man (23:7), and the narrator sets the two side by side without a syllable of comment.
verseByVerse.examples: And the reason a scrap of cloth troubles him: Samuel's robe tore in his hand at Gilgal, and the tearing was the sign — the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (15:27-28). David has just made the kingdom-tearing gesture himself, with a knife, on the king's own robe.

verseByVerse.quote: When Saul returned from following the Philistines, he was told, "Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi." Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel and went to seek David and his men in front of the Wildgoats' Rocks. And he came to the sheepfolds by the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting in the innermost parts of the cave. And the men of David said to him, "Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, 'Behold, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.'" Then David arose and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul's robe. And afterward David's heart struck him, because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe. He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed." So David persuaded his men with these words and did not permit them to attack Saul. And Saul rose up and left the cave and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Saul returned from following the Philistines, he was told, "Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi." Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel and went to seek David and his men in front of the Wildgoats' Rocks.'

He deals with the Philistine raid and comes straight back to the hunt, with three thousand picked men, for six hundred fugitives and one of them in particular.

Engedi is a spring above the Dead Sea, and the cliffs behind it are riddled with caves. It is good country to hide in and impossible country to search.

'And he came to the sheepfolds by the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting in the innermost parts of the cave.'

The narrator writes it exactly like that, without embarrassment and without a joke.

The king of Israel, at the head of three thousand men, steps into a cave for a private moment, and six hundred armed men who want him dead are sitting in the dark at the back of it watching him. He is alone, unarmed, in the one posture in which no man is dangerous.

It could hardly be more complete if it had been arranged.

'And the men of David said to him, "Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, 'Behold, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.'"'

Now read that sentence again and then look for the promise.

It is not in this book. Nowhere has God said to David that he would give his enemy into his hand, and nowhere has anybody said it on his behalf. Samuel anointed him and said nothing of the kind. Jonathan told him he would be king and said nothing of the kind. There is no such oracle.

The men have invented it.

Not cynically, most likely. They have watched this man hunted for years, they are exhausted and frightened, and here is their enemy in a cave with his trousers round his ankles. Of course this is God. What else could it possibly be?

It is exactly what Saul did one chapter ago. God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars (23:7). The same reasoning, the same confidence, about the same man — and the narrator answered Saul's version in his own words seven verses later.

He puts the two sentences one chapter apart and offers no comment on either. Both sides of this war read the circumstances as divine endorsement of what they already wanted, and only one man in the cave declines to.

Note also the second half of what they say: you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you. That is the part that gives the game away. A word from God that ends by handing you unlimited discretion is generally your own word.

'Then David arose and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul's robe.'

He goes forward with a knife and comes back with a piece of cloth.

'And afterward David's heart struck him, because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe.'

Here is the verse people stumble at. He did not kill him. He did not wound him. He did not so much as wake him. He cut a corner off a garment in the dark — and his conscience hit him for it.

It is not scrupulosity, and the reason is in chapter 15.

When Samuel turned to leave Gilgal, Saul grabbed the skirt of his robe and it tore, and Samuel said: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (15:27-28). The tearing of the robe was the sign. That is the language the kingdom changing hands is spoken in.

So when David crouches behind Saul in the dark and cuts the corner off his robe, he has just performed that sign himself, with his own hand, on the king's own coat. He has enacted the transfer of the kingdom rather than waiting for it.

Saul sees it too. Look ahead to verse 20: he is staring at a piece of his own robe in David's hand when he says now I know that you shall surely be king. Both men know what the cloth means.

'He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed."'

Twice in one sentence: the LORD's anointed.

This is the whole argument, and what it does not say matters as much as what it does. It does not say Saul is a good king; David knows exactly what he is. It does not say the throne is rightfully his; David has been anointed for it himself. It says that oil was poured on that man's head by Samuel at God's command, and that no reading of the circumstances gives a private citizen the right to undo it with a knife.

What God gave, God can take. David will not do God's work for him with a weapon in the dark, and this is the principle he will hold to for the next seven chapters, at enormous cost, twice.

'So David persuaded his men with these words and did not permit them to attack Saul. And Saul rose up and left the cave and went on his way.'

He has to persuade them, and the Hebrew is stronger than that — he tore into them. Six hundred armed men had already decided; he talked them out of it standing in the dark while the opportunity walked away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — A Dead Dog, a Single Flea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David comes out and calls after him, bowing to the ground: my lord the king! (vv. 8-9). He holds up the piece of cloth as evidence — see the corner of your robe in my hand... there is no wrong or treason in my hands (vv. 10-11). He quotes a proverb, out of the wicked comes wickedness, and asks: after whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a single flea! (vv. 13-14). And he hands the case over: may the LORD judge between me and you... but my hand shall not be against you (vv. 12, 15).
verseByVerse.theology: He calls him my father (v. 11), which is literally true — Saul is his father-in-law — and is also the last kindness left to offer a man who has been trying to kill him for years.
verseByVerse.examples: The self-description is not false modesty but strategy and theology at once. A dead dog and a flea are beneath a king's notice; he is telling Saul that the whole campaign is beneath him. And by handing the verdict to the LORD he takes the one course that lets him neither retaliate nor surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward David also arose and went out of the cave, and called after Saul, "My lord the king!" And when Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth and paid homage. And David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Behold, David seeks your harm'? Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD gave you today into my hand in the cave. And some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD's anointed.' See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand. For by the fact that I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you, you may know and see that there is no wrong or treason in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life to take it. May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you. As the proverb of the ancients says, 'Out of the wicked comes wickedness.' But my hand shall not be against you. After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea! May the LORD therefore be judge and give sentence between me and you, and see to it and plead my cause and deliver me from your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Afterward David also arose and went out of the cave, and called after Saul, "My lord the king!" And when Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth and paid homage.'

Consider what this takes.

He has just let the man go. Now he walks out into the daylight, in front of three thousand soldiers who could be on him in a minute, and calls out to make himself a target — and then puts his face on the ground.

He could have stayed in the cave and let Saul walk away not knowing. Instead he comes out, because a piece of cloth is no use as evidence unless somebody sees it.

'And David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Behold, David seeks your harm'? Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD gave you today into my hand in the cave."'

Note that he says the LORD did give Saul into his hand.

He does not deny the providence — he denies the conclusion drawn from it. God arranged the opportunity; that is not the same as God licensing the murder. This is the distinction his men could not make and Saul cannot make, and it is the whole difference between them.

'"And some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD's anointed.' See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand."'

See, my father.

He calls him father. It is technically accurate — Saul is his father-in-law, whatever has become of that marriage — and it is also the last tenderness available to a man who has spent years being hunted by the person he is speaking to.

Then the cloth. See the corner of your robe in my hand. The evidence is unanswerable and the whole speech turns on it: I was close enough to cut this, and you are alive.

'"For by cutting off the corner of your robe and not killing you, you may know and see that there is no wrong or treason in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life to take it."'

'"May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you."'

Here is the sentence to carry out of the chapter.

Notice that it is not a renunciation of justice. He asks God to avenge him — he believes he has been wronged, says so, and wants it answered. What he renounces is doing the answering himself.

None of that is pretending not to mind. David minds a great deal. He simply transfers the case to a court he cannot corrupt and whose judge is not a party to it, and then takes his own hand off the matter.

Paul is standing on this ground centuries later: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Rom. 12:19). The reason a Christian can let go of a grievance is not that grievances do not matter but that they are being handled.

'"As the proverb of the ancients says, 'Out of the wicked comes wickedness.' But my hand shall not be against you."'

He quotes a saying everybody in earshot knows, and he uses it carefully.

The proverb means that a wicked man's actions come out of what he is. David applies it as an argument: if I were what you say I am, you would be dead in that cave. My actions have shown you what I am. Judge by the fruit.

'"After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a single flea!"'

Then he makes himself as small as a man can make himself.

A dead dog is the most contemptible thing in that vocabulary — unclean, worthless, and not even alive. A single flea is a thing you cannot catch and would not want if you did.

It is genuine humility and it is also an extremely shrewd argument, and both at once. He is saying to the king, in front of the army: look at what you have become. Three thousand chosen men of Israel, marching round the wilderness of Engedi, after a flea. The Philistines are raiding the threshing floors and this is what the kingdom is doing.

'"May the LORD therefore be judge and give sentence between me and you, and see to it and plead my cause and deliver me from your hand."'

He ends where he began, and the verbs pile up: judge, give sentence, see to it, plead my cause, deliver me.

That last one is honest. He is not asking God merely to referee. He is asking to be got out of this, because he is not enjoying it, and he says so to Saul's face.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — You Are More Righteous Than I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Is this your voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice and wept (v. 16). He says it outright: you are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil (v. 17), and asks the question that answers itself — for if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe?
