(v. 19). Then: now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand (v. 20). He asks for an oath that David will not cut off his offspring (v. 21), gets it, and goes home — but David and his men went up to the stronghold (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The tears are real and they change nothing. He confesses, names David's righteousness and his own evil, concedes the kingdom, and then walks back to Gibeah and is hunting him again two chapters later. Feeling something deeply is not the same as repenting of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the last clause of the chapter. David does not go home with him. He hears every word of the confession, swears the oath he is asked for, and then goes back up to the stronghold — and the oath he swore he keeps, in the person of a lame grandson brought to his own table years later (2 Sam. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul lifted up his voice and wept. He said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil. And you have declared this day how you have dealt well with me, in that you did not kill me when the LORD put me into your hands. For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe? So may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day. And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand. Swear to me therefore by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father's house." And David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul lifted up his voice and wept.'

He weeps, and there is no reason to think the tears are fake.

Is this your voice, my son David? He has to ask, which tells you they are at a distance and shouting, and he calls him my son, which he has not done in a long time. Something in the man breaks for a moment.

'And he said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil."'

That is as clear a confession as anybody makes in this book.

He does not soften it or spread it about. You are more righteous than I. Good for evil, and he names which of them did which. He is entirely right about the facts and entirely honest about them.

'"And you have declared this day how you have dealt well with me, in that you did not kill me when the LORD put me into your hands. For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe? So may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day."'

For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe?

It is a rhetorical question with an obvious answer, and Saul is the proof of it: he has found his enemy repeatedly and thrown a spear every time. He is describing the ordinary way of the world, and he has just watched somebody not do it, and he cannot account for it except by calling it righteousness.

That is what non-retaliation does when anyone actually sees it. It is unaccountable. It does not fit the way the world runs, and it makes people ask what is different.

'"And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand."'

He says it out loud, standing on a hillside, holding nothing, looking at a piece of his own robe in the hand of the man who cut it.

Everyone has now said it. Samuel said it at Gilgal with a torn robe in his fist. Jonathan said it twice, in a field and in a wood. Abigail will say it in the next chapter before the year is out. And here is Saul himself, saying it in his own voice, weeping.

Not one of them changes what he does next.

'"Swear to me therefore by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father's house."'

This is what he is actually frightened of, and it is a reasonable fear. When a dynasty changed hands in that world the incoming king killed the old king's family as a matter of routine policy, and everybody knew it.

'And David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.'

He swore it, and he kept it.

Years later, on the throne, he asks: is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? and they bring him Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, crippled in both feet, who is terrified, and David gives him back all Saul's land and sits him at the royal table for the rest of his life (2 Sam. 9). The oath sworn on a hillside to a weeping enemy was still being kept a generation later by a man who had every power not to.

Now the last clause of the chapter, and it is the most important one.

Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.

David does not go with him.

He has just heard a full confession, an acknowledgment of his righteousness, a blessing, and a concession of the throne, and at the end of it he says nothing about coming back to court, and goes up into the rocks with his six hundred men.

He believes the tears were real. He does not believe they will last, and he is right; within two chapters Saul is out with three thousand men again, having heard from the Ziphites a second time.

That is a hard, useful thing to know about people, and it is not cynicism. A man can mean every word he says while he is saying it, weep genuinely, be perfectly accurate about his own sin, and be back at exactly the same behaviour within the month, because nothing underneath has changed. Real feeling is not repentance. Repentance is a turn, and Saul turns round and walks home.

25.title: Abigail: Wisdom That Stops a Fool
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Samuel died. And all Israel assembled and mourned for him, and they buried him in his house at Ramah. Then David rose and went down to the wilderness of Paran.<sup>2</sup>And there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. The man was very rich; he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. He was shearing his sheep in Carmel.<sup>3</sup>Now the name of the man was Nabal, and the name of his wife Abigail. The woman was discerning and beautiful, but the man was harsh and badly behaved; he was a Calebite.<sup>4</sup>David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.<sup>5</sup>So David sent ten young men. And David said to the young men, "Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal and greet him in my name.<sup>6</sup>And thus you shall greet him: 'Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have.<sup>7</sup>I hear that you have shearers. Now your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm, and they missed nothing all the time they were in Carmel.<sup>8</sup>Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a feast day. Please give whatever you have at hand to your servants and to your son David.'"<sup>9</sup>When David's young men came, they said all this to Nabal in the name of David, and then they waited.<sup>10</sup>And Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters.<sup>11</sup>Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers and give it to men who come from I do not know where?"<sup>12</sup>So David's young men turned away and came back and told him all this.<sup>13</sup>And David said to his men, "Every man strap on his sword!" And every man of them strapped on his sword. David also strapped on his sword. And about four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred remained with the baggage.<sup>14</sup>But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he railed at them.<sup>15</sup>Yet the men were very good to us, and we suffered no harm, and we did not miss anything when we were in the fields, as long as we went with them.<sup>16</sup>They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore know this and consider what you should do, for harm is determined against our master and against all his house, and he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him."<sup>18</sup>Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and five seahs of parched grain and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.<sup>19</sup>And she said to her young men, "Go on before me; behold, I come after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.<sup>20</sup>And as she rode on the donkey and came down under cover of the mountain, behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.<sup>21</sup>Now David had said, "Surely in vain have I guarded all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that belonged to him, and he has returned me evil for good.<sup>22</sup>God do so to the enemies of David and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him."<sup>23</sup>When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey and fell before David on her face and bowed to the ground.<sup>24</sup>She fell at his feet and said, "On me alone, my lord, be the guilt. Please let your servant speak in your ears, and hear the words of your servant.<sup>25</sup>Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I your servant did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent.<sup>26</sup>Now then, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, because the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from saving with your own hand, now then let your enemies and those who seek to do evil to my lord be as Nabal.<sup>27</sup>And now let this present that your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord.<sup>28</sup>Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD, and evil shall not be found in you so long as you live.<sup>29</sup>If men rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling.<sup>30</sup>And when the LORD has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you and has appointed you prince over Israel,<sup>31</sup>my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause or for my lord working salvation himself. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant."<sup>32</sup>And David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me!<sup>33</sup>Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand!<sup>34</sup>For as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from hurting you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, truly by morning there had not been left to Nabal so much as one male."<sup>35</sup>Then David received from her hand what she had brought him. And he said to her, "Go up in peace to your house. See, I have obeyed your voice, and I have granted your petition."<sup>36</sup>And Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he was holding a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. And Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until the morning light.<sup>37</sup>In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.<sup>38</sup>And about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.<sup>39</sup>When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD who has avenged the insult I received at the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. The LORD has returned the evil of Nabal on his own head." Then David sent and spoke to Abigail, to take her as his wife.<sup>40</sup>When the servants of David came to Abigail at Carmel, they said to her, "David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife."<sup>41</sup>And she rose and bowed with her face to the ground and said, "Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord."<sup>42</sup>And Abigail hurried and rose and mounted a donkey, and her five young women attended her. She followed the messengers of David and became his wife.<sup>43</sup>David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives.<sup>44</sup>Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.
25.overview:
Samuel dies in half a verse — the boy who heard his name in the dark at Shiloh, the judge of Ebenezer, the man who anointed both kings — and the writer moves straight on to a sheep farmer. Israel's great men die and God's purposes do not pause for the funeral.

The farmer is Nabal, which means fool, and the introductions are done before anyone speaks: he is harsh and badly behaved, his wife is discerning and beautiful. David's request at shearing time is courteous and his claim is true — his men were a wall to Nabal's shepherds by night and day, and the servants confirm every word. Nabal answers in Saul's own vocabulary (who is the son of Jesse?), files the king's son-in-law as a runaway slave, and counts his possessions three times in one sentence: my bread and my water and my meat.

So David straps on a sword. Hold the chapter between the two on either side of it: in chapter 24 he had Saul unarmed in a cave and would not touch him, in chapter 26 he stands over him asleep and will not touch him — and here he swears before God to kill every male in a household by morning because a farmer was rude to his messengers. It is easier to be magnificent about the great injury than decent about the small one.

Abigail meets him on the road with two hundred loaves and the wisest speech in the book. She takes the blame that is not hers, tells him God has restrained him while he is still armed, promises him a sure house in the words Nathan will use decades later, and reaches him with a sling: the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling. Then the argument that lands — not that this is wrong, but that he will have to carry it onto the throne. David blesses God for sending her. Ten days later the LORD strikes Nabal, and David gets the outcome without the bloodguilt.
25.theology:
Half a verse for Samuel (v. 1). All Israel mourned him, which is more than they gave him alive: they had demanded a king to be like the nations, he told them exactly what it would cost, and everything he warned of has now happened. The abruptness is the point.

The chapter's position is its argument. Twice on either side David refuses to lift a hand against the king who has hunted him for years, on principle, at mortal risk. In between he rides out to slaughter a household over an insult. Anybody who has behaved well under a great injury and lost their temper over a small one in the same week already understands this chapter.

Saving with your own hand (vv. 26, 33). Abigail names bloodguilt and saving with your own hand as one sin, and David repeats her phrase back word for word. Taking what God has promised by your own arm instead of waiting is precisely what he refused in the cave — and she says it in the vocabulary he would have used himself, which is why it lands.

She speaks in the past tense (v. 26). The LORD has restrained you — said to a man still sitting armed on the road. She does not ask him to stop; she tells him God has stopped him, that she is the stopping, and invites him to recognise it.

A sure house, and a sling (vv. 28-29). A farmer's wife on a hillside names the Davidic covenant before Nathan carries it to the palace (2 Sam. 7:11-16). And she reaches him with the one image in the language that could not miss: the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling. You did that once, and God will do it now; put the stone down.

The argument that works (v. 31). Not this is wrong, though it is; not pity for the servants, though she could. She argues forward into the reign he is going to have and asks what he will carry into it — pangs of conscience that will be in the room with him when he sits down on the throne. She is not asking him to be nicer. She is asking him to protect the man he will be from the man he is this afternoon.

Vengeance taken by somebody whose hands can afford it (v. 38). David wanted Nabal dead; Nabal is dead; David's hands are clean and he never lifted a finger. The LORD struck Nabal — the writer says who did it and does not hedge. That is Romans 12:19 in narrative: the promise is not that the wrong will be overlooked, but that it will be dealt with by someone who can bear the cost of dealing with it.

The flat ending (vv. 43-44). Two more notes, no comment: another wife, and Michal handed by her father to another man as though the marriage had not happened. This writer reports Gideon's ephod and Jacob's wives the same way, and silence is not endorsement. The damage that David's marriages do runs through 2 Samuel — Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah are sons of different mothers. The man talked out of a massacre on Tuesday is not a finished article by Friday, and Scripture refuses to tidy him up.
25.examples:
Then: A woman loaded two hundred loaves and five dressed sheep onto donkeys without telling her husband, rode down a mountain track into four hundred men coming the other way with swords drawn and an oath sworn, got off the donkey, put her face on the ground, and talked their commander out of a massacre — and he thanked her for it.

Now: Two things worth taking. Abigail's method, for anyone who has to stop somebody doing something terrible: she gave him somewhere to put the offence, told the truth about the offender without defending him, spoke in his own vocabulary, and then argued from the future he wanted back into the choice in front of him. Not one word of it is flattery and not one word is a lecture. And David's response, which is rarer than her speech: he did not say he had it under control. He blessed God for sending her, admitted out loud what he would have done by morning, and said I have obeyed your voice. Thanking the person who just stopped you is harder than being stopped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Who Is the Son of Jesse?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel dies and is buried at Ramah in half a verse (v. 1). Then a rich sheep farmer at Maon — three thousand sheep, a thousand goats, harsh and badly behaved — whose wife is discerning and beautiful (vv. 2-3). At shearing time David sends ten men with a courteous request and a true claim: his men guarded Nabal's shepherds and we did them no harm... they missed nothing (vv. 4-8). Nabal's answer: who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters. Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat... and give it to men who come from I do not know where? (vv. 10-11). David's answer is four hundred swords (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The insult is Saul's vocabulary. The son of Jesse is the name Saul uses when he will not say David (20:27; 22:7), and servants breaking away from their masters recasts the king's son-in-law as a runaway slave. Nabal knows perfectly well who he is; everyone in Judah did.
verseByVerse.examples: And count the possessives: my bread and my water and my meat. Three in one sentence, from a man whose shearing feast will be like the feast of a king nine verses later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Samuel died. And all Israel assembled and mourned for him, and they buried him in his house at Ramah. Then David rose and went down to the wilderness of Paran. And there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. The man was very rich; he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. He was shearing his sheep in Carmel. Now the name of the man was Nabal, and the name of his wife Abigail. The woman was discerning and beautiful, but the man was harsh and badly behaved; he was a Calebite. David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep. So David sent ten young men. And David said to the young men, "Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal and greet him in my name. And thus you shall greet him: 'Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have. I hear that you have shearers. Now your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm, and they missed nothing all the time they were in Carmel. Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a feast day. Please give whatever you have at hand to your servants and to your son David.'" When David's young men came, they said all this to Nabal in the name of David, and then they waited. And Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters. Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers and give it to men who come from I do not know where?" So David's young men turned away and came back and told him all this. And David said to his men, "Every man strap on his sword!" And every man of them strapped on his sword. David also strapped on his sword. And about four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred remained with the baggage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Samuel died. And all Israel assembled and mourned for him, and they buried him in his house at Ramah.'

Half a verse.

The boy who slept beside the ark and heard his name called in the dark. The judge who stood at Mizpah and set up a stone and called it Ebenezer. The man who anointed two kings, who tore his robe out of Saul's hand at Gilgal, who went to Bethlehem with a horn of oil and looked at seven sons before God told him to send for the eighth. The last of the judges, and the first of the prophets.

Now Samuel died.

All Israel came and mourned, which is right and is more than they gave him while he lived. They had asked him for a king to be like the nations, and he had told them exactly what it would cost, and they had said no! But there shall be a king over us. Everything he warned them about has now happened, and they bury him and go home.

The writer gives him one sentence and moves straight to a story about a sheep farmer, and the abruptness is the point. Israel's great men die and God's purposes do not pause for the funeral.

'And there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. The man was very rich; he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats... the name of the man was Nabal, and the name of his wife Abigail. The woman was discerning and beautiful, but the man was harsh and badly behaved.'

The introductions are complete before either character speaks, and the reader is told who is who.

Nabal means fool. Not a simpleton — in Hebrew the nabal is the moral fool of Proverbs, the man who says in his heart there is no God, whose folly is a settled disposition rather than a lack of intelligence. He is very rich, and his character is given in two words: harsh, and badly behaved.

His wife is discerning and beautiful, and the order matters. The first word is the wisdom vocabulary. She is put in front of us as the wise woman married to the fool, which is one of Proverbs' recurring nightmares.

'And David sent ten young men... "Ask him in my name of peace. And thus you shall greet him: 'Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have.'"'

The request is impeccably courteous, and the timing is deliberate.

Sheep-shearing was the harvest festival of a pastoral estate: a week of feasting, and the season when a wealthy man was expected to be open-handed. Nobody sent men to ask at shearing time unless they expected a yes.

'"And now your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm, and they missed nothing all the time they were in Carmel. Ask your young men, and they will tell you."'

The claim is verifiable and it is true; the servant confirms every word of it in verse 15.

Six hundred armed men had been living in the same hills as Nabal's flocks through the grazing season and had taken nothing. In that country, in those years, that is a substantial service, and David is asking to be paid something for it out of a feast that is already happening.

'And Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters."'

Listen to whose words those are.

The son of Jesse is Saul's phrase. It is what he calls David when he will not say his name — at the table when Jonathan defended him, under the tamarisk tree when he addressed the Benjaminites. And servants breaking away from their masters takes the king's son-in-law, the captain of the bodyguard, the man who killed Goliath, and files him as a runaway slave.

Who is David? Everybody in Judah knew who David was. Nabal is not ignorant; he is being insulting on purpose, and he is being insulting in the vocabulary of the court, which suggests he knows exactly which way the wind is blowing and has decided to be on the winning side loudly.

'"Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers and give it to men who come from I do not know where?"'

Count them. My bread. My water. My meat.

Three possessives in one sentence, and this from a man who is about to hold a feast like the feast of a king. It is not that he cannot afford it; it is that it is his.

And from I do not know where is the last twist of the knife: not merely no, but you are nobody, and I do not know you, and I do not propose to find out.

'And David said to his men, "Every man strap on his sword!"'

David, who would not lift his hand against a king, straps on a sword over a bad answer from a farmer.

Four hundred men go up and two hundred stay with the baggage — and that detail tells you this is not a raid to frighten somebody. That is a battle formation.

Hold this chapter next to the two on either side of it. In chapter 24 he had Saul unarmed in a cave and would not touch him. In chapter 26 he will stand over him asleep with a spear in the ground and will not touch him. And in between, a man is rude to his messengers and he sets off to kill every male in the household by morning.

He can restrain himself against the king who has been hunting him for years, on principle, at mortal cost. He cannot restrain himself against a fool who insulted him at a party.

That is not a contradiction anyone should find surprising. It is easier to be magnificent about the great injury than decent about the small one, and most people who have managed the first have lost their temper over the second in the same week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — One Cannot Speak to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A servant goes to Abigail, not to Nabal, and explains why: David's men were a wall to us both by night and by day, and he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him (vv. 14-17). She moves at once — two hundred loaves, wine, five dressed sheep, grain, raisins, fig cakes — but she did not tell her husband Nabal (vv. 18-19). And David, coming down the mountain, is swearing an oath: God do so to the enemies of David and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The household has already worked out that the master cannot be spoken to. The Hebrew behind worthless is the word for a son of Belial — the same term used of Eli's sons (2:12) and of the men who despised Saul at his coronation (10:27). It is not mere rudeness; it is a settled character.
verseByVerse.examples: Set David's oath beside the previous chapter. He would not lift a hand against a king who had hunted him for years, on principle, in a cave. He is now riding out to kill every male in a household because a farmer was rude to his messengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he railed at them. Yet the men were very good to us, and we suffered no harm, and we did not miss anything when we were in the fields, as long as we went with them. They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep. Now therefore know this and consider what you should do, for harm is determined against our master and against all his house, and he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him." Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and five seahs of parched grain and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys. And she said to her young men, "Go on before me; behold, I come after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal. And as she rode on the donkey and came down under cover of the mountain, behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them. Now David had said, "Surely in vain have I guarded all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that belonged to him, and he has returned me evil for good. God do so to the enemies of David and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he railed at them."'

Notice who he goes to.

He does not go to Nabal, and he does not go to the steward. He walks past the master of the house to the master's wife, and everyone in the story treats this as the obvious thing to do.

'"Yet the men were very good to us, and we suffered no harm, and we did not miss anything when we were in the fields, as long as we went with them. They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep."'

They were a wall to us both by night and by day.

The servant confirms David's claim in stronger terms than David made it. Not merely that they did no harm, but that they were the reason nothing else did. Shepherds in open country at night are the most vulnerable people in the economy, and for a season they had six hundred soldiers between them and the hills.

Nabal has just told the men who did that to go and find out who they are.

'"Now therefore know this and consider what you should do, for harm is determined against our master and against all his house, and he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him."'

There is the household's settled verdict on its head, delivered to his wife by a servant who does not expect to be contradicted.

One cannot speak to him. Not he will be angry, or he will need persuading. He cannot be spoken to. Everybody who works there has already established this and made their arrangements accordingly, which is why the servant is standing in front of Abigail instead.

The word behind worthless is the Hebrew for a son of Belial. It is what the narrator calls Eli's sons (2:12), and what the malcontents were called who despised Saul at his coronation (10:27). It is not describing a bad mood. It is a category.

'Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and five seahs of parched grain and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.'

Look at the size of it, and at the speed.

Two hundred loaves. Five dressed sheep. A hundred bunches of raisins, two hundred fig cakes. This is not a gesture; it is provision for six hundred men, assembled and loaded while an army is coming down the mountain. She has the whole estate moving inside the hour.

And note that she gives, generously and immediately, exactly what her husband refused — out of the same stores, on the same day.

'And she said to her young men, "Go on before me; behold, I come after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.'

She does not tell him.

The text states it flatly and does not defend it, and it needs no defending. He cannot be spoken to, there is no time, and four hundred armed men are on the road with an oath sworn to leave nobody alive. She acts to save his life, his household and his servants without his knowledge, because telling him would have cost all three.

'And as she rode on the donkey and came down under cover of the mountain, behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.'

'Now David had said, "Surely in vain have I guarded all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that belonged to him, and he has returned me evil for good."'

He is talking himself into it as he rides, and the grievance is legitimate. Every word of it is true. That is what makes it dangerous.

'"God do so to the enemies of David and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him."'

He has put himself under an oath, before God, to commit a massacre.

Every male in the household — which means the servants who did him no wrong, the shepherds whose lives his men guarded, the boy who ran to Abigail. Not one of them insulted anybody. They are to die by morning because their employer was rude.

This is the same man who two chapters ago said may the LORD judge between me and you, but my hand shall not be against you, and who told Saul he would not so much as touch him. He is about to save himself with his own hand, and he has sworn to God that he will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Bound in the Bundle of the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abigail dismounts, falls on her face, and speaks — taking the blame herself, naming her husband for what he is (Nabal is his name, and folly is with him), and then turning to David's own future: the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from saving with your own hand (vv. 23-26). The LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD (v. 28). The life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling (v. 29). And the point of it all: when God has done all he promised, my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause (v. 31). David: blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: She argues from his future backwards into his present. Not this would be wrong, though it would; but you are going to be king, and this is what you will have to remember about yourself when you are. That is the argument that lands.
verseByVerse.examples: And she uses a sling on the man who used one. She knows exactly who she is speaking to. A sure house is the promise Nathan will bring in full a few decades later (2 Sam. 7:11-16) — a farmer's wife on a mountain road names it first.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey and fell before David on her face and bowed to the ground. She fell at his feet and said, "On me alone, my lord, be the guilt. Please let your servant speak in your ears, and hear the words of your servant. Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I your servant did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent. Now then, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, because the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from saving with your own hand, now then let your enemies and those who seek to do evil to my lord be as Nabal. And now let this present that your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord. Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD, and evil shall not be found in you so long as you live. If men rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling. And when the LORD has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you and has appointed you prince over Israel, my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause or for my lord working salvation himself. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey and fell before David on her face and bowed to the ground. She fell at his feet and said, "On me alone, my lord, be the guilt."'

She puts herself between four hundred swords and a household, on the ground, and starts by taking the blame for something she did not do.

It is not grovelling and it is not flattery. It is the only opening that could work. A man riding to punish an offence has to be given somewhere to put it, and she takes it herself, immediately, before he can refuse.

What follows is one of the longest speeches by anyone in this book, and there is not a wasted sentence in it.

'"Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him."'

She is entirely candid about her husband, and she uses his name as the argument. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him.

She is not defending him. She is telling David that killing this man would be like being insulted by the weather and going to war with the sky.

'"Now then, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, because the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from saving with your own hand, now then let your enemies... be as Nabal."'

Here she does something remarkable with the tense.

She speaks of the restraint as already accomplished — the LORD has restrained you — while the man is still sitting on a horse with his sword on. She is not asking him to stop. She is telling him that God has stopped him, and that she is the stopping, and inviting him to recognise it.

And look at the phrase: from bloodguilt, and from saving with your own hand. Those two are the same sin here. Taking what is yours by your own arm, rather than waiting for the God who promised it, is exactly what he refused to do in the cave — and she names it in the language he himself would have used.

'"Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD, and evil shall not be found in you so long as you live."'

A sure house.

She is standing on a mountain track in front of a fugitive with a price on his head, and she tells him God will build him a lasting dynasty. That is not a compliment. That is the promise Nathan will carry to the palace decades later, in almost these words: the LORD will make you a house... and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me (2 Sam. 7:11-16).

A sheep farmer's wife says it first, on a hillside, to a man who is at that moment riding to commit murder.

'"If men rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling."'

Two images, and the second one should stop anybody reading.

Bound in the bundle of the living. The picture is of valuables tied up in a cloth and kept close — the way a traveller carried what he could not afford to lose. Your life, she says, is in God's bundle, tied at his belt. Nothing gets at it without going through him.

And then: the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling.

She uses a sling. To this man.

Everyone in Israel knew what David had done with a sling in the Valley of Elah, and she picks the one image in the language guaranteed to reach him, and turns it round: you did that once, and God will do it for you now. Put the stone down.

She has taken his measure completely, and she is using it to save lives.

'"And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant."'

One line for herself, at the end, and only after everything else.

'"my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause or for my lord working salvation himself."'

Here is the argument that actually lands, and here is why.

She does not tell him this would be wrong, though it would be. She does not appeal to his pity for the servants, though she could. She argues forward, into the reign he is going to have, and asks what he will have to carry into it.

There will be a throne. There will be a day when God has done everything he promised. And on that day, she says, you do not want to be a king who remembers a hillside full of dead shepherds killed over a rude answer. You will have pangs of conscience, and you will have them forever, and they will be in the room with you when you sit down.

That is the wisest thing anybody says to David in this book. She is not asking him to be nicer. She is asking him to think about the man he will have to be, and to protect that man from the man he is being this afternoon.

Keep that for the next time a person is owed something and can take it. The question is not only whether the thing is deserved. It is what you will be carrying afterwards, and for how long.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–44 — His Heart Died Within Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David blesses God for sending her — blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand — admits that by morning he would have left Nabal not one male alive, takes her gift and tells her I have obeyed your voice (vv. 32-35). She comes home to a feast like the feast of a king and a husband too drunk to be told, so she says nothing until morning — and when she does, his heart died within him, and he became as a stone (vv. 36-37). And about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died (v. 38). David blesses God for having returned the evil of Nabal on his own head, and sends for Abigail, who comes (vv. 39-42). The chapter ends with two flat notes: David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Saul had given Michal, David's wife, to another man (vv. 43-44).
verseByVerse.theology: The vengeance David was riding out to take is taken, ten days later, by somebody else. He gets the outcome without the bloodguilt — which is the whole of Abigail's argument proved, and exactly what Paul means by leaving room for the wrath of God (Rom. 12:19).
verseByVerse.examples: The last two verses are reported without a word of approval or disapproval. This narrator does that: he told us about Gideon's ephod and Jacob's two wives the same way. David now has three wives, one of them given away by her father to somebody else, and the trouble this makes in his house is a large part of 2 Samuel.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand! For as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from hurting you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, truly by morning there had not been left to Nabal so much as one male." Then David received from her hand what she had brought him. And he said to her, "Go up in peace to your house. See, I have obeyed your voice, and I have granted your petition." And Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he was holding a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. And Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until the morning light. In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me!"'

His first word is about God.

Not an agreement, and not a word of thanks — those come next. First: who sent you. He recognises inside about ten seconds that the woman standing in the road with a hundred bunches of raisins is God's answer to a prayer nobody prayed, and he says so out loud before he says anything else.

'"Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand!"'

Then her, by name and by quality — and he takes her exact phrase and repeats it back.

From bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand. That is her sentence from verse 26, word for word, and his using it is the sign that he has understood.

He is also being uncommonly honest. He does not say I had it under control. He says this woman prevented him, and blesses her for it. There is a particular strength required to say thank you to somebody who has just stopped you doing something dreadful, and most people cannot manage it in the moment.

'"For as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from hurting you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, truly by morning there had not been left to Nabal so much as one male."'

He confirms it. He would have done it. There is no minimising afterwards.

'Then David received from her hand what she had brought him. And he said to her, "Go up in peace to your house. See, I have obeyed your voice, and I have granted your petition."'

I have obeyed your voice.

The word is the ordinary one for obeying. The commander of six hundred men tells a woman he came to kill that he has done as she said, and does not appear to find it difficult.

Set that against another man in this book who was asked whether he had obeyed a voice, and said he had, and had not (15:20-22).

'And Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he was holding a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. And Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until the morning light.'

Like the feast of a king.

So the poverty was invented. The man who could not spare bread and water and meat for the soldiers who guarded his flocks is at that hour throwing a banquet fit for a monarch on the same supplies, and is too drunk to be told that his life was saved a few hours ago.

She tells him nothing until he is sober, which is judgment as well as prudence: there is no point saying anything true to a man in that condition.

'In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.'

Something breaks in him when he hears it.

The description is medical enough to be recognisable — a stroke, most likely, on hearing how close he came — and it is written in language that also says something about the man. His heart died within him. He became as a stone. The narrator has been telling us what Nabal was since verse 3, and this is the physical form of it.

'And about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.'

The vengeance David rode out to take is taken, ten days later, by somebody else.

The writer says who did it and does not hedge: the LORD struck Nabal. That is the same verb used of God's judgments elsewhere in the book, and it settles what has just happened.

This is Abigail's whole argument proved. David wanted Nabal dead. Nabal is dead. And David's hands are clean, and he has nothing to carry to the throne, and he never had to lift a finger. He got the outcome without the guilt, purely because a woman stood in the road and he listened.

It is what Paul means: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God... Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Rom. 12:19). The promise is not that the wrong will be ignored. It is that it will be dealt with by somebody whose hands can afford it.

verseByVerse.quote: When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD who has avenged the insult I received at the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. The LORD has returned the evil of Nabal on his own head." Then David sent and spoke to Abigail, to take her as his wife. When the servants of David came to Abigail at Carmel, they said to her, "David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife." And she rose and bowed with her face to the ground and said, "Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." And Abigail hurried and rose and mounted a donkey, and her five young women attended her. She followed the messengers of David and became his wife. David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives. Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD who has avenged the insult I received at the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. The LORD has returned the evil of Nabal on his own head."'

He blesses God twice, and for two different things.

For the judgment: the LORD has avenged the insult I received. He does not pretend he did not want this. He wanted it very much and rode out with four hundred men to arrange it.

And for the restraint: has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. He is as glad about the second as the first, and the order in which he says them shows he has grasped which of the two he was closer to losing.

'Then David sent and spoke to Abigail, to take her as his wife.'

In the same breath.

The narrator lets the two sentences stand next to each other without a syllable of comment, and a reader can make of the speed what they like. What is certain is that David has correctly identified the most valuable person he has met in years.

'And she rose and bowed with her face to the ground and said, "Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." And Abigail hurried and rose and mounted a donkey, and her five young women attended her. She followed the messengers of David and became his wife.'

She is consistent to the end: the woman who took the blame that was not hers offers to wash feet.

And she goes. Out of a large estate and a settled position, into a wilderness with a hunted man and six hundred soldiers, with five servants and no security whatever. She is captured with him at Ziklag before this is over (30:5).

She had told him on the road that God would build him a sure house. She now goes and lives as though she believed it.

'David also had taken Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives. Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.'

The chapter ends on two flat notes and no comment at all.

There is another wife, Ahinoam, mentioned for the first time as an established fact. And Michal — who loved him, who let him down through the window with a rope and put an idol in his bed — has been handed by her father to another man, as though the marriage had never happened. Saul is dissolving the connection by force.

Both notes are reported the way this writer reports everything: what happened, without approval or disapproval. He described Gideon's ephod the same way, and Jacob's two wives, and left the reader to notice. Silence here is not endorsement. David now has three wives, one of them given away by her father in his absence, and the wreckage that multiple marriages make in his household is a large part of the story of 2 Samuel — Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah are all sons of different mothers.

It is a strange ending to a chapter about restraint, and it is honest. The man who was talked out of a massacre on Tuesday is not a finished article by Friday. Scripture keeps saying this about its heroes and refuses to tidy them, which is one of the reasons to trust it.

26.title: David Spares Saul Again
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding himself on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the east of Jeshimon?"<sup>2</sup>So Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph.<sup>3</sup>And Saul encamped on the hill of Hachilah, which is beside the road on the east of Jeshimon. But David remained in the wilderness. When he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness,<sup>4</sup>David sent out spies and learned that Saul had indeed come.<sup>5</sup>Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had encamped. And David saw the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the commander of his army. Saul was lying within the encampment, while the army was encamped around him.<sup>6</sup>Then David said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Joab's brother Abishai the son of Zeruiah, "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" And Abishai said, "I will go down with you."<sup>7</sup>So David and Abishai went to the army by night. And there lay Saul sleeping within the encampment, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner and the army lay around him.<sup>8</sup>Then Abishai said to David, "God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice."<sup>9</sup>But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?"<sup>10</sup>And David said, "As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish.<sup>11</sup>The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. But take now the spear that is at his head and the jar of water, and let us go."<sup>12</sup>So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head, and they went away. No man saw it or knew it, nor did any awake, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.<sup>13</sup>Then David went over to the other side and stood far off on the top of the hill, with a great space between them.<sup>14</sup>And David called to the army, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, "Will you not answer, Abner?" Then Abner answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?"<sup>15</sup>And David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord.<sup>16</sup>This thing that you have done is not good. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now see where the king's spear is and the jar of water that was at his head."<sup>17</sup>Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And David said, "It is my voice, my lord, O king."<sup>18</sup>And he said, "Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is on my hands?<sup>19</sup>Now therefore let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is the LORD who has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering, but if it is men, may they be cursed before the LORD, for they have driven me out this day that I should have no share in the heritage of the LORD, saying, 'Go, serve other gods.'<sup>20</sup>Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains."<sup>21</sup>Then Saul said, "I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake."<sup>22</sup>And David answered and said, "Here is the spear, O king! Let one of the young men come over and take it.<sup>23</sup>The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the LORD gave you into my hand today, and I would not put out my hand against the LORD's anointed.<sup>24</sup>Behold, as your life was precious this day in my sight, so may my life be precious in the sight of the LORD, and may he deliver me out of all tribulation."<sup>25</sup>Then Saul said to David, "Blessed be you, my son David! You will do many things and will succeed in them." So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.
26.overview:
The Ziphites inform a second time, in almost the same sentence, and Saul comes out again with three thousand chosen men — after weeping on a hillside and conceding the throne. But this chapter is not a repeat of chapter 24, and the difference is everything. At Engedi the opportunity walked into the cave where David was hiding. Here he sends spies, confirms the report, observes where the king is lying and where the commander of the army is lying, and walks into the camp at night on purpose. Refusing what lands in your lap is one thing; building the opportunity and then refusing it is another.

Abishai — David's own nephew, and the first sample of the sons of Zeruiah who will trouble him for the rest of his life — asks once: God has given your enemy into your hand this day. That is the third time in four chapters somebody has read a circumstance and announced what God is doing, and not one of the three has asked God anything. David's answer goes further than at Engedi: the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish — and the third is what happens, on Mount Gilboa, five chapters from here.

They take the spear and the water jar and walk out through a camp God has put to sleep, and the narrator says so outright. God arranged the whole opportunity, and it still did not mean what Abishai said it meant: the opening was not the instruction.

Across the valley David humiliates Abner for sleeping through it, and the king's spear in his hand is both the proof of the charge and the proof of his own innocence. He tells Saul the thing that actually hurts — driven out of the land is driven from where God is worshipped, as good as being told go, serve other gods. Saul says I have sinned... I have acted foolishly, which is Samuel's word to him thirteen chapters late. David sends a boy for the spear rather than come near him. Then: David went his way, and Saul returned to his place. They never meet again.
26.theology:
The refusal that cost more. Chapter 24 was reactive; this one is deliberate. He constructed the chance over most of a day and then declined it, which is the harder version by a long way — and it settles that Engedi was principle and not panic.

Three men, one sentence, no enquiry (v. 8). Saul at Keilah (23:7), David's men in the cave (24:4), Abishai over the sleeping king. Each looks at circumstances that suit him and announces what God is doing, and there is an ephod in the camp the whole time. Abishai's I will not strike him twice is a professional offering to keep his commander's hands clean, which is its own kind of temptation.

God is not short of methods (v. 10). David names three ways Saul's end may come and says none of them needs him — and the third, he will go down into battle and perish, is exactly what happens at Gilboa (31:1-6). He says it standing over the man with a spear in reach. Anybody waiting for God to deal with someone should carry that verse: God has never once needed a believer to break faith in order to get something done.

The opening is not the instruction (v. 12). Here the narrator states outright what he left implicit at Engedi: a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them — three thousand men, a posted watch, and the commander of the army, all put under by God, in the same word used of Adam in the garden. God arranged the entire opportunity, and it still did not license what Abishai wanted. He set the camp asleep so that David could prove he would not do it.

Exile as idolatry (v. 19). Nobody said go, serve other gods to David. But to be squeezed out of Israel is to be squeezed away from the altar, the sacrifices and the feasts, into countries where every shrine belongs to somebody else, and he treats the two as one sentence. That is why the next chapter, where he goes to live in Philistia, is such a fall.

Discernment is not bitterness (vv. 21-22). Saul's confession is the clearest he ever makes, and I have acted foolishly is Samuel's own verdict at 13:13 finally repeated by the man himself. David answers it with complete courtesy, returns the spear, blesses him, takes no revenge — and sends a boy to fetch it rather than walk within reach. Both at once. He knows what the remorse is worth: real while it lasts, worth nothing tomorrow. Three chapters later Saul is consulting the dead at Endor.

Clarity that does nothing (v. 25). Saul understands his position better than almost anyone in Scripture — who God has chosen, that he himself is wrong, that he has been a fool — and he can bless the man to his face and prophesy his success. Then he goes home and dies in a battle he was warned about, having changed nothing. Knowing the truth about yourself and God is not the same as submitting to it.
26.examples:
Then: Two men walked into a camp of three thousand soldiers at night, stood over the sleeping king with his own spear planted in the ground beside his head, and one of them asked for permission to use it. The other said no, took the spear and the water jar, walked out unchallenged, and shouted across the valley at dawn to give them back.

Now: Verse 12 is the one to keep. God really had put that camp to sleep — the opportunity was genuinely his doing — and it still did not authorise a thing. An open door is not an instruction, and the fact that something has become easy is not evidence that it has become right; God may have opened it for a reason entirely unlike the one you have assumed. And verse 22 for the other half: forgiving somebody and trusting them again are two different decisions, and David made the first without making the second. He blessed Saul, prayed for him, gave him back his weapon — and sent a boy to carry it, and went his way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Deep Sleep from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ziphites inform on David a second time, in the same words as before, and Saul comes out again with three thousand chosen men (vv. 1-2). This time David does not stumble on the opportunity — he sends spies, confirms the camp, and goes down into it at night with Abishai (vv. 3-7). Saul is asleep in the middle of the camp with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. Abishai asks once: God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice (v. 8). David refuses (vv. 9-11), and they take the spear and the water jar and walk out, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the third time in four chapters that somebody reads a circumstance as a divine licence — Saul at Keilah, David's men in the cave, Abishai here — and it is the same sentence every time. Not one of the three asks God anything.
verseByVerse.examples: David's refusal here is a different order of thing from Engedi. There the opportunity found him; he was hiding in a cave and Saul walked in. Here he goes looking for it, at night, on purpose, and then declines it — which is the harder version by a long way.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding himself on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the east of Jeshimon?" So Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul encamped on the hill of Hachilah, which is beside the road on the east of Jeshimon. But David remained in the wilderness. When he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness, David sent out spies and learned that Saul had indeed come. Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had encamped. And David saw the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the commander of his army. Saul was lying within the encampment, while the army was encamped around him. Then David said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Joab's brother Abishai the son of Zeruiah, "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" And Abishai said, "I will go down with you." So David and Abishai went to the army by night. And there lay Saul sleeping within the encampment, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner and the army lay around him. Then Abishai said to David, "God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice." But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?" And David said, "As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish. The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. But take now the spear that is at his head and the jar of water, and let us go." So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head, and they went away. No man saw it or knew it, nor did any awake, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding himself on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the east of Jeshimon?"'

The same men, the same journey, almost the same sentence as three chapters ago.

They did it at 23:19 and they are doing it again. Nobody is paying them and nobody has threatened them; they simply keep informing on their own tribesman because he is losing and the king is not.

'So Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph.'

Three thousand chosen men, for the second time.

He has just wept on a hillside and confessed that David was more righteous than he was and that David would certainly be king. He is out again with the same army.

'David sent out spies and learned that Saul had indeed come. Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had encamped. And David saw the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the commander of his army.'

Here is the difference between this chapter and chapter 24, and it is the whole point of having both.

At Engedi, David was hiding in the back of a cave and the opportunity walked in on him. He did not seek it, could not have arranged it, and had about two minutes to decide.

Here he sends out reconnaissance, confirms the report, moves to the camp, and personally observes where the king is sleeping and where the commander of the army is lying in relation to him. He builds the opportunity himself, with care, over what must have been most of a day.

Refusing something that lands in your lap is one thing. Constructing it and then refusing it is another.

'Then David said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Joab's brother Abishai the son of Zeruiah, "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" And Abishai said, "I will go down with you."'

Two volunteers are asked and one answers, and the man who answers is David's nephew.

Zeruiah is David's sister, so Abishai and Joab are his sister's sons — and the sons of Zeruiah are going to be a recurring problem for the rest of David's life. They are magnificent soldiers and they solve every difficulty the same way. Years later David will say of them, in exasperation, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I (2 Sam. 3:39).

Here is the first sample of it, three verses on.

'So David and Abishai went to the army by night. And there lay Saul sleeping within the encampment, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner and the army lay around him.'

Note the spear, still.

The narrator has had it in Saul's hand at the table, at the tamarisk tree, in the throne room twice. Here it is planted in the ground beside his head while he sleeps, which is where a king put his spear to mark the royal place. It is the emblem of his kingship, and it is about to be carried off by a man he is hunting.

'Then Abishai said to David, "God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice."'

There is that sentence for the third time in four chapters.

Saul said it at Keilah: God has given him into my hand (23:7). David's men said it in the cave: here is the day of which the LORD said (24:4). Abishai says it standing over a sleeping king with a spear within reach.

Three times, in three different mouths, on three different sides — and on each occasion the speaker has looked at a set of circumstances that suits him and announced what God is doing. Not one of them has asked God anything, and there is an ephod in the camp.

The rest of Abishai's line reveals a good deal about him: I will not strike him twice. He is not asking permission to try. He is a professional soldier telling his commander that one thrust will be enough, and quietly offering to be the one who does it so that David's own hand stays clean.

'But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?"'

The same principle as the cave, and no more explanation than last time.

He does not argue that Saul deserves better, or that it would be impolitic, or that they would be caught. Oil was poured on that head at God's word; nobody unpours it with a spear.

'And David said, "As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish."'

Now this is new, and it is the deepest thing David says in either chapter.

He is not merely refusing to kill Saul. He is saying that Saul's end is already appointed, that God has more than one way of doing it, and that not one of those ways requires David's help. Three possibilities: God strikes him, or he simply reaches the end of his life, or he goes down in battle.

Hold that third one. He will go down into battle and perish.

That is exactly what happens. Five chapters from here, on Mount Gilboa, the archers find Saul, his three sons are killed around him, and he falls on his own sword (31:1-6). David names the manner of it standing over him in the dark with a spear in easy reach and declines to be the instrument.

Anybody waiting for God to deal with someone should carry that sentence. God is not short of methods, and he has never once needed a believer to break faith in order to get something done.

'"The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. But take now the spear that is at his head and the jar of water, and let us go."'

He takes the two things a soldier keeps closest: his weapon and his water.

'So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head, and they went away. No man saw it or knew it, nor did any awake, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.'

The narrator tells us plainly what was going on, which he did not do at Engedi.

Three thousand men, a posted watch, Abner the commander of the army lying next to the king — and every one of them unconscious, because God put them under. The word is the one used of the sleep that fell on Adam in the garden.

God arranged the whole opportunity. That is now established beyond argument. And it still did not mean what Abishai said it meant.

Which is the lesson of these three chapters together, put as plainly as it can be put: God may open a door in front of you for a reason entirely different from the one you assume, and the opening is not the instruction. He set that camp asleep so that David could prove he would not do it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Like One Who Hunts a Partridge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David crosses the valley, puts a hill between himself and the camp, and shouts — at Abner first. Are you not a man?... Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king?... you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now see where the king's spear is (vv. 14-16). Then to Saul: is this your voice, my son David? (v. 17). David asks what he has done, and says the thing that hurts most — they have driven him from the heritage of the LORD, as good as saying go, serve other gods (v. 19). The king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The rebuke to Abner is doing two things at once. It humiliates the commander in front of the whole army for a genuine failure — and it proves David's case by the same stroke, because the spear in his hand is the evidence that the king was his and he did not take him.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 19 is the real wound and it is a theological one. To be driven out of the land is to be driven from the place where God is worshipped and sacrifice is offered. That is why exile feels to him like an instruction to serve other gods — and it is why the next chapter is such a fall.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David went over to the other side and stood far off on the top of the hill, with a great space between them. And David called to the army, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, "Will you not answer, Abner?" Then Abner answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?" And David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord. This thing that you have done is not good. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now see where the king's spear is and the jar of water that was at his head." Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And David said, "It is my voice, my lord, O king." And he said, "Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is on my hands? Now therefore let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is the LORD who has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering, but if it is men, may they be cursed before the LORD, for they have driven me out this day that I should have no share in the heritage of the LORD, saying, 'Go, serve other gods.' Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David went over to the other side and stood far off on the top of the hill, with a great space between them.'

He puts a valley between himself and three thousand men before he says a word, which is simple good sense, and it is the same arrangement as the last time.

'And David called to the army, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, "Will you not answer, Abner?" Then Abner answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?"'

He addresses the commander of the army before the king, and the whole camp is listening.

'And David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord."'

The mockery is deliberate and it is not empty.

Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? — Abner is the commander-in-chief and Saul's own cousin, the most senior soldier in the kingdom. And he slept while two men walked into the middle of his camp and stood over the king.

'"This thing that you have done is not good. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now see where the king's spear is and the jar of water that was at his head."'

Notice what David has just done with a single sentence.

He calls Saul the LORD's anointed, to Abner, in front of the army — using the exact phrase that is his own reason for not killing him. He is telling three thousand soldiers, without saying it directly, that he holds their king's person sacred while their own commander could not stay awake.

And then the evidence: see where the king's spear is. The proof of the accusation and the proof of David's innocence are the same object. He is holding the king's spear, therefore the guard failed, therefore he could have used it, therefore he did not.

'Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And David said, "It is my voice, my lord, O king."'

Word for word what he said at Engedi (24:16). The writer is putting the two scenes on top of each other so that the differences show.

'And he said, "Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is on my hands?"'

'"Now therefore let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is the LORD who has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering, but if it is men, may they be cursed before the LORD."'

He divides the possibilities honestly, and the first half is remarkable.

If it is the LORD who has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering. If God is behind this, then there is sin in me somewhere that I cannot see, and I will bring a sacrifice and be forgiven and the matter is closed. He is prepared to entertain that he is the problem.

But if it is men — the Ziphites, the informers, whoever has been telling Saul that David is cunning — then let them answer for it.

'"For they have driven me out this day that I should have no share in the heritage of the LORD, saying, 'Go, serve other gods.'"'

Here is the thing that actually hurts, and it is not the running or the caves.

Nobody has said go, serve other gods to David. What has happened is that he is being squeezed out of Israel — and Israel is the land where the LORD is worshipped, where the altar is, where sacrifice is offered and the feasts are kept. To be driven out of the territory is to be driven away from all of it.

He treats the two as the same sentence, and in his world they were. Exile is not homesickness; it is being pushed out of reach of the means of grace, into countries where every shrine belongs to somebody else. That is what he is being made to do, and he says it is as good as being ordered into idolatry.

Remember that when the next chapter opens, because that is precisely where he goes.

'"Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains."'
