Two images and both of them belittle him on purpose.

A single flea is what he called himself at Engedi. And the partridge is a picture anybody in that country would recognise: the way you take one is to chase it until it cannot fly any more, because it can only manage short bursts. You do not out-fly it; you exhaust it.

That is what is being done to him, and he knows it. This is a man saying, in public, that he is being worn out on purpose by somebody with three thousand men and nothing better to do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — So David Went His Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul says it as plainly as he ever will: I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake (v. 21). David does not return. He holds up the spear and says let one of the young men come over and take it (v. 22), commits himself to the LORD who rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, and asks that his own life be as precious in God's sight as Saul's was in his (vv. 23-24). Saul blesses him: you will do many things and will succeed in them. So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: I have acted foolishly is Samuel's word to him at Gilgal thirteen chapters earlier — you have done foolishly (13:13). Saul finally says it about himself, and it is still not repentance, because nothing changes.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch what David does with the spear. He believes the confession enough to answer it and not enough to walk within arm's length of the man who made it — and he is right. This is the last time these two ever see each other or speak.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said, "I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake." And David answered and said, "Here is the spear, O king! Let one of the young men come over and take it. The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the LORD gave you into my hand today, and I would not put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. Behold, as your life was precious this day in my sight, so may my life be precious in the sight of the LORD, and may he deliver me out of all tribulation." Then Saul said to David, "Blessed be you, my son David! You will do many things and will succeed in them." So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul said, "I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake."'

It is the clearest thing he ever says, and every clause of it is true.

I have sinned. Not mistakes were made. He names it as sin, in the first person.

I have acted foolishly. And that phrase has a history. Samuel said it to him at Gilgal after the unlawful sacrifice, thirteen chapters ago: you have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God (13:13). Saul finally uses the word of himself, and by now the kingdom has been torn away, a priestly town has been massacred, and his son has told his enemy he will be king.

Still nothing changes, which is why the confession is not repentance. He said much the same at Engedi and wept while he said it. Within three chapters he will be at a medium's house at Endor, consulting the dead, on the night before he dies.

'And David answered and said, "Here is the spear, O king! Let one of the young men come over and take it."'

Read that carefully, because it is the most eloquent thing in the chapter and it is a piece of logistics.

He does not bring the spear back. He does not walk down the hill and hand it to Saul, and he does not accept the invitation to return.

Send a boy for it.

He has just heard a confession he believes to be sincere, from a man weeping and calling him son, and he will not come within arm's length of him. Two chapters ago he heard the same words and went up to the stronghold instead of going home. He has learned exactly what Saul's remorse is worth: real while it lasts, and worth nothing tomorrow.

Discernment about a person is not the same as bitterness toward them. David answers Saul with complete courtesy, gives him back his spear, blesses him and takes no revenge — and does not put himself in his power again. Both of those at once.

'"The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the LORD gave you into my hand today, and I would not put out my hand against the LORD's anointed."'

He says it a second time: the LORD gave you into my hand. He never denies the providence. He only ever denied the conclusion.

'"Behold, as your life was precious this day in my sight, so may my life be precious in the sight of the LORD, and may he deliver me out of all tribulation."'

This is the last thing David ever says to Saul, and it is a prayer.

He asks that God would treat him the way he has just treated Saul. That is a large thing to ask and he has earned the right to ask it twice over, and it is very close to a line the Lord Jesus put into the prayer he taught: forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors (Matt. 6:12).

He also adds deliver me out of all tribulation, which is honest. He is not pretending to be above it. He wants out.

'Then Saul said to David, "Blessed be you, my son David! You will do many things and will succeed in them." So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.'

That is the end of them.

So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place. They never see each other again. They never speak again. Everything that is left between them happens at a distance: David hears about Gilboa from a stranger with torn clothes, and composes a lament for the man who hunted him and for the friend he had lost.

Saul's last recorded words to David are a blessing and a prophecy, and they are accurate. You will do many things and will succeed in them. He has been told this by Samuel, by Jonathan, by Abigail, and now he says it himself for the second time, out loud, to the man's face — and then turns round and goes back to a kingdom he knows is not his.

There is a kind of clarity that does nothing at all. Saul understands his situation better than almost anyone in Scripture: he knows who God has chosen, he knows he is wrong, he knows he has been a fool, he can even bless the man. He goes home and dies in a battle he was warned about, having changed nothing. Knowing the truth about yourself and God is not the same as submitting to it, and Saul is the proof.

27.title: David Among the Philistines
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand."<sup>2</sup>So David arose and went over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath.<sup>3</sup>And David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.<sup>4</sup>And when it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he no longer sought him.<sup>5</sup>Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let a place be given me in one of the country towns, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?"<sup>6</sup>So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.<sup>7</sup>And the number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.<sup>8</sup>Now David and his men went up and made raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites, for these were the inhabitants of the land from of old, as far as Shur, to the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>And David would strike the land and would leave neither man nor woman alive, but would take away the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, the camels, and the garments, and come back to Achish.<sup>10</sup>When Achish asked, "Where have you made a raid today?" David would say, "Against the Negeb of Judah," or, "Against the Negeb of the Jerahmeelites," or, "Against the Negeb of the Kenites."<sup>11</sup>And David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, "lest they should tell about us and say, 'So David has done.'" Such was his custom all the while he lived in the country of the Philistines.<sup>12</sup>And Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant."
27.overview:
Then David said in his heart. That is the whole of the consultation. He has Abiathar, he has the ephod, he has Gad the prophet, and in chapter 23 he asked God four questions about one operation and got four answers — and on the largest decision of his fugitive years he asks nothing and talks to himself. Worse, the thing he tells himself is false: now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul, and Saul never touches him again. It comes immediately after a hillside where Saul wept and swore off the hunt, and days after God put an entire army to sleep so David could walk through it. He has never had more evidence, and this is the week he decides he is going to die.

So he goes to Gath. He has been to Gath before — alone, recognised, terrified, drooling into his beard in the gateway until Achish threw him out as a madman. This time he arrives with six hundred soldiers and is given a town. And one chapter earlier he had told Saul to his face that being driven out of Israel was as good as being ordered go, serve other gods. He knew exactly what he was doing, and he stays a year and four months.

Then the darkest passage in the book about him. He raids, takes the livestock, and leaves neither man nor woman alive — and the narrator gives the reason without a syllable of comment: lest they should tell about us. A survivor could reach Gath and contradict the story he is telling Achish, so whole settlements die to keep a lie standing up. And the lie works: Achish concludes David has made himself a stench to his own people and will therefore be his servant for good.
27.theology:
In his heart (v. 1). The omission is the chapter. Chapter 23 was built on a man who asked and was answered, set against a king who inferred and was wrong; here David has priest, ephod and prophet all three — he has them precisely because Saul destroyed the priesthood and Abiathar ran to him — and uses none of them. Fear is a poor analyst, and it does its best work when the pressure lifts. A man can hold together through years of being hunted and come apart in the week after, when there is finally room to think and what fills the room is the calculation he was too busy to make.

He knew what leaving the land meant (26:19). He had said it out loud, in public, weeks before: to be pushed out of the heritage of the LORD is to be pushed away from the altar and the feasts, and amounts to being told to serve other gods. Then he went, with six hundred households, for sixteen months.

It works perfectly, and that is the trouble (v. 4). Nothing in this chapter goes wrong for him. The plan is shrewd, the safety is real, the arrangement holds, and Saul gives up. It is entirely possible to solve a problem successfully and be in a far worse place at the end of it.

Lest they should tell about us (v. 11). The motive is stated by the narrator and it is not plunder and not judgment on Amalek: a living witness could reach Gath and break the story. Every man and woman in those settlements dies to keep a falsehood upright. The writer does not comment, exactly as he did not comment at Nob — and the silence is not approval, nor is it a space to be filled with excuses. There is no sentence in these verses that softens what is described, and manufacturing one serves nobody.

Why a passage like this is evidence for Scripture, not against it. Nobody constructing a national hero writes verse 11. Abraham lied about his wife twice, Jacob cheated his brother and his father-in-law, Moses killed a man and hid the body, Peter swore he had never met the Lord. These are not accounts written by admirers tidying up. And the same man wrote create in me a clean heart, O God; he understood what was in him better than his readers do.

He cannot get himself out (v. 12). Achish is certain he owns him — a man hated by his own nation has nowhere to go and will be loyal for good. David has bought safety by making a Philistine king sure he can never come home, and he has no route back that he can see. The next three chapters are God extracting him: suspicious Philistine commanders who refuse to have him in the battle line (29:3-11), and a burnt town that finally drives him to call for the ephod again (30:7). He asked God nothing in verse 1. His first recorded enquiry in sixteen months is made standing in ashes.
27.examples:
Then: A man with a priest, an ephod and a prophet in his camp decided his own future in a private conversation with himself, moved six hundred families into enemy territory for sixteen months, and then killed every inhabitant of the villages he raided so that nobody could contradict the account he was giving his host.

Now: The chapter is about the decision made in the quiet week after the crisis, not in the crisis. David held for years and then reasoned his way out of the land in a single sentence, alone, with every means of asking God sitting in his own camp. The tell was not that the plan was bad — it was excellent, and it worked. The tell was that he never put it to anybody: not to God, not to Gad, not to Abiathar. A decision you are reluctant to say out loud to somebody who will push back on it is usually the decision that most needs saying out loud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — David Said in His Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines" (v. 1). So he crosses over to Achish king of Gath with six hundred men and their households, and Saul stops looking for him (vv. 2-4). He asks for a country town rather than the capital, and is given Ziklag — where he stays a year and four months (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: He has a priest and an ephod in the camp, and in chapter 23 he asked God four questions and got four answers. Here he asks nothing. In his heart is the whole of the consultation, and it comes immediately after Saul has publicly sworn off the hunt.
verseByVerse.examples: The premise is also untrue. Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul — and Saul never touches him again, in this chapter or any other. Fear is a poor analyst, and it is at its most persuasive just after the danger has passed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand." So David arose and went over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath. And David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow. And when it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he no longer sought him. Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let a place be given me in one of the country towns, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?" So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day. And the number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines."'

Four words at the front of the verse carry the whole chapter: David said in his heart.

Count what he does not do. He does not call for Abiathar. He does not send for the ephod. He does not ask the LORD whether to go, as he did four separate times over one operation at Keilah, and he does not ask Gad the prophet, who is somewhere in the camp.

He talks to himself, and then he acts on it.

That is not a small omission in this book. Chapter 23 was built around a man who asked and was answered, set against a king who inferred and was wrong. David has the priest, the ephod and the prophet, all three, precisely because Saul destroyed the priesthood and Abiathar ran to him. And on the biggest decision of his fugitive years he uses none of them.

Now look at what he tells himself, because it is false.

Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul.

Saul never touches him. Not in this chapter, not in the next, not ever. In four chapters Saul will be dead on a mountain and David will be a hundred miles away, and the hand that kills Saul will be his own. The thing David is certain of does not happen.

Note the timing. This comes immediately after a hillside where Saul wept, confessed his sin, blessed him and swore off the hunt. Jonathan had told him the hand of Saul would not find him. Abigail had told him God would make him a sure house. He has just watched God put an entire army to sleep so that he could walk through it.

He has never had more evidence, and this is the moment he decides he is going to die.

Fear is a poor analyst, and it does its best work when the pressure lifts. A man can hold together through years of being hunted and come apart in the week afterwards, when there is finally room to think, and what fills the room is not gratitude but the calculation he was too busy to make.

'"Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand."'

The plan is shrewd, and shrewdness is not the issue.

It works exactly as designed — verse 4 says so. Everything wrong with it is upstream of its cleverness.

'So David arose and went over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath.'

Achish. King of Gath. He has been here before.

The last time David stood in front of this man he was alone, unarmed, recognised by the song, much afraid — and he saved his life by scratching at the gate and letting saliva run into his beard until Achish threw him out as a madman (21:12-15).

He comes back with six hundred soldiers and their families, and this time he is welcomed.

Remember what he said about this the last time he was in trouble, one chapter ago. To be driven out of Israel, he told Saul, was to be pushed out of the heritage of the LORD — away from the altar and the feasts and the sacrifices — and amounted to being told go, serve other gods (26:19).

He knew exactly what leaving the land meant. He said it out loud, in public, weeks earlier. And he goes.

'And when it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he no longer sought him.'

The plan works perfectly, which is the trouble with it.

Nothing in this chapter goes wrong for David. The safety is real, the arrangement holds, and the king of Israel gives up. It is entirely possible to solve a problem successfully and be in a far worse place at the end of it.

'Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let a place be given me in one of the country towns, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?"'

He asks to be moved out of the capital, and the reason he gives is deference. The real reason is distance: in a country town nobody watches what he does, and everything in the second half of the chapter depends on that.

'So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day. And the number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.'

Sixteen months.

Not a night's flight or a season's expedient. He settles, with six hundred households, under a Philistine king, on Philistine land, for a year and a third.

The aside about Ziklag — therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day — is the writer reminding us that God is still working, in the middle of all this. A town handed over by a Philistine to buy a mercenary's loyalty ends up permanently in the royal holdings of Judah. It is also where the news of Gilboa reaches David, and where he is sitting when the kingdom comes to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — Lest They Should Tell About Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Ziklag David raids the Geshurites, the Girzites and the Amalekites — and David would strike the land and would leave neither man nor woman alive (vv. 8-9). Achish asks where he has been raiding, and David names places in Judah's own territory, which is a lie (v. 10). The narrator then explains the killing: David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, "lest they should tell about us" (v. 11). And it works: Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant" (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason is given without a syllable of comment, and it is the plainest sentence in the chapter: he leaves nobody alive because a survivor could contradict the story he is telling his patron. This is killing to protect a lie, and the writer neither excuses it nor denounces it. He simply records it, as he recorded Nob.
verseByVerse.examples: One thing in the raiding does point forward: Amalek is on the target list, and Amalek is chapter 15's unfinished business, the nation Saul was told to devote to destruction and spared. It is not an excuse for verse 11, and the Amalekites will burn Ziklag over David's head three chapters from now.

verseByVerse.quote: Now David and his men went up and made raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites, for these were the inhabitants of the land from of old, as far as Shur, to the land of Egypt. And David would strike the land and would leave neither man nor woman alive, but would take away the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, the camels, and the garments, and come back to Achish. When Achish asked, "Where have you made a raid today?" David would say, "Against the Negeb of Judah," or, "Against the Negeb of the Jerahmeelites," or, "Against the Negeb of the Kenites." And David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, "lest they should tell about us and say, 'So David has done.'" Such was his custom all the while he lived in the country of the Philistines. And Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now David and his men went up and made raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites, for these were the inhabitants of the land from of old, as far as Shur, to the land of Egypt.'

He has to live, and six hundred families have to eat, and a mercenary in that arrangement fed himself by raiding. So far this is the ordinary economy of the situation.

Register one detail before the next verse. Amalek is on the list.

These are the people Saul was commanded to devote to destruction and did not, keeping the best of the flock and the king alive, and losing the kingdom over it (15:1-23). They are also the people who attacked Israel at the back of the column coming out of Egypt. David is finishing something Saul left, and the Amalekites will come back for Ziklag in three chapters and burn it over his head.

'And David would strike the land and would leave neither man nor woman alive, but would take away the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, the camels, and the garments, and come back to Achish.'

'When Achish asked, "Where have you made a raid today?" David would say, "Against the Negeb of Judah," or, "Against the Negeb of the Jerahmeelites," or, "Against the Negeb of the Kenites."'

Every one of those is a lie, and each is chosen with care.

He is naming his own people. Judah is his tribe. The Kenites are the clan of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, long settled among Israel and friendly — Saul warned them out of the way before the Amalekite campaign (15:6). David is telling the king of Gath that he has been raiding Israelites, because that is the news Achish wants, and it is the only story that keeps him safe.

'And David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, "lest they should tell about us and say, 'So David has done.'"'

There is the reason, given by the narrator, in the plainest sentence in the chapter.

He kills everybody because a survivor could talk.

Not for plunder, though he takes plunder. Not as judgment on Amalek, though Amalek is among them. The stated motive is that a living witness would reach Gath and contradict what he has been telling Achish, and the story has to hold. Every man and every woman in those settlements dies to keep a lie standing up.

The writer does not comment. He has not commented on anything in this chapter and he does not begin here. He does exactly what he did with the massacre at Nob: he states what happened, gives the reason, and moves on.

That silence should not be mistaken for approval, and neither should it be filled in with excuses. There is no sentence anywhere in these five verses that softens what is described, and producing one is not a service to anybody. This is the man after God's own heart, sixteen months into a foreign country he entered without asking God a single question, killing to protect a falsehood.

Scripture does this with all its people and it is one of the strongest reasons to believe it. Nobody constructing a national hero writes verse 11. Abraham lied about his wife twice, Jacob cheated his brother and his father-in-law, Moses killed a man and hid the body, Peter swore he had never met him. These accounts are not written by admirers tidying up. And the same David who appears here wrote create in me a clean heart, O God — he knew what was in him better than his readers do.

'And Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant."'

The deception is a total success, and the last verse says what it cost.

Achish believes he owns him. The reasoning is sound on the information he has: a man who has made himself hated by his own nation has nowhere else to go, and will therefore be loyal permanently. He shall always be my servant.

David has bought his safety by making a Philistine king certain that he can never go home. And that is the position he is in at the end of this chapter — secure, well supplied, established in a town of his own, trusted by his enemy, out of the land, out of reach of the altar, with the blood of whole villages behind him and no way back that he can see.

He will need to be got out of it, and he cannot do it himself. The next three chapters are God extracting him — by way of a company of suspicious Philistine commanders who refuse to have him in the battle line (29:3-11), and a burnt town that drives him to ask for the ephod again (30:7).

He asked God nothing in verse 1 of this chapter. The first recorded words of his enquiry after sixteen months are shall I pursue? — standing in the ashes of everything he had.

28.title: Saul and the Witch of Endor
28.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war, to fight against Israel. And Achish said to David, "Understand that you and your men are to go out with me in the army."<sup>2</sup>David said to Achish, "Very well, you shall know what your servant can do." And Achish said to David, "Very well, I will make you my bodyguard for life."<sup>3</sup>Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had put the mediums and the necromancers out of the land.<sup>4</sup>The Philistines assembled and came and encamped at Shunem. And Saul gathered all Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa.<sup>5</sup>When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.<sup>6</sup>And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.<sup>7</sup>Then Saul said to his servants, "Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her." And his servants said to him, "Behold, there is a medium at En-dor."<sup>8</sup>So Saul disguised himself and put on other garments and went, he and two men with him. And they came to the woman by night. And he said, "Divine for me by a spirit and bring up for me whomever I shall name to you."<sup>9</sup>The woman said to him, "Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the necromancers from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?"<sup>10</sup>But Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing."<sup>11</sup>Then the woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me."<sup>12</sup>When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul."<sup>13</sup>The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" And the woman said to Saul, "I see a god coming up out of the earth."<sup>14</sup>He said to her, "What is his appearance?" And she said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe." And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and paid homage.<sup>15</sup>Then Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul answered, "I am in great distress, for the Philistines are warring against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams. Therefore I have summoned you to tell me what I shall do."<sup>16</sup>And Samuel said, "Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy?<sup>17</sup>The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me, for the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David.<sup>18</sup>Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day.<sup>19</sup>Moreover, the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The LORD will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines."<sup>20</sup>Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night.<sup>21</sup>And the woman came to Saul, and when she saw that he was terrified, she said to him, "Behold, your servant has obeyed you. I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to what you have said to me.<sup>22</sup>Now therefore, you also obey your servant. Let me set a morsel of bread before you; and eat, that you may have strength when you go on your way."<sup>23</sup>He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to their words. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed.<sup>24</sup>Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she quickly killed it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread of it,<sup>25</sup>and she put it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.
28.overview:
Achish tells David to march out with the Philistines against Israel, and the bill for chapter 27 falls due. David answers with a sentence that means nothing and sounds like everything — you shall know what your servant can do — and is promoted to bodyguard for life. He cannot get himself out of this.

Across the valley Saul looks at the Philistine army and something goes out of him. He prays, and nothing comes back: neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. Three legitimate channels, all shut — and he closed one of them himself, because the Urim was carried in the ephod and he had every priest at Nob killed, after which the survivor carried it down to David. The man complaining that God will not speak destroyed the instrument God spoke through.

So he asks for a medium, and his own servants produce an address without pausing, which is what the purge was worth. He disguises himself to hide from his own law, travels by night around an enemy army, and swears as the LORD lives to protect a woman doing what the LORD forbade. She screams when it works — whatever she expected, this was not it.

Samuel's word is the old word with a date attached. The kingdom torn away and given to David; the reason named as Amalek, thirteen chapters on; the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy; and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. Saul falls full length on the floor. And the last meal he eats is cooked in the dark by the woman he had outlawed, out of the fattened calf that was everything she owned — the only kindness anyone shows him in the chapter. Then he walks back to Gilboa and takes his place at the head of the army.
28.theology:
He does pray (v. 6). Notice it before anything else: Saul goes to God first. And three channels answer nothing — dreams, the sacred lot, the living prophetic voice. Part of that is God's own withdrawal, announced at Gilgal and final. Part of it is Saul reaping precisely what he sowed: the Urim lived in the priestly ephod, and he had Doeg kill eighty-five priests at Nob, after which Abiathar carried the ephod to David (22:18-19; 23:6). The consequence arrived in the shape of the sin.

The silence, and what it is not. The most frightening thing God can do is not to refuse but to say nothing — a famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), no answer from God (Mic. 3:7), I never knew you (Matt. 7:23). And this must be said alongside it, because someone reading is in the dark: this is not what is happening to a Christian who feels God has gone quiet. Saul's silence is the end of a forty-year refusal after a specific and final rejection. The believer has a mediator whose blood speaks and a promise never to be left or forsaken. Feeling unheard and being unheard are not the same thing.

Swearing by the LORD to break the law of the LORD (v. 10). He invokes the living God as guarantor of a woman's safety while she does what God calls an abomination. He is not confused; he enforced that law himself. And the oath is sincere — he does mean to protect her. Saul never could tell the difference between meaning something and obeying.

Was it Samuel? Both views, honestly. Some, Calvin among them, held it was not — that God does not put his prophets at a witch's disposal, and that what appeared was a permitted impersonation or a vision. The strength of that view is its instinct about God's holiness. Others hold it was Samuel, raised by God's own act and not by her craft, and the text's weight seems to fall there: the narrator calls him Samuel flatly throughout, the woman screams (v. 12) at something she plainly did not arrange, the message is in Samuel's own manner and quotes his own earlier words, and the prophecy is fulfilled in detail within a day — and it is hard to see God letting a lying spirit deliver an accurate verdict in his name. On that reading God broke into her performance: he had refused to answer, and answered anyway, because there was one more thing to say and it was a sentence. Certainty is not available, and the chapter's argument does not need it. Both views agree on what matters: Saul went where he was forbidden, got what he asked for, and it destroyed him.

Become your enemy (v. 16). Not withdrawn, not disappointed, not standing back. The God who anointed him through this same prophet is on the other side of the field. Saul wants God's help and has God's enmity and cannot see that they are one relationship seen from two ends.

Still Amalek (v. 18). Not an accumulation of small failures — one day at Gilgal, one clear command, the best of the sheep kept back and called sacrifice. And while Saul kneels at Endor hearing it again, Amalekites are burning Ziklag and carrying off the families of the man who will replace him. The nation he spared is still in the story.

Jonathan is in the sentence (v. 19). You and your sons. The man who defended David to his father's face, gave away his own robe, and walked into a wilderness to strengthen a hunted man's hand in God, dies in his father's catastrophe. Scripture declines to tidy this up: the righteous are caught in the wreckage other people's sin makes, and nothing in this chapter explains it. What answers it is said elsewhere — the God who let Jonathan die on Gilboa took a death on another hill, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26).

The fattened calf (vv. 24-25). Not dinner — a poor household's savings, kept for a wedding. She kills it for a man told he dies tomorrow, having already taken her life in her hands for him, and the one voice Saul obeys in this chapter belongs to a medium. Nothing excuses her trade and the chapter does not try; and she is the only person in it who shows him any kindness. The writer records both and reconciles neither, as he did with Ahimelech's holy bread and David's burnt villages.

He walks back (v. 25). He could have run — disguised, behind the lines, with a night's start, and the throne gone anyway. He turns round and takes his place at the head of an army in a battle he has been told he will lose. Saul was never short of the raw material of a great king. He could face an army he knew would kill him, and could not face God and say he had been wrong.
28.examples:
Then: The king of Israel put on another man's clothes, walked at night around an enemy army on the eve of a battle, swore by the living God to protect a woman from a law he had made himself, and asked her to fetch up the prophet who had already told him everything he was about to be told again — and then lay full length on her floor while she killed her last calf to feed him.

Now: Saul is the warning for the season when the ordinary means seem to give nothing back — prayer flat, Scripture closed, no counsel available. The temptation is always to reach for something else, and something else is always findable; his servants had an address ready in a country where the trade was banned. Two things hold in that season. God's silence toward a believer is not God's silence toward Saul, and the difference is a mediator. And the illegitimate answer is still an answer — that is what makes it dangerous. Saul got exactly what he went for, and it put him on the floor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Neither by Dreams, nor by Urim, nor by Prophets
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Achish tells David he will march out with the Philistines against Israel, and David's answer is a masterpiece of ambiguity: you shall know what your servant can do. Achish makes him his bodyguard for life (vv. 1-2). Samuel is dead, and Saul had put the mediums and the necromancers out of the land (v. 3). The armies face each other at Shunem and Gilboa, and Saul was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly (vv. 4-5). And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Three channels, and all three shut. And Saul closed one of them with his own hand: the Urim was carried in the priestly ephod, and he massacred the priests at Nob, after which the survivor carried the ephod down to David (22:20; 23:6). The man complaining that God will not speak destroyed the instrument God spoke through.
verseByVerse.examples: Read David's answer to Achish twice. You shall know what your servant can do commits to nothing whatever and sounds like everything — and it is the trap of chapter 27 closing on him. He is now under orders to fight against Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war, to fight against Israel. And Achish said to David, "Understand that you and your men are to go out with me in the army." David said to Achish, "Very well, you shall know what your servant can do." And Achish said to David, "Very well, I will make you my bodyguard for life." Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had put the mediums and the necromancers out of the land. The Philistines assembled and came and encamped at Shunem. And Saul gathered all Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa. When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly. And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war, to fight against Israel. And Achish said to David, "Understand that you and your men are to go out with me in the army."'

There is the bill for chapter 27.

David went to Philistia because he decided in his own heart that he would die by Saul's hand. Sixteen months of successful deception later, his host requires the thing a host of that kind always eventually requires: come and fight my war.

The war is against Israel. He is being ordered into the field against his own nation, alongside the people he made his name killing, in the battle where Saul and Jonathan are going to die.

'David said to Achish, "Very well, you shall know what your servant can do." And Achish said to David, "Very well, I will make you my bodyguard for life."'

Read David's answer twice, because it says nothing at all.

You shall know what your servant can do. It is not a promise, not a refusal, and not a lie in any form that could be pinned on him. It is a sentence with two meanings, and both of them are true, and Achish hears the one he wants.

It is also a man out of room. He cannot say no without ending the arrangement that is keeping six hundred families alive, and he cannot say yes and mean it. So he says something clever, and gets promoted for it, and is now the Philistine king's personal bodyguard with a battle coming.

He cannot get himself out of this. Somebody else will have to, and in the next chapter somebody does.

'Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had put the mediums and the necromancers out of the land.'

The narrator puts two facts side by side, and the whole chapter is in the gap between them.

Samuel is dead. That is the door Saul would have used, closed by ordinary mortality.

And the mediums are gone, because Saul removed them. That was obedience: the law is explicit and severe about consulting the dead (Lev. 19:31; Deut. 18:10-12), and driving them out was one of the right things he did. The writer mentions it now so that we know exactly what Saul is about to do, and that he knows it too.

'The Philistines assembled and came and encamped at Shunem. And Saul gathered all Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa. When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.'

He looks across the valley and something goes out of him.

This is a soldier. He has beaten the Philistines before, at Michmash and elsewhere; he has spent his reign at war with them. What he is looking at is not worse than what he has faced. But the man looking at it is not the man who faced it.

'And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.'

Here is the verse the chapter turns on, and it should be read slowly.

He asks. Notice that before anything else: Saul does pray. He goes to God about it before he goes anywhere else.

And nothing comes back.

Three channels are named, and they are the three legitimate means by which God spoke to Israel. Dreams — God had spoken that way to Jacob, to Joseph, to Solomon. Urim — the sacred lot carried in the high priest's breastpiece, the means of asking a direct question and getting a direct answer. Prophets — the living voice, which is how Samuel had come to him for years.

All three, silent.

Now hold that against something the reader knows and Saul appears not to have thought about. The Urim was carried in the ephod, and the ephod was in the hands of the priests, and Saul had every priest at Nob killed by an Edomite because one of them gave David bread (22:18-19). The single survivor of that massacre ran to David carrying the ephod, and it has been in the fugitive's camp ever since (23:6).

God is silent through the Urim because there is no Urim to be silent through. Saul destroyed it himself, and he is now complaining about the result.

That is not all of it — the dreams and the prophets are God's own withdrawal, and Samuel had told him at Gilgal that the rejection was final. But it is a substantial part of it, and it is the pattern of the whole reign: the consequences arriving in the shape of the thing he did.

And a word about the silence itself, because it is one of the terrors of Scripture and it is not only Saul's.

The most frightening thing God can do is not say no. It is say nothing. Amos names it as a judgment worse than famine: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11). Micah says of the false prophets that there shall be no answer from God (Mic. 3:7). And the Lord Jesus describes men on the last day who will list their credentials and hear I never knew you (Matt. 7:23).

What must be said alongside that, because it matters enormously to anyone reading in the dark: this is not what is happening to a Christian who feels God has gone quiet. Saul's silence is the end of a forty-year refusal, announced in advance, after a specific and final rejection. The believer in a dry season has a mediator whose blood speaks, and a standing promise never to be left or forsaken. Feeling unheard and being unheard are different things, and Saul is the second.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Seek Out for Me a Woman Who Is a Medium
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Saul said to his servants, "Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her." They know where one is immediately (v. 7). He disguises himself, goes by night, and asks her to bring up whomever he names (v. 8). She refuses: you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the necromancers from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life? (v. 9). So Saul swears — as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing (v. 10). Bring up Samuel for me (v. 11). And when she sees him, the woman cried out with a loud voice... "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul" (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: His servants produce a medium at once, which tells us what the purge was worth. He expelled them as royal policy; nobody in his own household has any difficulty finding one at short notice.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is the chapter in one line. He swears as the LORD lives — taking an oath in God's name to guarantee the safety of a woman doing what God forbade — because God will not talk to him. And verse 12 matters for what follows: she screams. Whatever she expected, this was not it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to his servants, "Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her." And his servants said to him, "Behold, there is a medium at En-dor." So Saul disguised himself and put on other garments and went, he and two men with him. And they came to the woman by night. And he said, "Divine for me by a spirit and bring up for me whomever I shall name to you." The woman said to him, "Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the necromancers from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?" But Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing." Then the woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me." When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul." The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" And the woman said to Saul, "I see a god coming up out of the earth." He said to her, "What is his appearance?" And she said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe." And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and paid homage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul said to his servants, "Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her." And his servants said to him, "Behold, there is a medium at En-dor."'

They answer immediately. They know one.

Four verses ago the writer told us Saul had cleared the mediums out of the land, and here his own staff produce an address without pausing to think. The purge was policy, not conviction. Everyone knew where these people were, and everyone had gone on knowing.

And note the verb Saul uses: inquire. It is the same word used of asking the LORD. He has asked God and heard nothing, so he will ask someone else with the same word.

Endor is also on the far side of the Philistine lines. To get there he has to travel by night around an enemy army, on the eve of a battle, away from his own camp, with his kingdom at stake. That is the measure of what he wants.

'So Saul disguised himself and put on other garments and went, he and two men with him. And they came to the woman by night. And he said, "Divine for me by a spirit and bring up for me whomever I shall name to you."'

The disguise is the detail that gives everything away.

Consider what it means. He puts on other clothes so that a woman practising a craft he made illegal will not know she is talking to the king who made it illegal. He is hiding from his own law, in order to break it, in the dark, wearing somebody else's coat.

Look back at what he was. In chapter 9 he was a head taller than everybody in Israel and hiding among the baggage because he did not want a crown. In chapter 10 the Spirit rushed on him and he prophesied among prophets, and people asked whether Saul was one of them. This is the same man, on a track in the dark, in disguise, going to a witch.

'The woman said to him, "Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the necromancers from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?"'

She is frightened, and she is right to be.

She thinks this is entrapment — a stranger arriving at night asking her to do the one thing that carries a death sentence. She has survived by being careful and this is not careful.

'But Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing."'

There is the sentence that should stop anybody reading.

As the LORD lives.

He takes an oath in the name of the God of Israel, invoking the living God as guarantor, to reassure a woman that she may safely do the thing that God's law calls an abomination and commands Israel to punish with death.

He is not being blasphemous by accident. He knows the law; he enforced it. He is using the name of the God who will not speak to him as collateral in a transaction God forbade.

It is also, in a terrible way, sincere. He does mean to protect her. The oath is honest and the use of it is monstrous, and Saul has never been able to tell the difference between meaning something and obeying.

'Then the woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me."'

Of course it is Samuel.

The man who anointed him, who confronted him at Gilgal, whose robe tore in his hand, who told him the kingdom was gone and then went home and did not see him again until the day he died. The last person who ever brought him a word from God.

He wants Samuel back, and he has been told what Samuel will say, and he wants him anyway.

'When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul."'

She screams.

Hold on to that, because it is the hinge of the whole question this chapter raises. Whatever this woman normally did in her sessions, and whatever she was expecting to happen, what happened terrified her.

Now the question that has occupied serious readers for two thousand years, and it must be put honestly: is this really Samuel?

Godly men have taken it different ways, and both deserve to be heard.

Some, Calvin among them, have held that what appeared was not Samuel at all — that God does not put his prophets at the disposal of a witch's summons, that the dead are at rest and not subject to being fetched, and that what came up was a spirit permitted to impersonate him, or a vision God caused her to see. The strength of this view is its instinct about God's holiness: it will not have the Lord's servant on call to necromancy.

Others — and this is where the weight of the passage seems to fall — hold that it was Samuel, brought up by God's own act and not by the woman's craft at all.

The reasons are in the text. The narrator simply calls him Samuel, repeatedly, without a hint of qualification anywhere in the chapter. The woman's terror suggests she got something she had not arranged and could not control. What is said is true, specific, and entirely in Samuel's own manner — a rebuke, a reference back to his own earlier words, and a prophecy which comes to pass in detail within twenty-four hours. And it is very hard to see God permitting a lying spirit to deliver an accurate final verdict in his own name.

On that reading, God broke into her performance. She began a fraud or a ritual, and the God who had refused to answer Saul through dreams, Urim and prophets answered him after all — not because she compelled anything, but because he had one more thing to say, and it was a sentence. Which would be entirely in character: the silence was judgment, and so was the breaking of it.

Certainty is not available and does not need to be. What both views agree on is what matters, and the chapter's own argument does not depend on the answer: Saul went where he was forbidden to go, got what he asked for, and it destroyed him.

'The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" And the woman said to Saul, "I see a god coming up out of the earth."'

'He said to her, "What is his appearance?" She said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe." And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and paid homage.'

Wrapped in a robe.

That is how Saul knows him, and the robe has a history between these two. Samuel wore it; Saul grabbed at it as the prophet turned to leave Gilgal and it tore in his hand, and Samuel said the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (15:27-28).

The last thing Saul ever saw of Samuel alive was a piece of that robe in his fist. The first thing he sees of him now is the robe again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Tomorrow You and Your Sons Shall Be with Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up? Saul explains: the Philistines are here, God has turned away and answers neither by prophets nor by dreams (v. 15). The answer is merciless. Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy? (v. 16). The kingdom is torn away and given to David; and the reason is named: because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day (vv. 17-18). And then: tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing here is new. Every word of it was said at Gilgal thirteen chapters ago (15:26-28), and Amalek is named again as the cause. The last word Saul ever receives from God is the first word repeated, with a date attached.
verseByVerse.examples: Become your enemy is the most frightening phrase in the book and it should not be softened. And tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me is exact: by the next evening Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua are dead on Gilboa and Saul has fallen on his own sword.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul answered, "I am in great distress, for the Philistines are warring against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams. Therefore I have summoned you to tell me what I shall do." And Samuel said, "Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy? The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me, for the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David. Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day. Moreover, the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The LORD will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?"'

The first words are a reproach, and they are about rest.

Why have you disturbed me? He was somewhere, and it was somewhere he did not wish to be called out of. There is no eagerness here, no gladness at the reunion, and no interest in the occasion. He wants to know why he has been troubled.

'Saul answered, "I am in great distress, for the Philistines are warring against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams. Therefore I have summoned you to tell me what I should do."'

His explanation is entirely accurate and it condemns him as he says it.

God has turned away from me and answers me no more. He knows. He is not confused about his position; he states it in one sentence, correctly, without excuse.

And then: therefore I have summoned you. There is the whole man in one word. God will not answer, therefore I will go round him. Not therefore I have repented, or therefore I am afraid, or even therefore tell me what I must do to be forgiven. Therefore I have found another way to get an answer.

Notice too what he wants. Tell me what I should do. He is after tactics. He is on the eve of a battle he expects to lose and he wants advice, from a man who told him years ago that the problem was never a shortage of advice.

'And Samuel said, "Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy?"'

Read the last three words again, and do not soften them.

Become your enemy.

Not withdrawn from you. Not disappointed in you. Not standing back. The God who anointed him through this same prophet, who gave him the Spirit and a new heart and victory after victory, is now on the other side of the field.

It is a sentence the Bible does not use lightly and does not withdraw when it uses it, and it is addressed to a man who is still king of Israel and still, at some level, wants God's help. He wants the help and he has the enmity, and he cannot see that they are the same relationship viewed from two ends.

'"The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me, for the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David."'

Nothing new. Not one syllable of this is information.

As he spoke by me — Samuel is quoting himself. He said it at Gilgal with the torn robe in his hand: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (15:28). The only thing added in thirteen chapters is the name.

Saul travelled through enemy lines in the dark, broke his own law, and risked his kingdom for an answer he was given years ago and did not accept.

'"Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day."'

Amalek. Thirteen chapters later, it is still Amalek.

The kingdom did not slip away over an accumulation of small things. It was one day at Gilgal when he was given a clear command and kept the best of the sheep and the king alive and told Samuel it was for sacrifice. To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams (15:22).

And there is one more turn of that knife which the chapter does not spell out and the reader can hardly miss. He was told to destroy the Amalekites and did not; and at that very hour, while Saul is on his knees in a hut at Endor, Amalekites are burning Ziklag to the ground and carrying off the families of the man who will replace him. The nation Saul spared is still in the story, and it is not finished.

'"Moreover, the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The LORD will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines."'

Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me.

He came for a battle plan and he is given a date.

The word is exact and it is fulfilled in the next chapter but two. Tomorrow: the Philistines overtake Saul and his sons on Mount Gilboa, and Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchishua are killed, and Saul falls on his own sword (31:1-6). You and your sons. All of it happens.

Which means Jonathan is included in the sentence.

Jonathan, who defended David to his father's face and was nearly speared for it. Who took off his own robe and gave it away. Who walked into a wilderness to strengthen a hunted man's hand in God. Who said you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you and went home to his father's house.

He dies in his father's catastrophe. He was the best man in the book and he is killed on his father's mountain in his father's lost battle, and the text offers no comfort about it at all.

This is one of the places where Scripture simply declines to tidy the world up. The righteous are caught in the wreckage that other people's sin makes; Job knew it, the psalms know it, and it is not explained here. What is said elsewhere, and is the only thing that answers it, is that the God who let Jonathan die on Gilboa took a death of his own on another hill, and that the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26). Jonathan is not lost. But nothing in this chapter says so, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest to the text.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — She Killed the Fattened Calf
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear, having eaten nothing all day and all night (v. 20). The woman comes to him. Behold, your servant has obeyed you. I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to what you have said to me. Now therefore, you also obey your servant (vv. 21-22). He refuses, and his servants and the woman together urge him until he gets up off the ground and sits on the bed (v. 23). She kills the fattened calf she has, bakes unleavened bread, sets it before them — and they eat, and go out into the night (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The last meal Saul eats is cooked for him in the dark by a woman he had outlawed on pain of death, out of her own last animal, after he has been told he dies tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples: And she is the only person in the chapter who shows him any kindness. She is doing something forbidden, and the narrator does not pretend otherwise — and he also records, without comment, that she took her own life in her hands, argued him up off the floor, and fed him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night. And the woman came to Saul, and when she saw that he was terrified, she said to him, "Behold, your servant has obeyed you. I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to what you have said to me. Now therefore, you also obey your servant. Let me set a morsel of bread before you; and eat, that you may have strength when you go on your way." He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to their words. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed. Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she quickly killed it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread of it, and she put it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night.'

He goes down like a felled tree.

The narrator gives both causes and does not rank them: terror at what he has heard, and the plain fact that a frightened man has not eaten for twenty-four hours. The tallest man in Israel is lying full length on the floor of a hut at Endor.

'And the woman came to Saul, and when she saw that he was terrified, she said to him, "Behold, your servant has obeyed you. I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to what you have said to me."'

She comes to him, which nobody else in this chapter does.

And she uses the word. Your servant has obeyed you. It is the vocabulary of this whole book — obeying a voice, listening, doing what you were told — and it is put in the mouth of a woman breaking the law of God, speaking to a king who was destroyed for not obeying. The writer does not draw attention to it and it sits there all the same.

I have taken my life in my hand is simply true. She did. She had every reason to think this was a trap and she did it anyway.

'"Now therefore, you also obey your servant. Let me set a morsel of bread before you; and eat, that you may have strength when you go on your way."'

'He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to their words. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed.'

They have to argue him up off the floor.

Two soldiers and a witch, standing over a collapsed king in the dark, persuading him to sit on a bed and take some food. And the narrator notes, with what may be the driest line in the chapter, that he listened to their words — the one voice Saul obeys in this chapter belongs to a medium at Endor.

'Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she quickly killed it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread of it, and she put it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.'

She kills the calf.

A fattened calf in a poor house is not dinner; it is the household's savings, the animal you keep for a wedding or a feast. She kills it for a man who has just been told he will be dead by tomorrow evening, and bakes bread with her own hands, and sets a table in the middle of the night.

It is the last meal Saul eats. It is cooked for him by a woman he had outlawed on pain of death, in a village behind enemy lines, out of the best thing she owned.

Nothing in this excuses what she did, and the chapter does not offer it as a defence. The law against her trade was God's law and Saul was right to enforce it, and she was practising it that night for money or fear or both.

She is the only person in this chapter who shows Saul the slightest kindness. Not his servants until she prompted them. Not Samuel. Not God. A woman he had criminalised got up, took a risk she had already been paid nothing for, and fed him.

The writer records both things and reconciles neither, which is how he handles most people. He told us Ahimelech gave holy bread to a liar and the Lord Jesus later praised him for it. He told us David killed villages to protect a story. He is not in the business of sorting characters into piles.

'Then they rose and went away that night.'

Out he goes into the dark, back around the Philistine lines, to Gilboa.

He knows what is coming. He has been given the day and the outcome and the names, and he goes back and takes his place at the head of the army anyway, and dies there with his sons.

There is something in that last walk it would be wrong not to say. He does not run. He could have. He is in disguise, behind the lines, with two men and a night's start, and the throne is gone regardless. He turns round and goes back to his army to fight a battle he has been told he will lose.

It is courage, and it is the courage of a man who has nothing left, and it saves nothing and no one. Saul was never short of the raw material of a great king. He was short of one thing from the day at Gilgal onward, and that is the whole tragedy: he could face an army he knew would kill him, and he could not face God and say he had been wrong.

29.title: David Sent Away from the Battle
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines had gathered all their forces at Aphek. And the Israelites were encamped by the spring that is in Jezreel.<sup>2</sup>As the lords of the Philistines were passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were passing on in the rear with Achish,<sup>3</sup>the commanders of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me now for days and years, and since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him to this day."<sup>4</sup>But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him. And the commanders of the Philistines said to him, "Send the man back, that he may return to the place to which you have assigned him. He shall not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here?<sup>5</sup>Is not this David, of whom they sing to one another in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"<sup>6</sup>Then Achish called David and said to him, "As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you.<sup>7</sup>So go back now; and go peaceably, that you may not displease the lords of the Philistines."<sup>8</sup>And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"<sup>9</sup>And Achish answered David and said, "I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up with us to the battle.'<sup>10</sup>Now then rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you, and start early in the morning, and depart as soon as you have light."<sup>11</sup>So David set out with his men early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
29.overview:
The armies muster, and the man God anointed to be king of Israel is marching at the back of the Philistine column with the king of Gath, toward the battle in which Saul and Jonathan will die. Every part of the position is his own doing: he went to Philistia because he told himself Saul would kill him, without asking God, and the arrangement that kept six hundred families fed has now presented its bill. He cannot refuse to march and cannot march and fight.

What gets him out is not David. The Philistine commanders see the Hebrews in the line and refuse to have them — and their reasoning is exactly right: a man with that record would be an appalling risk, and everything they suspect about his loyalties is true. How could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here? They have thought it through better than Achish, and better than David appears to have. And then they quote the song — the same song that made Saul reach for a spear, and that was thrown at David in this very city on the day he saved his life by feigning madness. It ruined him twice and now it rescues him.

Achish, who is the most decent man in the chapter and wrong about everything, swears by the God of Israel that David has been honest and calls him blameless as an angel of God. David protests — and his protest can be read two ways, and the writer does not settle it. Then the two parties separate on the road, and God has extracted his anointed from a trap he built himself, using a committee of enemy generals who did not care whether he lived.
29.theology:
The rescue comes from men with no interest in rescuing him (v. 4). The Philistine commanders are protecting a flank, not saving anybody, and they are professionally correct about the risk. God uses accurate suspicion from irritated enemies to get his anointed out of the battle line.

The song, three times (v. 5). Sung by the women after Goliath, it made Saul eye him and throw a spear (18:7-9). Quoted by the courtiers of Gath, it drove him to drool in a gateway to stay alive (21:11-13). Quoted by the commanders of Gath, it sends him home before he has to choose between his nation and his cover. Nothing about the fact changed; his circumstances changed, and God used the same fact both ways.

Blameless as an angel of God (vv. 6, 9). A Philistine king swears by the covenant name to certify the honesty of a man who has deceived him for sixteen months. The narrator sets it down and does not tell us what to feel. Achish is generous, loyal, and completely wrong, and he deserved better than he got.

Verse 8 is left open, and should be. The enemies of my lord the king is either a lie sustained to the last inch, or the exact truth in a sense only David can hear — his lord being the LORD, whose enemies are the men standing round him. Most readers take the protest as theatre required by the part, and that may well be right. It may also be that a man sixteen months into a deception can no longer find its edge. The writer does not say, and it is not honest to decide for him. It is the last thing David says in Philistia, and it is ambiguous — a fitting close to a chapter of his life that began with him settling matters privately in his own heart.

What Romans 8:28 does and does not promise. David built this trap himself; not one part of it was done to him. God got him out using a committee of enemy generals and a decade-old song. But all things work together for good does not mean all things are good, or that the foolish decision was secretly wise. Chapter 27 was a failure and the bill is still unpaid — he comes home in the next chapter to a burnt town and his wives in Amalekite hands. The promise is that God is not stopped by his people's stupidity, and that he works with material which has no intention of serving him.
29.examples:
Then: A committee of Philistine generals, annoyed with their own king and quoting an Israelite folk song about a man killing ten thousands, refused to let David into the battle line — and so kept the future king of Israel out of the fight in which his predecessor and his best friend were killed.

Now: For anyone who has walked themselves into a corner and cannot see the way out: the exit here did not come from David, and it did not look like rescue while it was happening. It looked like being dismissed, in front of everybody, from a job he had argued to keep. Deliverance frequently arrives disguised as a closed door, administered by people who are not thinking about you at all. That is not a reason to make the chapter-27 decision; the cost of that is still coming. It is a reason not to conclude that a mess of your own making has put you beyond God's reach.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The armies muster at Aphek and Jezreel, and David and his men march in the rear with Achish (vv. 1-2). The Philistine commanders see them: what are these Hebrews doing here? (v. 3). Achish vouches for him — a deserter from Saul who has given him no cause for complaint in over a year. The commanders are angry and will not have it: send him back, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here? (v. 4). And then they sing: is this not David, of whom they sing to one another in dances, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands"? (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Their military judgment is exactly right. A man with David's record and following would have been an appalling risk in that line, and everything they suspect about his loyalties is true. God rescues his anointed here by means of accurate suspicion from men who are trying to protect their own flank.
verseByVerse.examples: That song has now done three things. It made Saul watch David with a spear in his hand (18:7-9). It was quoted back at him by the courtiers of Gath on the day he saved his life by feigning madness (21:11). And now it gets him out of the worst position of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines had gathered all their forces at Aphek. And the Israelites were encamped by the spring that is in Jezreel. As the lords of the Philistines were passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were passing on in the rear with Achish, the commanders of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me now for days and years, and since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him to this day." But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him. And the commanders of the Philistines said to him, "Send the man back, that he may return to the place to which you have assigned him. He shall not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here? Is not this David, of whom they sing to one another in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the Philistines had gathered all their forces at Aphek. And the Israelites were encamped by the spring that is in Jezreel.'

'As the lords of the Philistines were passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were passing on in the rear with Achish,'

There is the picture, and it is the worst position David has ever been in.

The Philistine army is marching to the battle in which Saul and Jonathan will die, and the man God anointed to be king of Israel is walking at the back of the column with the king of Gath.

Everything about it is his own doing. He went to Philistia because he told himself in chapter 27 that Saul would kill him, without asking God, and the arrangement that kept six hundred families fed has now presented its bill.
