He cannot refuse to march. He cannot march and fight. And he appears to have no plan for what happens when the lines close.

Watch what gets him out, because he does not do it himself.

'the commanders of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me now for days and years, and since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him to this day."'

Achish defends him warmly, and every word of the defence is built on a lie.

Since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him. That is sixteen months of raids David reported as attacks on his own tribe, and villages emptied of every living person so that nobody could come to Gath and correct the story (27:8-12). The trust is total and it is manufactured.

'But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him. And the commanders of the Philistines said to him, "Send the man back, that he may return to the place to which you have assigned him. He shall not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us."'

The commanders are not fooled, and they are right.

Their reasoning is sound soldiering. You do not put a foreign contingent with divided loyalties in your own line, and this particular foreigner is the most famous Israelite soldier alive. If he turns in the middle of an engagement your formation collapses from the inside.

'"For how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here?"'

That is precisely the question, put by people who have no interest in David at all.

How does a man in his position buy his way back into Israel? By turning in the battle and arriving home with Philistine heads. They have thought it through better than Achish, and better than David appears to have.

'"Is this not David, of whom they sing to one another in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"'

That song again.

Follow what it has done. The women sang it in the streets when he came home from killing Goliath, and from that day Saul eyed David and threw a spear at him (18:7-9). The courtiers of Achish quoted it at him the first time he came to Gath, alone and terrified, and he saved his life by drooling into his beard (21:11-13). It has followed him for a decade and cost him everything he had.

Here it is a third time, in the mouths of enemy commanders, and it is the thing that gets him out.

The reputation that made him a fugitive is the reputation that will not let a Philistine army have him in its ranks. Nothing about the song changed. His circumstances changed, and God used the same fact both ways.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — As the LORD Lives, You Have Been Honest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Achish tells him: as the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me... nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you (vv. 6-7). David protests — what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king? (v. 8). Achish is unmovable and gracious about it: I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God, but the commanders have spoken (v. 9). So David rises early and goes back to the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines go up to Jezreel (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: A Philistine king swears by the God of Israel, and calls a man who has lied to him for sixteen months blameless as an angel. The deception in chapter 27 has been that complete, and the narrator lets the irony stand without a word.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is the uncomfortable one. The enemies of my lord the king can mean Achish's enemies, which would make it a lie carried to the last inch — or it can mean the LORD's, which would make it true in a sense only David knows. The writer does not tell us which, and it is not honest to decide for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Achish called David and said to him, "As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you. So go back now; and go peaceably, that you may not displease the lords of the Philistines." And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?" And Achish answered David and said, "I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up with us to the battle.' Now then rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you, and start early in the morning, and depart as soon as you have light." So David set out with his men early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Achish called David and said to him, "As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day."'

A Philistine king swears by the God of Israel.

As the LORD lives. He uses the covenant name, presumably as a courtesy to the Israelite he is addressing, and he uses it to certify that David has been honest with him.

David has not been honest with him about anything for sixteen months.

The narrator sets it down and moves on. He does not tell us what to feel about it. It is simply there: the God whose name is being sworn by knows exactly what has been going on, and the man being called honest is standing in front of him.

'"Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you. So go back now; and go peaceably, that you may not displease the lords of the Philistines."'

'And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"'

Here is the hardest verse in the chapter, and the honest thing is to leave it open.

He argues to be allowed to stay. He is being handed the way out of an impossible position and he pushes back on it, and he pushes back using the words the enemies of my lord the king.

Which lord? Which king?

Read it one way and it is a lie sustained to the last possible inch: he means Achish, he wants to march, and he is protesting his loyalty to a Philistine because that is the character he has been playing for a year and a third.

Read it the other and it is exactly true in a sense only he can hear: his lord is the LORD, his king is God, and the enemies of that king are the men standing round him — so that every syllable is honest and Achish hears the opposite.

The writer does not tell us which, and it is not right to settle it for him. It may well be that the protest is theatre, required by the part, and that David is enormously relieved — that is the reading most people take, and it may be correct. It may also be that he had genuinely lost his bearings by this point; a man who has been lying for sixteen months is not always able to find the edge of it any more.

What can be said is this: it is the last thing he says in Philistia, and it is ambiguous, and that is a fitting end to the chapter of his life that began with him deciding matters privately in his own heart.

'And Achish answered David and said, "I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up with us to the battle.'"'

Blameless as an angel of God.

It is the highest thing a man can say about another man, and it is said by a deceived king about somebody who has been systematically deceiving him, in the language of the deceived man's own religion.

Achish is the most consistently decent character in these chapters and he is completely wrong about everything. He has been generous, given David a town, defended him to his own officers, sworn by his guest's God, and gone on believing him against professional advice. He deserved better.

'"So rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you, and start early in the morning, and depart as soon as you have light."'

'So David set out with his men early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.'

The two parties separate on the road, and the chapter ends.

Now stand back and look at what has just happened, because it is the point of having this chapter at all.

David built this trap himself. Not one part of it was done to him. He decided in his own heart without asking God, went to live in enemy country for sixteen months, secured his position by deception, and ended up marching in the enemy's rear guard toward the battle where his own king and his closest friend would die. There was no honourable way out that he could see, and by the evidence of verse 8 he was not looking very hard.

God got him out.

Look at the instruments. A committee of Philistine generals, protecting their own flank, irritated with their king, who did not care in the slightest what happened to David and would cheerfully have killed him — and an old song sung by Israelite women a decade earlier that had already ruined his life twice.

Not one of these things was trying to help him.

That is the grammar of Romans 8:28, and its terms should be stated exactly. For those who love God all things work together for good — not that all things are good, and not that the foolish decision was secretly wise. Chapter 27 was a failure and the bill for it is still to be paid; he comes home in the next chapter to a burnt town and his wives in Amalekite hands. The promise is that God is not stopped by his people's stupidity, and that he uses material which has no intention of serving him.

Anyone who has walked themselves into a corner and cannot see the exit should read this chapter slowly. The exit did not come from David and it did not look like rescue while it was happening. It looked like being sacked.

30.title: David Strengthened Himself in the LORD His God
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid against the Negeb and against Ziklag. They had overcome Ziklag and burned it with fire<sup>2</sup>and taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They killed no one, but carried them off and went their way.<sup>3</sup>And when David and his men came to the city, they found it burned with fire, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.<sup>4</sup>Then David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep.<sup>5</sup>David's two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.<sup>6</sup>And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.<sup>7</sup>And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.<sup>8</sup>And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?" He answered him, "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue."<sup>9</sup>So David set out, and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed.<sup>10</sup>But David pursued, he and four hundred men. Two hundred stayed behind, who were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor.<sup>11</sup>They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. And they gave him bread and he ate. They gave him water to drink,<sup>12</sup>and they gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. And when he had eaten, his spirit revived, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights.<sup>13</sup>And David said to him, "To whom do you belong? And where are you from?" He said, "I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite, and my master left me behind because I fell sick three days ago.<sup>14</sup>We had made a raid against the Negeb of the Cherethites and against that which belongs to Judah and against the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire."<sup>15</sup>And David said to him, "Will you take me down to this band?" And he said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will take you down to this band."<sup>16</sup>And when he had taken him down, behold, they were spread abroad over all the land, eating and drinking and dancing, because of all the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.<sup>17</sup>And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day, and not a man of them escaped, except four hundred young men, who mounted camels and fled.<sup>18</sup>David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.<sup>19</sup>Nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken. David brought back all.<sup>20</sup>David also captured all the flocks and herds, and the people drove the livestock before him, and said, "This is David's spoil."<sup>21</sup>Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow David, and who had been left at the brook Besor. And they went out to meet David and to meet the people who were with him. And when David came near to the people he greeted them.<sup>22</sup>Then all the wicked and worthless fellows among the men who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the spoil that we have recovered, except that each man may lead away his wife and children, and depart."<sup>23</sup>But David said, "You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He has preserved us and given into our hand the band that came against us.<sup>24</sup>Who would listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike."<sup>25</sup>And he made it a statute and a rule for Israel from that day forward to this day.<sup>26</sup>When David came to Ziklag, he sent part of the spoil to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, "Here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD."<sup>27</sup>It was for those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negeb, in Jattir,<sup>28</sup>in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa,<sup>29</sup>in Racal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, in the cities of the Kenites,<sup>30</sup>in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, in Athach,<sup>31</sup>in Hebron, for all the places where David and his men had roamed.
30.overview:
David comes home on the third day to a burnt town and no families. The Amalekites did it — the nation Saul was commanded to destroy and spared, whose survival cost him the kingdom, and who were burning Ziklag at the hour Saul lay on the floor at Endor hearing their name again. Nobody was killed, because live captives are worth money. Six hundred soldiers stand in the ashes and weep until they physically cannot, and then they start picking up stones — and they are not being irrational. He chose Ziklag. He marched north with the Philistines and took every fighting man with him.

But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God. The verb is Jonathan's: at Horesh, Jonathan came and strengthened his hand in God. Here there is nobody — Samuel buried, Jonathan a day from Gilboa, Abigail in enemy hands, the six hundred turned. So he does for himself what his friend once did for him. Not a mood: a location. He takes hold of something outside the situation.

Then bring me the ephod — the first recorded enquiry since Keilah, sixteen months of deciding privately finally broken by a burnt town. He is told to pursue, and given more than he asked: you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue. Two hundred cannot cross the brook. In a field they find a dying Egyptian slave dumped by his Amalekite master, feed him before asking him anything, and he turns out to be the only man alive who knows where the raiders went.

David brought back all. Then the quarrel over the spoil, which David settles in one sentence — not what we recovered but what the LORD has given us — and the equal share for the men at the baggage becomes a statute for Israel. He sends the rest to thirteen towns of Judah, ending with Hebron. He thinks he is being generous. He is being made king.
30.theology:
He strengthened himself in the LORD his God (v. 6). The word is the one used of Jonathan at 23:16, and the difference is everything: there somebody came and put David's grip back on what he already knew, and here there is nobody at all. The verse does not say his circumstances improved, that he felt better, or that he pulled himself together — it names a place he went. What that looks like is written across his own psalms: why are you cast down, O my soul?... hope in God (Ps. 42:5), a man asking his own soul a question and answering it out loud with what he knows about God whether he feels it or not. It is not positive thinking, which has nothing outside itself to hold. Every believer will need this, because Ziklag comes and the friend who would normally do it is not there.

And he was not always able to do it. Three chapters earlier the same man said in his heart now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul and talked himself out of the land. Same practice, opposite direction. Everything turns on what he is telling himself and whom he is telling it about.

Bring me the ephod (v. 7). The last enquiry was Keilah. Nothing before Philistia, nothing at Gath, nothing on the march to Aphek — and Abiathar and the ephod were in the camp the whole time. It took a burnt town and a mutiny to get the question asked. And the answer gives more than was asked for: he wanted to know if he would overtake them, and was told he would surely rescue.

The man his master threw away (vv. 11-15). Four hundred men in desperate haste, with their own children in enemy hands, stop for a stranger dying in a field — and feed him before they question him. Nobody knows yet that he is useful. God's you shall surely overtake arrives in the form of a discarded slave, and his two conditions say what his life had been: do not kill me, and do not give me back to my master. He would rather face four hundred armed men than be returned.

Still not finished (v. 17). Four hundred escape on camels. Saul was told to destroy Amalek and did not; centuries later Haman the Agagite — of the line of the king Saul spared — tries to have every Jew in the Persian empire killed (Esth. 3:1-6). Sin not dealt with when it is commanded does not stay where it was left.

What the LORD has given us (v. 23). The objectors say the spoil that we have recovered; David says what the LORD has given us, and the argument is over. If the four hundred won it they may ration it; if God gave it, it is not theirs to allocate. And the facts are with him: they were half dead when they started, they found the camp because a slave happened to be lying where they passed, and they had been told in advance they would succeed. Nobody earned anything. He also calls them my brothers, days after they discussed stoning him.

The statute, and the vineyard (vv. 24-25). Equal shares for the men at the front and the men at the stores, made permanent law. The two hundred were not skiving; they were finished, and the baggage had to be guarded by somebody. The same complaint appears in a vineyard where men hired at five o'clock are paid a full day and the all-day workers object, and the answer is the same: do you begrudge my generosity? (Matt. 20:1-16). There will be Christians in glory who came in at the eleventh hour and Christians who carried the work for fifty years, and they will be given the same Christ.

Made king while sharing out spoil (vv. 26-31). Two of the towns on the list, the Jerahmeelites and the Kenites, are the very people he told Achish he had been raiding (27:10) — his cover story now receives a share of the plunder. And the list ends at Hebron, where the men of Judah will shortly anoint him king (2 Sam. 2:1-4). Thirteen towns will have had a gift from David in their hands for a week when the news from Gilboa arrives.
30.examples:
Then: A commander stood in the ashes of his own town with his wives taken, his men discussing whether to stone him, and every human support gone — and the next thing recorded about him is not what he did but where he went: he strengthened himself in the LORD his God. Then he asked God a question for the first time in sixteen months.

Now: Verse 6 is the practical gift of the whole book. There will be a day when the people who normally hold you up are unavailable, unaware, or part of the problem, and the only thing left in the room is what you actually know about God. That day is not the time to start learning it. What David did is repeatable and it is unglamorous: he spoke to himself about God, out loud, in the ruins, ahead of his feelings — and then he asked God what to do, and did it. And verse 24 for the other half: the people who could not cross the brook were not lazy, they were spent, and they got the same share. That is a rule worth having in any church, in any family, and in your own head on the days you are one of the two hundred.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — David Strengthened Himself in the LORD His God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David comes home to Ziklag on the third day and finds it burned to the ground, the women and children carried off, nobody killed (vv. 1-3). He and his men wept until they had no more strength to weep — and his own two wives are among the captives (vv. 4-5). Then: And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything has gone at once: the town, the families, and the loyalty of the men. And he is genuinely responsible for the first two — the decision to live at Ziklag was his, and so was marching off with the Philistines and leaving it undefended.
verseByVerse.examples: The verb is Jonathan's. At Horesh, Jonathan... strengthened his hand in God (23:16) — somebody else took hold of David's grip and put it back. Here there is nobody: Jonathan is a day from death, Samuel is buried, and the six hundred are collecting stones. So he does for himself what his friend once did for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid against the Negeb and against Ziklag. They had overcome Ziklag and burned it with fire and taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They killed no one, but carried them off and went their way. And when David and his men came to the city, they found it burned with fire, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive. Then David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep. David's two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid against the Negeb and against Ziklag. They had overcome Ziklag and burned it with fire.'

The Amalekites.

Of all the peoples in the region, it is that one. These are the nation Saul was commanded to destroy and did not, keeping the best of the flock and the king alive and losing his throne for it (15:1-23). Two chapters ago Samuel named them as the reason the kingdom was torn away, and while Saul was on the floor at Endor hearing it, they were putting a torch to Ziklag.

And David has been raiding them himself from this very town (27:8). This is a reprisal.

The unfinished business of chapter 15 does not stay unfinished. It comes back and takes David's own family.

'and taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They killed no one, but carried them off and went their way.'

Nobody is dead. That is the one mercy in the verse, and it is not mercy — live captives are worth money and dead ones are not.

'And when David and his men came to the city, they found it burned with fire, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.'

'Then David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep.'

Six hundred soldiers standing in a burnt town crying until they physically cannot.

The phrase is not decorative. It means what it says: they wept to the point of exhaustion, until the body would not do it any more. These are hard men, most of them the distressed and indebted and bitter who gathered at Adullam, and they are on the ground in the ashes of their houses.

'David's two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.'

Abigail is among them. The woman who came down the mountain track with two hundred loaves and stopped him committing a massacre is now in an Amalekite column somewhere south with a rope on her.

'And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters.'

Now everything is gone.

Not just the town and the families. His men — the six hundred who followed him out of caves and wildernesses for years, who went where he said and asked nothing — are picking up stones.

And they are not being irrational. Somebody let this happen and it was him. He chose Ziklag. He chose to march north with Achish and take every fighting man with him, leaving a town of women and children on the southern frontier with no garrison at all, in country he had spent sixteen months raiding. The Amalekites did not stumble on Ziklag; they came for it, and they came while he was away, and he is the reason it was empty.

Every one of the fathers standing in that ruin has worked this out.

So: the consequence of his own decision, arriving all at once, with no one to blame and nobody left to turn to. Samuel is dead. Jonathan is a day's march from his own death on Gilboa. Abigail is in the hands of the enemy. And the men are bitter in soul.

'But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.'

There is the verse, and it is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament.

Take the word first, because it has a history in this book. At Horesh, when Saul had come out to hunt him and David could see it, Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God (23:16). Somebody came, took hold of a grip that was going slack, and put it back where it belonged.

Here there is nobody. There is no Jonathan on the road, no Samuel to send for, no Abigail to argue with him, no six hundred men at his back — the six hundred are the threat. He is completely alone in the middle of a crowd that wants him dead.

So he does for himself what his friend once did for him.

And notice what the sentence does not say. It does not say his circumstances improved, or that he felt better, or that he received a vision, or that he pulled himself together. It says he strengthened himself in the LORD his God — which is a location, not a mood. He went and took hold of something outside the situation.

What that looks like in practice is written all over the psalms, because this is the man who wrote them. Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God (Ps. 42:5). That is a man talking to himself — asking his own soul a question and then answering it with what he knows about God, out loud, whether he feels it or not.

It is not positive thinking, which has nothing outside itself to hold. It is the deliberate act of taking what you already know to be true about God and applying it, by force if necessary, to the place you are standing in.

Every believer needs this and every believer will need it, because there comes a day when the people who would normally do it for you are not there. Ziklag arrives. The friend is unavailable, the church is far away, and the crowd has turned. The question that day is whether you know enough about God to say it to yourself in the ashes.

He was not always able to do it. Three chapters ago he said in his heart now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul, and talked himself out of the land. The same man, the same practice of speaking to himself — and everything turns on what he is telling himself, and whom he is telling it about.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." He asks two questions and gets an answer with a guarantee in it: pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue (vv. 7-8). Six hundred set out; two hundred are too exhausted to cross the brook Besor and stay with the baggage (vv. 9-10). In a field they find an Egyptian, half dead, who has had nothing for three days and nights — his master abandoned him when he fell sick. They feed him first (vv. 11-13). He guides them to the raiders on one condition: swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first recorded enquiry since Keilah. He asked God nothing before going to Philistia, nothing at Gath, nothing on the march to Aphek — sixteen months of deciding in his own heart. The first question he asks is asked standing in ashes.
verseByVerse.examples: And the whole rescue turns on a man somebody threw away. An Amalekite raider dumped a sick slave in a field to die; David gave him bread, figs and water before asking him a single question, and that man is the only person alive who knows where the raiders went.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought the ephod to David. And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?" He answered him, "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue." So David set out, and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed. But David pursued, he and four hundred men. Two hundred stayed behind, who were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor. They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. And they gave him bread and he ate. They gave him water to drink, and they gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. And when he had eaten, his spirit revived, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights. And David said to him, "To whom do you belong? And where are you from?" He said, "I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite, and my master left me behind because I fell sick three days ago. We had made a raid against the Negeb of the Cherethites and against that which belongs to Judah and against the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire." And David said to him, "Will you take me down to this band?" And he said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will take you down to this band."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.'

Four words, and they are the sound of a man coming home.

Bring me the ephod. Count how long it has been. The last recorded enquiry was at Keilah in chapter 23, where he asked four times about one operation and was answered four times. Since then: chapter 27, where he decided to leave Israel in his heart and asked nothing. Sixteen months in Philistia and no question put to God once. The march to Aphek. The argument with Achish.

Abiathar and the ephod have been in the camp the whole time.

The first thing David does after strengthening himself in the LORD is to ask the LORD something, and it takes a burnt town and a mutiny to get him there.

'And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?" He answered him, "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue."'

Two questions, and the answer contains more than was asked for.

He asked whether to go and whether he would catch them. He is told to go, that he will surely overtake, and — which he did not ask — that he will surely rescue. Not go and see. Not it may be that. A guarantee, twice, in the emphatic form.

That word is what the next twenty verses run on, and it is what makes the difference between six hundred exhausted men marching south and six hundred exhausted men marching south with something.

'So David set out, and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed. But David pursued, he and four hundred men. Two hundred stayed behind, who were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor.'

A third of the force cannot go on.

They have marched a long way north with the Philistines, been dismissed, marched three days back again, found their homes burnt, wept themselves to a standstill, and are now expected to chase mounted raiders across the Negeb. Two hundred of them reach a stream and cannot get over it.

Remember them, because there is going to be an argument about them.

'They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. And they gave him bread and he ate. They gave him water to drink, and they gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. And when he had eaten, his spirit revived, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights.'

Read the order of operations. They feed him, and then they ask him questions.

Four hundred men in a desperate hurry, chasing an enemy with a three-day start and their own children in his hands, stop for a half-dead stranger lying in a field. They give him bread and water, and then figs and raisins, and they wait while he comes round.

Nobody in that party knows yet that he is useful. They do not stop because it is efficient. They stop because he is dying in a field.

'And David said to him, "To whom do you belong? And where are you from?" He said, "I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite, and my master left me behind because I fell sick three days ago."'

An Egyptian slave, sick, dumped in open country by his owner three days ago and left to die.

That sentence is the whole character of the Amalekites in one line. They took the women and children of Ziklag alive because captives are worth money, and they threw away a slave who had stopped being worth anything, and the two decisions are the same decision.

'"We had made a raid against the Negeb of the Cherethites and against that which belongs to Judah and against the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire."'

He knows exactly where they went, because he was with them until three days ago.

The only man alive who can find the raiders is a slave his master threw away, kept alive by soldiers who fed him before they knew he could help them.

God's answer — you shall surely overtake — comes in the form of a discarded man in a field. There is nothing in the promise about how it would be done, and this is how.

'And David said to him, "Will you take me down to this band?" And he said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will take you down to this band."'

His two conditions tell you what his life has been.

Do not kill me — which is what he expects from armed men. And do not give me back to my master — which he fears more, and he has just been left in a field to die by that master, and he would still rather face the four hundred than be returned.

David swears it. And the last we hear of this man is that he guided them to the camp; the writer does not tell us what became of him, which is a pity, because he is one of the more moving people in the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — So Shall His Share Be Who Stays by the Baggage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They find the Amalekites eating and drinking and dancing, because of all the great spoil they had taken, and David strikes them from twilight to the evening of the next day — only four hundred young men escape on camels (vv. 16-17). David recovered all... nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken. David brought back all (vv. 18-19). Then the quarrel: wicked and worthless fellows among the four hundred say the two hundred who stayed shall have nothing but their own wives and children (v. 22). David refuses — you shall not do so, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us... as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike (vv. 23-24). And it becomes law: a statute and a rule for Israel from that day forward to this day (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is met exactly. You shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue, and the writer labours the completeness of it — nothing missing, small or great, and David brought back all. God's word, acted on, does precisely what it said.
verseByVerse.examples: The narrative itself calls the objectors wicked and worthless, and David's answer moves the ground under their feet: it is not our spoil to allocate, it is what the LORD has given us. That settles it, and it becomes a permanent statute. It is also the logic of the vineyard, where the men hired at the eleventh hour are paid a full day (Matt. 20:1-16).

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken him down, behold, they were spread abroad over all the land, eating and drinking and dancing, because of all the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah. And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day, and not a man of them escaped, except four hundred young men, who mounted camels and fled. David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives. Nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken. David brought back all. David also captured all the flocks and herds, and the people drove the livestock before him, and said, "This is David's spoil." Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow David, and who had been left at the brook Besor. And they went out to meet David and to meet the people who were with him. And when David came near to the people he greeted them. Then all the wicked and worthless fellows among the men who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the spoil that we have recovered, except that each man may lead away his wife and children, and depart." But David said, "You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He has preserved us and given into our hand the band that came against us. Who would listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike." And he made it a statute and a rule for Israel from that day forward to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when he had taken him down, behold, they were spread abroad over all the land, eating and drinking and dancing, because of all the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.'

They are having a party.

Spread out over the ground, no watch set, eating and drinking and dancing, with the women and children of Ziklag sitting somewhere in the middle of it. They think there is nobody left to come after them.

'And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day, and not a man of them escaped, except four hundred young men, who mounted camels and fled.'

Nearly a full day of fighting.

Four hundred exhausted men who could not persuade two hundred of their comrades to cross a brook fight from dusk to the following evening, and hold.

Note also the four hundred who get away on camels, because it matters. This is still not finished. Saul was told to destroy Amalek and did not; David destroys most of what he can reach and four hundred ride off into the desert. Centuries later a man called Haman the Agagite — of the line of Agag, the Amalekite king Saul spared — will try to have every Jew in the Persian empire killed (Esth. 3:1-6). Sin that is not dealt with when it is commanded does not stay where it was left.

'David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives. Nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken. David brought back all.'

The writer will not let this go by quickly, and he is not padding.

Nothing was missing. Small or great. Sons or daughters. He lists the categories and then says it again in three words: David brought back all.

Because he is measuring it against something. God said you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue, and the account is being reconciled against that sentence line by line. The promise said surely twice; the outcome is all, and nothing missing.

Every family in Ziklag got back every person they had lost. It is the only unmixed good news in the last ten chapters of this book.

'Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow David... And David came near to the people and greeted them.'

He greets them. That is the first thing he does, and it settles the argument before it starts.

'Then all the wicked and worthless fellows among the men who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the spoil that we have recovered, except that each man may lead away his wife and children, and depart."'

The narrator does not wait for us to form an opinion. He tells us who is talking: wicked and worthless fellows, and the phrase is the one used of Eli's sons and of Nabal.

And listen to the shape of the proposal, because it is more calculated than simple greed. They are not saying the two hundred get nothing; they are saying the two hundred may have their own wives and children back, and nothing else. It has the form of fairness. You did not fight, so you get no plunder — but we are not monsters, take your family and go.

It is the reasoning of men who have decided that what they hold, they earned.

'But David said, "You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He has preserved us and given into our hand the band that came against us."'

With one sentence he takes the ground out from under them.

They said the spoil that we have recovered. He says what the LORD has given us. That is the entire argument and there is nothing to add to it. If the four hundred won this, they may distribute it as they please. If God gave it, it is not theirs to ration.

He has the facts on his side. Four hundred men did not out-fight an army by being strong; they were half dead when they started. They found the camp because a discarded slave was lying in a field where they happened to pass, and they were told in advance that they would surely rescue. Nobody in that company earned anything.

Note also my brothers, said to men who were talking about stoning him a few days ago.

'"Who would listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike."'

There is the rule, and it repays being kept word for word.

The men at the front and the men at the stores get the same. Not a token for the stragglers and the bulk for the fighters — the same share, because the two hundred were not skiving. They were finished. They had marched to Aphek and back and buried nothing but ashes and could not cross a stream, and they stayed and guarded the baggage, which had to be guarded by somebody.

'And he made it a statute and a rule for Israel from that day forward to this day.'

It goes into the law. A decision made by an exhausted commander in a wadi becomes permanent Israelite practice, and the writer notes that it was still being applied when he wrote.

It is not only a rule about plunder. The principle in it turns up again in a vineyard, where men hired at five in the afternoon are paid the same as men who worked from dawn, and the ones who worked all day complain, and the owner asks: do you begrudge my generosity? (Matt. 20:1-16). The complaint in both places is identical, and so is the answer: it was never yours to allocate.

There will be Christians in heaven who came in at the eleventh hour, and Christians who have carried the work for fifty years, and they will be given the same Christ. Anyone who finds that uncomfortable should read verse 23 slowly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–31 — To the Elders of Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sends part of the spoil to his friends, the elders of Judah, with a message: here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD (v. 26). Then a list of thirteen towns — Bethel, Ramoth of the Negeb, Jattir, Aroer, Hebron and the rest — and to all the places where David and his men had roamed (vv. 27-31).
verseByVerse.theology: He calls it a present and it is also politics of the best kind. These are the towns of his own tribe, which sheltered him, informed on him, and watched him hunted for years; and he is putting Amalekite plunder into the hands of their elders while Saul is dying on a mountain forty miles north.
verseByVerse.examples: Note where the list ends. Hebron — and it is at Hebron, in the very next chapter of the story, that the men of Judah come and anoint David king (2 Sam. 2:1-4). He is being made king while he thinks he is only sharing out the spoil.

verseByVerse.quote: When David came to Ziklag, he sent part of the spoil to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, "Here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD." It was for those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negeb, in Jattir, in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa, in Racal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, in the cities of the Kenites, in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, in Athach, in Hebron, for all the places where David and his men had roamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When David came to Ziklag, he sent part of the spoil to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, "Here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD."'

He gives it away.

Having just argued that the plunder was not his to withhold from his own men, he now sends a large part of it out of his camp altogether, to the elders of Judah.

Note the phrase he sends with it: from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD. Not my enemies. He is telling the elders of Judah that the Amalekites were God's enemies and that this is God's plunder, which is exactly what he told the four hundred.

'to those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negeb, in Jattir, in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa, in Racal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, in the cities of the Kenites,'

Two of those names should stop a careful reader.

The Jerahmeelites and the Kenites are on the list of places David told Achish he had been raiding (27:10). They were his cover story — the towns he named as his victims to convince a Philistine king that he had made himself hated in Israel.

He now sends them a share of Amalekite spoil.

The writer does not comment, as usual. But the man who lied about attacking these people is putting plunder into their hands, and whatever else it is, it is the beginning of undoing sixteen months of damage.

'in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, in Athach, in Hebron, for all the places where David and his men had roamed.'

The list ends at Hebron, and 1 Samuel ends one chapter later.

Hebron is where the men of Judah will come, very shortly, and anoint David king over the house of Judah (2 Sam. 2:1-4). The last name on this list of towns receiving a gift is the town where he receives a crown.

The phrase all the places where David and his men had roamed covers the whole story: these are the towns of Judah that sheltered him, informed on him, fed him, refused him, and watched him hunted for years. Keilah is that country. Ziph is that country. The men of both handed him over or tried to.

He sends every one of them a present.

It is generosity and it is also politics, and there is no reason to pretend otherwise or to think less of him for it. He is putting himself in the memory of every elder in the south as the man who fights their enemies and shares the proceeds, at the exact hour — the reader knows it and David does not — when Saul is dying forty miles north on Mount Gilboa.

By the time the news reaches Ziklag, thirteen towns in Judah will have had a gift from David in their hands for a week.

He thinks he is being generous to his friends. He is being made king.

31.title: The Death of Saul
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.<sup>2</sup>And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.<sup>3</sup>The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers.<sup>4</sup>Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.<sup>5</sup>And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him.<sup>6</sup>Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together.<sup>7</sup>And when the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. And the Philistines came and lived in them.<sup>8</sup>The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.<sup>9</sup>So they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines, to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people.<sup>10</sup>They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.<sup>11</sup>But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,<sup>12</sup>all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.<sup>13</sup>And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
31.overview:
Thirteen verses for the end of a forty-year reign, and no preamble at all: the Philistines fight, Israel runs, and the men of Israel fall on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan dies in half a clause, in a list of three names — the man who went up a cliff with one armour-bearer, who gave away his own robe and sword, who told his father the truth about David and was nearly speared for it, who walked into a wilderness his father's army was searching to strengthen a hunted man's hand in God. He goes home to his father's house one last time and dies in it. The chapter offers nothing to soften that.

Saul is brought down by the archers and asks his armour-bearer to finish him — lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me. His last recorded words are about being laughed at, which has been the shape of him all along (honor me now before the elders of my people). The man will not do it, so Saul falls on his own sword, and the armour-bearer, who could have walked away, falls on his beside him. Two nights earlier at Endor: tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me.

The Philistines send the good news round their temples, put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth and his body on the wall of Beth-shan. Israel asked for a king like all the nations, and the nations are celebrating in their shrines. Then the men of Jabesh-gilead hear, and go all night into occupied territory to take the bodies off the wall — the town Saul rescued from an Ammonite in his very first act as king, forty years before. They bury the bones under a tamarisk and fast seven days.

The book ends in a gap: no coronation, no resolution, David at Ziklag not yet knowing. But not one word God spoke has fallen to the ground — and the frame was set at the start by a woman nobody was listening to, singing about the horn of his anointed before there was a king in Israel at all.
31.theology:
Jonathan, in five words (v. 2). The best man in the book dies in his father's lost battle, on his father's mountain, for his father's sin, and the text records it in a list and moves on. Scripture keeps declining to tidy this: consequences do not stop at the edge of the person who caused them, and the righteous are caught in the wreckage. Nothing here explains it. What answers it has to be brought from elsewhere and is the only answer there is — the God who let Jonathan die on Gilboa came and took that kind of death himself, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26). Saying that too quickly, though, cheats the reader of what the chapter actually says.

His last fear (v. 4). Not death — he is already bleeding out — but being made sport of. It is the same man who at Gilgal, with the kingdom just torn away, asked only honor me now before the elders of my people (15:30); who hid in the baggage on his coronation day; who could not bear a song that praised somebody else more. It should be said without contempt. Most people know that fear better than they would like to, and it is a small and human thing to be ruined by.

He went back (v. 3). Told at Endor precisely what would happen, disguised and behind enemy lines with a night's start and the throne gone anyway, he turned round and stood in the line until the archers found him. And his armour-bearer, who had already refused one order and was free to leave, chose to die beside him. At the very end there was still one man who would not leave Saul, and nobody recorded his name.

Like all the nations (v. 10). The armour dedicated in the temple of Ashtaroth, the body nailed to a public wall, runners carrying good news to every Philistine shrine. Israel had demanded a king to be like all the nations (8:5), and the nations are celebrating that their gods have won. They had tried making the LORD a trophy once before, when the ark went into the house of Dagon and Dagon was found face down and then broken on the threshold (5:1-5). Saul's armour stays where they put it.

The circle closes at Jabesh-gilead (vv. 11-13). Of every town in Israel, that one. Saul's first act as king was to march all night and save Jabesh-gilead from Nahash, who intended to gouge out every right eye in the place — and the Spirit of God had rushed upon him when he heard it (11:1-11). Forty years later the men of Jabesh go all night for him: across Philistine-held country, to take four bodies off a public wall in an occupied city, with no reward possible and the dynasty finished. He had not been a good king for a long time, and they came anyway. David calls it hesed when he hears of it (2 Sam. 2:5) — covenant love that keeps going after the reason for it has gone.

Not one word fell to the ground. Eli's sons dying on one day and his house cut off (2:31-34); the kingdom torn from Saul and given to a better neighbour (15:28); tomorrow you and your sons; the anointing of the eighth son in his father's house and the failure of every spear, ambush and army sent after him. That is the book's argument, and the writer never once stops to point at a fulfilment. He trusts the reader.

Hannah's frame. The LORD kills and brings to life... he brings low and he exalts... he will guard the feet of his faithful ones — and then he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (2:6-10). There was no king in Israel when she sang it and the office did not exist. Everything between that song and this grave is God bringing it about. And the horn is not lifted yet: there is a man at Ziklag who is anointed and not crowned, and who will take another man's wife and murder her husband. David is not the answer either. The horn is finally raised a thousand years later, in David's own town, when another woman with nothing sings almost Hannah's song (Luke 1:52) over a child called a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).
31.examples:
Then: A body was nailed to the wall of an occupied city and the armour hung up in a foreign temple as evidence that a foreign goddess had beaten the God of Israel — and a group of men from a town two days' march away walked all night through enemy country to take it down, brought it home, buried the bones under a tree and went without food for a week, for a king who had been failing them for years and could never repay them.

Now: The men of Jabesh-gilead are the last picture in the book and the one to keep. They remembered one night forty years earlier when a young man came for them and the Spirit of God was on him, and they held on to that after the man himself had gone wrong in almost every way a man can. There was nothing in it for them. Loyalty like that — to a person who has disappointed everybody, at cost, with no prospect of return — is the nearest thing in this chapter to the love God has for people who have gone wrong in almost every way a person can. And it is what David called it when he heard: hesed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Word Came True on a Tuesday
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines fight Israel, the men of Israel flee, and they fall on Mount Gilboa (v. 1). The pursuit overtakes Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchishua, the sons of Saul (v. 2). Saul is badly wounded by the archers and asks his armour-bearer to finish him — lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me — and the man will not (v. 4). So Saul takes his own sword and falls on it, and his armour-bearer does the same (vv. 4-5). Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together (v. 6). And the towns of the valley are abandoned to the Philistines (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel had said it two nights earlier at Endor: tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me (28:19). Every clause of it happens, in order, and the writer does not stop to point it out.
verseByVerse.examples: Jonathan dies in half a clause, in a list of three names. The man who gave away his robe on a hillside, who twice told a fugitive he would be king, who walked into a wilderness to strengthen his friend's hand in God — and the text records it in five words and moves on to his father.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul. The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers. Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him. Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together. And when the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. And the Philistines came and lived in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.'

No preamble, no speeches, no build-up. The battle is over in one verse and Israel has lost it.

The writer has spent thirty chapters on the reign of this king and gives the end of it thirteen verses, and the first thing he says is that the army ran.

'And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.'

Jonathan.

Five words in a list of three names, and then the narrator goes straight on to Saul's wound. That is all he gets.

Take a moment over it, because he has earned it. This is the man who went up a cliff with one armour-bearer and started a rout, and said nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few. Who stripped off his own robe and armour and sword and belt and gave them to a shepherd boy. Who told his father the truth about David and was nearly speared for it at his own table. Who walked into the Wilderness of Ziph while his father's army was searching it, for no reason except that his friend was frightened, and strengthened his hand in God. Who said you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you and then went home to his father's house.

He goes home to his father's house one last time, and dies in it.

The chapter offers nothing to soften this and neither should anyone reading it. The best man in the book dies in his father's lost battle, on his father's mountain, for his father's sin. He was not less faithful than anybody, and he is dead at the same hour as Saul.

Scripture keeps declining to tidy this up. Job knew it, and the psalms know it, and the world runs on it: the consequences of one man's choices do not stop neatly at the edge of the man who made them, and the righteous are caught in the wreckage. Nothing in this chapter explains it.

What answers it is not here and has to be brought from elsewhere, and it is the only answer there is: the God who let Jonathan die on Gilboa did not stay at a distance from that kind of death. He came and took one, on a hill, at the hands of an occupying army, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26). Jonathan is not lost. But this chapter does not say so, and saying it too quickly cheats the reader out of what the chapter does say.

David will say the true thing about him within a fortnight: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women (2 Sam. 1:26).

'The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers.'

He is still on the field.

Whatever else is true of Saul, it is true that he went back. He was told at Endor exactly what would happen, he could have run in the dark with a night's start, and he came back and stood in the line and fought until archers brought him down. His sons died around him.

'Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly.'

His last recorded words are about being humiliated.

Lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me. The verb means to abuse, to make sport of. He is not afraid of dying; he is bleeding to death already. He is afraid of being laughed at.

That has been the shape of him the whole way through. At Gilgal, with the kingdom just torn away, what he asked Samuel for was honor me now before the elders of my people (15:30). He hid among the baggage on the day he was made king. He raged when the women sang a better number about somebody else. The thing he could never bear was how it looked.

It should be said without any contempt. Most people understand that fear better than they would like to, and it is a small and human thing to be frightened of, and it ruined a man who had everything else.

The armour-bearer will not do it. He is the last person in the book to refuse Saul an order, and he refuses out of fear rather than principle — but the guards at Nob refused too, and one of the quiet threads of this book is ordinary men declining to do what a king tells them.

'Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him.'

He falls on his own sword, and his armour-bearer follows him.

Do not pass that second death by. The man was not required to do it. He had already refused an order, the king was dead, and he could have gone. He chose to die beside him — which means that at the very end there was still somebody who would not leave Saul, and we do not know his name.

'Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together.'

The sentence is deliberately flat, and it counts them.

Saul. His three sons. His armour-bearer. All his men. On the same day together.

Two nights ago in a hut at Endor an old prophet said tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me, and here is the accounting. The writer does not point at the fulfilment. He has spent thirty-one chapters showing that what God says happens, and he trusts his reader to see it.

'And when the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. And the Philistines came and lived in them.'

The whole valley empties.

This is the last thing 1 Samuel says about the state of the nation, and it should be set beside the first. The book opened with the Philistines beating Israel at Aphek, capturing the ark, and a woman dying in childbirth naming her son Ichabod — the glory has departed from Israel (4:21).

Israel demanded a king to fix precisely this. That we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles (8:20). They got him, and forty years later the Philistines are living in Israelite towns and the king is dead on a mountain.

A king was never going to be enough. That is one of the two things this book was written to say.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The next day the Philistines find the bodies, cut off Saul's head, strip his armour, and send the news round their temples and their people (vv. 8-9). They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan (v. 10). Then the men of Jabesh-gilead hear of it, and all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan (vv. 11-12). They burn them, bury the bones under the tamarisk tree at Jabesh, and fast seven days (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel asked for a king like all the nations (8:5). Their king's armour is now a dedication in the temple of a foreign goddess and his body is nailed to a city wall, and the nations are sending word round their villages that their gods have won.
verseByVerse.examples: And of every town in Israel, it is Jabesh-gilead that comes. Saul's first act as king, forty years earlier, was to rescue that town from an Ammonite who intended to gouge out every right eye in it (11:1-11). They never forgot. They walk all night into Philistine-held territory to take his body off a wall.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. So they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines, to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people. They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan. But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there. And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. So they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines, to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people.'

The good news. That is what the word is, and the Philistines are the ones using it.

They send runners to every town and every temple. This is a religious event to them: their gods have beaten Israel's God, and the proof is on a stretcher.

'They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.'

Two things, and both of them are the end of an argument that began in chapter 8.

His armour goes into a temple. It is dedicated to Ashtaroth as a thank-offering — the war gear of the LORD's anointed laid up in a shrine as evidence that a Canaanite goddess is stronger than the God of Israel.

And his body is nailed to a city wall for people to walk past.

Now go back to what the nation asked for. Give us a king to judge us like all the nations (8:5), and Samuel told them exactly what it would cost, and they said no! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations.

They wanted to be like the nations. The nations are at this moment celebrating in their temples because their king is a trophy on a wall.

One more thing in it, which the reader has been set up for since chapter 5. When the Philistines captured the ark they put it in the temple of Dagon, and in the morning Dagon was face down on the floor in front of it, and the next morning his head and hands were broken off on the threshold (5:1-5). They tried to make the LORD a trophy once. It did not go well for them.

Saul's armour stays where they put it.

'But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,'

Jabesh-gilead.

Of every town in Israel, that one, and it closes a circle forty years wide.

Turn back to chapter 11. Nahash the Ammonite besieged Jabesh-gilead and offered terms: he would make a treaty on condition that he gouge out the right eye of every man in the town, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel (11:2). They sent messengers begging for help, and the messengers came to Gibeah, and Saul was behind the oxen coming in from the field. And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled (11:6). He raised the whole nation, marched all night, and cut the Ammonites to pieces in the morning watch.

That was his first act as king, and it was magnificent, and he did it because the Spirit came on him.

They never forgot.

'all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.'

Went all night.

The same phrase as the night march that saved them. Saul went all night for Jabesh-gilead, and forty years later the men of Jabesh-gilead go all night for Saul.

Look at what it costs them. Beth-shan is a Philistine-held city in the middle of the valley they have just abandoned. These men cross enemy country in the dark, take four bodies off a public wall in an occupied town, and carry them home — and there is nothing whatever in it for them. The king is dead, the dynasty is finished, and no reward is coming. They do it because of something that happened when their grandfathers were young.

He had not been a good king for a long time. They came anyway.

'And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh and fasted seven days.'

Under a tamarisk tree, which is where we last saw him sitting with a spear in his hand at Gibeah (22:6). And seven days of fasting, which is the full mourning of a household for its own.

The last recorded act in the book of 1 Samuel is a kindness done for a failed king by a town that remembered when he was good.

That is where the writer chooses to stop, and it is a remarkable place to stop. He could have ended on the Philistines celebrating, or on the head on the wall, or on David at Ziklag. He ends with a burial and a fast.

David will hear about this and send them a message: may you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyal love to Saul your lord and buried him (2 Sam. 2:5). He calls it hesed — covenant kindness, the word for love that keeps going when the reason for it has gone.

Now stand at the end of the book and look back down it.

There is no coronation here, no triumph and no resolution. David is at Ziklag with a burnt town and thirteen crates of Amalekite spoil delivered to the elders of Judah, and he does not yet know that Saul is dead. The book ends in a gap.

But every single thing God said has happened.

The man of God told Eli that both his sons would die on one day and that his house would be cut off (2:31-34), and Hophni and Phinehas died at Aphek and the priests of Nob died at Gibeah. Samuel told Saul at Gilgal that the kingdom was torn away and given to a neighbour better than he was (15:28), and it was. Samuel told him at Endor that he would die tomorrow with his sons, and he did. David was anointed in his father's house in front of seven passed-over brothers, and every attempt to kill him failed — the spears, the ambushes, the three thousand chosen men, twice.

Not one word fell to the ground.

The frame around the whole of it was set at the start by a woman nobody was listening to. Hannah stood at Shiloh with her son and sang: the LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up. The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust... he will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness (2:6-9).

And then the last line of it, which nobody could have understood when she sang it: he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (2:10).

There was no king in Israel when Hannah said that. The word had not been spoken and the office did not exist. She sang about the LORD's anointed while she was handing a weaned child over to an old priest whose own sons were stealing the sacrifices.

Everything between her song and this grave is God bringing it about — through a barren woman, a corrupt priesthood, a captured ark, a demanded king, a rejected king, a hunted shepherd, and a mountain covered in the dead.

The horn is not exalted yet. That is why the book stops where it does. There is a man at Ziklag who has been anointed and is not yet crowned, and even when he is crowned he will be a king who takes another man's wife and murders her husband, and his sons will tear his kingdom apart. David is not the answer either.

The horn Hannah sang about is finally lifted a thousand years later, in the town David came from, when another woman with nothing sings almost her song — he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52) — over a child who is called a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).

1 Samuel ends with a king dead on a mountain, his armour in an idol's temple, and a good man buried under a tree. It was always pointing somewhere else.
